While employed by K-T, Padlo was principally   engaged in marketing and teaching K-T's programs to industry and government groups.  He did not write the texts and outlines used to teach the programs, but did prepare an outline for his personal use.  Before he came to K-T, Padlo had little formal writing experience; however, while   there he became familiar with K-T's materials.  Carabio, on the other hand, did draft some K-T materials in preliminary form, primarily those used to teach K-T salesmen-instructors how to teach the programs.  He also taught and prepared an outline for his own use.
BPI was formed by Padlo on July 18, three days after he left K-T.  He had begun work on a set of program materials while he was still technically on K-T's payroll.  As early as July 11 he sent worksheets to be used in the BPI programs to the printer.  By the first of September Padlo had generated a set of teaching materials that were rought but complete enough to market.   It was at this time he was joined by Carabio, who had tendered his resignation to K-T two weeks earlier.  Carabio immediately performed a final revision and review of BPI's materials. On September 27 BPI obtained its first major customer, Chrysler Corporation, a former   customer of K-T.
The Creation Of BPI's Materials

When Padlo left K-T, he surrendered all "formal documents" (copyrighted teaching materials).  He retained his personal outline (prepared from K-T's works).  In preparing BPI's materials, Padlo assembled all the information he could gather pertaining to the teaching of problem-solving programs.  Much of this consisted of materials used by K- T's competitors. Padlo also used his personal K-T outline and drew upon his familiarity with K-T's materials.  From this base of raw data, Padlo selected those ideas and approaches he felt were most effective.  He tried to avoid direct copying.

Defendants admit similarity between BPI's materials and K-T's.They concede, even emphasize, similarity between BPI's materials and those of some of K-T's competitors. Defendants deny any direct copying of K-T's materials. Padlo kept no notes of his preparation.
The Contentions Of The Parties

K-T asserts there was substantial   copying. It emphasizes that the BPI materials were prepared in a very short time by one with little formal writing experience on a low budget.  (BPI operates out of Padlo's home and its capitalization is only $2,000.) Coupling this with numerous asserted similarities in format, outline and phrasing, and the fact the some of BPI's materials were prepared while Padlo was still on K-T's payroll, K-T contends a finding of copyright infringement is warranted.  The case is sealed, K-T argues, by the marked-up K-T work sheets subpoenaed from the printer which, with only minor changes, were later marketed as part of BPI's material (see Plaintiff's Exhibit 13).  Padlo admitted at trial that were BPI's materials used exactly the same phrasing to describe a concept or idea, the phrase was copied.
Defendants argue that although there are major similarities between BPI's material and K-T's, this is attributable to the limited ways the ideas taught by K-T can be expressed.  In support of this, Defendants produced copies of the materials used by many of their competitors. I find a great deal of similarity among them.   K-T, while arguing that Defendants' copying from others who, in turn, copied   from K-T, it no defense, did not offer proof that any of the third-party materials had been copied from K-T.
Defendants also introduced evidence of K-T's competitive behavior in the program market, which I accept.  K-T dominates the problem-solving market.  Thalthough there are scores of competitors, the majority are small with little impact.  Many college professors teach these programs on a part-time basis.  There are also several companies of BPI's size or larger which sell the same product   as K-T.  some large corporations which have been or might otherwise be K-T customers maintain in-house staffs to teach problem-solving techniques.  Some are licensed by K-T.
Many of K-T's competitors are former K-T employees.  K-T monitors them closely and is constantly on guard against copyright    infringement. Dr. Blanchard Smith, a K-T employee who testified, has prepared a number of formal comparisons between K-T's material and its competitors'. (These are called "side-by-sides" and one of them, Plaintiff's Exhibit 11, comparing K-T and BPI materials, contains the substance of K-T's claim here.) K-T maintains an aggressive posture towards those it feels infringe its copyrights, often writing letters to them, but the instant litigation is the first to be brought domestically.
BPI contends that K-T's market position weakens its case from an equitable standpoint.  Defendants emphasize that K-T has produced thousands of pages of copyrightable material over the years in this area and to some extent pre-empted further discussion.  K-T responds by arguing that notwithstanding the volume of material it has produced, there are nearly infinite ways to express the ideas it purveys.    Through Dr. Smith, K-T introduced a sample paragraph it claims restates the idea contained in BPI's explanation of the "problem statement" in a manner which would not infringe K-T's copyright.  (Plaintiff's Exhibit 12) I find this proffer scarcely any more different from K- T's than BPI's, and considerably less clear.  I also conclude that though this is not an anti-trust case, K-T's dominant market position should not be encouraged, nor should its copyright policy be directed toward lessening competition.  A copyright suit is equitable in nature, and thus I may consider such factors.  Tempo Music Inc. v. Myers, 407 F.2d 503, 507 n. 8, 160 USPQ 707, 709-710, n. 8 (4th Cir. 1969); M. Witmark & Sons v. Jensen, 80 F.Supp. 843, 850, 79 USPQ 6, 11-12 (D.Minn. 1948), 3 M. Nimmer, Nimmer on Copyright, §§ 1309[A] & [B].
The Copyrighted Materials

Much has been said of the copyrighted material at issue.  My analysis builds on their singular nature, so I describe them in detail.

K-T teaches 5-day programs in what might be called applied reasoning and common sense in problem-solving techniques.  Defendants teach a 3-day program.  K-T has three levels of programs.  "Apex II" is targeted   at middle and top level executives; "Genco II" aims at front-line management and supervisors; and "LDI" is used to instruct Apex II and Genco II teachers.  Each program has basically the same format and approach, keyed to what K-T apparently believes are the three major intellectual processes needed in corporate management.  These are "problem-solving", "decision making" and "planning" techniques.  (BPI teaches a fourth category called "concern analysis" which is an introductory analysis of the areas of inquiry that must "concern" anyone facing a management decision.  See Plaintiff's Exhibit 8 pp. 000049-000068.) Each of these three areas is presented to the student through four devices.  First, an outline of the material; second, textual exposition, which essentially follows the outline; third, "cases" or problem examples in prose form; and, fourth, worksheets -- blank grids of varying structure highlighted by keyword headings and used by the student in systematic application of the logical sequence of analysis being taught. BPI's materials use the same basic approach, with the addition of concern analysis.  BPI has only one set of materials in contrast to K-T's three.
The two   companies' products are also similar in that they aim at the same markets.  Except for the length of the programs, they are taught in the same manner -- a combination of lecture, student-teacher interaction and group analysis using sample problems.  At the conclusion of the program, the "graduate" receives a certificate of attendance (See Sec. 2 of Plaintiff's Exhibit 11), and is allowed to take away a supply of worksheets, presumably to be used at the office or plant.
More specifically, the two program approaches teach the same kind of analysis.  The problem-solving portion of both sets of materials proceeds by first stating the problem.  BPI calls this the "problem statement" (Plaintiff's Exhibit 8, p. 000008), whereas K-T calls it the "Deviation Statement." Next, the inquiry is narrowed by describing the problem, i.e., by asking what the problem "is" and what it "is not", where it is and where it is not, and so forth.  At this stage the analysis is characterized by the use of a litany "what-where-when-extent/magnitude" each followed by "is-is not" in both sets of materials.  The other steps are, in order: Ask how is this problem different from other problems and from the absence   of the problem; ask what changed when the problem first appeared (i.e. what are the possible causes); ask what are the possible causes (or, as others in the field have asked, what are the probable causes, potential causes, etc., see Table 1 in Defendants' Post Trial Brief); test for the most probable alternative; and, verify (document) the cause.  I will not labor this further, sufficient it to say that the other sections of the problem-solving portion of K-T's materials track the outline, and that the other general topics (i.e., decision making and planning) follow the same sort of approach.
Plaintiff alleges infringements in each of four sections of BPI's work (outline-text, teaching outline, worksheets and cases).  The substance of the alleged infringement is reproduced in Plaintiff's Exhibit 11.  Before commenting on the factual comparison basis for the infringement, I will discuss how the law applies.
I.  K-T's Materials Are Copyrightable

In BPI's post-trial memorandum (p.8) it asserts K-T's materials are not copyrightable, arguing the ideas presented are inextricable from their straightforward explanation.  To protect K-T's material would protect the idea, 17 U.S.C. §   102(b).  Although I reject this argument's applicability, Defendants are on the right track, and have presented the key to this dispute.

 The originality an author must contribute to a subject for his work to be copyrightable is extremely small. Puddu v Buonamici Statuary, Inc., 450 F2d 401, 402, 171 USPQ 709, 710-711 (2nd Cir. 1971) A number of highly similar copyrights may exist around a common theme.  Id., at 403, 171 USPQ at 711; Alfred Bell & Co. v Catalda Fine Arts, 191 F.2d 99, 103, 90 USPQ 153, 157 (2nd Cir. 1951); Ricker v General Electric Co., 162 F2d 141, 142, 73 USPQ 458, 459-460 (2nd Cir. 1947) K-T's concepts admit sufficient variety of expression that their materials are copyrightable.
II.  Unity Of Idea And Expression

The insight that if an idea and its expression are of necessity close, the expression is not copyrightable, received its furthest extension in Morrissey v Proctor & Gamble Co., 379 F2d 675, 154 USPQ 193 (1st Cir. 1967). There the court held a contest rule uncopyrightable on the rationale that the rule's concept could be expressed in only a limited number of ways.  The court wrote:

"… When the uncopyrightable subject matter is very narrow, so that   'the topic necessarily requires,' Sampson & Murdock Co. v. Seaver-Radford Co., 1 Cir., 1905, 140 F. 539, 541; cf. Kaplan, An Unhurried View of Copyright, 64-65 (1967), if not only one form of expression, at best only a limited number, to permit copyrighting would mean that a party or parties, by copyrighting a mere handful of forms, could exhaust all possibilities of future use of the substance.  In such circumstances it does not seem accurate to say that any particular form of expression comes from the subject matter.  However, it is necessary to say that the subject matter would be appropriated by permitting the copyrighting of its expression.  We cannot recognize copyright as a game of chess in which the public can be checkmated." 379 F.2d at 678-9


Nimmer thinks this is a questionable extension of the unity of idea and expression" concept.  3 M. Nimmer, Nimmer on Copyright, § 13.03[A] (1978).  That may be, but the case focuses the most important feature of this case; namely, when a subject can only be explained in limited ways, the degree of protection copyright affords is correspondingly more limited.  Crume v Pacific Mut. Life Ins. Co., 140 F.2d 182, 183, 60 USPQ 359, 359-360  (7th Cir. 1944)
III.  What Does Copyright Cover?

The first question is to determine exactly what K-T's copyright protects.  In Nichols v Universal Pictures Corp., 45 F2d 119, 7 USPW 84 (2nd Cir. 1930), Judge Learned Hand observed:

"Upon any work… a great number of patterns of increasing generality will fit equally well, as more and more of the incident is left out.  The last may perhaps be no more than a general statement of what the play is about,… but there is a point in this series of abstractions where they are no longer protected, since otherwise the playwright could prevent the use of his "ideas," to which, apart from their expression, his property is never extended… Nobody has ever been able to fix that boundary, and nobody ever can…" 45 F2d at 121, 7 USPQ at 86-87.

The task is to determine in K-T's materials where the idea leaves off and its expression begins.  In works of fiction this occurs at a fairly high level of abstraction.  There are infinite themes, plots and characters that many be expressed in such variety that they may be given wide berth with no stifling effect by those who wish to express similar ideas.  As to such works, a judge's instinctive   impressions serve as well as any indicator whether there has been an infringement. But, such cases lead to pat formulations as the following from Miller Brewing Co. v Carling O'Keefe Breweries, 452 F Supp 429, 439, 199 USPQ 470, 479 (W.D. N.Y. 1978):

"… a copyright does not protect the holder from another's use of themes or plots, but rather the gist of copyright infringement is the pirating of particular expressions of thematic concepts by use of similar details, scenes, events and characterization."

  In cases like this one, more penetrating analysis is called for.  Instinct alone will not serve.  Unthinking application of the "substantial similarity" test may produce the wrong result.  A plaintiff can claim no protection for a more abstract level than he created.  If the only original aspect of a work is its literal expression, only a nearly identical copy will infringe. 3 M. Nimmer, Nimmer on Copyright § 13.03 [A] [1].
K-T enjoys no protection for its "approach" to problem-solving,  namely, the analysis summarized in its outlines. K- T has no monopoly over the handling of a problem by stating it, then narrowing the inquiry by the "is-is not" technique, and so forth.
The most useful analysis of this problem, which has not been much improved through the years, is set forth in Baker v Selden, 101 U.S. 99 (1880). The Court considered a system of ruling books in which accounts were kept which consisted of an introductory essay explaining the system and a series of ruled forms with headings.  The Court noted, "The truths of a science… are the common property of the whole world [and] any author has the right to express the one, or explain and use the other, in his own way." The hard question in the case was presented because "[in] describing the art, the illustrations and diagrams employed happen to correspond more closely than usual with the actual working performed by the operator who uses the art."
Likewise, K-T has no exclusive right to package its problem-solving techniques and market them as a seminar to business and industry.  Nor may K-T lay claim to solving problems or making decisions using the logical sequence outlined earlier.  K-T has no   monopoly on any pedagogical technique, such as the "outline-text-worksheets- cases" approach it uses, and it had no exclusive right to present any of its material in an outline or text format.
An interesting contrast with my conclusion is presented by Nutt v National Institute Incorporated, 31 F2d 236 (2nd Cir. 1929), cited by K-T.  there the plaintiff claimed an infringement of three copyrighted lectures on memory improvement.  The court agreed, stating:

The appellant here, not only uses the underlying theme of the lectures, but treats the ideas and topics in the same way.  He used identical associations and key words, and makes it inconceivable that he does so without copying appellee's copyrighted work…  A comparison shows appellant following the plan and arrangement of the appellee, and more than a substantial part has been appropriated.  Copying is not confined to a literary repetition, but includes various modes in which the matter of any publication may be adopted, imitated, or transferred with more or less colorable alteration.  31 F2d at 238

This case may have been correctly decided at the time, but if I was presented with it today, I might disagree. Copyright analysis   has become more sophisticated.  I would hesitate to even imply protection could attach to isolated "key words", "theme", "arrangement" and "plan".  These are abstract rather than concrete expression, and in a technical or applied art context, they perhaps have little, if any protection.
IV.  The Extent Of Copyright's Protection

Having expressed what K-T's copyright does not protect, I now take up its extent.  I conclude K-T has what might be called a "thin" shell of protection around its materials.

This concept may be illustrated by the following quotation from Herbert Rosenthal Jewelry Corp. v Kalpakian, 446 F 2d 738, 170 USPQ 557 (9th Cir. 1971), cited in Sid & Marty Krofft Television v McDonald's Corp., 562 F 2d 1157, at 1167, 196 USPQ 97, at 104-105:

What is basically at stake is the extent of the copyright owner's monopoly -- from how large an area of activity did Congress intend to allow the copyright owner to exclude others?

The court continued, observing:

The coincidence of idea and expression may occur in works other than "things." Baker v. Selden, supra, held that blank accounting books are not subject to copyright protection.  Yet if any information is contained   in those banks, copyright protection is available.  See Edwin K. Williams & Co. v Edwin K. Williams, etc., 542 F. 2d 1053, 1060-61, 191 USPQ 563, 568-570 (9 Cir. 1976) (account books with explanation); Guthrie v. Curlett, 36 F. 2d 694, 4 USPQ 1 (2 Cir. 1929) (2(dex of freight tariffs); American Code Co. v. Bensinger, 282 F. 829 (2 Cir. 1922) (codes). Id., at 1168, 196 USPQ at 105-106 (footnote omitted)
Although Kalpakian involved a jewelry bee and Sid & Marty Krofft involved a    television program, both speak to the extent of copyright protection.  Both illustrate how the concept of "thin" protection can be developed.

Another crucial observation is that the "substantial similarity" test for infringement is much too simplistic.  In this case it would, if not applied with precision, yield an incorrect result.

The usual statement of the rule is: to prove infringement the plaintiff must show copying of his work, Universal Athletic Sales Co. v Salkeld, 511 F 2d 904, 906-7, 185 USPQ 76, 77-78 (3rd Cir. 1975) , and that it resulted in a work "substantially similar" to plaintiff's.  Id. Substantial similarity, it is said, should be judged by "whether an average lay observer [i.e.,    one within the audience at which the work is addressed] would recognize the alleged copy as having been appropriated from the copyrighted work." Ideal Toy Corp, v Fab-Fu, Ltd., 261 F Supp 238, 241, 152 USPQ 500, 501-50 (S.D. N.Y. 1966) This is useful shorthand, but should not substitute for reasoned analysis.  In practice the test is much modified; its contours depend on the subject matter of the copyright and a number of other factors.
The first of these is the already noted distinction between literary works and those which teach or explain a useful art or scientific process.  This factor modifies the "substantial similarity" test.  In a literary work, plot, theme, character and, as said in Sid & Marty Krofft, supra, at 1167, 196 USPQ at 104-105, "The total concept and feel" of the work, are important.  This is because in literature, these things are wholly the creature of the writer.  There is an unlimited variety which may be invented.  Authors are not confined.  In addition, there is no societal interest in many variants on a single theme or plot, nor is there the likelihood that by extending broad protection, entry to the market for   literary works will be foreclosed.  But with respect to the useful arts, there is a societal interest in having many offer the art in the marketplace.  Our economy functions best under competition.  And, if many can present variants on the copyrighted material, we hope that advances in its teaching will result.  As a consequence, more similarity between two works of a commercial and useful character is required to find infringement than between two literary works.  Two useful works might bear resemblance that would show infringement if literary, but which is not because they are technical.  The "substantial similarity" test is modified.
The problem can be approached from another angle.   Many cases say an idea and its expression may be closely related.  It is the strong policy of copyright not to protect ideas.  Free interchange of thought is paramount. To avoid protecting ideas, courts have limited the concept of substantial similarity. Two works explaining or embodying the same idea will necessarily be somewhat alike.  For example, consider two biographies of a famous person, Rosemont Enterprises, Inc. v Random House, Inc., 366 F 2d 303, 306-7, 150 USPQ 715, 718-719 (2nd Cir.   1966), two law treatises, Orgel v Clark Boardman Co., 301 F 2d 119, 120, 133 USPQ 94, 95 (2nd Cir. 1962), and two model airplanes, Monogram Models, Inc. v Continental Insurance Co., 448 F 2d 284, 287 (6th Cir. 1971). "Substantial similarity" is further modified.
In yet another vein, the simpler the thing described, the more alike two explanations will be.  To cite an extreme, how many ways may one describe how to draw a circle with a compass? To be sure, many outlandish methods using eccentric styles could be conceived.  But there is no societal value in that.  For better it is to narrow the protection to the first writer, in the interest of competition.

K-T has tried t deny that its material describes something simple.  But the problem-solving K-T exalts is nothing more than what everyone with common sense does automatically.  By describing it and elaborating on it, K-T cannot expropriate it.
The best example of this is K-T's explanation of the Problem Statement.  (See Plaintiff's Ex. 12 also) A problem statement is a statement of the problem; a definition of the undesired state of things, and so forth.  There are only so many ways it can be said, and they all sound alike.    Once one accepts that K-T has no monopoly on its process or approach, only limited protection may exist.  For this reason Morrissey v Proctor, supra, is important:

… the matter of infringement is so closely related to, if not actually dependent on, the extent of protection to which plaintiff is entitled by virtue of his copyright as to require some consideration of the latter [in determining if there is an infringement].  Crume v Pacific, supra, 140 F 2d at 183, 60 USPQ at 359-360
K-T's copyrights rest on an unstable foundation; barely copyrightable material.

In addition to these reasons for K-T's "thin" copyright, other factors weigh heavily.     K-T dominates the market as to the programs it teaches. Defendants freely admit that a major selling point of their programs is that they are similar to K-T's.  To succeed in this market, one must imitate K-T.  K-T is a known quantity and industry's expectations have been molded in its direction.  This is a tribute to K-T, but it does not give them a monopoly. Thus, a certain similarity may be expected.
This point was influential in McGraw-Hill, Inc. v Worth Publishers, Inc., 335 F Supp 415, 172 USPQ 482 (S.D. N.Y. 1971). The   court noted that some similarity to Professor Paul Samuelson's economics text is essential to any introductory text.  The college professors who teach basic economics all want to use their notes from years past, and those notes all conform to Samuelson.  The court reasoned, no text not modelled to some extent on Samuelson would sell, so similarity to Samuelson was permissible.  The principle applies here.
McGraw-Hill also notes that in teaching, a noticeable style is a hindrance.  Two simple and straightforward explanations of an economic law or principle must bear a close resemblance, so greater similarity must be allowed. Id., at 420, 172 USPQ at 485-486. Ricker v General Electric Co., 162 F 2d 141, 142, 73 USPQ 458, 459-460 (2nd Cir. 1947). The same holds true here.  K-T and BPI both strive for a clear and simple way to express a very basic idea.  The law of copyright cannot mean that BPI is required to resort to an eccentric style or the kind of obfuscation in Plaintiff's Exhibit 12 to avoid infringement.
Another constraint on the expression available to BPI is the presentation format it chooses to follow, namely, the instructor-taught seminar with class participation.  Some   similarity must result when two undertake to present the same information in the same manner.  At trial K-T showed that there are several different basic approaches to "problem-solving".  They included "brainstorming," mathematical or computer oriented approaches, and some others.  From this K-T concludes there is a great variety of expression available to one desiring to teach problem solving.  But K-T has no monopoly on the problem-solving process it developed.  Its copyright gives it no right to require BPI to adopt another approach.  This is patent's province.  The similarities which necessarily result must be tolerated.
One final point is, the amount of protection enjoyed depends upon the amount of protectible originality in the original work.  Wilson & Co. v Irving J. Dorfman Co., 268 F Supp 711, 713, 154 USPW 226, 228-229 (S.D. N.Y. 1967) K-T's material contains some originality that is not protectible.  The only protectible aspect of K-T's materials is that measure by which it goes beyond the unprotectible underlying ideas.  K-T can protect only the expression of that it has added to our store of knowledge on problem solving.  Peter Pan Fabrics, Inc. v Martin Weiner Corp., 274   F 2d 487, 489, 124 USPQ 154, 155-156 (2nd Cir. 1960) As stated in another context in Dorsey v Old Life Ins. Co., 98 F 2d 872 (10th Cir. 1938), "The degree of protection afforded by the copyright is measured by what is actually copyrightable in the publication and not by the entire publication." 98 F 2d at 874
This can be illustrated by two fabric cases.  In Lanratex v Textile Corp. v Citation Fabric Corp., 328 F Supp 554 (S.D. N.Y. 1971), the plaintiff copyrighted a fabric design that was only a slight variation on a general one in the public domain.  The defendant produced a design that was a slight variation of plaintiff's design.  The court held no violation because, though the two were similar, the plaintiff's design contained so little that was new, it would be improper to find defendant's design a violation.  In Concord Fabrics, Inc. v Generation Mills, Inc., 328 F Supp 1030, 169 USPQ 470 (S.D. N.Y. 1971), the same holding resulted from similar facts.  That court reasoned that the defendant had the right to draw upon all that had gone before in making its design, just as did the plaintiff, and concluded that if the plaintiff makes only a small variation on a general theme,    he is entitled to little protection.
In our case, K-T has contributed to its field.  But much of its effort is not protectible.  It consists of ideas in the public domain.  See Wilson & Co. v Irving J. Dorfman Co., 268 F Supp 711, 713, 154 USPQ 226, 228-229 (S.D. N.Y. 1967). K-T's outlines are the bare bones of the ideas.  Any exposition of the ideas will be similar to the outlines, which are nearly uncopyrightable because so close to the ideas.
V.  Infringement

The ultimate question remains.  I find that although K-T has what I have called a "thin" copyright, BPI has infringed it in certain minor respects.
1.  Worksheets

I find no violation with respect to the worksheets. They are similar to K-T's due to defendants having drawn ideas from K-T.  But the Baker v Selden problem    predominates.  The worksheets contain so little expression and there is so much difficulty separating the expression from the idea; the protection they enjoy extends little beyond actual xerographic reproduction.  An analogous case as to this issue is Taylor Instrument Companies v Fawley- Brost Co., 139 F 2d 98, 100, 59 USPW 384, 386-387 (7th Cir. 1943).  There the plaintiff designed a blank chart   to be used with certain weather recording machinery that it also produced.  The court concluded that the essential distinction was whether the chart's value was explanation or use.  See Synercom Technology v University Computing Co., 462 F Supp 1003, 1011, 199 USPQ 537, 544-545 (N.D. Tex.) (1978) (forms accompanying computer instruction manuals)) It found it was use, and held it uncopyrightable.  In this case, the forms are slightly explanatory; they have some informative value.  But they are primarily a student's tool for applying what he has learned.  The student uses them as he would use a compass or straightedge if he was studying geometric constructions.

I have approached the worksheet problem from the infringement standpoint rather than copyrightability, unlike Baker v Selden and other cases, because I think this case is distinguishable.  But the result (i.e., the answer to: "Is there an infringement?) can be arrived at from either direction.  The same considerations apply.
2.  The cases

The cases are the opposite end of the scale from   the worksheets. In them I find the greatest room for "literary" creativity and divergence of expression from idea.
(a) Handmixers v Auto Heaters -- Infringement

BPI's case is an obvious copy.  The differences are trivial and only point out the similarity. Most obviously, each product comes in three models, is assembled on highly similar assembly lines, and suffers from a defect in its finish caused by something the employees wear on their hands.
(b) Dairyland Corp. v Tamworth Petrochemical Corp. -- Infringement

Once again BPI's case is an ingenious theft of K-T's.  Both products are flat and square, are similarly distributed, suffer from an unknown reaction to electromagnetic radiation, and engender nearly identical customer problems. There are an infinite number of defective-product cases that could be written to illustrate exactly the same concepts.
3.  The Outlines and the Text (Sec. 1 of Ex. 11)

Analyzing these sections of the two sets of materials is the most difficult.  On the one hand, K-T has no monopoly on its ideas or on the sequence in which they are presented.  K-T has no exclusive property in the outline format. More important, K-T has no monopoly on the use of common words to carry it meaning.  It has no proprietary interest i such words as "is" or "is not".  The same holds true for "what, where, when and extent." As said in Alexander v Haley, 460 F Supp 40, 46, 200 USPQ 239, 243 (S.D. N.Y. 1978):

…  Words and metaphors are not subject to copyright protection; nor are phrases and expressions conveying an idea that can only be, or is typically, expressed in a limited number   of stereotyped fashions… [citing four cases]

This is especially true in scientific or technical areas where certain words become terms of art.  Orgel v Clark Boardman Co., supra, 301 F2d at 120, 133 USPQ at 94-95, Caddy-Imli Creations, Inc. v Caddy, 299 F2d 79, 81, 132 USPQ 384, 385-386 (9th Cir. 1962); Ricker v General Electric Co., supra, 162 F2d at 144, 73 USPQ at 460- 461; Dorsey v Old Surety Life Ins. Co., supra, 98 F2d at 872. And where an explanation of a technical matter is at issue, the simpler the language, the more nearly idea and expression coincide.
However, BPI has infringed the copyright of K-T as to the text and outline in Ex. 11.  My conclusion stems mainly from the numerous obvious paraphrases which appear throughout this section.  For example, see: sentence four on page I-Oa and sentence two on I-Ob; sentence seven on I-Oa and sentence seven in I-Ob.  Likewise, page I-2a infringes I-2b because of the horizontal "is-is not" juxtaposed with the vertical "what-where-when-extent/magnitude". None of these modes of expression is itself protectable but the unique and idiosyncratic juxtaposition presents too great a similarity, especially considering the relationship   of the parties.  Defendants could use alternate phrasings to convey the same meaning.  For example, for "is" could be substituted "describe the problem" or "explain the problem."

Even so, I am troubled by the Seventh Circuit's statement in Crume v Pacific Mutual Life Insurance, supra, 140 F2d at 184-5, 60 USPQ at 360-362:

…  To hold that the idea, plan, method, or art described in a copyright is open to the public but that it can be used only by the employment of different words and phrases which mean the same thing, borders on the preposterous. It is to exalt the accomplishment of a result by indirect means which could not be done directly.  It places a premium upon evasion and makes this the test of infringement.

To a certain extent, I do this here.

It is an unhappy result.  However, it is what the law requires.  In Section 1 of Ex. 11, Defendants have copied, either consciously or unconsciously, Bright Tunes Music Corp. v Harrisongs Music Corp., 420 FSupp 177, 180-1 (S.D. N.Y. 1976), K-T's material and produced a result so similar that it is an appropriation of K-T's effort.  College EntranceBook Co. v Amsco Book Co., 119 F2d 874, 49 Uspq 517, 519-520 (2nd Cir. 1941).
The changes required are small.  BPI is free to borrow K-T's ideas.  Reyher v Children's Television Workshop, 533 F2d 87, 88, 190 USPQ 387 (2nd Cir. 1976). Competition is health.  K-T should not use its copyright to enhance its already undesirable market dominance.
VII.  Conclusion

No statement rings more true than Judge Hand's in Peter Pan Fabrics, Inc. v. Martin Weiner Corp., 274 F2d 487, 489, 124 USPQ 154, 155-156 (2nd Cir. 1960):

Obviously, no principle can be stated as to when an imitator has gone beyond copying the "idea" and has borrowed its "expression." Decisions must therefore inevitably be ad hoc.

In the end, my judgment must prevail.   But there is nothing in the law that precludes one author from saving time   and effort through the labors of others.  This waste of energy the ban n copyright of ideas prevents.  Rosemont Enterprises, Inc. v. Random House, Inc., 366 F2d 303, 310, 150 USPQ 715, 721-722 (2nd Cir. 1966) I have been guided in this case by the observation    that one work does not infringe another if their similarity results from the limits on expression I have described.  Harold Lloyd Corp. v Witmer, 65 F2d 1, 17 (9th Cir. 1933). And of paramount importance, I think, is the public interest in the advancement of art, science and industry. Sometimes this must be placed ahead of the copyright holder's interest in the maximum profit from his creation. Rosemont Enterprises, Inc. v Random House, Inc., supra, at 307, 150 USPQ at 719; Berlin v E. C. Publications, Inc., 329 F2d 541, 544, 141 USPQ 1, 3 (2nd Cir. 1964). This fundamental distinction underlies the difference between patent and copyright.  K-T's real concern in this case is that BPI has stolen its ideas and is profiting from them.  Copyright simply does not remedy this.  Universal v Salkeld, supra, 511 F2d at 908, 185 USPQ 78-79.

An appropriate order may be submitted and a hearing date will be set to address the proper remedy.
Supplemental Opinion And Order

On April 20, 1979 I issued an opinion finding that Defenants had infringed Plaintiff's copyright in minor, yet definite, respects.  Since then the following events have transpired:
1.  Defendants submitted their first post-trial revision of the infringing sections of their teaching materials.
2.  Plaintiff responded to the revisions; agreed some charges were adequate, but asserted continued challenge to other parts of the Defendants' materials.  Plaintiff accepted: the revisions of the two infringing problems from § 4 of Plaintiff's Exhibit 11; the revisions of Defendant Business Processes, Inc.'s "Decision Making" text (pp. I-15a -- 1- 26a of § 1 of Plaintiff's Exhibit 11).  It rejected changes pertaining to pp. I-1a -- I-10a of Exhibit 11 (BPI's "Problem Solving" text), and to pp. I-27a -- 1-35a of Exhibit 11 (BPI's "Planning" text).  See Plaintiff's Exhibit 8.  Some of the revised materials were neither expressly accepted nor expressly challenged, namely, certain revised pages from "Problem Solving" and "Planning".  Additionally, Defendants did not revise every page in "Problem Solving" and "Planning." With respect to any materials that   were not objected to in Plaintiff's 5/29/79 Report, as well as the acceptable revised materials, I conclude Plaintiff has no continued copyright claim.
3.  I issued an interim order enjoining use of the unrevised infringing materials, allowing the use of the revised set of materials, denying impoundment, deferring discovery, and requiring BPI to make a diligent effort toward removing the infringing materials from the market.
4.  BPI submitted a second post-trial revision of its teaching materials.  In a letter accompanying this submission (dated 6/8/79) it is pointed out that BPI's "Introduction" and "Concern Analysis" (pp. I-11a -- I-14a of Exhibit 11) passed the Plaintiff's Report without objection.  However, "Concern Analysis" was rewritten anyway.  Due to Plaintiff's post-Report silence as to both of these sections, I assume there is no objection to them and do not discuss them further.
The questions before me are: (1) whether the second revised set of BPI materials continues to infringe Plaintiff's copyrights; (2) what Copyright Act, that of 1976 or 1909, governs this case;    (3) what monetary and further injunctive relief is necessary; (4) what, if any discovery is necessary to effect the remedy; (5) and whether BPI is making (or has made) "diligent, good faith" efforts to remove infringing materials from the market place.
1.  The Second Revision

Judged by the principles set forth in my first opinion, I conclude BPI's second revised set of materials does not infringe Plaintiff's copyrights.  BPI's revised "Problem Solving" text largely leaves behind the outline format found in Plaintiff's Exhibit 8 and in the Concept Rational Breakdown portion of the LDI material, and Apex II's strong reliance on the horizontal "is-is not" vertical "what-where, etc." structure.  Its emphasis has also shifted from a fairly detailed treatment of each subconcept through an outline to the use of more general prose passages highlighted with a recurring example tied to the more abstract concepts under discussion.

The same observations apply to BPI's revised "Planning" section.  Emphasis has shifted from simple presentation of the concepts to a format structured around problems that arise in a typical situation calling for "planning" techniques.

  This conclusion makes unnecessary any further injunction against the Defendants; the "Permissive Injunction" section of the Interim Order will be modified to permit Defendants to use the second revised set of materials.
2.  The Applicable Copyright Act

Plaintiff argues that though it makes little or no difference which Act -- 1909 or 1976 -- applies, most of the conduct complained of is governed by the 1970 Act.  Plaintiff's position is that a "cause of action" for infringement arose each time Defendants either copied or distributed its materials.  Thus, the initial copying and the first few distributions were governed by the 1909 Act, whereas every distribution made after January 1, 1978 is governed by the 1976 Act (page 3 of Plaintiff's Brief of 6/15/79).

BPI argues that the "cause of action" for this lawsuit arose in 1977, when the actual copying occurred and when BPI began its corporate existence.  BPI opposes the consecutive application of the two Acts, but agrees that the question of which Act applies is immaterial.

I conclude that it is important to determine which Act applies.  First, under the 1976 Act, Plaintiff elects either the combination of actual damages   and attributable profits, or statutory "in lieu" damages.  3 M. Nimmer, Nimmer on Copyright, §§ 14.01 [A] & [B]; 17 U.S.C.  § 504(b) (hereinafter" Nimmer at").  The election of "in lieu" damages precludes the right to recover both actual damages and the Defendants' profits, 3 Nimmer at § 14.01 [B], contrary to some earlier decisions.  Under the 1909 Act, "in lieu" damages may be awarded when damages or profits are not established, but do not always preclude them.  4 Nimmer at Appendix 16, p. 165.  More importantly, there is authority for the proposition that under the 1909 Act, the election is not the Plaintiff's but the Court's.  4 Nimmer at Appendix 16, p. 16-6.


Second, "In lieu" damages are measured differently under the 1909 and 1976 Acts. 3 Nimmer at § 14.04[E][2][a]. Under the 1909 Act separate minimum damage awards must be awarded for each "infringement", as that term is defined in the cases.  Under the 1976 Act "[a] single infringer of a single work is liable for a single amount between $250 and $10,000, no matter how many acts of infringement are involved in the action and regardless of whether the acts were separate, isolated, or occurred in a related   services." [footnote 65 omitted] 3 Nimmer at § 14.04 [E][2][a] [quoting from H.R. Rep. No. 94-1476, 94th Cong., 2d Sess. 162 (1976)] Thus, an award of statutory damages under the 1909 Act would be very likely larger than under the 1976 Act.

Third, under the 1909 Act "it was mandatory that full costs be awarded to the prevailing party in a copyright infringement action." 3 Nimmer at § 14.09; 17 U.S.C.  § 116 (… full costs shall be allowed…) Under § 505 of the new Act, "the court in its discretion may allow the recovery of full costs" (emphasis supplied) against any party, even the winner.  3 Minner at § 14.09.

Thus, in at least three respects (and possibly others) the 1909 and 1976 Acts differ materially.
The issue of which Act applies is, as BPI notes, "unsettled".  Transitional and Supplemental Provision § 112, Public Law #94-553, 90 Stat. 2600, reproduced in 17 U.S.C.  § 501 note, provides: "All causes of action that arose under Title 17 before January 1, 1978, shall be governed by Title 17 as it existed when the cause of action arose." But, what is a "cause of action"?  It may be defined as "the fact or combination of facts which give rise to a right   of action; the existence of which affords a party a right to judicial interference in his behalf." Helmers v Anderson, 156 F2d 47, 50 (9th Cir. 1946) aff'd 331 U.S. 461 (1947). A more elegant definition is set forth in Vnson v Graham, 44 F2d 772, 776 (10th Cir. 1930), where the court described a cause of action as

a primary right possessed by the plaintiff, and a corresponding primary duty devolving upon the defendant [and] a delict or wrong done by the defendant which [consists] in a breach of such primary right and duty.

Plaintiff argues each seminar session is a separate "cause of action".  In support it cites several cases where, for minimum statutory damages purposes, separate publications were held to be separate causes of action for which cumulative minimum statutory damage amounts must be awarded.  Thus, Plaintiff contends that consecutive application of the 1909 and 1976 Acts is appropriate.  However, this analysis does not fully address the issue.  The considerations    which led courts to the rules governing whether one or many minimum damage awards is appropriate are considerably   different from those involved in determining which of two consecutive Acts applies, even though both derive nominally from the meaning ascribed to the phrase "cause of action".
To achieve a definition of "cause of action" that comports with the aim of § 112, it must be noted that copyright infringement nearly always occurs over a period of time and involves a number of connected or related acts.  That is its nature.  Plaintiff's definitions of "cause of action" are not completely satisfactory when applied to course-of- conduct-type infringements. Thus, construing § 112 according to the usual meaning of "cause of action" yields an unsatisfactory result.  The new Act, as mentioned earlier, recognizes this inherent tendency of copyright violation and prescribes that for a single work there can be only one statutory damage award no matter how many "infringements" occur.  3 Nimmer at § 14.04[E][2][a].  When the phrase "cause of action" in § 112 interpreted in the light of the sort of thinking embodied in the new act, it is reasonable to conclude that the 1909 Act is to apply to all infringements which originated or ripened into a condition where suit was possible before January   1, 1978. Thus, the phrase "cause of action" for purposes of § 112 acquires a broad meaning, encompassing all of the conduct complained of in this lawsuit, rather than the narrower meaning, which is derived from cases that define the minimum amount of conduct that is actionable under copyright law, but do not address the problem of how to define "cause of action" for purposes of a sensible allocation of the relative temporal spheres of application of the 1909 and 1976 Acts.  I conclude the 1909 Act applies to this case in its entirety.
3.  Monetary and Injunctive Relief

A.  Statutory "in lieu" Damages vs. Actual Damages and Profits .

Plaintiff argues that under   the 1909 Act it is entitled to elect the greater of Defendants' actual profits or its own damages, or, 2f those two amounts cannot be ascertained, statutory damages.  17 U.S.C.  § 101(b).  In support, Plaintiff cites Sid & Marty Krofft Television Productions, Inc. v McDonald's Corp., 562 F2d 1157, 1172-1179, 196 USPQ 97, 109-116 (9th Cir. 1977), where at page 1179, n. 7, 196 USPQ at page 115 n.7, the court says (without citation) that an award of "in lieu" damages cannot deprive the plaintiff of his right to the greater of damages or profits when both are ascertained or to either one if only one is ascertained.  I do not agree.  The Supreme Court has never explicitly so held nor do I read the affirmance of Gordon v Wier, 111 FSupp. 117, 97 USPQ 387 (E.D. Mich. 1953), aff'd, 216 F2d 508 (6th Cir. 1954)), by the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, as mandating this result.
There is considerable disagreement on questions concerning § 101(b).  For example, some courts seem to say that if either damages or profits are not established, statutory damages are mandatory, e.g., Jewell-LaSalle Realty Co. v. Buck, 283 U.S. 202, 9 USPQ 22 (1931); other decisions indicate   they are only permissible, e.g., F. W. Woolworth Co. v. Contemporary Arts, Inc., 344 U.S. 228, 95 USPQ 396 (1952). See 4 Nimmer at Appendix 16, p. 16-2.  Another example may be found by comparing Judge Carter's dissent in Sid & Marty Krofft with the majority's holding in that case.  The majority held that the plaintiff was entitled to the larger of profits or damages.  Id., at 1179, 196 USPQ at 115-116.  Judge Carter, however, marshalled a great body of authority in support of a cumulative award, citing inter alia the new Act, § 504(b).  Id., at 1179-1181, 196 USPQ at 115-118.
I conclude that the lack of uniformity on these and other issues is partly attributable to the "impenetrable" and "unreadable", Robert Stigwood Group Ltd. v. O'Reilly, 530 F2d 1096, 1101, 189 USPQ 453, 457-458 (2d Cir.), cert. denied, 429 U.S. 848 (1976), language of § 101(b), but even more to the nearly infinite variety copyright infringements exhibit.  The hallmark of copyright law is flexibility in nearly every regard.  For example, the minimum "in lieu award is $250, whereas the maximum is $5,000.  This is a great difference.  In effect, the trial judge can, at his discretion, impose an unpayable large   award, or one so small as to be nearly nominal.  Likewise, the award of an attorney's fee is discretionary; under the new Act, the losing party may be awarded the fee.  And, though an award of costs is not discretionary under the 1909 Act, some courts refused to allow them.  3 Nimmer at § 14.09.  The list of areas in which    the court has wide discretion could be continued, but the point is that the law of copyright is, and must be, as flexible as the artistic and commercial public which invokes its aid.  Thus, I conclude that I should award the minimum statutory damage amount of $250 for each infringement by Defendants of Plaintiff's copyrighted works.
This conclusion results from the singular character of this case.  It was, from its inception, more a competitive tactic against a successful upstart competitor (see Defendants' Exhibits 20-22, 24-31) than a vindication of Plaintiff's right to the exclusive control of its copyrighted material.  As Defendants argued, materials do not sell seminars, seminars sell materials.  The copyrights in suit here were merely the vehicle by which an already dominant Plaintiff sought to mitigate competition.  Moreover, the copyright protection enjoyed   by Plaintiff is very limited; the violations were technical rather than substantive.
The cases support this approach.  In American Visuals Corp. v. Holland, 261 F2d 652, 119 USPQ 482 (2d Cir. 1957), the award was $5,000 in statutory damages though the defendants' profits were proved to be in excess of $7,000.  Citing Woolworth, supra, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed the award as being within the trial court's discretion.  The case of Masspequa Pub. Co. v Observer, Inc., 191 FSupp 261, 262, 128 USPQ 418, 418-419 (E.D. N.Y. 1961) is in accord.  There the court said: [we] think the statute empowers the trial court in its sound exercise of judicial discretion to determine whether on all of the facts a recovery upon proven profits and damages or one established within the statutory limits is just.


See generally 4 Minner at Appendix 16, p. 16-6; cf.  Smothers v Columbia Broadcasting Systems, 359 FSupp 723, 726 (C.D. Cal. 1973) (Judges Hauk rejected the plaintiff's proof of damages and profits and in his discretion awarded "neither plaintiff's actual damages nor defendant's profits, but rather 'such damages as to the court… [appeared] to be   just.' [citations omitted]"
The Number of Copyrighted Works at Issue

The foregoing conclusion presents "one of the most difficult problems in applying the statutory damages provision," namely, "when the mandatory minimum of $250 must be multiplied by reason of multiple infringements." 3 Nimmer at § 14.04[E].  This problem has two parts: first, it must be determined how many copyrights were infringed; second, how many infringements occurred as to each.  In general, the total statutory damage award must equal at least the following sum: $250 times the number of works infringed times the number of infringements of each.  3 Nimmer at §§ 14.04[E][1] & [2].
Plaintiff claims there are three copyrighted works at issue.  (Plaintiff's Proposed Findings of Fact, p. 2) They are: "Apex II" (Plaintiff's Exhibit 1); "Genco II" (Plaintiff's Exhibit 2); and "LDI" (Plaintiff's Exhibit 3).  Copyright certificates dated July 29, 1978 were issued on Apex II and Genco II, whereas the LDI materials are covered by 16 separate certificates (Plaintiff's Exhibits 4, 5 and 6, respectively).  Whether two separately copyrighted works are distinct for purposes of multiple damage awards is generally   determined by the objective of each separate copyright; would each be viable even if not presented in conjunction with other related copyrights.3 Nimmer at § 14.04[E][1] Although related by common theme, content and format, it appears that Apex II and Genco II are sufficiently distinct in terms of the audiences at which they are aimed and their relative levels of sophistication to meet the "separate work" test.
The LDI materials are a closer case.  They are by nature derivative, being used to teach other show to teach Apex II and Genco II.  In fact, some portion of the LDI material are verbatim reproductions of material found in Genco II and Apex II.  Moreover, the LDI materials would be useless if Apex II and Genco II did not exist.  The LDI materials could not "live their own copyright life," Stigwood, supra, at 1105, 189 USPQ at 460-461, because without Genco and Apex they would have no purpose.   The authority on this point is somewhat limited, being confined to clear cases involving the multiple-vs-single work question: E.g., L. A. Westermann Co. v Dispatch Printing Co., 249 U.S. 100 (1919) (illustrations of women's clothing); Lottie Joplin Thomas Trust v Crown Publishers,    592 F2d 651, 658 n. 10, 199 USPQ 449, 454 n.10 (2d Cir. 1978) (songs); Smothers v Columbia Broadcasting Systems, supra (television programs).  However, I conclude that for purposes of a multiple award of    statutory damages, the LDI copyright will not be considered as a separate work.
The Number of Infringements

How many infringements of Plaintiff's two copyrights occurred?  The government case is L. A. Westermann, supra, which held two publications of a single copyrighted drawing in two editions   of the same newspaper in two separate advertisements by two customers were two infringements for minimum damages purposes.  The court indicated that the standard by which these questions are judged is whether subsequent publications were new and distinct or merely continuations or repetitions of the first.  In making this determination, a number of factors are considered by the courts, among which are: the time interval between succeeding publications; whether separate transactions generated were the same or different parties involved); were there new business arrangements made for each successive publication; were the succeeding publications made in the same or different locales?  See generally 3 Minner at § 14.04[E][a]; Stigwood, supra, 530 F2d at 1102-1103, 189 USPQ at 458-459.
Plaintiff argues that each seminar session should be counted as a separate infringement, likening the holding of a seminar to the performance of a musical composition or the publication of an illustration.  I disagree, and hold that a separate "infringement" occurred each time Defendants acquired a new client and taught at least one seminar on its behalf.  Each successive seminar is merely a repetition   of the first.  The same contracting parties are involved, the business arrangements for the succeeding seminars are much the same as for the first, whereas the time interval and geographic locale factors seem to be more fortuitous than related to any considerations of law or policy.  In the competitive market, the real damage occurs each time a new account is obtained because the parties at the time of the initial contract contemplate an ongoing relationship.

Thus, the total amount of damages to which Plaintiff is entitled is: the minimum statutory award     $250     times the number of copyrights violated     2     times the number of customers BPI has obtained.   For example, if BPI has sold seminars to ten clients, Plaintiff would receive $250x2x10, which equals $5,000.
B.  Separability of Infringing and Non-Infringing Material

Plaintiff asserts that because Defendants' seminars were sold as a unit, 2t is entitled to all of the profits flowing from Defendants' seminar (and presumably third party licensing) business.  Plaintiff   cites Callaghan v Myers, 128 U.S. 617, 66 (1888) in support of its claim.  I note that Callaghan has been modified by a subsequent Supreme Court case, Sheldon v Metro-Goldwyn Pictures Corp., 309 U.S. 390, 44 USPQ 607 (1940), and retains little vitality today.  See 3 Nimmer at § 14.03[C].  In any event, my decision to award statutory damages in lieu of damages and profits makes this issue moot.
4.  Discovery

Plaintiff suggests Defendants be ordered to produce for inspection and copying all documents, etc., pertaining to the operation of BPI since 1977.  Because of my holding with respect to damages, there is no need for such wide ranging discovery. See generally Rule 26(a)(1) F.R.C.P.; 8 C. Wright & A. Miller, Federal Practice and Procedure §

2009; 4 J. Moore, Moore's Federal Practice P26.56.  The discovery I order is as follows: BPI must forthwith produce a list of its clients, indicating whether any single account contains two or more subdivisions   or departments that are so distinct as to reasonably represent not one but two or more separate accounts.  BPI shall also be required to produce a list of all corporations, partnerships or individuals with whom it has contracted or licensed to market or distribute its materials, if any part of that contract or license pertains to any of the materials that infringe Plaintiff's copyrights.
5.  Good Faith Effort

By a letter to me dated June 22, 1979 Defendants' counsel provided me with a copy of the form letter being sent by BPI to each of its customers as its "diligent, good faith efforts to remove the infringing materials from the marketplace." In a letter dated June 26, 1979 Plaintiff's counsel complains that the BPI letter is not sufficient, arguing that the recipient will not understand that BPI is revising its materials pursuant to a finding of copyright infringement. I disagree.  The important objective is to remove the infringing materials from the market.  The letter does this.
Summary and Conclusion

(1) Defendants' second revised set of materials does not infringe Plaintiff's copyrights.

(2) The 1909 Act applies to this case.

(3) Plaintiff will receive the minimum   statutory damage award of $250 for each infringement of its copyrights by Defendants.  In this regard, the Defendants infringed two of Plaintiff's copyrights.  Furthermore, the number of infringements is equal to the number of BPI's clients.  Plaintiff will receive no attorney's fee.  Defendants must pay the costs of this litigation.  No further injunctive relief is necessary except for the above-mentioned changes in the permissive and prohibitive portions of the Linterim Order.

(4) Plaintiff shall be allowed to discover, and Defendants shall be required to produce, a list of BPI's customers. Plaintiff shall also be allowed to discover whether any client has two or more subdivisions so separate as to make it reasonable and just to treat them as separate customers for damage purposes.

(5) Defendants have made a diligent, good-faith effort to remove the infringing materials from the market.

An appropriate order is entered herewith.

a.Validity of the Copyrights
Defendants   have challenged the validity of plaintiff's copyrights on the grounds that (a) some tape recordings of plaintiff's sales wraparound or sales pitch were distributed without proper copyright notice, (b) the publication date stated on them is September 1, 1977 rather than January, 1977, and (c) the entity claiming copyright upon publication in January or February of 1977, namely, Dealer Advertising Development, Inc., a Tennessee corporation, was not then in existence. The final paragraph of a letter dated April 7, 1977 and sent by Allan Horn, Sr., corporate defendant's president, to Don Roy, plaintiff's president, states:

In determining the presence of substantial similarity for purposes of copyright infringement, the test is "whether the work is recognizable by an ordinary observer as having been taken from the copyrighted source."

Proof of this element does not require that the infringing material correspond verbatim to the copyrighted material, since "in copyright law paraphrasing is equivalent to outright copying." Donald v. The similarities between these extracts are sufficiently numerous and striking and the variations to minor and artificial that it appears that one is a copy of the other.  A less striking but also significant similarity exists between two of the newspaper cartoons of each   campaign.
In Gordon v. Weir , 111 F.Supp. 117 (E.D. Mich. 1953), aff'd 216 F.2d 508 (6th Cir. 1954), the owner of an original copyrighted advertisement for licensing to merchants was approached by defendant with a view to marketing the campaign for their mutual benefit. Pursuant to former 17 U.S.C.  § 101(b),    a copyright infringer is liable to the copyright proprietor for
"such damages as the copyright proprietor may have suffered due to the infringement, as well as all the profits which the infringer shall have made from such infringement."
The standard of proof is also set forth in this section:
"[I]n proving profits the plaintiff shall be required to prove sales only, and the defendant shall be required to prove every element of cost which he claims, or in lieu of actual damages and profits, such damages as to the court shall appear to be just."
While there is disagreement as to whether both damages and profits are to be included in an award for copyright infringement, there is agreement that the prevailing party is entitled to at least the greater of damages or profits.  Sid & Marty Krofft Television Productions, Inc. v. McDonald's Corp ., 562 F.2d 1157, 1172 (9th Cir. 1977).
The burden of proving the amount of damages sustained or profits realized rests with the moving party and although they need not be established with precision, they cannot be assessed on the basis of speculation. No evidence whatsoever was introduced which would establish the number of sales by defendants of the "Come Grow With Us" series, the amount of profit realized thereon, or the number or value of sales lost by plaintiff attributable to defendants' infringements. The Court thus has no basis upon which to assess or award actual or statutory damages or profits.

Traditionally, the remedy against unauthorized copying of published literary property must first be sought under the federal copyright statutes.  Globe Newspaper Co. v. The second allegation of Count 8, that defendants utilized the giggle track of the "Timmy" series in their "Come Grow With Us" series, is undisputably demonstrated by plaintiff's exhibit 123.  This use of the giggle track without plaintiff's permission violates plaintiff's joint ownership rights under the April 1, 1976 Agreement.  (Pl's Ex. 47).  The issue is whether this violation constitutes actionable misappropriation as alleged.
It is settled law that each joint owner of a copyrighted work is a holder of an undivided interest in the whole, akin to a tenant in common.  Pye v. Mitchell , 574 F.2d 476, 480 (9th Cir. 1978); Picture Music, Inc. v. Weiner , 353 F.2d 41 (9th Cir. 1965), cert. denied , 384 U.S. 928 (1966); Edward B. Marks Music Corp. v. Jerry Vogel Music Co ., 140 F.2d 266 (2d Cir. 1944). Rather, the unilateral exploitation of a joint work by one of the co-owners without the permission of the other results in the creation of a constructive trust for the mutual benefit of both co- owners and imposes a duty upon the unilateral user to account to the other for all compensation thereby obtained. Donna v. Dodd, Mead & Co., Inc ., 374 F.Supp. 429, 43031 (S.D.N.Y. 1974); Picture Music, Inc. v. Bourne, Inc., supra , 314 F.Supp. at 646-47. 1 Nimmer on Copyright, supra , § 6.12.
The issue here is not the unilateral exploitation of a jointly owned work but, rather, the unilateral exploitation of a portion of a jointly owned work.  The seminal case on this question is Shapiro, Bernstein & Co. v. Jerry Vogel Music Co ., 221 F.2d 569 (id Cir. 1955), modified on rehearing 223 F.2d 252 (2d Cir. 1955), commonly known as the "12th Street Rag" case.  In that case, the composer   of an instrumental piano solo assigned all of his rights in the composition to a publisher who commissioned lyrics to be written for the work.  The court held that the resulting combination of music and lyrics constituted a joint work for the use of which each party had to account to the other. However, no obligation to account arose from the publisher's use of the music alone.
Professor Nimmer views the distinction narrowly, suggesting that when a joint owner uses or licenses only that portion of the joint work which he has himself contributed, the claim of the other joint owner to an accounting of profits turns on "whether that portion of the joint work which was licensed was itself created prior to the joint work and is the subject of a separable and subsisting copyright." 1 Nimmer on Copyright, supra , § 6.12[B], p. 6-29. Other commentators view the distinction more broadly and contend that a co-owner in no case needs to account for profits derived from the separable part attributable to him alone:
"since in most cases the author (or the owner) of an artistic creation who agrees to join his work with that of another for the purpose of publishing the resulting combination   probably does not intend to surrender any right to exploit the product of his (or his predecessor's) genius separately."
It is true that in some cases the subsequent popularity of one separable portion may be partially attributable to the initial popularity of the combined work.  For example, music which is not melodious enough to win wide acclaim by itself may, through the addition of clever lyrics, become familiar to the public, and thus later prove profitable even in instrumental form.  It would be desirable to allow an accounting for the portion of such subsequent   popularity attributable to the other section of the combined work.  But since the estimation of such a factor is impossible, the choice must be between two extremes: either an accounting in all cases of separate exploitation, or in none.  The latter seems generally to be the better.

Count 8 alleges that plaintiff has infringed defendants' copyrights in violation of the federal Copyright Act and the common law.    Specifically, if alleges that plaintiff, without the authority of defendants, has reproduced, printed, copied, published, and sold the "core theme" of Barbara Allan's "It's The Little Things That Count" script as the central theme in its "Little Kids" campaign, as well as other materials of Barbara Allan protected under common law copyright.

Although plaintiffs' motions are deceptively simple, they raise an issue which has received some conflicting treatment by the courts and which has never been completely resolved either by the Supreme Court of the United States or the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals.  The issue is whether an action for infringement of a copyright is equitable or whether it is a legal claim to which the defendant is entitled to its rights under the Seventh Amendment to the Constitution of the United States.  Although the principal relief sought by the plaintiffs is equitable, they cannot avoid the conclusion that some of the relief smacks of   an action at law.  Thus they have pleaded in their amended complaint a hybrid action in both law and equity, although of course these common law distinctions are not generally significant under the Federal Rules.  The issue to be decided is, in our opinion, whether the plaintiffs have converted a complaint which was basically one at law into one in equity.
Count I of the Amended Complaint alleges that plaintiffs obtained a copyright of their 1977 and 1978 Multistate Bar Examinations and that defendant has been copying and using a large number of the questions which appeared on one of these examinations.  Plaintiffs therefore seek the relief of (1) statutory damages; (2) reasonable disbursements and attorneys' fees; and (3) delivery to plaintiffs of all "infringing materials and all plates and other materials for making" them.  Plaintiffs also seek an injunction for further infringements, all of which relief is provided for in 17 U.S.C.  §§ 501 et seq. Count II alleges false representations and false designations of origin in violation of 15 U.S.C.  § 1125 and Ill. Rev. Stat. ch. 121 1/2, § 311-318.  This count also seeks an injunction and attorneys' fees and costs.  It is obvious   therefore that plaintiffs seek more than mere equitable relief, particularly in Count I.
However, §  504(c)(2) of the Copyright Act provides:

In a case where the copyright owner sustains the burden of proving, and the court finds, that infringement was committed willfully, the court in its discretion may increase the award of statutory damages to a sum of not more than $ 50,000.

Thus the reference in the statute to the "court" and to "statutory damages" leads the plaintiffs to contend that Congress did not contemplate use of a jury in awarding damages and that the award of statutory damages does not involve an action of law.  Apparently plaintiffs would agree that the award of punitive damages could require the use of a jury, however.
It is well-settled that willful or wanton conduct is the basis for punitive damages, and § 504(c)(2) is based solely upon willful conduct of the defendant.  Even the statutory damages which can be awarded under § 504(c)(1) are not less than $ 250 and not more than $ 10,000.It has generally been understood that Congress provided for these liquidated damages because of the difficulty of proving actual damages.  Brady v. Daly, 175 U.S. 148,    154 (1899). This is further illustrated by some of the cases relied upon by plaintiffs in which the playing of musical numbers by a jukebox constitutes the infringement, where there is no practical way of determining the number of times that has occurred and the amount of royalties of which the plaintiff has therefore been deprived.  See Cayman Music, Ltd. v. Reichenberger, 403 F.Supp. 794 (W.D. Wis. 1975) and Broadcast Music, Inc. v. Papa Johns, Inc., 201 U.S.P.Q. 302 (N.D. Ind. 1979).
We cannot agree, however, that damages up to $ 50,000 as provided in § 504(c)(2) are of the same type as those provided in § 504(c)(1), although both subsections refers to "statutory damages." Section 504(c)(2) musr be concerned with punitive damages, since a plaintiff would not ordinarily be entitled to five times more damages for an infringement which is willful than for one which was not.  We therefore believe that  the language of § 504(c)(2) (supra p. 3) should be construed to submit the question of willfulness to the jury and leave it to the court to assess the amount of these damages if willfulness is found by the jury.
Finally,  the question of infringement itself is one which can ordinarily be determined by a jury, as is done on occasion in   patent cases.  It so happens that the subject matter in the case at bar involves questions testing the legal qualifications of applicants for admission to the bar, but in most infringement cases the subject matter is more likely to be literature or musical compositions with which jurors are more conversant.  The right to a jury cannot depend upon the nature of the subject matter, however.  In any event,  if the question of infringement or non-infringement appears to be without substantial dispute on the facts, the court can either direct a verdict for one side or the other   or can set aside an unsupported verdict.
The Supreme Court's decision in Dairy Queen, Inc. v. Wood, 369 U.S. 469 (1962) dealt with a case where the plaintiff sought a money judgment based on an accounting and also an injunction for infringement and for breach of a contract which restricted the use of a trademark.  The trial court struck the defendant's jury demand, the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit refused a mandamus, and the Supreme Court, by Justice Black, reversed and ruled that mandamus should issue.  The court held in substance that plaintiff was entitled to a trial by jury in a hybrid case involving both equitable and legal issues and that a prayer for an "accounting" did not render the case one merely in equity.  The court applied Federal Rule 18(b) and followed Beacon Theaters, Inc. v. Westover, 359 U.S. 500 (1959) in concluding at p. 479:

I am disposed to accept the view, strongly pressed at the bar, that this complaint seeks an accounting for alleged trademark infringement, rather than contract damages.  369 U.S. at 480.

He concludes, as did Justice Black, that:

[a] jury, under proper instructions from the court, could readily calculate the damages flowing from this alleged trademark infringement, just as courts of law often do in copyright and patent cases.  369 U.S. 480-81.
The Supreme Court did not touch upon the issue of statutory damages for infringement in the foregoing case, because plaintiff had a contract to rely on. We have been referred to no case which has attempted to resolve this problem. However, we think it is clear that Justice Harlan was of the opinion   that a case involving merely infringement of a copyright is subject to the Seventh Amendment right of a jury trial in civil cases if damages are sought by the plaintiff.
We have been referred to two decisions in our circuit which have denied plaintiff the right to a jury trial. Broadcast Music, Inc. and Cayman Music, Ltd., supra, p. 4.  Neither of these cases involved punitive damages and both judges were careful to point out that the relief sought was limited to an injunction and minimum statutory damages.

Nor was the question of attorney's fees discussed in either case.  We therefore find that they are distinguishable from the one at bar, and in any event they apparently were not appealed.
On the other hand the Supreme Court in holding that a jury is required for statutory damage in a statutory Civil Rights case in Curtis v. Loether, 415 U.S. 189 (1974) stated at p. 196, "… the relief sought here - actual and punitive damages - is the traditional form of relief offered in the courts of law." Acc. Barber v. Kimbrell's, Inc., 577 F.2d 216 (4th Cir. 1978), cert. denied 439 U.S. 934 (1978). Another court in Chappell & Co., Inc. v. Pumpernickel Pub, Inc., 79 F.R.D. 528 (D. Conn.    1977) refused to strike a jury demand in a copyright infringement action even when plaintiff was only seeking the minimum statutory damages.  Acc. Broadcast Music, Inc. v. Moor-Law, 203 U.S.P.Q. 487 (D. Del. 1978).
In applying the criteria set out in Ross v. Bernhard, 396 U.S. 531 (1970), we must also deny plaintiff's motion to strike the jury demand.The  practice classically followed in questions of this sort prior to the merger of law and equity was to look for the legal rights being enforced, not the form of action being employed (at p. 533 et seq.). (1) the purpose and character of the use, including whether such use is of a commercial nature or is for nonprofit educational purposes;

(2) the nature of the copyrighted work;

Cl. 1973), affirmed 420 U.S. 376 (1975).
