This is an action for injunctive relief and damages based upon the alleged infringement of a copyright under 17 U.S.C. § 501 (1976). Plaintiff Lauratex Textile Corp. ("Lauratex") is a New York corporation engaged in the business of converting greige goods into printed textiles for apparel.  The plaintiff accuses the defendants Allton Knitting Mills, Inc., a New York corporation, and Martin Levine, its president and sole employee, of duplicating a fabric design which plaintiff had created, copyrighted and successfully sold in the market.  The defendants allegedly sold this copied version to several of plaintiff's customers at a lower price. Less than one month after the complaint was filed, the defendants consented to a preliminary injunction from the further production of this fabric design.  The parties were unable to agree, however, on an appropriate measure of damages.  Consequently, a one day non-jury trial was held before me on January 8,    1981.  The following shall constitute my findings of fact and conclusions of law.
I
This is not a case where the alleged infringement results from a design which is similar but not identical to that belonging to the plaintiff.  See, e.g., Harlequin v. Gulf and Western Company, 644 F.2d 946 (2d Cir. 1981); Malden Mills Inc. v. Regency Mills Inc., 626 F.2d 1112 (2d Cir. 1980). Here, the defendant has produced a fabric which is virtually identical to that produced by the plaintiff.  The lines, shapes and colors of the fabric designs on both parties' products are the same.  The only perceivable distinctions are a slight difference in the shade of the background color and the absence, in the defendant's fabric pattern, of black lines around the bow-like figures which appear in both patterns.  The background color difference can be explained by the respective manufacturing methods used by the parties.  The plaintiff printed the design on a 100 percent polyester fabric using a screen-printing process.  The defendant Martin Levine testified that he also used 100 percent polyester fabric but imprinted the design by way of a heat-transfer method.  The absence of black lines around the figures   in the defendant's pattern amounts to an insignificant distinction between the two fabric designs. [***522]
Mr. Jerry Sander, a stylist for Lauratex, testified that Lauratex purchased the design in question from an English design studio in August, 1979.  The invoice from that sale was introduced into evidence at    trial.  Plaintiff began to make fabric with this design in January, 1980 and obtained a copyright for the design in April, 1980.  The defendant Levine testified that he came upon the same design at a fashion show in Milan, Italy in November, 1979. He purchased a piece of the fabric which contained the pattern design at that time.  Levine began producing about 3,100 yards of the fabric in September, 1980.
Regardless of where the defendant claims he actually obtained the pattern, it is clear that the plaintiff had a valid copyright on the design, that the defendants had a reasonable opportunity to copy that design since January, 1980 when plaintiff first sold it, and that the defendants produced an identical design thereafter.  From the credible evidence adduced at trial, there is substantial proof that the defendants copied plaintiff's design and thereby infringed its   copyright within the meaning of 17 U.S.C. § 501. See Novelty Textile Mills v. Joan Fabrics Corp., 558 F.2d 1090 (2d Cir. 1977).
II
Having determined that an infringement has occurred, the question remains as to what is an appropriate remedy. The plaintiff has asked for a permanent injunction, statutory damages in the sum of $ 50,000, and attorneys' fees in the sum of $ 10,000.
A permanent injunction to prevent or restrain the infringement of a copyright is provided for in 17 U.S.C. § 502 and is appropriate where money damages would not suffice.  Here, the evidence shows that there exists a strong probability that the defendant will, in the future, continue to infringe plaintiff's copyright.  The defendants already have sold several thousand yards of fabric containing the design.  Moreover, the defendant Levine has the engraving to produce more.  For these reasons, a permanent injunction will issue.

Turning to the question of money damages, the plaintiff has requested statutory damages under 17 U.S.C. § 504 (1976).   This section provides in part that the court may, in its discretion, award damages up to $ 50,000 where the plaintiff copyright owner proves that the infringement   was committed wilfully.  17 U.S.C. § 504(c)(2).  If the infringement is not found to be willful, damages of between $ 250 and $ 10,000 may be awarded. Id. § 504(c)(1).
In general, statutory damages are appropriate where, as here, the measure of actual damages is difficult to prove.  See Russell v. Price, 612 F.2d 1123 (9th Cir. 1979), cert. denied, 446 U.S. 952, 100 S. Ct.    2919, 64 L. Ed. 2d 809 (1980). The broad discretionary power given courts to make such an award serves the dual purposes of the Copyright Act: to compensate copyright owners and to provide a deterrent for would-be infringers. Lottie Joplin Thomas Trust v. Crown Publishers, 592 F.2d 651 (2d Cir. 1978).  Actual damages to the copyright owner usually are measured in terms of lost profits.  It is often difficult to speculate, however, what the  [***523] plaintiff's sales would have been had there been no infringement. Here, computing plaintiff's lost profits is complicated by the lower price which defendant charged for their infringing goods.  At trial, the defendant Levine testified that he charged $ 1.67 per yard. The plaintiff charged $ 2.60 per yard. It is quite possible that defendants' lower price resulted in more sales volume than would have been achieved by the plaintiff.  Thus, applying defendants' sales volume to plaintiff's price in order to compute lost profits would   be misleading.  It is possible, on the other hand, to compute defendants' profits from the evidence presented at trial and use that as an

519 F. Supp. 730, *732; 1981 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 13770, **4; 215 U.S.P.Q. (BNA) 521, ***522

approximate measure of plaintiff's damages.  Levine testified that he produced approximately 3,100 yards of the fabric and sold it to two of plaintiff's customers. This amounts to gross profits of $ 5,177.  The defendants did not offer any proof of expenses or costs related to these sales.  This figure will provide a basis for examining an appropriate amount of statutory damages.
To determine what amount of statutory damages should be awarded, it must be decided whether the defendants willfully copied the plaintiff's protected fabric design.  The record before me mandates an affirmative answer to this question.  The defendant Levine claims that he purchased a piece of fabric containing the design in Europe in November, 1979.  He did not mass produce the fabric design and sell it, however, until September, 1980, nearly nine months after the plaintiff had already established a successful market in the design and five months after the plaintiff copyrighted it.  At no time did the defendant Levine attempt to copyright the design he allegedly obtained   in Europe.  When he finally produced it, he went directly to one of plaintiff's best customers. Under the circumstances, the defendant can hardly be called an innocent infringer. Although no specific proof has been presented to show that Levine knew of the plaintiff's copyright, it is clear that, at the very least, he acted with a reckless disregard for the rights the plaintiff had in the design.
In addition, the plaintiff presented at trial docket sheets in six copyright infringement cases brought within the last three years against Levine.  Four of these cases have been settled.  This provides one more indication that the business of encroaching upon others' copyrights is not unfamiliar to the defendant.  For these reasons, the defendant appears to have infringed plaintiff's copyright willfully.

At the conclusion of this trial, the defendant Levine moved to dismiss the action on the theory that all of his acts proved at trial were really those of the corporate defendant.  As a result,    it is asserted that he should not be held individually liable for any damages to plaintiff.  Cf.  Walkovszky v. Carlton, 18 N.Y.2d 414, 276 N.Y.S.2d 585, 223 N.E.2d 6 (1966) (corporate veil not pierced because of absence of fraud).  This argument is unavailing because of the defendant Levine's control over the corporate defendant.  Levine is the sole stockholder and officer of Allton Knitting Mills, Inc.   Where an individual directly causes a corporate defendant to infringe and personally participates in the acts constituting the infringement, he is jointly and severally liable for the infringement. See Lottie Joplin Thomas Trust v. Crown Publishers, 456 F. Supp. 531 (S.D.N.Y.1977), aff'd 592 F.2d 651 (2d Cir. 1978). Thus, both defendants are jointly and severally liable for the plaintiff's $ 40,000 damage award.

FAIR USE DOCTRINE

As indicated by the district court, the analysis of whether the recording was infringement does not end with the statutory language. While the old Act was in effect, the courts pronounced a rule of law known as the doctrine of "Fair Use." This doctrine has been appropriately described as "the most troublesome in the whole law of copyright." Dellar v. Samuel Goldwyn, Inc., 104 F.2d 661 (C.A.2 1939). From its inception,    the doctrine has presented members of the judiciary with among the most elusive views that the courts are called upon to decide. It has been said that the doctrine is entirely equitable and is so flexible as virtually to deny definition.  Time, Inc. v. Bernard Geis Associates, 293 F. Supp. 130 (S.D.N.Y.1968). Time after time the courts have ruled on the Fair Use doctrine, but no real definition of the concept has ever emerged. One of the better definitions is that of the Second Circuit in Rosemont Enterprises, Inc. v. Random House, Inc., 366 F.2d 303, 306 (C.A.2 1966), cert. denied, 385 U.S. 1009, 87 S. Ct. 714, 17 L. Ed. 2d 546 (1967), where it is said that fair use is "a privilege in others than the owners of a copyright to use the copyrighted material in a reasonable manner without his consent, notwithstanding the monopoly granted to the owner" by the copyright. The Congress in the legislation of 1976 attempted to define fair use in § 107 which reads:
"Notwithstanding the provisions of section 106, the fair use of a copyrighted [***769]  work, including such use by reproduction in copies or phonorecords or by any other means specified by that section, for purposes such as   criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching (including multiple copies for classroom use), scholarship, or research, is not an infringement of copyright. In determining whether the use made of a work in any particular case is a fair use the factors to be considered shall include--

(1) the purpose and character of the use, including whether such use is of a commercial nature or is for nonprofit educational purposes; (2) the nature of the copyrighted work; (3) the amount and substantiality of the portion used in relation to the copyrighted work as a whole; and (4) the effect of the use upon the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work."
It is noteworthy that the legislative history of § 107 makes it clear that its statements of the fair use doctrine offers some guidance to users in determining when the principles of the doctrine apply. However, it is there emphasized that the endless variety of situations and combinations of circumstances that can arise in particular cases precludes the formulation of exact rules.
The history states that the legislation endorses the purposes and general scope of the judicial doctrine of fair use, but there is no   disposition to freeze the doctrine in the statute. We quote from the closing sentence of the history:

"Section 107 is intended to restate the present judicial doctrine of fair use, not to change, narrow, or enlarge it in any    way." U.S.Code Cong. & Admin.News 1976, 5680. Consequently, and despite what is said by the district court, this fair use analysis is equally applicable to alleged violations under both the Old and the New Act. It is interesting to note that appellees have not suggested that home video recording would not violate the Old Act in the absence of a finding of fair use.
Despite the nebulous character of the doctrine, previous case law and the general copyright scheme do provide us with considerable guidance. As the first sentence of § 107 indicates, fair use has traditionally involved what might be termed the "productive use" of copyrighted material. See 66 Va.L.Rev. at 1012-1014. The purposes listed in § 107 are simply illustrative and not limitative, but they do give some idea of the general orientation of the doctrine. It is noteworthy that the statute does not list "convenience" or "entertainment" or "increased access" as purposes   within the general scope of fair use.
Leon Seltzer, in his illuminating book Exemptions and Fair Use in Copyright (1978) states:

Supp. at 450, and quoting Nimmer's critique of the opinion, Id. at 451, used Williams & Wilkins Co.'s distortions of the fair use rationale to justify an application of the doctrine which, in our opinion, stretches fair use beyond recognition and undermines our traditional reliance on the economic incentives provided to authors by the copyright scheme.
In Williams & Wilkins Co., the Court of Claims found that copying by the National Institute of Health (NIH) and the National Library of Medicine (NLM) of entire articles published in plaintiff's journals was  [***770]  fair use. Plaintiff was the publisher of certain medical and scientific journals. We believe that Williams & Wilkins Co. is clearly distinguishable. It appears that the Court of Claims was primarily concerned about the serious damage to medical science that would result if it held for the plaintiff. In this case,   there is no corresponding countervailing societal benefit to "weigh" against the copyright interests of the author. We do not mean to suggest that increased access to such Disney products as "Chip and Dale/Mixed Nuts" is not a benefit to society. We only mean to say that the consequences attendant upon reduced consumer control of access do not in any way correspond to the deleterious consequences of reduced access identified by the Court of Claims in Williams & Wilkins Co.
Aside from the obvious distinctions between Williams & Wilkins Co. and the instant case, we believe that the Court of Claims' approach--in treating intrinsic use of such work as within the bounds of fair use--created doctrinal confusion that raises the spectre of the evisceration of the traditional workings of the copyright scheme. As Seltzer has stated:

"The traditional fair use notion has had to do with the sort of access that the mind of a user has to a copyrighted work: the work is instantly accessible on sight or hearing, and the question is what the second user would or should be allowed to 'do' with it--or, more accurately, what the creator of the work ought to have expected him freely to   do with it. Use for photocopying and phonorecording involves a different sort of access: the possibility--and the capability--of instant reproduction of the work in the same mode and for the same purpose the original was in the first place acquired. [Emphasis added.] Seltzer concludes that exemptions from the normal workings of the copyright scheme, because they involve the reallocation of costs, are matters for Congress, not the courts.
We hold that, particularly in the context of new technology, there is a danger to including the sort of copying involved in Williams & Wilkins Co. within the scope of the fair use doctrine.  New technology, which makes possible the mass reproduction of copyrighted material (effectively taking   control of access from the author), places a strain upon the fair use doctrine. A court, if it decides that fair use is applicable, is required to weigh--in "balancing the equities"--the "benefit" of an extremely popular increase in access with the "harm" to a plaintiff. The harm to a copyright plaintiff is inherently speculative, and as Williams & Wilkins Co. and the district court decision indicate, a plaintiff is faced with the unenviable task of proving the nonexistence of fair use, which has typically been viewed as a defense.
The costs are also important. They fall primarily into two categories. First, the result of applying fair use to intrinsic use cases like Williams & Wilkins Co. and this case is a fundamental restructuring of the copyright system not justified by the statutory scheme or traditional notions of fair use. Second, the framework for copyright litigation this view establishes is ultimately hostile and extremely adverse to the rights of copyright holders. It places them in the unenviable position of proving damage in a context in which extreme difficulty is acknowledged.
As a society, we may decide that these costs are acceptable. But, that branch   of  [***771]  public policy determination is preeminently a decision for the legislative branch.
It is our conviction that the fair use doctrine does not sanction home videorecording.  Without a "productive use", i. e.    when copyrighted material is reproduced for its intrinsic use, the mass copying of the sort involved in this case precludes an application of fair use. An analysis of the four factors listed in § 107 does not dictate a contrary result.

LIABILITY OF CORPORATE DEFENDANTS

We disagree with the district court's conclusion that even if it were to hold that home-use copying was an infringement under the Old and the New Acts and was not fair use, the court could not find the appellees Sonam, Sony, DDBI and the four retail stores liable for this type of infringement. 480 F. Supp. at 457.
At the outset, it is necessary to make a couple of observations about the district court's analysis. The court relied heavily on a "staple item of commerce"  theory in rejecting appellants' claims. The district court stated that "Selling of a staple article of commerce--e.g., a typewriter, a recorder, a camera, a photocopying machine-- technically contributes to any infringing use subsequently made thereof, but this kind of 'contribution,' if deemed sufficient as a basis for liability, would expand the theory beyond precedent and arguably beyond judicial management." 480 F. Supp. at 461. This reliance on the "staple article of commerce" theory was inappropriate. Appellees' analogy of videotape records to cameras or photocopying machines may have substantial benefit for some purposes, but does not even remotely   raise copyright problems.  Videotape recorders are manufactured, advertised, and sold for the primary purpose of reproducing television programming. Virtually all television programming is copyrighted material. Three days after the filing of the complaint Kamakazi sought a preliminary injunction and Robbins cross-moved to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction or alternatively for a stay pending arbitration of the dispute under the Agreement.  After a number of motions, the hearings and further motions, the arbitrator's awards were confirmed in opinions dated August 3, 1981 and September 15, 1981.  This motion to amend the complaint was served on defendants on December 7, 1981. It is therefore collaterally estopped from urging that its acts were authorized by the Agreement.

LUMBARD, Circuit Judge:

Kamakazi Music sued Robbins Music, both being New York corporations, in the Southern District of New York for infringing its copyrights in the sheet music of pop star Barry Manilow.  Kamakazi sought a preliminary injunction, damages and attorneys fees under the Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. §§ 502-05 (Supp. IV 1980). Robbins responded that it had licensed the copyrights from Kamakazi, that there was no federal jurisdiction as Kamakazi's suit was for breach of contract and, in the alternative, it sought arbitration as provided   in the contract. Judge Sweet took jurisdiction and sent the case to arbitration. The arbitrator awarded Kamakazi an injunction, $250,000 in damages, and $50,127.72 in attorney's fees under 17 U.S.C. § 505. Judge Sweet confirmed the award. Robbins appeals, arguing again that the federal court has no jurisdiction to hear what Robbins terms a suit for breach of contract, and stated further that the arbitrator exceeded his authority in basing his remedies on the Copyright Act. We affirm. That Robbins interposed a contract as defense does not turn Kamakazi's suit under the Copyright Act into a suit for breach of contract. As for the challenged award, the arbitrator exercised only the jurisdiction which Robbins itself pressed upon him.
Kamakazi's complaint, filed on May 19, 1980, clearly stated claims under the Copyright Act. It did not mention breach of contract as a theory of liability. Kamakazi sought a preliminary injunction, damages and attorneys fees under the Copyright Act. Robbins interposed its interpretation of the contract as a defense, claimed that Kamakazi's suit was for breach of contract and contended that the district court lacked   jurisdiction.  Robbins sought in the alternative to compel arbitration under § 20 of the contract, which provided that "any controversy or claim arising out of, or relating to this agreement or the subject matter thereof, or the breach hereof shall be settled by arbitration" in New York City according to the rules of the American Arbitration Association. On June 5, 1980, Judge Sweet ruled that the district court had jurisdiction because Kamakazi had sued under the Copyright Act, but ordered the case to arbitration    pursuant to the arbitration clause. Judge Sweet denied Kamakazi's request for a preliminary injunction for fear of pre-empting the arbitration.
The arbitration began August 12, 1980, with Kamakazi's opening statement that it was suing for copyright infringement. At the hearing on September 5, the parties discussed the damages to be considered by the arbitrator, and the arbitrator summarized the colloquy as follows:

Mr. Frankel [for Kamakazi] indicated that the testimony here would probably be duplicative of the testimony to be given in the Southern District case, and that perhaps in an effort to save time, I might consider not hearing the damage issue.   Mr. Osterberg [for Robbins] raised the potential that he might argue in the Federal Court, Southern District case that the award of damages and the arbitration might limit Judge Sweet and that, therefore, he did not believe that the damage issue should be waived at this hearing.

After considering the arguments, I determined and expressed to Mr.  Frankel my opinion that the arbitration between the two parties, which was referred to the American Arbitration Association pursuant to Judge Sweet's opinion, should be a total resolution of the claims and liabilities between the parties; that is, Kamakazi Music

684 F.2d 228, *228; 1982 U.S. App. LEXIS 17288, **1 and Robbins Music, and that I was not prepared to exercise discretion, if I have any, to not hear the damage issue, and that I would hear testimony as to damages. (Emphasis added.)
The arbitrator made his award on liability and damages on March 6, 1981, ruling for Kamakazi on the disputed issues of fact. He found that "personality folios" were not included in the contract's provision for "mixed folios," and therefore Robbins had no right to sell "personality folios" after December 31, 1979. The arbitrator found that Robbins wilfully continued to sell "personality folios"   in violation of 25 copyrights owned by Kamakazi,  and he awarded Kamakazi statutory damages of $10,000 per copyright infringed under 17 U.S.C. § 504(c). He also granted a permanent injunction against Robbins' publication or sale of Kamakazi copyrights. On April 7, the arbitrator made a supplemental award of $50,127.72 in attorney's fees under 17 U.S.C. § 505. On August 3, Judge Sweet confirmed the award subject to a hearing as to the validity of Kamakazi's copyrights.  522 F. Supp. 125 (S.D.N.Y. 1981). He found the copyrights valid on September 15, 1981.
We agree with Judge Sweet that the district court had jurisdiction.  Kamakazi's suit is, was, and always has been based on the Copyright Act. Kamakazi sued Robbins for publishing Manilow works after the contract between the two had expired. Once the contract had expired, Robbins was liable for infringement of Kamakazi's copyrights. Given the explicit language of Kamakazi's complaint, and the acts complained of, it is frivolous for Robbins to contend that its contractual defense makes Kamakazi's suit one for breach of contract.    The district court had jurisdiction because the claim was for copyright infringement. The claim sent to the arbitrator was for copyright infringement. The damages calculated by the arbitrator at Robbins' urging were for copyright infringement.
In the circumstances of this case, the arbitrator had jurisdiction to make an award under the Copyright Act. We agree with Judge Sweet that the arbitration clause was broad enough to encompass Copyright Act claims which required interpretation of the contract. Even if the arbitration clause did not encompass Kamakazi's claims, it is hornbook law that  parties by their conduct may agree to send issues outside an arbitration clause to arbitration. See Amicizia Societa Navegazione v. Chilean Nitrate and Iodine Sales Corp., 274 F.2d 805, 809 (2d Cir.), cert. denied, 363 U.S. 843, 4 L. Ed. 2d 1727, 80 S. Ct. 1612 (1960); Ficek v. Southern Pacific Co., 338 F.2d 655, 656 (9th Cir. 1964),   cert. denied, 380 U.S. 988, 14 L. Ed. 2d 280, 85 S.  Ct. 1362 (1965); Capital City Telephone Co. v. Communication Workers of America, 575 F.2d 655, 658 (8th Cir. 1978). Robbins forced Kamakazi to submit its claim to arbitration and urged the arbitrator to consider all of the issues between the parties. Robbins by its conduct clearly agreed to submit all claims under the Copyright Act to the arbitrator, including Kamakazi's claim -- pressed from the start -- for attorney's fees under 17 U.S.C. § 505.
We find no merit in Robbins' other arguments on appeal. Robbins contends that "public policy" prohibits submission of copyright claims to arbitration, but   it cites no case for this proposition and we can find none.  Public policy does prohibit submission of some securities, patent and antitrust claims to arbitration. See Scherk v. Alberto-Culver Co., 417 U.S. 506, 512-13, 41 L. Ed. 2d 270, 94 S. Ct. 2449 (1974) (securities); American Safety

684 F.2d 228, *230; 1982 U.S. App. LEXIS 17288, **5

Equipment Corp. v. J.P. Maguire & Co., 391 F.2d 821, 826-27 (2d Cir. 1968) (antitrust); N.V. Maatschappij Voor Industriele Warden v. A.O. Smith Corp., 532 F.2d 874, 876 (2d Cir. 1976) (per curiam) (patent).  The only "public interest" in a copyright claim concernsthe monopoly inherent in a valid copyright. The validity of the copyrights here, and therefore the existence of the monopoly, was not determined by the arbitrator, but by the district court. Consequently, we see no public policy against arbitration of this claim for the infringement of a valid copyright.
Robbins challenges the arbitrator's award of attorney's fees on the ground that New York law, which controlled the arbitration procedure, prohibits the award of such fees unless the contract so   provides. N.Y.  C.P.L.R. 7513. Robbins misconstrues the import of that statute, which provides in pertinent part:

 Unless otherwise provided in the agreement to arbitrate, the arbitrators' expenses and fees together with other expenses, not including attorney's fees, incurred in the conduct of the arbitration, shall be paid as provided in the award. (Emphasis added.)
The statute does not bar the award of attorney's fees; it merely does not grant authority to do so. In this case, the arbitrator drew upon an independent source of authority -- the Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. § 505 -- to award attorney's fees. The federal statute grants authority to award attorney's fees; the failure of New York law to grant such authority is irrelevant. Cf.  Morris v. Government Employees Insurance Co., 81 A.D.2d 880, 439 N.Y.S.2d 163 (2d Dep't 1981) (C.P.L.R. 7513 is not inconsistent with Insurance Law § 675 which allows recovery of attorney's fees.)
We have considered Robbins' other arguments and find them without merit, largely for reasons enunciated in Judge Sweet's opinion of August 3, 1981.

Affirmed.

Professor Treacy is a Spanish language expert and an expert in translation from Spanish into English, who is also knowledgeable about Spanish food and cuisine.  Professor Treacy   testified that in many instances the Marlings had brought a considerable amount of skill, judgment and originality to the task of translating Spanish to English.  For example, "Tapas," which is translated in Marling (p. 8) as "In-between meal snacks' and in Ellison (p. 67) as "In between meal snacks," is a simple two-syllable word that stands for a complex Spanish custom of eating small amount of a variety of foods while drinking at a series of bars at particular times of the day.  Professor Treacy's testimony reinforces the conclusion that Ellison's identical English rendition of this term was copied from the Marling book.  Another example is the term "Especialidades Ahumadas" which means literally "smoked specialities." The Marlings translate this term (p. 16) as "special smoked fish appetizers." That Ellison (p. 26) has the identical English translation of this term, I find to be not a matter of coincidence, but further evidence of copying.
Professor Treacy also illuminated instances in which the Marlings made errors in their translation of Spanish terms into English.  I find this to be especially significant in this case, since many of these errors were copied by Ellison in   his book.  It is well recognized that the existence of common errors in two similar works is perhaps the strongest evidence of copying. I find that Ellison copied errors from the Marlings as well as their accurate translation work.  For example, the Marlings (p. 97) translated "Toston (asado)" as "a young suckling pig; spit-roasted." Ellison (p. 71) translated the same term as "spit-roasted young suckling pig." The evidence discloses that every suckling pig is young pig, thus the use of the word "young" is superfluous.  The Marlings also erred in translating the term "Chuleta de Anojo" (p. 76) as "a chop * * * from an older sheep, a mutton chop, since "Anojo" means a yearling lamb (or calf).  The Marlings error may have been in the spelling of the Spanish, since the similar word "Anejo" means "old, aged." Which was their error, however, Ellison followed it on page 15 of his book, where he translates "Chuletas de Anojo" as mutton chops."
In deposition testimony elicited during cross examination of Professor Treacy by counsel for defendant (p. 142), Professor Treacy summarized her conclusion as follows:

"I have found examples of what I considered to be direct copying. I have found   examples of excessive borrowing.  And I have found examples of what I believe to be use of the Marling book to determine what entries to make into the Ellison book.  So I do not find it just mere copying. I find it more than that."
The findings recited above and those to follow represent the findings of the Court.  I further find, based upon the credible evidence adduced at trial, based upon a comparison of the works themselves, and based upon the assistance provided by the expert testimony of Professor Treacy, that Ellison copied the Marlings' translation work in the Spanish books.
This Court finds that the Marlings employed considerable effort, expertise and judgment in the development of American English translation for the German terms listed in their German Menu-Master.  This Court finds further that Ellison's German Menu Reader borrows the Marlings' American English translations of Germans menu terms wholesale.
Examples of verbatim copying of the Marlings original translations may be found throughout Ellison's German Menu Reader.  Thus "Paprikahanchen "ungarisch"" is translated by the Marlings (p. 65) as "Chicken braised in a paprika sauce with sour cream and tomato paste."    Ellison (p. 46) translates this term as "Chicken braised in paprika sauce with sour cream and tomato paste." The Marlings' translation for "Cordon Rouge" (p. 47) is "Veal or beef filet with mushrooms, chicken livers and tarragon." For Ellison this term means (p. 8): "Veal or beef filet with mushrooms, chicken livers and tarragon." The terms "Blatterteigpastete mit Geflugelragout" is translated by the Marlings (p. 19) as "Patty shell with diced chicken or other fowl in rich cream sauce." In Ellison (p. 54) the translation is "Patty shell with chicken or other fowl in rich cream sauce." The Marlings render the term "Hawaii" (p. 21) as "With pineapple garnish;" for Elison the same term mean (p. 25) "With pineapple garnish." The entry "Krabbenmayonannais is translated in the Marling book (p. 22) as "Shrimp in mayonnaise dressing." Ellison translates this entry (p. 36): "shrimps in mayonnaise dressing." I find that the verbatim replication by Ellison of the Marlings'   original translations, as in the foregoing examples, is the product of unlawful plagiarism.
Many other Ellison translations, though less than verbatim, still retain the key words and word order of the Marlings' original.    For example, "Schwedenplatte" is rendered by the Marlings (p. 25): "Swedish smorgasbord plate of mixed appetizers"; and by Ellison (p. 59): "Swedish smorgasbord or mixed appetizers." The Marlings translate "Falscher Hase" (p. 47) as: "False Hare -- a meat loaf of seasonal chopped beef, veal, and pork, covered with a sauce of creamed pan juices. " (Emphasis added.) Ellison translates this term (p. 12): "Meat loaf with beef, veal pork and creamed pan juices." The entry Pastete Kapuzinerart" is translated by the Marlings (p. 23) as: "Capucine Monk's style -- a delicate meat stew served in a patty shell. " (Emphasis added.) Ellison translates this term (p. 46): "Meat stew in patty shell." In other cases, Ellison retains the key words and the gist of the Marlings' translation, but makes alterations in word order.  Thus, the entry "Mayonnaisesalat" is translated by the Marlings (p. 23) as: Pieces of cooked meat or fish, vegetables in mayonnaise dressing." Ellison renders this term (p. 41): "Fish or meat and vegetables in mayonnaise." "Kasseler Saftrippe" appears in the Marings book (p. 22) as: "Juicy pickled and smoked pork loin chop," and in the Ellison book (p. 34) as "Pickled and smoked   pork loin chop."
Plaintiffs presented by deposition the testimony of Professor Fritz Fleischmann, a native speaking German language expert and expert in translation of German into English.  Professor Fleishmann's testimony was of value to the Court in identifying instances in which the Marlings erred in their translation of German terms into English. This has an important bearing on the case at hand, since, as discussed, common errors in similar works are regarded as perhaps the strongest evidence of copyright infringement. In the instant case there are numerous examples in which Ellison copies errors from the Marling menu-Master from Germany.  At page 84 of their book, the Marlings erroneously defined the term "Krapfen" as "fritters." The word means yeast doughnut according to Professor Fleishmann.  Ellison (p. 36) also renders this term "Fritters," even though he correctly defines it elsewhere in the very next entry, as a "yeast doughnut." The Marlings also erred in translating the term "Eierschaum" (p. 82) as: "Beaten egg yolks and sugar * * *".  The term actually means beaten egg white with sugar, according to Professor Fleishmann.  Ellison (p. 10) repeats substantially the   same error with his translation: "Beaten egg with sugar." Yet another Marling error is their translation of "Gepokelt" (p. 21) as "Pickled." Ellison (p. 20) uses the identical translation. In fact, the term is generic for pickled or cured and hence could mean pickled, smoked or salted, according to Professor Fleishmann.  Another Marling error replicated in Ellison (p. 41) is their translation of "Meeresfruchte" (p. 23) as "Seafood." In fact, this term refers to shell fish and octopus; it is a German version of a famous Italian dish, according to Professor Fleishmann.  Hence, the American term "seafood" which includes fish as well as shellfish, is an erroneously overboard and imprecise translation of this term.
The Marling translation of "Krabbenmayonnaise" (p. 22) erroneously restricts the dish to shrimp, when "the fish used in this dish are not necessarily or not usually shrimp." Deposition of Professor Fleischmann, p. 73.  Ellison replicates this error on page 36 of this book.  The Marlings translate "Puterschinken" (p. 65) as "Turkey leg;" literally the term means turkey ham.  See Deposition of Professor Fleischmann, p. 74.  Ellison follows this error on page 49 of his book.    These common errors demonstrate the convincingly, and the Court finds, that Ellison's Menu Reader for Germany, published in 1977, copied in substantial measure from The Marling Menu-Master for Germany, which was published in 1970.
Professor Fleischmann stated his finding upon comparing the two German language books as follows:

"Mr. Ellison lists the identical menu categories also listed in the Marlings' book.  And he has selected a number of other dishes not necessarily on a German menu reader which are also present in the Marling book.  Both works contain a number of identical mistakes."
This Court finds, as a matter of factual conclusion, identical menu categories in both books, copying by Ellison of the Marlings' editorial selection work in the dishes and entries included, and copying by Ellison of the Marlings' judgment in their translation of German terms into American English.
In summary, this Court finds that Ellison's German Menu Reader exhibits substantial similarity to the Marling Menu- Master for Germany, both with respect to editorial selection and with respect to translation into American English. This Court further finds that Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader exhibits   substantial similarity to the Marling Menu-Master for Spain, both with respect to editorial selection and with respect to translation into American English.Plaintiffs also contend that Ellison's Swiss Menu Reader exhibits substantial similarity in editorial selection and in translation from German into English   to the Marling Menu-Master for Germany.  However, plaintiffs presented little evidence of these similarities. There was some suggestion of copying in that Ellison's Swiss Menu Reader seems to replicate materials from Ellison's German Menu Reader in its German language section.  Some of these materials as they appeared in Ellison's German Menu Reader may have been copied from the Marling Menu- Master for Germany.  However, Ellison's Swiss Menu Reader contains an intermixture of French, Italian, and German terms, such that the German terms themselves are but a portion of the book.  No attempt was made by plaintiffs to show copying by Ellison with respect to the French and Italian entries in the Swiss book.  Under these circumstances, I conclude that insufficient evidence has been presented to me to establish substantial similarity between Ellison's Swiss Menu Reader and The Marling   Menu-Master for German, with respect to either editorial selection or translation of German terms into American English.
Conclusions of Law

 A claim of copyright infringement is established by showing (1) a valid copyright and (2) copying by the defendant.  See generally 3 Nimmer On Copyright, § 13.01, page 13-3 (1981).  The validity of plaintiffs' copyrights in the Marling Menu-Master for Spain and the Marling Menu-Master for Germany is well established on this record and also uncontested.  Copying may be shown by proof that defendant had access to plaintiffs' works and by proof that defendant's infringing works are substantially similar to plaintiffs'work.  Id., pp. 13-5 ff.  Access of Ellison to the Marling book is here uncontested, since defendant admitted access in his response to plaintiffs' request for admission.  I find and rule that the ordinary user of the books here in question can readily perceive the substantial similarity both in editorial selection and in translation that is set forth in the Court's finding of fact above.  Plaintiffs' initial claim is that defendant has infringed their copyrights in their Spanish and German books by copying their editorial selection   work in his Spanish and German books respectively.  In   17 U.S.C.  § 101, a compilation is defined as

"A work formed by the collection and assembling of pre-existing materials or of data that are selected, coordinated, or arranged in such a way that the resulting work as a whole constitutes an original work of authorship."

 Under 17 U.S.C.  § 103(a), "the subject matter of copyright * * * includes compilations * * *"
A long line of cases has recognized  the right of the compilation author to protection under the copyright law for his original selection, combination or arrangement of various forms of public domain materials.  See, e.g., Schroeder v. William Morrow & Co., 566 F.2d 3, 198 USPQ 143 (7th Cir. 1977) (rival gardening directories); Adventures in Good Eating, Inc., v. Best Places to Eat, Inc., 131 F.2d 809 (7th Cir. 1972) (restaurant guides); College Entrance Book Co., Inc. v. Amsco Book Co., Inc., 119 F.2d 874, 49 USPQ 517 (2d Cir. 1941) (French language examination word lists); Leon v. Pacific Telephone and Telegraph Co., 91 F.2d 484, 34 USPQ 237 (9th Cir. 1937) (telephone directories); Hartfield v. Peterson, 91 F.2d 998, 28 USPQ 142 (2d Cir. 1937) (cable and telegraphic   code books); W.H. Anderson Co. v. Baldwin Law Publishing Co., 27 F.2d 82 (6th Cir. 1928) (rival publications of an annotated statute); Jeweler's Circular Publishing Co., 281 F. 82 (2d Cir. 1922) (directory of trademarks and tradenames used by jewelers); Frank Shepard Co. v. Zachary P. Taylor Publishing Co., 193 F. 991 (2d Cir. 1912) (legal citation systems); List Publishing Co. v. Keller, 30 F. 772 (S.D. N.Y.) (directories of fashionable New Yorkers); Lawrence v. Dana, 15 Fed. Cases 26, Case No. 8, 136 (D. Mass. 1869) (annotations to legal treatise).  These cases rest upon the rationale that the author is entitled to copyright protection for the originality of his selection, arrangement and organization of public domain materials, and that one should not freely reap the benefit of another's industry in selecting and organizing public domain facts.  As the Court stated in Orgel v. Clark Boardman Co., 301 F.2d 119, 120, 133 USPQ 94, 95 (2d Cir. 1962) cert. denied 371 U.S. 817, 135 USPQ 502 (1962): "Appropriation  of the fruits of another's labor and skill in order to publish a rival work without the expenditure of the time and effort required for independently arrived at results is   copyright infringement."
Based on the evidence in this case, including the books in question, the documentary evidence and the more persuasive testimony, I rule that Ellison appropriated the Marlings' editorial selection work in large part in order to publish rival menu translators. Thus, as discussed above, of 59 Spanish menu terms for food courses in The Marling Menu-Master for Spain culled by the Marlings from at least 113 such terms found on Spanish menus, Ellison utilized 54 in Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader, and included no   other food course terms.  Similarly, the Marlings included 56 out of at least 168 food course terms found on German Menus in The Marling Menu- Master for Germany.  Ellison took 53 of these and listed no others in Ellison's German Menu Reader.  As the Court stated, in Jeweler's Circular Publishing Co. v. Keystone Publishing Co., supra, 281 F. at 94, "it is almost impossible to conceive of two individuals working independently and arriving at practically the same classification."
I also rule, based on the cogent and credible evidence before me, that Ellison unlawfully copied the Marlings' editorial selection work in the choice of dishes and variations in   preparations to be included.  The Marlings painstaking editorial selection of dishes and preparations to be included in The Marling Menu Master for Spain, has been copied in Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader for almost all of the basic Spanish dishes. Thus Ellison takes eight Marling entries for "Entremeses," fourteen of fourteen Marling entries for "Cerdo," eight of eight Marling entries for "Rinones," twenty-two of twenty-three Marling entries for "Consome," and numerous other entries, as noted in the Court's findings above.  Similar copying of the editorial selection work that is the heart of a compilation is evidenced in Ellison's extensive borrowings from The Marling Menu-Master for Germany, for use in Ellison's German Menu Reader.  Of 1800 entries in The Marling Menu-Master for Germany, Ellison replicates almost 1100, or almost 60% of the Marlings selections, in his German book.  Similarly, of 1900 entries in The Marling Menu-Master for Spain, Ellison has over 1325, or approximately 70% of the Marlings choices for entries.
These substantial borrowings show, and this Court rules, that Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader copied the very essence of the authors' work from The Marling Menu-Master   for Spain and that Ellison's German Menu Reader copied the very essence of the author's work from The Marling Menu-Master for Germany.  Ellison's substantial copying of the Marlings' original selections of food course terms and individual entries amounts to "[a]appropriation of the fruits of another's labor and skill in order to publish a rival work without the expenditure of the time and effort required for independently arrived results [and] is [therefore] copyright infringement." Schroder v. William Morrow & Co., supra, 566 F.2d at 6, 198 USPQ at 146; Adventures in Good Eating, Inc. v. Best Places to Eat, Inc., supra, College Entrance Book Co., Inc. v. Amsco Book Co., Inc., supra; List Publishing Co. v. Keller, supra.
Plaintiffs next contend that defendant has infringed their copyrights in their Spanish and German books by copying their original translations in his Spanish and German books respectively.   The copyright law gives explicit protection to translations from a foreign language into English.  17 U.S.C.  §§ 101, 103(a); Toksvig v. Bruce Publishing Co., 181 F.2d 664, 85 USPQ 339 (7th Cir. 1950), even where the transition is of the list of relatively simply, basic   terms.  College Entrance Book Co., Inc. v. Amsco Book Co., Inc., 119 F.2d 876, 49 USPQ (2d Cir. 1941) (French word list for language examination).  In the College Entrance Book Co. case the Court noted that plaintiff employed "quite a considerable amount [of originality] in its choice of translations appropriate for the purpose." Id. at 876.
Successful translations of hundreds of difficult and sometimes exotic Spanish and German menu terms at issue in the instant litigation requires experience with the relevant cuisine and restaurants, knowledge of the foreign language in question and of food-handling techniques in that country, careful thought and the exercise of judgment. The Marlings applied skill and effort to produce carefully tailored, original translations in their books.  William Marling testified in some detail about the time, research and travel invested in the production of the books in question.  He and his wife visited 50 cities and towns in Germany; 46 in Spain; they visited five to six hundred restaurants; consulted experts, cookbooks and encylopedia for reference and in Germany obtained from two to three hundred menus. Mr. Marling testified more would have been   collected but were not because file cards and notebooks were used to store information.  Some of the notebooks were available at trial.  In Spain, William Marling conferred with Manuel Gorce, a teacher at Waiters School, studied butchering and talked with waiters, chefs and others knowledgeable in the food dissemination business.  I have little doubt that the Marlings in a quite professional way, exercised ingenuity and judgment in developing the works involved here.  I rule that Ellison's verbatim and near-verbatim replications of hundreds of the Marlings' original translations from The Marling Menu- Master for Spain and The Marling Menu-Master for Germany in his Spanish and German books respectively constitute copyright infringement.
"It may be added that one of the most significant evidences of infringement exists frequently in the defendants' volumes, namely, the copying of errors made by" the Marlings   .  Callaghan v. Myers, 128 U.S. 617, 662 (1888). Adventures in Good Eating, Inc., v. Good Places to Eat, Inc., 131 F.2d 809, 811-812 (7th Cir. 1942); Jewelers' Circular Publishing Co., Inc. v. Keystone Publishing Co., 281 F.82 95 (2d Cir. 1922).  As the Court stated in Frank Shephard   Co. v. Zachary P. Taylor Publishing Co., 193 F. 991, 993, (2d Cir. 1912):

"The inference from the unfair use of the complainant's work in these instances of erroneous citations in that it was similarly used as to the correct citations to an extent that cannot be determined."

Here Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader replicates errors in The Marling Menu-Master for Spain and Ellison's German Menu Reader copies errors in The Marling Menu-Master for Germany.  As already suggested, the evidence was particularly interesting in this regard.  Note also the use of taburette (Marling p. 95; Ellison p. 67).  William Marling got this term from Mr. Garces and found it in only one restaurant. It was not found in any reference books.  William Marling testified as to other "finds" in obscure a Spanish areas, which were used by Mr. Ellison.  (See p. 35, Marling and p. 32, Ellison with reference to Huevas Cubanana; Marling, p. 99 and Ellison, p. 72 regarding villa godia de vaca).  I conclude that Ellison's near verbatim reproduction of hundreds of original translations from the Marlings' books, including a few erroneous translations, constitutes unlawful infringement of the Marlings' copyrights. 17   U.S.C.  §§ 101, 103(a); Toksvig v. Bruce Publishing Co., supra; College Entrance Book Co., Inc., v. Amsco Book Co., Inc., supra.
Defendant contended at the trial that he did not copy from the Marlings in the production of his Spanish, German and Swiss books.  As noted above, I have found that insufficient evidence was presented to establish that Ellison's Swiss Menu Reader was copied from The Marling Menu-Master for Germany.  I have found, as a factual conclusion, however, and I so rule, that Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader was copied form The Marling Menu-Master for Spain and bears a substantial similarity to the Marling book.  I have further found, and I rule, again, contrary to defendant's contention, that Ellison's German Menu Reader is in substantial part copied from The Marling Menu- Master for Germany and bears a substantial similarity to the Marling book.  Defendant did not attempt to assert a fair-use defense with respect to the substantial similarity of his Spanish and German books to the Marlings' Spanish and German books respectively, with respect to both editorial selection and translation. In any event, I find and rule on the facts before me that a fair use defense is   unavailable to defendant Ellison.
Four factors are set forth in the statute, 17 U.S.C.  § 197, for evaluation of fair-use defenses, and defendant Ellison fails to satisfy any one of them.  The clear purpose of his menu readers was to make a profit.  Indeed, Ellison testified on cross examination that he lied to his employees about the purpose of the work they were doing, because he wanted to keep the idea a secret. The nature of the works in question is also significant here.  It is noted above in my findings of fact, that the menu translators have characteristics of a compilation or collection of facts, as to which relatively greater license to use portions of a copyrighted work will be permitted.  However, as is also noted in my findings of fact, the menu translators also have a large translation component, which involves a high degree of originality, inventiveness and creativity.  As to creative and inventive works, fair use is severely restricted.  Since the evidence shows that Ellison copied literally from the Marling's translation work in both his Spanish and German books, he has gone well beyond the concept of fair use.  The third factor identified by the statute is the   "amount and substantiality of the portion used in relation to the copyrighted work as a whole." In Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader, both with respect to editorial selection work and with respect to translation, the copying from The Marling Menu-Master for Spain is substantial.  In Ellison's German Menu Reader, both with respect to editorial selection and with respect to translation, the amount of material copied from The Marling Menu Master for Germany is substantial.  Hence, I rule that Ellison has engaged in copyright infringement and may not rely on the fair-use defense.  Finally with respect to the fourth factor mentioned in the statute -- "the effect of the use upon the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work" -- I find that the Ellison books were aimed at the identical market as the Marling books.  Both sets of books were aimed at the American tourist market, either here or abroad; both were distributed on a national basis, though plaintiffs' books were largely directed to the American market in Europe.  There may, however, have been some impact on the plaintiffs' market.
For all of these reasons, I rule that this case is plainly distinguishable from the case of   New York Times Co. v. Roxbury Data Interface, Inc., 434 F.Supp. 217, 194 USPQ 371 (D.N.Y. 1977), where a fair-use defense was upheld.  In that case defendant had produced a name index to the New York Times Index.  There, unlike here, the work in question was strictly a compilation, defendant provided a   public serve in addition to seeking a profit, the amount of materials of plaintiff's that were used was small and the defendant's work did not compete at all with customers of plaintiff's work.  Indeed, the Court found that the defendant's work may well increase business for the plaintiff, since defendant's work was useless to someone who did not own the plaintiff's work.  Here, by way of contrast, Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader and Ellison's German Menu Reader were indirect competition with The Marling Menu Master for Spain and The Marling Menu Master for Germany, respectively, copied both the Marlings' compilation efforts and their original and creative translation efforts and the copying was substantial.  I rule and conclude that Ellison is liable for copyright infringement.
An appropriate remedy is the next matter requiring discussion.   The copyright law provides that the copyright owner may obtain an injunction against infringement. 17 U.S.C.  § 502(b).  I rule that plaintiffs are entitled to a permanent injunction restraining defendant from further infringement of their copyrights.  I further rule that plaintiffs are entitled to an order which requires the defendant to deliver to this Court for destruction any copies of Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader and Ellison's German Menu Reader that the defendant presently has in his possession or under his control, to prevent their further dissemination into commerce.  I further rule that plaintiffs are entitled to an order requiring defendant to notify all retail outlets having copies of his work on consignment that they must be returned to him for deliver to this Court or destroyed.
Plaintiffs are entitled to recover from a copyright infringer both (a) the actual damages suffered by the copyright owner and (b) the infringer's profits.    17 U.S.C.  § 504(a)(1).In establishing the infringer's profits, plaintiffs need prove only the infringer's gross revenue and the defendant has the burden of proving any deduction from this amount.  17 U.S.C.  § 504(b).  Defendant has himself admitted gross sales of 4,000 of Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader and 4,000 of Ellison's German Menu Reader, with a gross profit margin of approximately 50 per each book. The defendant testified however that he had lost between $50,000.00 and $60,000.00 dollars in this venture.  No specific allocation of this total loss was directed to a particular menu book.
At any time before a final judgment, the plaintiffs may elect to recover statutory damages.  17 U.S.C.  § 504(c)(1). For each copyrighted work that is infringed, the plaintiffs are entitled, under ordinary circumstances, to recover not less than $250.00 or more than $10,000.00.  Id.  Where, as here, two copyrighted works are infringed, these limits are multiplied by two.  Id.  See Also H.R. No. 94-1476, 94th Cong., 2 Sess., on S.22 (the Copyright act of 1976),

page 12 (item 3), reprinted as Appendix 4 in 4 Nimmer On Copyright App. 40135 -- 4-136.  Prior copyright law provides a useful   guide in awarding statutory damages in usual circumstances: "$1 for every infringing copy made or sold by or found in the possession of the infringer or his agents or employees." 27 U.S.C.  § 101(b), as in effect prior to enactment of the Copyright Act of 1976, reproduced at 4 Nimmer On Copyright App. 6-19.  Even under prior law, however, the one dollar per copy measure could be increased or decreased by a court in its discretion.  E.g., Fleischer Studios, Inc., v. Freundlich, 14 F. Supp. 401, 30 USPQ 125 (S.D.N.Y. 1936).
Ellison has admitted access to plaintiffs' works at the time his infringing works were prepared.  Paragraph 5.7 of Defendant's Pre-Trial Stipulation; Response dated November 7, 1979, to Plaintiffs' Request for Admissions, Nos. 1 through 7, dated October 15, 1979.  Ellison, a lawyer, "instructed" his staff "not to copy." Ellison disposition, p. 7,   lines 9-18 (lawyer), pp. 15-16, 63-64 (copyright).  Under these circumstances, this Court finds that Ellison engaged in substantial copying, that he knew or should have known of such copying and that his infringement is thus willful.
The plaintiffs have elected to accept statutory damages.  The gross profit above described may be used as a guide. There was no evidence presented by either side as to the defendant's "net" profit except for his testimony that he lost between fifty and sixty thousand dollars.  This type of case is not, and this was not, easy to determine.  The questions presented concerned the use of words many of which must necessarily be used by one writing on the subjects in question.  Yet, plaintiffs presented a persuasive, indeed compelling case, meeting in my opinion, their burden and justifying relief.  On damages, however, the evidence, almost necessarily, was wanting and I find little upon which to award that plaintiffs seeks, except the number of defendants' books sold.  This does afford some basis upon which an award can be fashioned.  It can properly be argued that the plaintiff should have actual damages of $4,000, based   on the gross profit margin of 50 per copy of defendant's books.
In considering actual damages, however, I have concern about the adequacy of the proof in view of the defendant's testimony (though wholly unsupported by documentation) that he lost considerable money in his venture.  His testimony is unrefuted.
In any event, plaintiffs have elected to recover statutory damages.  Within the limits provided by applicable law, the Court must award such damages as appear to be just and fair.  Under the circumstances of this case, the Court finds that the plaintiffs are entitled to $4,000.00 ($2,000.00 for each violation).
For the foregoing reasons, it is therefore,

Ordred and adjudged that defendant is hereby permanently enjoined from infringing in any manner the plaintiffs' copyrights in the Marling Menu-Master for Spain and The Marling Menu-Master for Germany, and from publishing, selling, marketing, or otherwise disposing of copies of Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader and Ellison's German Menu Reader.  It is further

Ordered that defendant deliver up to this Court for destruction all copies of Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader and Ellison's German Menu Reader in his possession or under his control.  It is further,

Ordered that defendant notify all retail outlets who may have copies of Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader and Ellison's German Menu Reader   on consignment that they must   return same to him for delivery to this Court for destruction.  It is further,
ordered that defendant deliver up to this Court for destruction all plates, molds, matrices, masters, tapes, film negatives or other articles by means of which copies of Ellison's Spanish Menu Reader or Ellison's German Menu Reader may be reproduced.  It is further

Ordered that plaintiffs, Wiliam E. and Clare F. Marling have and recover of and from defendant, Al Ellison, the sum of Four Thousand Dollars ($4,000.00), statutory damages, plus their costs herein expended.  It is further,

Ordered that plaintiffs are entitled to the costs of suit and to a reasonable attorney's fee for the services of their attorneys.  It is further,

CONNER, D.J.:

Plaintiff Pret-A-Printee, Ltd. ("Pret-A-Printee") seeks damages, injunctive relief and attorney's fees against defendants Allton Knitting Mills ("Allton"), Holland Fabrics, Inc. ("Holland") and Martin Levine ("Levine") for the alleged infringement of plaintiff's copyrighted fabric design.  Both plaintiff and defendant corporations are textile converters who process greige goods into printed fabrics for resale to garment manufacturers.  Allton and Holland share the same business premises and both corporations are controlled by Levine, who is the sole officer, director and shareholder of each.  Pret-A-Printee claims that defendants have duplicated and marketed its Pattern No. 5012.  The case was tried by the Court without a jury; the following opinion incorporates the Court's findings of fact and conclusions of law pursuant to Rule 52, F.R.Civ.P.
Liability

 In order to prove   infringement of a copyright, a plaintiff must show ownership of a valid copyright and copying by the defendant.  Novelty Textile Mills v. Joan Fabrics Corp., 558 F.2d 1090, 1092 (2d Cir. 1977). At trial, Pret-A-Printee introduced Certificate of Copyright Registration No. VA 10-773, which was obtained for Pattern No. 5012 on November 6, 1978.  This certificate constitutes prima facie evidence of ownership and validity of the copyright, see id. at n.1, and in the absence of contrary evidence the Court must presume that the ownership and validity requirements are satisfied.  See Id. In the present case, defendants offered no evidence denying the ownership or validity of the copyright.  Moreover, plaintiff introduced the testimony of its former head stylist, who described the process by which Pattern No. 5012 was created from an original, purchased sketch by putting the sketch into a repeat design suitable for printing of a textile fabric. This evidence further supports the conclusion that plaintiff has a valid copyright on Pattern No. 5012 since the adaptation of the original artwork of another to form a repeat design constitutes the necessary originality.  See Soptra Fabrics Corp. v.   Stafford Knitting Mills, Inc., 490 F.2d 1092, 1094 (2d Cir. 1974).
In addition to showing ownership of a valid copyright, plaintiff must also establish copying by defendants. Copying is generally proven by showing: (1) that the defendant had access to the plaintiff's design and (2) that the defendant's design is substantially similar to that of the plaintiff.  See Novelty Textile Mills, supra, 558 F.2d at 1092.
In this case, there is no question that defendants had access to Pret-A-Printee's Pattern No. 5012.  The pattern was the subject of an earlier lawsuit between the parties.  See Pret-A-Printee, Ltd. v. Holland Fabrics, Inc., Martin Levine, et al., 79 Civ. 704 (WCC).  This prior lawsuit was commenced in 1979 and a stipulation of settlement and discontinuance, containing a permanent injunction, was entered on April 18, 1980.  In the present case, Levine testified that the allegedly infringing design, Pattern No. 201, was created in 1980.  Clearly, by 1980 defendants were aware of plaintiff's Pattern No. 5012 by virtue of the earlier suit.
The test for "substantial similarity" is whether an ordinary observer would regard the aesthetic appeal of the two designs as the same.    In Peter Pan Fabrics, Inc. v. Martin Weiner Corp., 274 F.2d 487 (2d Cir. 1960), the court articulated the following standard:

In the case of designs, which are addressed to the aesthetic sensibilities of an observer, the test is, if possible, even more intangible.  No one disputes that the copyright extends beyond a photographic reproduction of the design, but one cannot say how far an imitator must depart from an undeviating reproduction to escape infringement. In deciding that question one should consider the uses for which the design is intended, especially the scrutiny that observers will give to it as used.  In the case at bar we must try to estimate how far its overall appearance will determine its aesthetic appeal when the cloth is made into a garment.  Both designs have the same general color, and the arches, scrolls, rows of symbols, etc. on one resemble those on the other though they are not identical. Moreover, the patterns in which these figures are distributed to make up the design as a whole are not identical. However, the ordinary observer, unless he set out to detect the disparities, would be disposed to overlook them, and regard their aesthetic appeal as the   same.  That is enough; and indeed, it is all that can be said, unless protection against infringement is to be denied because of variants irrelevant to the purpose for which the design is intended.


Id. at 489. See also Malden Mills, Inc. v. Regency Mills, Inc., 626 F.2d 1112 (2d Cir. 1980) (where designs reflect like subject matter, style of representation, shading, composition and relative size and place of components, designs are substantially similar); Soptra Fabrics Corp. v. Stafford Knitting Mills, Inc., 490 F.2d 1092 (2d Cir. 1974) (uses for which designs are intended important factor in considering substantial similarity; where designs to be used in dresses small differences apparent under courtroom scrutiny do not negate substantial similarity).
In the present case, examination of Pret-A-Printee's Pattern No. 5012, see Trial Exhibit 19, with defendants' Pattern No. 201, see Trial Exhibit 20, reveals the obvious similarity of their overall effect.  Both designs are floral prints on a black background with a color combination which emphasizes both wine and brown stems, and violet buds.  In addition, the placement and size of the vines, leaves and flowers are substantially   duplicated in the two designs.  The identical placement of the floral components is highlighted by Trial Exhibit 21, which is an acetate drawing of each of the two designs.  The exhibit demonstrates that each element of Pattern No. 5012 has a match in Pattern No. 201.
As illustrated by Exhibits 19 and 20, there are certain apparent differences in the two designs.  For instance, in plaintiff's design, the blossoms of the large flowers are oriented so that one side is toward the viewer while the corresponding blossoms in Pattern No. 201 are turned to face the viewer.  In addition, the designs on the individual flower petals differ as do the leaves on the vines. While these features ensure that the patterns are not identical, they do not negate the substantial similarity of the designs.  The virtually identical placement of the flowers, stems, buds and vines, together with the comparable color schemes, create an impression of similarity that cannot be ignored.
At trial, defendants offered evidence in support of their claim that Pattern No. 201 was an independent creation. Levine testified that in 1979 he purchased in Italy a sketch that became the basis for Pattern No. 201.  This  testimony is suspect for several reasons.  First, the sketch, which was marked as Exhibit A, bears scant resemblance to Pattern No. 201.  The sketch is merely a drawing of flowers, stems and leaves in no particular pattern and without vines. Second, the flowers in the sketch are not the same shape, size or coloring as the main flowers in Pattern No. 201.  Third, although Levine testified that he purchased the sketch in 1979, defendants did not produce the design on fabric until May of 1981, after plaintiff had established a market for its pattern.  Fourth, defendants' past record of copyright infringement indicates a practice of copying despite claims of independent creation. Two of the actions resulted in the award of statutory damages against defendants and in all cases permanent injunctions were granted either as a part of a settlement or after trial. Novelty Textile   Mills, supra, 558 F.2d at 1092 n.2. Damages

Pret-A-Printee seeks injunctive relief, statutory damages in the sum of $50,000, costs and attorney's fees.  Section 502 of Title 17 U.S.C. provides the remedy of a permanent injunction to prevent or restrain infringement of a copyright. That injunction will continue in effect, with the addition of defendant Allton Mills.
As for monetary damages, Pret-A-Printee has elected statutory damages under 17 U.S.C.  § 504(c) (1978).  HN4[

] This section provides, inter alia, that the court in its discretion may award up to $50,000 in statutory damages where it finds that the violation was willful. See 17 U.S.C.  § 504(c) (2).  If the infringement is not judged to have been willful, the court may award damages of between $250 and $10,000.See id. Section 504(c) (1).
An award of statutory damages is appropriate where the measure of actual damages is difficult to ascertain.  See Peter Pan Fabrics v. Jobela Fabrics, Inc., 329 F.2d 194, 196 (2d Cir. 1964). Moreover, "[t]he broad discretionary power given the   courts to make such an award serves the dual purposes of the Copyright Act: to compensate copyright owners and to provide a deterrent to would-be infringers." Lauratex Textiles Corp. v. Allton Knitting Mills, 519 F. Supp. 730, 733 (S.D.N.Y. 1981), citing Lottie Joplin Thomas Trust v. Crown Publishers, 592 F.2d 651 (2d Cir. 1978).
I find that statutory damages should be awarded in this case both because actual damages are difficult to measure, see Peter Pan Fabrics v. Jobela Fabrics, Inc., 329 F.2d 194, 196 (2d Cir. 1964), and because defendants willfully copied plaintiff's design.  Levine testified that he purchased the original sketch for the design in 1979.  He did not produce the design or fabric, however, until May of 1981, after plaintiff had already established a market for the design and after he had consented to a permanent injunction in settlement of Pret-A-Printee's earlier action against him in connection with Pattern No. 5012.  Moreover, Levine immediately sold the fabric to Royal Green, which had previously been purchasing Pattern No. 5012 from plaintiff.  These actions, given Levine's clear knowledge of plaintiff's copyright and the similarity of the patterns, compel   a finding of willfulness.  Given also the fact that Levine and his corporations have been repeatedly pursued in court for the very kind of violation at issue here, the almost unavoidable inference is that Levine has built a business based on deliberate infringement of the copyrights of other converters.  Consequently, an award of statutory damages is appropriate as a deterrent. See Lauratex Textile Corp. v. Allton Knitting Mills and Martin Levine, 517 F. Supp. 900, 903-04 (S.D.N.Y. 1981).
Turning to the amount of the statutory damages, plaintiff argues that the maximum award of $50,000 is necessary in this case to compensate it and to deter defendants.  Pret-A-Printee calculates that the compensatory element of the award alone should be set at $45,112.61.  Plaintiff arrives at this figure by estimating its lost profits at $13,234.61 and defendants' profits at $31,878.  Thus, plaintiff argues that $45,112.61 is necessary to compensate it and that the maximum should be awarded in an effort to deter defendants from future violations.
The Court concludes that plaintiff's base figure of $45,112.61 is overstated.  Actual damages to the copyright owner usually are calculated by assessing   lost profits.  Attempting to estimate what sales plaintiff would have made in the absence of an infringement, however, is inherently speculative.  In the present case, the parties have stipulated that defendant Allton Mills sold 19,320.6 yards of Pattern No. 201 to two customers, Royal Green, Ltd. and Canasta Frocks, Inc.  Plaintiff contends that it should be credited for those sales and awarded its profit margin ($.685 a yard) for a total of $13,234.61.  This computation of plaintiff's actual loss is somewhat misleading, since defendants sold their fabric at $1.65 a yard while plaintiff sold its fabric at $2.025 a yard. Thus, defendants' lower price might have resulted in greater sales than plaintiff could have obtained at its higher price.
Actual damages can also be estimated by computing defendants' profits and using that as an approximate measure of plaintiff's damages.  The parties stipulated that defendant Allton Mills received $31,878 in gross revenue from the two sales.  However, there was no evidence as to defendants' costs and expenses related to these sales.  As a result, it is not possible to determine defendants' profits with any degree of certainty.
After considering the evidence of plaintiff's loss and defendants' willful infringement, I conclude that statutory damages should be awarded in the sum of $30,000.  Although defendants' past record normally would suggest that a higher sum would be appropriate in an effort to deter future violations, it seems that defendants have not been involved in any new litigation, other than this suit, since 1980.  Accordingly, it appears to the Court that defendants may be feeling the effects of previous statutory damages awards and that the maximum award is not warranted here.
Pret-A-Printee also seeks recovery of its costs and attorney's fees as allowed by 17 U.S.C.  § 505 (1978).Defendants have not submitted any papers in opposition to plaintiff's motion and the Court concludes that such an award is justified.   The determination of the actual amount of fees to be awarded involves a number of factors, including the amount of time spent on the case, the amount of work necessary, the skill employed, the monetary amount at stake and the result achieved.  See Orgel v. Clark Boardman Co., 301 F.2d 119, 122 (2d Cir.), cert. denied, 371 U.S. 817 (1962). In the present case, plaintiff's counsel   has submitted his affidavit setting forth his hours spent on various stages of the litigation.  In total, plaintiff seeks to recover for 102 hours of work at $100 an hour.  Having reviewed counsel's affidavit and having no opposition from defendants, I
find that the affidavit establishes services in the amount of $10,200, which I find reasonable and accordingly award together with statutory costs.
In addition to the relief discussed above, Pret-A-Printee also seeks to have a magistrate appointed to determine its damages in the previous action, 79 Civ. 704 (WCC).  The final stipulation of settlement and discontinuance in that case provides in part:

4.  In the event that any of the defendants shall violate any of the terms hereof, or in the event that any representation   herein shall be false, plaintiff shall be relieved of its agreement hereunder as to such defendant and shall be entitled, upon five (5) days notice served upon such defendant or their attorneys of record herein, to apply for and obtain an order from this Court for the appointment of a Master to fix damages, if any, as set forth in the complaint herein, and such violating defendant hereby consents to the entry of such order.

The order was signed by defendant Holland Fabrics, Inc. and Martin Levine in his personal capacity.
Defendants concede that the prior lawsuit was based on plaintiff's Pattern No. 5012 but argue that because the infringing patterns in the two cases are different, plaintiff cannot establish a causal connection.  That argument is meritless.  By marketing Pattern No. 201, defendants Levine and Holland Fabrics violated the permanent injunction restraining them from infringing plaintiff's copyright on Pattern No. 5012.  That defendants used a different pattern on the second occasion or that time elapsed between settlement of the first case and the second infringement does not alter the situation.  Levine agreed to a determination of damages from the first suit if   the injunction were violated and that agreement forecloses argument now.  Accordingly, a magistrate will be appointed to determine the damages, if any, arising from the first action.

Britannica Educational Corp. v. Crooks, supra at 1171. A contributory infringer is one who, with knowledge of the infringing activity, induces, causes or materially contributes to the infringing conduct of another.  Id. at 1162. In this respect,

a defendant's mistake as to the legal consequences of his actions does not constitute an excuse for an infringement. It is only necessary that a copyright defendant have knowledge of the infringing activity.

While the end result of this calculation is to award plaintiff judgment for defendants' gtross sales, this award is provided for by statute, see 17 US.C.  § 504(b). Carousel Handbags, 592 F.2d 126, 130 (2d Cir. 1979).   Additionally, as noted by Magistrate Sinclair, there is a very real possibility that defendants made other sales of the infringing fabric than plaintiff was able to establish.  Accordingly, the Court concludes that the award of damages for defendants' gross sales is proper.
Before Magistrate sinclair, plaintiff also sought recovery of "contempt" damages based upon defendants' violation of the permanent injunction. The Magistrate, however, properly denied this request on the ground that the $30,000 in statutory damages awarded by this Court in the September 16 Opinion and Order afforded an adequate remedy. Since the 1981 sales have already been covered through the award of statutory damages, there is no need to assess further damages for contempt.

A "work made for hire" is defined in section 101 of the Act in two ways. Mr.    Rodack for MSR did more, however, than originate the idea for the wagons.He provided explicit and detailed instructions for their manufacture.These instructions constituted the necessary expression of the idea for the wagons and were entitled to copyright protection.  Mr. Rodack provided Richard Viola with specifications for drawings of the Coca-Cola logo which was to be incorporated on the Coke wagon. Neither Mr. Viola nor the Taiwanese manufacturer of the wagons had the slightest discretion to change the specifications as set forth by Mr. Rodack or to provide any creativity to the products.  The Telex communications between Mr. Rodack and his agent Mr. Chang (Ex. P-15 & P-20) evidence that Mr. Rodack's approval was needed for any modification of his original specifications.  Mr. Viola and the Taiwanese manufacturer contributed no "originality" to the works and it is originality which is protected by a copyright.  Id.

Even though Mr. Viola was not an employee of MSR or Mr. Rodack in the usual sense of the word, that which he designed was under the complete control and   direction of Mr. Rodack.
