Video Views, Inc., the appellant and cross-appellee, is a corporation engaged in the business of sub-licensing "adult films" for video arcade exhibition on the premises of "adult entertainment businesses." The appellees and cross-appellants (who will be referred to collectively as "Studio 21") are Studio 21, Ltd.,    and its principal shareholder, Joseph Sclafani.
Video Views brought this action under the Copyright Act of 1976, 17 U.S.C. § 101 et seq., alleging that Studio 21 had been infringing its exclusive right to perform certain adult films publicly. After a six-day trial, the jury returned a verdict finding that Studio 21 had willfully infringed Video Views' copyrights in two of the seven adult films involved in the action. The district court granted Studio 21's motion for a judgment notwithstanding the verdict on the issue of willfulness, but awarded Video Views statutory damages in the amount of $ 5,000 for each infringement. Both parties raise a number of issues on their respective appeal and cross-appeal. We affirm.
I.
Video Views is engaged solely in the business of licensing what have come to be known as "adult films" for display in video arcades at "adult entertainment businesses," enterprises commonly referred to as "adult book stores." Video Views does not create adult films; it enters into sub-licensing agreements with adult book stores, such as Studio 21, which provide their customers with the opportunity to view adult films in viewing rooms located on premises. Video    Views must first obtain from the respective copyright owners the exclusive right to perform those films publicly in video arcades. See 17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 106(4). Video Views obtains that particular strand in the bundle of property rights designated by the Copyright Act by entering into licensing agreements with the respective copyright owners (typically the producers of the films). In effect, the copyright owners grant Video Views a limited exclusive right to sub-license the video arcade exhibition of particular adult films, in video cassette format, on business premises.
Studio 21 operates an "adult entertainment business" in Addison, Illinois. It provides video facilities of the type that Video Views would ordinarily sub-license. During the time period relevant to this action, Joseph Sclafani was the owner of all shares in Studio 21. He served as its president, and, along with his wife, Theresa, discharged other responsibilities vital to the operation of Studio 21, such as ordering goods, bookkeeping, and making personal decisions. Studio 21 built six "video arcade booths" on its premises wherein customers view adult films (such as those that had been licensed to Video Views)    by the use of video arcade equipment operated by tokens. Customers could purchase tokens, for one dollar each, which would entitle them to view five minutes of selected adult films. At the time the customers purchase the tokens, they also noted the responsible Studio 21 employee of the film they would like to view. Studio 21 has a large inventory of these films, which are also available for home rental or purchase. Apparently, Studio 21 is aware of the scope of the copyright laws: on occasion, it learns from   the owner of the exclusive public performance right that it has no authority to perform a particular video cassette in its video booths. As to such films, Studio 21 places a prominent "for sale or rental only" sticker on the video cassette to alert its employees. The alternative would be for Studio 21 to enter into a sub-licensing agreement to acquire that aspect of the public performance right from its owner.
When Video Views came to suspect that Studio 21 was providing its customers with the opportunity to view on its premises films that had been licensed to Video Views, Jerry Greenberger, Video Views' president, approached Mr. Sclafani, seeking to enter into a sub-licensing agreement   with Studio 21. Studio 21 declined to do so. The filing of this action followed, initially resulting in the entry of a preliminary injunction barring Studio 21 from infringing Video Views' exclusive rights.
At trial, Video Views sought money damages for Studio 21's alleged willful infringement of the following films: Nothing to Hide, Baby Cakes, Black on White, Women in Love, Chocolate Candy, Doctor Desire, [***1755]  and Our Major is Sex. It sought statutory damages, an option available to it under the Copyright Act, see 17 U.S.C. § 504(c), instead of electing to prove and recover actual damages and Studio 21's profits, see 17 U.S.C. § 504(b). It also made a motion to strike Studio 21's demand for a jury trial, which was denied. The issues of liability and willfulness were tried to a jury. During the trial, William Mahr, a private investigator hired by Video Views, testified that he had viewed the films Nothing to Hide and Baby Cakes in a video arcade booth at Studio 21 on April 12, 1984. Mr. Greenberger also testified that he had visited Studio 21 on April 5, 1985, when he purchased 35-40 tokens and viewed the other five films involved in this action (coincidentally,    the ones that Mr. Mahr had not). Although Theresa Sclafani testified that she saw Mr. Greenberger at Studio 21, another Studio 21 employee, Noble Butler, testified that he had been working that day but that he had never seen anyone purchase that many tokens.
The jury found that Studio 21 had willfully infringed the films Nothing to Hide and Baby Cakes, but had not infringed the other five films. Based upon the jury verdict, the district court assessed statutory damages pursuant to § 504(c)(1) ($ 5,000 per infringement) and increased statutory damages pursuant to § 504(c)(2) ($ 10,000 per

925 F.2d 1010, *1012; 1991 U.S. App. LEXIS 1711, **2; 17 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1753, ***1754

infringement). The court ordered the entry of judgment in the total amount of $ 30,000. However, upon Studio 21's motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict, the district court found the jury's verdict on the issue of willfulness to be unsupported by the evidence and vacated the award of any increased statutory damages. The district court also concluded that neither party had "prevailed" and declined to award either litigant costs and attorney's fees. This appeal followed.
II.
Section 504  of the Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. § 504, provides the copyright owner with an election  between two forms of monetary recovery from a copyright infringer.  As in ordinary tort cases, the copyright owner is entitled to prove and recover its actual damages and profits, pursuant to § 504(b). In addition, § 504(c) grants an alternative form of recovery available to the copyright owner:

 (1) Except as provided by clause (2) of this subsection, the copyright owner may elect, at any time before final judgment is rendered, to recover, instead of actual damages and profits, an award of statutory damages for all infringements involved in the action, with respect to any one work, for which any infringer is liable individually, or for which any two or more infringers are liable jointly and severally, in a sum not less than $ 250 [$ 500] or more than $ 10,000 [$ 20,000] as the court considers just. . . .

(2) In a case where the copyright owner sustains the burden of proving, and the court finds, that infringement was committed willfully, the court in its discretion may increase the award of statutory damages to a sum of not more than    $ 50,000 [$ 100,000]. In a case where the infringer sustains the burden of proving, and the court finds, that such infringer was not aware of and had    no reason to believe that his or her acts constituted an infringement of copyright, the court it [sic] its discretion may reduce the award of statutory damages to a sum of not less than $ 100 [$ 200]. . . .

17 U.S.C. § 504(c) (1976) (brackets show section as amended October 31, 1988).
On its appeal, Video Views challenges the granting of a jury trial, contending that the entire action should have been tried without a jury because it sought only statutory damages. Studio 21 urges that the seventh amendment to the Constitution required a jury trial in this copyright infringement action, despite the fact that Video Views sought statutory instead of actual damages.
This question has been the subject of some conflict among (and within) the circuit courts of appeal that have touched upon it, complicated by the fact that these decisions have been under both the Copyright Act of 1976 and the now-repealed Copyright Act of 1909. See, e.g., Chappell & Co. v. Palermo Cafe, 249 F.2d 77 (1st Cir. 1957) (no right to a jury trial under 1909 Act); Mail & Express Co. v. Life Publishing Co., 192 F. 899 (2d Cir. 1912) (right to a jury trial under 1909 Act); Oboler v. Goldin, 714 F.2d 211   (2d Cir. 1983) (per curiam) (no right to a jury trial under the 1976 Act); Gnossos Music v. Mitken, Inc., 653 F.2d 117 (4th Cir. 1981) (right to a jury trial under the 1976 Act); Twentieth Century Music Corp. v. Frith, 645 F.2d 6, 7 (5th Cir. 1981) (per curiam) (no right to a jury trial under either the 1909 Act or the 1976 Act); National Football League v. McBee & Bruno's, Inc., 792 F.2d 726, 729 n. 4 (8th Cir. 1986) (noting the conflict between circuits but declining to address the question); Sid & Marty Krofft Television Productions, Inc. v. McDonald's Corp., 562 F.2d 1157, [***1756]  1177 (9th Cir. 1977) (under the 1976 Act, statutory damages determined by judge, not the jury); Cable/Home Communication Corp. v. Network Productions, Inc., 902 F.2d 829, 852-53, 15 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1001 (11th Cir. 1990) (no right to a jury trial under the 1976 Act).
Because § 504(c) does not resolve the question, we must address the constitutional issue as to entitlement to a jury trial. Cf., Lorillard v. Pons, 434 U.S. 575, 577, 98 S. Ct. 866, 55 L. Ed. 2d 40 (1978); see also Tull v. United States, 481 U.S. 412, 417 n. 3, 107 S. Ct. 1831, 95 L. Ed. 2d 365 (1986) ( when statute is silent there is no recourse but to address the constitutional issue); Curtis v. Loether, 415 U.S. 189, 192 n. 6,    94 S. Ct. 1005, 39 L. Ed. 2d 260 (1974). There is little question that  the right to a jury trial exists in a copyright infringement

925 F.2d 1010, *1013; 1991 U.S. App. LEXIS 1711, **6; 17 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1753, ***1755

action when the copyright owner endeavors to prove and recover its actual damages, as determined by a jury, pursuant to § 504(b).  Arnstein v. Porter, 154 F.2d 464, 468 (2d Cir. 1946) (Frank, J.) (1909 Act). It is also clear that  it is for the district court and not for a jury to determine the appropriate award of statutory damages, within the limits prescribed in §§ 504(c)(1) and (2), respectively. But see Gnossos Music, 653 F.2d at 120 (jury to assess statutory damages within the limits prescribed). However, § 504 is completely and unambiguously silent on our central issue: whether there is a right to a jury trial on the underlying factual issues of infringement and willfulness when the plaintiff opts for statutory damages instead of actual damages. See Gnossos Music, 653 F.2d at 119 (noting that the language is "not sufficiently clear to mandate either a bench trial or jury trial").
The seventh amendment to the Constitution provides that  "In all suits at common law, where the value in controversy exceeds twenty dollars, the right to a jury trial shall   be preserved. . . ." See also Rule 38(a), Federal Rules of Civil Procedure ( "The right to a trial by jury as declared by the Seventh Amendment to the Constitution or as given by a statute of the United States shall be preserved to the parties inviolate."). The Supreme Court has determined that  whether the right to a jury trial has been "preserved" in a given case "depends on the nature of the issue to be tried rather than the character of the overall action." Ross v. Bernhard, 396 U.S. 531, 538,    90 S. Ct. 733, 24 L. Ed. 2d 729 (1970). In Ross, the court suggested that:

The "legal" nature of an issue is determined by considering, first, the pre-merger [of courts of law and courts of equity through the adoption of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure in 1938] custom with reference to such questions; second, the remedy sought; and third, the practical abilities and limitations of juries.

396 U.S. at 538 n.10 (noting that the first consideration may require "extensive and abstruse historical inquiry").
The determination of the factual issues of infringement and willfulness in a copyright infringement action do not appear to be "beyond the practical abilities and limitations of juries," and, thus, this   matter must be settled by the remaining two considerations. See Curtis v. Loether, 415 U.S. 189, 195, 94 S. Ct. 1005, 39 L. Ed. 2d 260 (1974) (jury trial available if the action "involves rights and remedies of the sort typically enforced in an action at law").
At common law, copyright infringement created a cause of action entitling the copyright owner to a recovery "analogous to recovery for a number of tort actions recognized at common law." Gnossos Music, 653 F.2d at 120 (citations omitted). A qualifying plaintiff who asserted both a claim for copyright infringement and the inadequacy of a remedy at law might have been entitled to proceed before a court of equity. However, for all other plaintiffs -- namely those who could not assert the inadequacy of a remedy at law -- remedies for copyright infringement "traditionally would have been enforced at law." Gnossos Music, 653 F.2d at 120. There is no reason to believe that, at common law, the injured copyright owner would have been treated far differently from the trademark owner. See Dairy Queen v. Wood, 369 U.S. 469 & n. 15, 82 S. Ct. 894, 8 L. Ed. 2d 44 (1962) (Trademark Act preserved right to jury trial) (citing Arnstein v. Porter, 154 F.2d 464 (2d Cir. 1946) (a copyright case)).    Thus,  actions both for copyright and trademark infringement may fairly be viewed as actions at law to vindicate a tortious interference with a property right, namely that of intellectual property. However, we acknowledge the fact that Congress has seen fit to provide somewhat different statutory remedies for each.
The remedy that Congress has provided in § 504(c) defies blanket characterization as either "equitable" or "legal." In some cases, the statutory damage award will be intended to approximate the actual damages suffered; in others, as in those cases where only minimum statutory damages are sought, it may not.  In determining the measure, within the specified limits, of statutory damages to be awarded a copyright owner, the district court may consider various factors such as "the difficulty or impossibility of proving actual damages, . . . the circumstances of the infringement, . . . and the efficacy of the damages as a deterrent to future copyright infringement." F.E.L. Publications, Ltd. v. Catholic Bishop of Chicago, 754 F.2d 216, [***1757]  219 (7th Cir.) (decided under the 1909 Act) (citing F.W. Woolworth Co. v. Contemporary Arts, Inc., 344 U.S. 228, 232-33, 73 S. Ct. 222, 97 L. Ed. 276 (1952), and Douglas    v. Cunningham, 294 U.S. 207, 209, 55 S. Ct. 365, 79 L. Ed. 862 (1935)), cert. denied, 474 U.S. 824, 106 S. Ct. 79, 88 L. Ed. 2d 64 (1985). See also Lottie Joplin Thomas Trust v.

925 F.2d 1010, *1014; 1991 U.S. App. LEXIS 1711, **10; 17 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1753, ***1756

Crown Publishers, Inc., 592 F.2d 651, 657 (2d Cir. 1978) (court will resort to statutory damages when proof of actual damages is "virtually impossible").
However,  it cannot be said that statutory damages are "equitable" in nature rather than "legal" in nature simply because the copyright owner is relieved of the necessity of proving its actual damages. The availability of statutory damages is premised on a far less demanding standard than the "inadequacy of an adequate remedy at law" standard; it is premised simply upon the copyright owner's election -- for whatever reason. We do not overlook the possibility that the requirement that equitable relief be made available only where there is no adequate remedy at law was intended "to guard the right of trial by jury preserved    by the Seventh Amendment and to that end it should be liberally construed." Ross, 396 U.S. at 539 (quoting Schoenthal v. Irving Trust Co., 287 U.S. 92, 94, 53 S. Ct. 50, 77 L. Ed. 185(1932)).
The goal of deterrence that statutory damages have been thought to serve "reflects more than a concern to provide equitable   relief." Tull, 481 U.S. at 423. This court has recently upheld as "wholly proper" an award of statutory damages that the district judge imposed to "penalize" the infringer for "illbegotten profit and to deter future violations." Illinois Bell Telephone Co. v. Haines and Co., 905 F.2d 1081, 1089, 15 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1353 (7th Cir. 1990). To the extent that it is correct to view statutory damages as some sort of a penalty, there is undoubtedly still greater justification for characterizing them as a "legal" remedy.  Tull, 481 U.S. at 422 ("remedies intended to punish culpable individuals . . . were issued by courts of law, not courts of equity"); Curtis, 415 U.S. at 197 (HN13[

] punitive damages are "legal" rather than "equitable"). Moreover, the discretion that § 504(c) vests with district judges to determine the amount of an award of statutory damages does not parallel the types of discretion that the Supreme Court has termed "equitable." Curtis, 415 U.S. at 197 (noting the "equitable" nature of a statute that grants a district judge the discretion to award backpay in an employment discrimination action).
We do not think that by vesting district judges with flexibility in determining the appropriate   award of statutory damages for copyright infringement, Congress intended to divest completely either copyright owners or alleged infringers of their right to a jury trial. Cf.  Tull, 481 U.S. at 427 (Clean Water Act vested district judge with the authority to assess civil penalties for noncompliance but entitled defendants to jury trial on issue of liability). We believe that the statutory damage provisions of the Copyright Act were intended to relieve the aggrieved copyright owner of the task of proving its actual damages, not to relieve the alleged infringer of its right to a jury trial on other factual issues, such as infringement, or in appropriate cases, willfulness. We conclude that,  when monetary damages of any kind are sought, the issues of infringement and willfulness are for the jury to resolve.  The fact that the district judge is given the responsibility to assess the statutory damages does not, without more, transform the proceeding -- one in which monetary relief is sought -- from one legal in nature to one equitable in nature.
The most compelling opposing argument is judicial economy; indeed, we concede that jury trials may result in delays in the administration of   justice in particular cases. This appears to be an implicit consideration in those decisions that have deemed there to be no right to a jury trial when the copyright owner seeks only "minimum" statutory damages, incidental to equitable relief. See, e.g., Twentieth Century Music Corp. v. Frith, 645 F.2d 6 (5th Cir. 1981) (per curiam). However, we think to deny the right to a jury trial in those instances would fly in the face of Beacon Theatres Inc. v. Westover, 359 U.S. 500, 510-11, 79 S. Ct. 948, 3 L. Ed. 2d 988 (1959), where the Supreme Court cautioned that  the right to a jury trial could not be lost by characterizing a "legal" claim as "merely incidental to" an equitable claim. Moreover, apart from the fact that the Supreme Court has recently cautioned that  considerations of judicial economy are "an insufficient basis for departing from our longstanding commitment to preserving a litigant's right to a jury trial," see Lytle v. Household Manufacturing, Inc., 494 U.S. 545, 110 S. Ct. 1331, 1337, 108 L. Ed. 2d 504 (1990), we do not think our ruling overlooks those considerations.
The  evidentiary record upon which an award of statutory damages is based need not be developed to the same extent as one in which an award of actual damages is sought.  If a copyright   owner seeks only "minimum" statutory damages, the record on damages need not be developed at all. If a greater amount of statutory    damages is sought, the district court may make the appropriate award when the evidentiary

925 F.2d 1010, *1015; 1991 U.S. App. LEXIS 1711, **14; 17 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1753, ***1757 record adequately [***1758]  supports that determination.  Morley Music Co. v. Dick Stacey's Plaza Motel, Inc., 725 F.2d 1, 3 (1st Cir. 1983) (district court that has before it sufficient evidence to form a basis for statutory damages may award them).  The district court is accorded wide and almost exclusive discretion in determining the size of the statutory damage award.  Douglas, 294 U.S. at 210. However,  concerns of due process and the opportunity for meaningful, if limited, appellate review contemplate that the district court would provide some explanation of the factual findings that underlie this exercise of discretion to award greater than minimum statutory damages.
We disagree with Video Views' contention that Studio 21 was not entitled to a jury trial because the action was one for statutory damages under § 504(c). Had Video Views sought only an injunction, Studio 21 certainly would have had no entitlement to a jury trial. Here, however, Video Views sought   increased statutory damages pursuant to § 504(c)(2). Studio 21 vigorously (and not unsuccessfully) defended against Video Views' allegations of willful infringement. After Video Views' motion for a summary judgment was denied, there remained jury questions of infringement and willfulness. Before it was entitled to recover any damages, Video Views was obligated to convince the jury that Studio 21 had infringed one or more of the seven adult films involved in this action. See 17 U.S.C. §§ 106(4), 501. The district court correctly submitted the factual questions of infringement and willfulness to the jury, and based on its verdict, determined the appropriate award of statutory damages, as directed by § 504(c).
B.
At trial, Video Views proffered evidence suggesting that Studio 21 had infringed its exclusive right to perform seven adult films publicly in video cassette format at "adult entertainment centers." The jury partly disagreed, finding that Studio 21 infringed only two of those films. On this appeal, Video Views contends that the district court erred by denying its motion for a new trial on the issue of infringement. It urges that we upset the jury's determination that   five of the seven adult films at issue had not been infringed as being against the manifest weight of the evidence. In its cross-appeal, Studio 21 contends that Video Views' evidence failed to present a jury question on the issue of infringement.
Section 501(a) of the Copyright Act provides that

 Anyone who violates any of the exclusive rights of the copyright owner as provided by sections 106 through 118 . . . is an infringer of the copyright.

17 U.S.C. § 501(a). Section 106 of the Act, entitled "Exclusive rights in copyrighted works," provides:

 Subject to sections 107 through 118, the owner of copyright under this title has the exclusive rights to do and to authorize any of the following: * * * (4) in the case of . . . motion pictures and other audiovisual works, to perform the copyrighted work publicly. . . .

17 U.S.C. § 106(4). Section 101 of the Act defines "audiovisual works" as

. . .  works that consist of a series of related images which are intrinsically intended to be shown by the use of machines or devices such as projectors, viewers, or electronic equipment, together with accompanying sounds, if any, regardless of the nature of the material objects, such as films    or tapes, in which the works are embodied.

17 U.S.C. § 101.
To prevail in an action alleging the infringement of the exclusive right to perform publicly a copyrighted work, a plaintiff is obligated to prove the following: (1) that it was the owner or assignee of the particular right asserted; (2) that the defendant either publicly performed or authorized the public performance of the work; and (3) that the defendant did not have permission to perform the work. See, e.g.,    Paramount Pictures Corp. v. Sullivan, 546 F. Supp. 397, 398 (D. Me. 1982).
In this case, Studio 21 did not dispute that each of the films were original works entitled to the copyright protection. Nor did it assert that the formalities of the Copyright Act had not been satisfied. It did not claim to have had any license or other authorization to perform these films publicly. The infringement question turned upon whether Video Views was the "owner" of the rights it claimed and whether Studio 21 had performed the films publicly.
The initial determination is whether Video Views was the "owner" of the property right it sought to enforce against Studio 21. Section 201(d)  of the Copyright Act provides for the transfer   of ownership of any or all of the exclusive rights comprised in a copyright:

 (1) The ownership of a copyright may be transferred in whole or in part by any means of conveyance or by operation of law. . . .

(2) . . . The owner of any particular exclusive right is entitled, to the extent of [***1759]  that right, to all protection and remedies accorded to the copyright owner by this title.

17 U.S.C. § 201(d). While Video Views was not the "copyright owner" of the adult films involved in this action, it claimed that it had entered into exclusive licensing agreements with the copyright owners of those films. By virtue of each of those agreements, Video Views asserted that it was the "owner" of the exclusive right -- allegedly infringed by Studio 21 -- to perform publicly those films in video arcades.
It is clear that  a licensing agreement cannot create property rights enforceable under the copyright laws. 17 U.S.C. § 201(d)(2) (limiting protections to "the extent of th[e particular] right"); cf.  F.E.L. Publications, Ltd. v. Catholic Bishop of Chicago, 506 F. Supp. 1127, 1134 (N.D. Ill. 1981), rev'd on other grounds, 754 F.2d 216 (7th Cir. 1985). A licensing agreement is an assignment of    preexisting property rights, in this case, rights created under the Copyright Act of 1976. Any other obligations or liabilities created by the licensing agreement exist only between the parties to that agreement -- Video Views and the copyright owners of the respective films. Studio 21 concedes the existence of these licensing agreements but, by virtue of its cross-appeal, rigorously challenges the scope of those agreements -- in particular, those pertaining to the two films it was found to have infringed, Nothing to Hide and Baby Cakes.
On July 1, 1983, Video Views executed separate licensing agreements with Cal Vista International, Ltd., and Essex Distributing, Inc. (which will be referred to as the "Cal Vista" and "Essex" licenses, respectively). Each license granted Video Views ownership of the exclusive right to sub-license the "video arcade exhibition" of numerous adult films. The Cal Vista license, which governed the film Nothing to Hide, was recorded with the Copyright Office on February 2, 1984. In pertinent part, it provided (with emphasis added):

NOTE: The rights granted to LICENSEE hereunder for on-premises video software exhibition to patrons of adult entertainment   businesses is to have those adult entertainment businesses that have adult motion picture arcade-type viewing facilities, and not to video theatres.

"Adult motion picture arcade facilities" are defined as any place to which the interested adult public is permitted or invited, wherein coin or slug operated, or electronically, electrically or mechanically controlled image- producing devices utilizing the works in video software format are maintained to show images to two (2) [to five (5)] patrons per image-producing device at any one time. The bracket material was lined out on the original agreement.

The Essex license, governing the film Baby Cakes, and recorded with the Copyright Office on March 27, 1984, provided in pertinent part (with emphasis added):

"Adult motion picture arcade facilities" are defined as any place to which the interested adult public is permitted or invited; wherein coin or slug operated, or    electronically, electrically or mechanically controlled image-producing devices utilizing the Works in video software format are maintained to show images to two (2) to five (5) patrons per image-producing device at any one time.
Studio 21 urges that the licensing   agreements apply only when two persons, in the case of the Cal Vista license, and from two to five persons, in the case of the Essex license, occupy the type of facility described for the purposes described. It may be that these licenses are neither models of clarity or draftsmanship; we offer no opinion on that subject. Nevertheless, we decline to adopt the crabbed construction of those agreements urged by Studio 21. We conclude that the licensing agreements describe the capacity of the "place" where the films would be shown and are not so narrow in scope as Studio 21 urges. We have little trouble concluding that Studio 21's viewing booths are the type of "facilities" contemplated by a reasonable construction of the license: namely "adult motion picture arcade facilities . . . maintained to show images to" two to five persons. That the booths may, at a particular time, in fact be occupied by one person or six persons does not alter the fact that the booths are maintained to accommodate two to five persons.
The remaining question is whether the works had been "performed publicly" by Studio 21 within the meaning of the Copyright Act. Once again, we begin with the language of the   Copyright Act, namely §  101 of the Act, which generally provides that to "perform" a copyrighted work is

under past license agreements. We specifically upheld this approach in Kowalczyk. See 855 F.2d at 382-83.   The fact that the figure was not exactly three times the license amount is not troubling. The court was not required to follow any rigid formula. Indeed, district courts enjoy wide discretion in awarding fees and may consider various factors such as "the difficulty or impossibility of proving actual damages, the circumstances of the infringement, and the efficacy of the damages as a deterrent to future copyright infringement." See F.E.L. Publications v. Catholic Bishop of Chicago, 754 F.2d 216, 219 (7th Cir.) (citations omitted), cert. denied, 474 U.S. 824, 88 L. Ed. 2d 64, 106 S. Ct. 79 (1985); see also Harris v. [***1718]  Emus Records Corp., 734 F.2d 1329, 1335 (9th Cir. 1984) (court has wide discretion to award any amount within the statutory guidelines). Moreover, when the    infringement is willful, the statutory damages award may be designed to penalize the infringer and to deter future violations. See Illinois Bell Tel. Co. v. Haines & Co., 905 F.2d 1081, 1089, 15 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1353 (7th Cir. 1990); Kowalczyk, 855 F.2d at 383. Under the statute, the court potentially could have awarded up to $ 900,000, or in other words, 22.5 times the amount   that it actually awarded. Instead, the district court attempted to fashion a remedy more equitably tailored to the specific facts of the case. In essence, Charlie Club contends that the court did not base recovery on a figure that accurately measured the plaintiffs' losses. It is precisely because of the difficulty in measuring such losses, however, that statutory damages exist. Accordingly, we conclude that the district court's damages award did not constitute an abuse of discretion.

This appeal concerns copyright infringement of a reference guidebook, compiled by plaintiff, U.S. Payphone, Inc. ("Payphone"), which provided information concerning the coin-operated telephone market. The district court held that defendant, Executives Unlimited of Durham, Inc. ("Executive"), et al, had infringed Payphone's copyright and awarded   Payphone in actual damages $ 15,000 and $ 20,486 of Executive's profits from the infringement. Executive appeals the judgment and damage award; Payphone cross-appeals the damage award. We affirm, except to remand for further explication of the $ 20,486 profit award, and reverse that part of the judgment allowing prejudgment interest.
I. Factual Background

After Congress deregulated the business of coin-operated telephones in 1984, any private   company or individual could own and operate pay telephones, subject to compliance with state tariffs. In 1986, Payphone prepared the "Payphone Magazine Reference Guide" ("Guide"), which is the subject of this litigation. The Guide, one hundred sixty pages in length, included a fifty-one page section on state tariffs. That section, which provides the basis of Payphone's infringement claim, summarized the state tariffs regulating the fees payable to telephone utilities by owners and operators of pay telephones. The President of Payphone, Mark Ostrofsky, with the assistance of three lawyers, compiled the Tariff Section. He collapsed voluminous tariff information into a format of one sheet per state. Payphone contends that the one-page format   of the Tariff Section made it easy for readers to use and was the "heart" of the Guide.
Payphone first published the Guide on May 5, 1986. On November 13, 1986, it applied for and obtained a Certificate of Copyright Registration from the United States Copyright Office, and a notice of copyright was affixed to the Guide's front page. Payphone sold 254 copies of its Guide, at a price of approximately $ 195 per copy. Payphone's market dominance, however, was brief. In late 1986, Executive published the Executive Manual ("Manual"), a guide to Amway Corporation distributors interested in getting into the pay telephone business. During preparation of the Manual, an Executive employee telephoned an employee of National Telephone Services for information about the private payphone business. In response, the latter sent a "ten-inch high stack" of materials to Executive regarding the payphone telephone business, which included the Tariff Section from Payphone's Guide. The material, however, did not contain any notice of copyright. Executive, unaware of the source of the Tariff Section, included it in its Manual, under the heading "Tariffs and Regulations Information." When Payphone filed   this action for copyright infringement on March 20, 1987, Executive immediately halted all sales of the Manual. At that time, Executive had sold approximately 6,609 copies of the Manual, at a price of $ 25 per copy.
The district court held that, though Executive did not intentionally infringe Payphone's copyright, the Guide was copyrightable material and Executive had "failed to overcome the presumption of validity which attached to the copyrighted work." The court awarded Payphone actual damages in the amount of $ 15,000 and Executive's profits from the infringement in the amount of $ 20,486 and prejudgment interest on these sums.
II. The Copyright Judgment

Executive admitted copying   the Tariff Section of Payphone's Guide, but argues as a matter of law that the material cannot be copyrighted. Its core contention is that Payphone simply created a form and printed legislative material on it. Executive argues that Payphone's Tariff Section did not evince the requisite "subjective judgment and selectivity" necessary to constitute copyrightable material.
Payphone's  registration of its copyright is, of course, prima facie evidence that the copyright is valid and that the material is original.  M. Kramer Mfg. Co. v. Andrews, 783 F.2d 421, 434 (4th Cir. 1986); Blumcraft of Pittsburgh v. Newman Bros. Inc., 373 F.2d 905, 906 (6th Cir. 1967). The  Copyright Act of 1976 provides protection for "original works of authorship fixed in any tangible medium of expression." 17 U.S.C. § 102(a). Executive correctly notes though that legislative enactments are in the "public domain" and, therefore, normally not copyrightable. However, a "compilation"  of material in the public domain is copyrightable if the author exercises some "subjective judgment and selectivity in choosing items" which comprise his compilation.  Dow Jones & Co. v. Board of Trade of City of Chicago, 546 F. Supp. 113, 115 (S.D.N.Y. 1982).    The evidence suggests that the Tariff Section could have been organized in many different ways and that Payphone expended a great deal of time creating the single-page-per-state format. The Guide, according to Payphone, is the result of hundreds of hours of reviewing, analyzing, and interpreting state tariffs and regulations of the fifty states and the District of Columbia. During discovery,   Payphone produced 2700 pages of documents relating to the review, selection, coordination and arrangement of the compiled data which ultimately it organized in a "simple and readable format" of fifty-one pages.
The district court concluded that the Tariff Section clearly met the standard that we enunciated in Kramer. We agree. In Kramer, we stated:

   Copyrightability of a compilation or derivative work does not turn on whether the component parts of the collective work are original or in the public domain. Section 103 of the Act makes this plain. It declares that the validity of a copyright of a compilation or derivative work depends on the originality of the compiler's individual contribution to the work or material regardless of whether the individual items in the material have been or ever could have been subject to copyright. It follows that the validity of the Plaintiff's copyright does not depend on the copyrightability of the components represented by the underlying work but by the originality of its own contribution to the copyrighted work.

Kramer, 783 F.2d at 440 (citing Apple Barrel Prod., Inc. v. Beard, 730 F.2d 384, 387-88 (5th Cir. 1984)).
Concerning the notion of "originality," the Supreme Court has recently stated:

1991 U.S. App. LEXIS 7599, *3; 18 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 2049, **2050

 To be sure, the requisite level of creativity is extremely low; even a slight amount will suffice. The vast majority of works make the grade quite easily, as they possess some creative spark, "no matter how crude, humble or obvious. . . ."

. . .

 A compiler   may settle upon a selection or arrangement that others have used; novelty is not required. Originality requires only that the author make the selection or arrangement independently (i.e., without copying that selection or arrangement from another work), and that it display some minimal level of creatively. Presumably, the vast majority of compilations will pass this test, but not all will.

Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Tel. Serv. Co., 59 U.S.L.W. 4251, 4253, 4256 (1991) (citation omitted); see also Kramer, 783 F.2d at 437-38.

We are persuaded that Payphone's selection and organization of the state tariff material was sufficiently subjective and original to make the Tariff Section copyrightable material and that, therefore, Executive's inadvertent copying constituted infringement.
III. The Damage Award

 Under § 504(b) of the Copyright Act, a copyright owner may recover:

the actual damages suffered by him or her as a result of the infringement, and any profits of the infringer that are attributable to the infringement and are not taken into account in computing the actual damages.

17 U.S.C. § 504(b). The district court awarded Payphone   actual damages of $ 15,000, Executive's profits from the infringement in the amount of $ 20,486, and prejudgment interest on these sums. Both parties contest the award.
A. Actual Damages

Payphone sold 254 copies of its Guide. The district court found that, had not Executive infringed Payphone's copyright, the latter would have sold more Guides. However, it also found that because of the constant need to update the material to keep abreast of changes in the regulatory environment, the Guide had a very short "useful life," -- estimated at three years. The court also noted the probability of only "sporadic" sales over the course of those three years.  As a result, it found actual damages in the amount of $ 15,000. Implicit in that determination, we think, is a finding that, had Executive not infringed Payphone's copyright, the latter would have sold approximately eighty more Guides. Mindful that  when "establishing lost sales due to sales of an infringing product, courts must necessarily engage in some degree of speculation," we are not prepared to say that the district court erred   in its computation of actual damages. Stevens Linen Assoc., Inc. v. Mastercraft Corp., 656 F.2d 11, 14 (2d Cir. 1981).  

1991 U.S. App. LEXIS 7599, *7; 18 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 2049, **2051
B. Executive's Profits

Section 504(b) states, in pertinent   part:

 In establishing the infringer's profits, the copyright owner is required to present proof only of the infringer's gross revenue, and the infringer is required to prove his or her deductible expenses and the elements of profit attributable to factors other than the copyrighted work.

17 U.S.C. § 504(b). The parties stipulated that Executive received gross revenues from sales of the Manual in the amount of $ 101,749. The district court found that Executive had incurred deductible expenses of $ 50,512, thus realizing a pretax profit of approximately $ 51,282.  Additionally, the district court found that the Tariff Section represented forty percent of the value of the Manual and, thus, concluded that Payphone was entitled to forty percent of the profits from the sale of the Manual--$ 20,486.
Courts are necessarily concerned with the proper application of § 504(b)'s language restricting recovery of an infringer's profits to   those that are not taken into account in computing actual damages. The Seventh Circuit, for example, has stated, "if  the profits the owner would have made but for the infringement are equal to the profits the infringer made by selling the copyrighted item, . . . the 'not taken into account' clause . . . bars the owner from receiving an additional award of damages based on the infringer's profits." Taylor v. Meirick, 712 F.2d 1112, 1120 (7th Cir. 1983) (citations omitted); see also Robert R. Jones Assoc. Inc. v. Nino Homes, 858 F.2d 274, 281 (6th Cir. 1988). However, "if the infringer makes greater profits than the copyright owner lost, because the infringer is a more efficient producer than the owner or sells in a different market, the owner is allowed to capture the additional profit even though it does not represent a loss to him." Taylor, 712 F.2d at 1120. From the record, we are unable to determine what portion, if any, of $ 20,496 resulted from sales by Executive that were "not taken into account" when the district court calculated Payphone's actual damages. To justify the "profits" portion of the award, all of the 6,609   Executive Manuals would necessarily have had to have been sold to persons or companies that would not have purchased Payphone's Guide, which was sold at a much higher price. Stated differently, any of Executive's sales which resulted in lost opportunities for sales by Payphone and were, therefore, calculated in the latter's actual damages, could not be considered as part of Executive's profits which Payphone could again recover. Because the district court made no finding in this respect, we remand for that determination.
C. Prejudgment Interest

 The Copyright Act of 1976 does not provide for prejudgment interest. We recognize that, even in the absence of legislative direction, a court may award it if necessary to further a statute's purposes. See Rodgers v. United States, 332 U.S. 371, 373 (1947); Robert R. Jones Assoc., 858 F.2d at 282. Generally stated, the purpose of § 504(b) of the Copyright Act of 1976 is to compensate the copyright owner and to discourage the infringer by disgorging his profits.  Kleier Advertising Co. v. James Miller Chevrolet, Inc., 722 F. Supp. 1544 (N.D. Ill. 1989); see also Taylor, 712 F.2d at 1120.    Although we do not intend to state a universal rule, we are persuaded that the award to Payphone of its actual damages plus Executive's profits, if any, will sufficiently compensate Payphone for its loss, and, since the infringement was not intentional, any additional sanction would serve no purpose.

This is an action for copyright infringement commenced by Hukafit Sportswear, Inc. ("Hukafit") against K-Mart Apparel Corporation ("K-Mart"), alleging that K-Mart's sale of 4400 dozen sweaters purchased from Selective Knitwear, Inc. ("Selective") in the fall of 1987 infringed a copyright in a Damask design owned by Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear Productions, Limited ("Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear") of London, England. Hukafit asserts that at the time of the alleged infringement it was Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear's exclusive licensee in the United States, and had full authority to prosecute the alleged infringement.

K-Mart denies any infringement, and has filed a third-party complaint against Selective, alleging breach of a contract of indemnification, and demanding contribution. Selective has not contested its obligation to indemnify K- Mart should liability for infringement be established.

Selective asserts that the design of its sweaters (the "Selective Style 9001 Sweaters") were independently created and based upon the design of an Israeli sweater, that it had no access to Hukafit's (Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear's) Damask   design, and that in any case the Damask design is not susceptible to copyright protection because it is a common and familiar design rooted in Ottoman and Victorian antecedents.

The Court granted summary judgment to K-Mart and Selective on count three of the Amended Complaint on September 26, 1989. Selective dismissed its counterclaim against Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear on March 15, 1990. The parties agreed to bifurcate the trial, deferring the issue of damages until after liability is decided. A non-jury trial commenced on October 18, 1990, and was completed on November 15, 1990, after a three-week continuance to accommodate the English witnesses. Final post-trial papers were filed by counsel on February 15, 1991. This opinion constitutes the Court's findings of fact and conclusions of law in the liability phase of the proceedings.
The Agreement

In 1984 Hukafit and Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear entered into an Agreement pursuant to which Hukafit was granted an exclusive license to manufacture, use and sell Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear's designs in ladies' sweaters in the United States. JX 18.  The initial term of the Agreement was to expire on May 31, 1987. Id. para. 4. Hukafit was  entitled to renew the Agreement for one-year periods commencing on June 1 of 1987, 1988 and 1989 by giving written notice, at least nine months before the relevant renewal date, to Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear of an intention to renew. Id. para. 5. The parties agreed to royalty payments calculated at a fixed rate, id. 13, and guaranteed minimum royalties. Id. 15. David Binder, the principal of Hukafit, personally guaranteed the discharge of all of Hukafit's obligations to Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear. Id. 18. Hukafit was obligated to obtain, in the name and on behalf of Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear, copyright registration in the United States of the latter's designs. Id. 22. It was further obligated, if it became aware of infringement of Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear's designs, to notify Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear immediately of the infringement and to assist Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear, if requested, in taking steps to defend the copyright, provided that Hukafit could take reasonable, necessary and appropriate steps to protect its rights under the Agreement without prejudicing any right or interest of Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear. Id. para. 23. Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear reserved the right   to terminate the Agreement immediately if Hukafit breached any of its obligations, but any asserted Hukafit breach not involving non-payment of royalties had to be the subject of formal notice by Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear, and could be remedied within thirty days of the notice of such breach. Id. paras. 28(4), 36. All amendments to the Agreement had to be in writing. Id. para. 35. The Agreement, which was to be governed by and construed in accordance with English law, id. para. 40, was drafted by Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear's solicitor, John Rosenheim. Tr. 784-85; 961-62.
Hukafit obtained, in Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear's name, as copyright claimant, a copyright registration for a design entitled Damask, effective December 6, 1984. Tr. 110-111, 352-53. More than 125 other   copyrights were obtained in the name of Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear by Hukafit for Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear designs. Tr. 84-85. Hukafit's sales volume from 1984 through 1987 ranged between 10 to 14 million dollars annually. Tr. 54-55. For the period 1984-85, 80% to 95% of its sales volume was based upon Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear's designs; for 1986, the figure was 40% to 70%, and in 1987, about 40%. Tr. 61-62. Indeed, the defendants do not contest the substantial role that Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear designs played in the economic viability of Hukafit's business, or the essential role of aggressive copyright enforcement in defending that business. Pursuant to the Agreement, Hukafit paid Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear $ 300,000 in general royalties, another $ 150,000 to $ 200,000 in royalties under the 10% provision of paragraph 5(b) of the Agreement, and bought more than a million and a half dollars of merchandise from Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear. JX 18, Tr. 380-81.
During the course of their relationship, Hukafit initiated numerous infringement actions in the United States in the name of Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear and in consultation with Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear's counsel or staff. Even though John Rosenheim,    legal counsel to Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear, was not advised prior to the initiation of several copyright actions filed by Hukafit at the inception of the relationship, he did not object, as he could have, under the Agreement. Indeed, he found the procedure "perfectly acceptable". Tr. 815. This comfortable and flexible informality was to characterize the relations of the parties throughout most of their business dealings. Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear routinely supported, when asked to do so, Hukafit's enforcement efforts in the United States. Tr. 1022-1027. There were numerous cases in which Jeffrey Rogers and David Binder, the principals of their respective firms, discussed matters, and in which Rogers largely ceded to Binder the authority to resolve the cases. These cases were the "Miss Erica" litigation, Tr. 86-88, 440-41, 475, 490, 857-59, 856-66, 970-72, 1017-18; the Brooks Fashions case, Tr. 88-89, 92-93, 1027-1028; the Macy's infringements, Tr. 98-99; the consolidated Kellwood and Sweater Bee cases, Tr. 99-100, 974, 1032-38, 1043-44; the Oak Hill action, Tr. 101, 972-73; the Petrie matter, Tr. 101; the "Mr. Noah" case, Tr. 101-102; the Tangiers matter, Tr. 102-03, 1032, 1079-80; and   the Knit-Maven situation, Tr. 482-83. Mr. Rosenheim was also informed of an action against Step Up/Cherry Stix, Tr. 921, HX 109, 110, 112. In March 1985 Rogers told Binder, referring to Hukafit's United States copyright enforcement of Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear's designs, "Whatever you do on your side of the pond is your business." Tr. 105-106.
In July 1985, Jeffrey Rogers authorized Binder to act as his agent in signing settlement papers in the "Miss Erica" case, notwithstanding the fact that para. 26 of the Agreement prohibits this. Tr. 93, 97-98, 475-76, 795-98, 867-68, 1021-22; HX 18. In August 1985 the same was done in the Brooks Fashion case. Tr. 476-77, 795-98. Donald Binder testified that his enforcement efforts on behalf of Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear designs were in all respects reasonable, necessary and appropriate, and that, in conformity with para. 23 of the Agreement, they in no way prejudiced the right or interest of Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear. "[Rogers'] copyrights weren't disturbed. They were upheld in every case. Most people that we went after stopped doing it [copying]. And we certainly did protect these copyrights." Tr. 110. Indeed, Jeffrey Rogers' solicitor, John Rosenheim,    admitted that, in this regard, no notice of breach under para. 36 of the Agreement was ever given to Hukafit. Tr. 859, 891-93.
The central issue in this lawsuit is whether the 1984 Agreement was renewed beyond its expiration date, May 31, 1987. As is apparent from its text, the Agreement itself sets forth the terms and conditions for its renewal, and no new "renewal" document is required to come into existence. Hukafit was required, however, to give written notice of its intent to renew to Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear nine months before the expiration date. JX 18, para. 5(a) (b); Tr. 802- 04.

In November 1986, Binder spoke to Rogers by telephone and told him that he wished to renew the Agreement for another year, and Rogers agreed. Tr. 134. Furthermore, in January 1987, Hukafit sent one of its senior sales persons, Barry Roth, to London to pick up the new line from Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear, as was conventionally done at that time of year, beginning a process that ends with shipping goods based upon the line to customers in the following fall, in this case, of 1987. Tr. 1057, 134-37. Additionally, during December 1986 and January and February 1987 Binder urged Rogers to come to the United   States to testify in the Oak Hill infringement case, and Rogers appeared and testified in June 1987. This is especially strong evidence that the agreement had been renewed, and that Rogers considered it renewed. Any doubt about the matter is dissipated by Rogers' own testimony at the June 30, 1987 Oak Hill deposition. Three times he stated in clear terms that the Agreement was then in effect and had been renewed. Tr. 506; HX 59.
Q. Do you license others to use your designs as well as sell garments which you have had manufactured with your designs?

A. No. The only license is with David [Binder].

HX 61 p. 11.

Q. Is this contract still in force?

A. Yes.

Id. p. 86.

Q. Has the agreement been renewed?

A. Yes.

Q. Is there a written renewal document?

A. No, it's not necessary.

* * *

Q. What did you mean when you said that the agreement had been renewed?

A. I mean that we shook hands and I said that I would continue to supply Mr. Binder for a further year, and to me, that is the agreement.

Id. at 104.
The following day, in New York, Binder asked Rogers to give him a letter confirming his testimony in the deposition that the Agreement had in fact been renewed,    in order, obviously, to avoid the need to relitigate the point in any future enforcement suits initiated by Hukafit. Tr. 142-43. Jeffrey Rogers signed and sent such a letter to Hukafit two weeks later, on July 16, 1987, in which he stated: "This is to confirm that In Design [Hukafit] and Jeffrey Rogers shall continue to work together for a further period, until May '88, when we will rediscuss our association. . ." HX 21. It is noteworthy that, consistent with the original terms of the Agreement, this renewal was for one year, terminated in the month of May, and contemplated further renewal.
At the trial, Rogers repudiated his aforementioned testimony and asserted that the Agreement "was finished" as of May 31, 1987, and that his letter did not relate to the Agreement, but rather that it was his intention to "revert back" to the relationship [with Hukafit] that was in existence prior to the Agreement. The Court examined Rogers closely on the obvious connection between the sending of the letter and his sworn testimony in the Oak Hill matter that the Agreement had in fact been renewed.

THE COURT: Let me ask you this, Mr. Rogers: Are you swearing here that there was no connection between  the letter that you sent and the testimony you gave in the deposition?

THE WITNESS: I can't recollect any connection between the two, your Honor. THE COURT: When you say you can't recollect, you are saying there may have been a connection or may not have been a connection but you can't say?


THE WITNESS: I cannot sit here and say that I really know where there was a connection between the two, no.

THE COURT: You have no recollection so you can't tell us definitively that there was no connection either, correct?

THE WITNESS: Asked like that, yes.

THE COURT: He has pointed out to you that there is certainly a coincidence here that is notable in the sequence of events. He has pointed that out to you in an effort to stimulate your recollection. You have indicated that it does not stimulate your recollection.

THE WITNESS: Correct.

THE COURT: You don't have a recollection. You can't deny that there was a connection?

THE WITNESS: I asked and asked myself why July 16th, not two days after I came back from America as an example. So that is why I really don't know why the two should necessarily be connected.

Tr. 1072-73.
We are reluctant, but compelled, to say that Jeffrey   Rogers' trial testimony on the question of whether the Agreement had been extended beyond May 31, 1987, is conspicuously unbelievable and untruthful, and that his credibility as witness in a United States Court, and as an honorable businessman in international commerce, is fatally impugned. We reject his testimony entirely. We are distressed with the testimony of his counsel, John Rosenheim, a member of the English bar, but will say only that we find it generally unconvincing. We find his purported advice to Rogers with respect to the July 16, 1987 letter to be of no consequence to the resolution of the issues before us.
We find that adequate notice of intention to renew the Agreement was given orally by Hukafit to Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear in November 1986, that the parties agreed that written and strictly timely notice could be dispensed with, that the parties in fact renewed the Agreement prior to its expiration on May 31, 1987, and that Jeffrey Rogers intended to evidence his renewal of the Agreement by his Oak Hill testimony and his July 16, 1987 letter. We specifically find that the Agreement was renewed and not amended.
Finally, we find that Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear, through its   counsel John Rosenheim, in the spring of 1988 authorized Hukafit a) to proceed against K-Mart in this lawsuit, and b) to protect its interests through enforcement of its copyrights against K-Mart. HX 15.
The Damask Design

Hukafit obtained, in the name of Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear, as copyright claimant, a copyright registration for the Damask design, Registration No. 172-938, effective December 6, 1984. Tr. 110-11, 352-3. This design originated in the London studios of Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear, and was given to David Binder, who brought it back to the United States in the third quarter of 1984. Tr. 111-115, 471-72. The original artwork is signed by Dennis Ashworth, a senior designer at Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear, is dated August 10, 1984, and carries a copyright legend. SX W, 79-80; HX 86, 82-85.
Hukafit manufactured and sold, during 1985 and 1986, 24,000 sweaters bearing the Damask design, having a wholesale value of $ 400,000 to $ 500,000 and a retail value of $ 1 million. These sweaters carried copyright notices, and photographs of the Damask sweaters were available for the scrutiny of buyers at Hukafit's showroom. Tr. 117-23; JX 19, 20; HX 19, 20. These Damask sweaters were   sold in more than 3,000 retail stores across the country. Tr. 123-30; 457-59; HX 13. Frank Ruggiero, who appeared as a representative of Selective, testified that "it is our business to constantly . . . shop . . . and see what people wear," and that he routinely shopped all the major department stores to inform himself of popular sweater designs. Tr. 541-61. Kathy Foley performed the same function for K-Mart. Tr. 524-25. K- Mart's buying agent, Fashion House, obtained 240 of the Damask sweaters from Hukafit on April 10, 1985. HX 13, Tr. 130-33. We find, accordingly, that both Selective and K-Mart had access to the Damask pattern in issue.
The parties have stipulated, and we so find, that the design of the Selective Style 9001 sweater is substantially similar to the Hukafit Damask sweater. Tr. 405-06; JX 14, 19, 20.

On or about April 8, 1987, Ruggiero, on behalf of Selective, displayed a sample of its 9001 sweater to K-Mart and advised that it was available for production and sale. Tr. 508-09, 517-18, 568. K-Mart's Merchandise Description Worksheet describes in detail the specifications of the 9001 sweater, and volume and price required. KX A; JX 2, 2- 1. This worksheet was initiated   on April 1, 1987. Tr. 511. K-Mart issued a purchase order to Selective dated April 8, 1987 for 4400 dozen of the 9001 sweaters. Tr. 520; JX 3 & 4. This order conditioned acceptance by Selective upon its agreement to indemnify K-Mart fully for any liability resulting from the sale and use of the sweaters. Id. On May 30, 1987, Selective issued a worksheet to N & Z Knitting Mills for the manufacture of the sweaters. JX 5; Tr. 601-606. Selective delivered the 9001 sweaters to K-Mart in late November 1987 for sale to the public. Tr. 406-408.
The Flexo-Craft Defense

Selective called Abraham Klein to assert a defense based on a certain engraving which purported to embody the Damask design before its creation by Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear's studio. Klein was the sole witness on this point. He is employed by Flexo-Craft Prints, a Brooklyn firm that prints heat transfer paper to be used on fabric. Tr. 645-46.
Klein's testimony focused on SX F, a computer printout of all of the style numbers for designs which Flexo-Craft Prints engraved, along with other data, including the date of engraving, the status of each style number, and the name of the customer to whom each style was sold.    Tr. 648-649. Selective sought to show through Klein that a transfer sheet film, SX E, with a "Floral Damask" design was engraved and used for printing in 1983.
Klein began to work for Flexo-Craft Prints in December 1984 or January 1985, Tr. 649-651, and therefore did not work for Flexo-Craft prints in 1983, which is the date on the transfer sheet film itself, SX E. Nor was he an employee of Flexo-Craft Prints when the data relating to the "Floral Damask" design was entered into the computer. As Mr. Klein testified, ". . . that wasn't my time." Tr. 669.

Klein testified that before he began working for Flexo-Craft Prints, his father worked there and was familiar with the computer system. Tr. 653-654. We observe that Selective did not call as a witness Klein's father, a principal in the business and the person who was presumably in charge in about 1983, when the Flexo-Craft Prints engraving was supposedly created. Selective failed to show that Klein's father could not have been subpoenaed to appear at the trial to obviate the speculative nature of his son's testimony on the origin and use of the "Floral Damask" design.
The computer printout in question was actually printed on March 8,    1988, at the request of Moses Schlesinger, an employee of Selective and the son of the principal of Selective, Abraham Schlesinger. Tr. 612-613, 651. Moses Schlesinger and the younger Klein are acquaintances from the same neighborhood. Tr. 610, 672-673.
Klein testified that during the course of his employment with Flexo-Craft Prints, from about February 1985 to the present, others routinely entered data into the computer program that produced the printout. Tr. 651, 654-655, 682- 83. Indeed, there were at least three and possibly as many as seven different people who had access to that computer. Tr. 682, 687. Klein had no knowledge of which employee actually typed the "Floral Damask" information into the computer. Tr. 688.
With respect to information contained on the printout, Klein testified that of the four digits of a style number appearing on the printout, the first number indicated a certain color. The rest of the numbers are assigned in sequence as those next available. Tr. 657-658. However, on page one of the printout, Style No. 1111 is described as "Thin Pin Stripe 1/4 Neg" and was purportedly engraved on 1/1/80, and Style No. 1112 was engraved on the same date, while a pattern   with a lower number, namely Style No. 1101 for Floral Damask, was engraved on a later date, 6/08/83. Similarly, Style No. 1105 was purportedly engraved on 1/6/86, while a later style number, Style No. 1110, was purportedly engraved on an earlier date, 11/5/84. Tr. 677-678.
Klein attempted to address this inconsistency by saying that before his coming to the company in 1985, the prior computer operators had grouped designs by type. Tr. 660, 676. However, "Floral Damask", clearly a floral design, is given Style No. 1101, while another floral design, "Monotone Leaf", shown on page six and purportedly engraved on 1/17/84, has Style No. 1807, but is not grouped in any way with Style No. 1101. Tr. 706. Klein also stated that, in the last five years while he has been at Flexo-Craft, the entries have been done in numerical order, while previously, they were not done in numerical order. Tr. 678-679. Under cross-examination, however, Klein admitted that he did not know the previous system. Tr. 686-687.
Klein gave no explanation for the very odd coincidence that in a 50-page printout with dates running from as early as 1980 through as late as the beginning of 1988, the one design in which Selective   was most interested for the purpose of defeating Hukafit's claim was the very first one on the first page of this large list. Tr. 679-680.

While the printout has a column entitled "Date Engrv", which would presumably be understood to mean the date the engraving was made, Klein testified that that date is simply the date the data is entered into the computer, which in turn is taken from the customer purchase order; it is not the date any engraving takes place. Tr. 658-659, 689-690, 708-709. Hence, even if a customer placed an order which would cause a date to be placed under the engraving date heading, and then later cancelled the order, that date would remain in the computer. Klein conceded that at most a date under the heading "Date Engrv" means that an order had been put in, but is no evidence that an engraving was actually made or that a product was shipped to a customer. Tr. 690.
Moreover, Flexo-Craft Prints' computer program is seriously flawed with respect to the dates it carries. An examination of printout page 16, for example, shows there is a date of engraving of "05/15/8", Tr. 713, and of course, there is no such date; on page 18 there is a date of engraving of "07/10/",    and of course, the date is incomplete; and the computer shows a date of "2/30/87" for Style Number 4120 on page 19, which is also obviously in error, since there is no such date. Tr. 713-714; SX F.
Klein was not sufficiently familiar with the details of the printout to be convincing as a witness. He did not know how data for the "Last Print" column got into the computer, Tr. 659, and he did not know why a large number (10) of styles on page 2 had "00/00/00" as the "last Print" date, Tr. 693.
We emphasize that Klein was not employed at Flexo-Craft Prints when the "Floral Damask" pattern was allegedly produced. Tr. 669; 680-681. Klein's only knowledge of the "Floral Damask" pattern arose when Moses Schlesinger came to him and, after consulting the printout, he went with Mr. Schlesinger to the Flexo-Craft Prints' bins to see what Style No. 1101 actually was. Tr. 701. As to the film itself, the only knowledge that Mr. Klein had of it was by reading the date on it, which states "1983". Tr. 680-681. Flexo-Craft Prints has no samples of fabric bearing its Damask design. Tr. 671-672, 697.
Klein further testified that not every film is dated by his company in the ordinary course of its business.    These films are dated only when the customer asks Flexo-Craft Prints to do so. Tr. 671. Thus, since admittedly Mr. Klein was not at the company in 1983, he has no direct knowledge of a request by one of the firm's customers, Delta Fabrics, asking Flexo-Craft in 1983 to put a date on the file relating to the "Floral Damask" design.

Klein testified that a date would be put on the transfer film itself only when a customer wanted the print for its exclusive use. Tr. 671-672. This is indicated by the use of the letter "C" to designate the style as confined to the indicated customer. Tr. 671. We observe, however, that while there are some "C"s in the printout, there is no "C" on the line for Pattern No. 1101 as, apparently, the system according to Klein required. SX F.
Klein stated that about 57,000 yards of this transfer paper were printed from the Flexo-Craft Prints engraving, and that he had gotten that information from the firm's computer shortly before testifying. Tr. 672. Selective's counsel, however, failed to ask Mr. Klein to bring a printout of this information to Court so it could be examined. Tr. 692.

Klein also agreed that in any case, even if some transfer paper was delivered   to Delta Fabrics, he has no knowledge of what that firm did with it. Tr. 694.
Selective failed to produce any invoices or other documents to show that Flexo-Craft Prints actually made a sale of 57,000 yards of its design to Delta Fabrics. Selective failed to produce a computer printout showing that 57,000 yards had actually been printed. Selective failed to produce any employee of Delta Fabrics to testify that they received 57,000 yards of this design from Flexo-Craft, and did not explain why it did not do so.
Based on the foregoing, the Court finds that the computer printout on its face is so full of deficiencies that it is not a trustworthy document to prove that Style No. 1101 Floral Damask was actually engraved on June 8, 1983. Indeed, it is a most dubious exhibit, and we give it no weight.
Since the only witness on this point, Klein, was not at the company in 1983 when the "Floral Damask" engraving was purportedly made and had no knowledge of the engraving until it was found by himself and Moses Schlesinger in March 1988 during the course of this litigation, the Court finds that there is no credible proof that heat transfer paper with that design was ever printed, delivered to   a customer, or used by any customer to print fabric. We specifically find that the asserted Delta Fabric transaction has not been established by any credible proof.
The Israeli Sweater Defense

Selective introduced SX J, K & L into evidence, which are derived from an investigation undertaken by Hukafit of the so-called "Israeli" sweater. Tr. 451-452; SX W, pp 248-51.
SX J is a facsimile letter dated November 16, 1987 from a firm of patent attorneys in Israel to plaintiff's counsel. In this document, Zwi Bregman reports the results of his November 12, 1987 visit to the Miss Segal store, where the "Israeli" sweater was allegedly bought by Ms. Naomi Moskowitz, daughter of a principal of Selective. One "Albert", the store proprietor, is reported to have said that with respect to the sweater's "Gimal" label, it "is unfamiliar to him", although "he does not pay too much attention to the names appearing on labels and it may be that in the past such a label could have been attached to women's clothing sold in the store".

When shown a receipt purportedly given by his store to Ms. Moskowitz, Albert is reported in this same document by Bregman to have said that this was an invoice of   the type originating with his store, but he "did not recognize the writing on this particular invoice" and he further stated that "it could have belonged to any one of the people working in his store at that time". SX J.
In another facsimile letter of December 7, 1987, SX L, Bregman confirms that he has checked and there is no Israeli trademark application or registration for "Gimal" for clothing, even though there is an "R" in a circle on the label. SX A and Tr. 598. There is also a confirmation by Bregman that Albert had said that he was "not quite sure as to the signature on the receipt".

The receipt in question, SX C, is dated October 18, 1984. The Court finds that even if this receipt were proven to be for the "Israeli" sweater relied upon by Selective, its date is after the date when Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear employee, Dennis Ashworth, created the Damask design in England, on or before August 10, 1984. HX 86. Furthermore, it is after the October 8, 1984 publication date, JX 21, on which Hukafit first showed a Damask sweater in its own showroom. Thus, even if we were to find that the "Israeli" sweater existed as of October 18, 1984, a fact we are not disposed to find, it could    have been copied from a Jeffrey Rogers Knitwear sweater bearing the Damask design in England or from a Hukafit sweater with the Damask design in the United States. Tr. 772-773.
Selective's primary witness on the origin of the "Israeli" sweater was Naomi Moskowitz, the daughter of Abraham Schlesinger, the principal of Selective, Tr. 546, and an employee of Selective Tr. 715-716. Ms. Moskowitz testified that she bought the "Israeli" sweater in Israel in September or October 1984, Tr. 717, and that she obtained a receipt for it and that the receipt says it was purchased on October 18, 1984. Tr. 718, SX C. She also said that she took the receipt home from Israel and put it together with all of her paper work that she keeps at home. Tr. 719-720. She said that she wore the "Israeli" sweater to work in November or December of 1984 and that "somebody noted they liked the style of the sweater and then I sold it to Selective". Tr. 720. She was paid about $ 20 in cash for the sweater. Tr. 721.
Ms. Moskowitz admitted that she didn't "remember the exact store" where she had purchased the sweater, and when asked for the name of the store by her counsel, Ms. Moskowitz read its name, "Ms. Segal",    from the exhibit in front of her. Tr. 718-719. She conceded that she has gone to Israel "a lot of times" and has bought 12 to 15 sweaters there. Tr. 722-723.
Ms. Moskowitz insisted that, even though she buys sweaters continuously, she remembered that the sweater in front of her at trial had been bought in Israel the first time she went there. Tr. 724. When asked why she testified at her prior deposition that she did not recall during what year and on what trip to Israel she bought the "Israeli" sweater, Ms. Moskowitz replied as follows:

Q. . . . So my question is why is it that you now say 1984 when your passport shows that you made trips in 1984 and 1986 and apparently you didn't know at the deposition which trip you bought the sweater on?

A. We have been discussing this sweater at the deposition and as we go along. And I did remember the receipt for 1984 and I did go to Israel in 1984, and at a later time, I did recall that I did bring it home on the 1984 trip. So everything got together.

Q. But is it correct that when I took your deposition on March 21st of this year at that time on that date, you did not recall which of the two earlier trips you bought the sweater on?

A.    At that time, I did not recall.

At her deposition, Ms. Moskowitz had testified that she really had no recollection of the receipt unless she read it, Tr. 732, and that she had no recollection that that receipt went with the "Israeli" sweater. Tr. 733-734.
Q. It is really the discussion with your father and this proceeding which has helped you to remember this information about the 1984 receipt?

A. Yes.

Id.
At her deposition, in answer to the question, "Is this Exhibit 9 the only receipt you received in Israel in 1984", Ms. Moskowitz stated, "I don't remember", and, when asked, "How do you know that this receipt goes with this sweater", she stated, "because going back to 1984, I remember it. Today I don't remember." Tr. 736.
At trial, Ms. Moskowitz initially stated that she first wore the "Israeli" sweater to Selective's office in November or December of 1984. Tr. 720, 729. However, at her deposition, Ms. Moskowitz had no recollection of even the year in which she first wore the "Israeli" sweater to work. Tr. 729. When asked why she didn't remember that date at her deposition but remembered it at trial, Ms. Moskowitz stated: "I can't tell you why I didn't remember at that  time. This time I believe that I came back in October and I wore it in November." Tr. 729-730. When Ms. Moskowitz was asked on cross-examination whether she was certain of her answer or whether it was open to question, she stated: "It is open. It is not certain." Tr. 730.
It was pointed out to Ms. Moskowitz on cross-examination that at her deposition, on two occasions, she had testified that no one ever asked her for the sweater and no one ever said to her something like "we want to use the sweater". Tr 730-731. Tr. 730-731.

He   teaches basic and advanced knitting. Tr. 744. Tay is "basically a technician", Tr. 747, 768, and has no formal training in cultural, industrial, or art history of any kind.

K-Mart conceded that the "Snowflake" design was on a K-Mart garment bearing the "Tough Gear" label, and the vendor is named in a K-Mart affidavit to be K-Mart. Tr. 321-322; HX 80. K-Mart took full responsibility for the offending garment. Tr. 270-271.

Mr. Pokotilow has repeatedly stated to the court that K-Mart in absolute good faith    wants to and will take steps to remove the merchandise from the shelves. He states furthermore that in addition to taking all such reasonable steps K-Mart will guaranty that it will not restore the merchandise without reasonable notice to the plaintiffs, sufficient to allow the plaintiff adequate opportunity to come back to court to block any resumption of the selling before it can take place. When asked on cross-examination at this trial if she had taken steps to check on whether the allegations by Hukafit's counsel were correct, Ms. Marjorie Alfus, K-Mart's house counsel, could only state, "I cannot tell you what steps I did   take." Tr. 259-260. This litigation also resulted in a Consent Judgment against K-Mart, with damages awarded to Hukafit. Tr. 183, 184, 261, 269; HX 47.

K-Mart is prepared to comply with your demand and remove the sweater from the marketplace and it will not be necessary to commence an action to obtain such a result. Therefore, we are sending this album intended for Mr. Binder to your office and request you advise your client that unless we are supplied with other photographs or samples depicting additional designs, we will assume that this collection numbered 1 through 179 does depict all the copyrighted designs owned by In-Design.
