Noted is the fact that James had given Graham a license to use the James-C version on PDSI-004-1.
Following the falling-out of the parties, Graham had the monochromatic bug corrected by another programmer, Peter Armenia,  and also had James's copyright notice removed on a "recut" of PDSI-004-1 (Pltf's Exh 7) (I:215/22 to I:216/13). Shortly thereafter Graham released PDSI-004-2 (Pltf's Exhs 32 & 40),  PDSI-005   (Pltf's Exh 8), PDSI-006 (Pltf's Exh 34), PDSI-006-1 (Pltf's Exh 24) and NOPV-6 (Pltf's Exh 25).  Later versions of disputed file retrieval programs are included on Graham's CD-ROMs   NOPV-7 (Pltf's Exh 26)(alleged to have been authored by Brian Martin), NOPV-8 (Pltf's Exh 28) (also alleged to have been authored by Martin) and NOPV- 9 (Pltf's Exh 36) (alleged to have been authored by Phil Swanson).
It is clear that, at least prior to trial, Graham considered the file retrieval program included on his products to be the best on the market. James claims such standing for the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE. Graham disagrees, but his testimony on this point is wildly inconsistent and wholly self-serving. For instance, at the preliminary injunction hearing -- where it behooved him to show irreparable harm etc. --, Graham stated that his then-current file retrieval program was the best on the market. He had also claimed, however, that such superiority attached to a file retrieval program   created, not by James, but by Martin (Preliminary Injunction Hearing Transcript at 105:10-18). As it has evolved, that statement was false. Such is made clear by simply noting that, at trial, it was shown that the Martin version of NIGHT.EXE (Pltf's Exh 20) was not released until several months after the preliminary injunction hearing. Thus, it is readily apparent that Graham, during the relevant time period, considered the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE (Deft's Exh 2) to be the best on the market. It is also of note that Graham testified that the James-C program was worth at least $ 60,000 (e.g., I:294/25 to I:295/9).
Because what is now determined to be the Martin version of NIGHT.EXE was not released until several months after the preliminary injunction hearing, it is also clear that what Graham had then represented to be the Martin program (submitted at trial as Pltf's Exh 19) is not such. At trial, Graham himself referred to Pltf's Exh 19 as "Larry's program with the bugs fixed *** from Brian Martin" (I:306/10-11; see also id. at I:293/15 to I:294/19). Martin did not testify. James testified that Pltf's Exh 19 was his code -- i.e., Deft's Exhs 1 & 2 -- minus his copyright   screen and certain other minor elements. (E.g., I:I779/15 to I:I786/22, I:I788/8 to I:I790/10). Based on such testimony and a simple review of the source codes in Pltf's Exh 19 and Deft's Exhs 1 & 2, this Court finds that these three versions of NIGHT.EXE are nearly identical, right down to the numerous spelling errors contained therein. For instance, Deft's Exh 2 contained the following misspellings which were mirrored in Deft's Exh 1 and Pltf's Exh 19: "cateqory," [sic] "extention," [sic] "avantage," [sic] "varibles," [sic] "Apend," [sic] "Unziping," [sic] "implimented" [sic] and "openning." [sic] Pltf's Exh 19 cannot be considered anything but a copy of Deft's Exh 2. It is also nearly identical to Deft's Exh 1 which is a printout of the source code of the program which James attempted to market after he had parted company with Graham and prior to the imposition by this Court of the preliminary injunction -- essentially Pltf's Exh 19 with a different title and with James's copyright notice intact. Martin's changes to Pltf's Exh 19 are deemed inconsequential. The source code of the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE contained in Deft's Exhs 1 and 2 and Pltf's Exh 19 appears on PDSI-004-1 (recut version), PDSI-004-2, PDSI-005, PDSI-006,    PDSI-006-1 and NOPV-6 (see I:300/22 to I:302/19, I:343/24 to I:344/8, I:1034/21 to I:1035/1 ; Pltf's Exh 33.
The literal elements of a computer program -- e.g., its source code -- are clearly copyrightable material under the Act. Computer Associates Intern., Inc. v. Altai, Inc. 982 F.2d 693, 702 (2d Cir. 1992).  The Act provides in pertinent part:

"Copyright protection subsists, in accordance with this title, in original works of authorship fixed in any tangible medium of expression, now known or later developed, from which they can be perceived, reproduced, or otherwise communicated, directly or with the aid of a machine or device. Works of authorship include the following categories:

(1) literary works ***." 17 U.S.C. § 102(a).

Congress intended that computer programs be classified as literary works.  Apple Computer, Inc. v. Franklin Computer Corp., 714 F.2d 1240, 1247-1252 (3rd Cir. 1983), cert. dismissed, 464 U.S. 1033 (1984). The Act defines a computer program as "a set of statements or instructions to be used directly or indirectly in a computer in order to bring about a certain result."    17 U.S.C. § 101.
To establish copyright infringement, a party must show both ownership of a valid copyright and a copying of the constituent elements of the work that are original.  Lotus Development Corp. v. Borland Intern., Inc., 49 F.3d 807, 813 (1st Cir. 1995), aff'd without op.,     U.S.    , 116 S. Ct. 804 (1996); Computer Associates, 982 F.2d at 701. A valid copyright registration is prima facie evidence of the validity of a copyright.  Fonar Corp. v. Magnetic Resonance Plus, Inc., 920 F. Supp. 508, 512-513 (S.D.N.Y. 1996) (citing Durham Indus., Inc. v. Tomy Corp., 630 F.2d 905, 908 (2d Cir. 1980). Both parties have introduced   such and so rebut the presumption raised by the other in that this Court has found that they cover the same material -- the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE as shown in Pltf's Exh 19 and Deft's Exh 1 & 2. See Pltf's Exh 14; Deft's Exh 17. There is little dispute that the James- C version of NIGHT.EXE is an original work.  Contentions to the contrary are without merit. Hence, the issue comes down to who owns the program.
As the parties agree, the essential issue herein is whether James was an employee of Graham when he wrote the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE. The Act states:

 "(a) Initial Ownership.--Copyright in a work protected under this title vests initially in the author or authors of the work. ***

"(b) Works Made for Hire.--In the case of a work made for hire, the employer or other person for whom the work was prepared is considered the author for purposes of this title, and, unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise in a written instrument signed by them, owns all of the rights comprised in the copyright." 17 U.S.C. § 201.

There was no such written agreement between the parties. Thus, if the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE is considered a work made for hire, Graham owns any copyright to such.  Section 101 of the Act defines a "work made for hire" as "a work prepared by an employee within the scope of his or her employment." Hence, it must be determined if the program was prepared by James as an employee of Graham. Under the Act, the determination whether a person is an employee is dictated by the "general common law of agency" -- Community for Creative Non-Violence   v. Reid ("Reid"), 490 U.S. 730, 751, 104 L. Ed. 2d 811, 109 S. Ct. 2166 (1989):


 "We consider the hiring party's right to control the manner and means by which the product is accomplished. Among the other factors relevant to this inquiry are the skill required; the source of the instrumentalities and tools; the location of the work; the duration of the relationship between the parties; whether the hiring party has the right to assign additional projects to the hired party; the extent of the hiring party's discretion over when and how long to work; the method of payment; the hired party's role in hiring and paying assistants; whether the work is part of the regular business of the hiring party; whether the hiring party is in business; the provision of employee benefits; and the tax treatment of the hired party. *** No one of these factors is determinative." Id. at 751-752.
The hiring party in Reid was a nonprofit organization ("CCNV") dedicated to eliminating homelessness. It had endeavored to construct for display in the District of Columbia a Christmas Nativity scene featuring, in lieu of the Holy Family, a homeless family. Reid was hired to and did sculpt   the family; CCNV was responsible for the other elements of the project. There was never any discussion regarding the copyright to the work. After the initial negotiations and subsequent hiring of Reid, the parties then collaborated on the early stages of the project to ensure that Reid's sculpture met CCNV's specifications. In analyzing the parties' roles and relationship, the Court noted that Reid, as a sculptor, was engaged in a skilled occupation. He was hired for a set fee, paid in installments (as opposed to a salary) and such fee was in consideration for one specific job. He did not have any payroll taxes withheld from such fee and did not receive any employee benefits; CCNV did not contribute to unemployment insurance or workers' compensation funds. The tools Reid used were his own and he worked out of his Baltimore studio, making daily or other immediate supervision by CCNV impracticable. He was retained for less than two months and had, except for having to meet a completion date, absolute freedom as to how long and when he worked and, if necessary, the hiring of assistants. Both during and after this time period, CCNV did not have the right to assign him additional projects.    It was also determined that CCNV was not in the business of creating sculptures. Hence, Reid was determined to be an independent contractor. Id. at 733-735, 751-752.
The Reid criteria were utilized and expounded upon in Aymes v. Bonelli, 980 F.2d 857 (2d Cir. 1992), which addressed a copyright dispute involving a computer program developed by an individual to maintain a swimming pool retailer's business records. After the programmer and the retailer had parted company and the retailer had begun using such program at its other locations, the programmer registered the program with the Copyright Office and brought an infringement action wherein the retailer defensively asserted that the program was a work for hire. Aymes ruled that several of the Reid factors were of universal significance -- viz., the hiring party's right to control the manner and means of creation, its right to assign additional projects, the skill required and the provision of employee benefits to and the tax treatment of the hired party -- and should be given more weight in determining the true nature of the employment relationship.
The retailer in Aymes was found to have exercised significant   control over the program's creation, which finding weighed in favor of a conclusion that the programmer was an employee, but, because of other facets of the relationship between the parties, the Court accorded less weight to this factor. It was also noted that the computer program therein at issue demanded a certain level of programming skill and that several other courts had held programmers to be "highly skilled independent contractors." Id. at 862.
Of greatest import to the Aymes Court were the facts that the programmer did not receive any employee benefits and did not have any payroll taxes withheld. These two factors were held to be "virtual admissions" by the retailer that the programmer was an independent contractor. It had benefitted in treating him as such when it came to the providing of benefits and the paying of a percentage of his payroll taxes, although ten years later and in court opportunistically sought to deny him that status when the issue of copyright infringement hinged thereupon. Ibid. Under the facts of that case, the method of payment, the regular business of the retailer (selling pools), the programmer's discretion over how and when to work, the   duration of the relationship, location of the work done, source of tools and the programmer's authority to hire assistants were accorded little weight. For instance, although programming work was not a part of the retailer's regular business of selling swimming pools, the Court noted that many employees of the retailer -- e.g., a custodian -- would not engage in the retailer's regular business of selling pools. Based on the above -- with greatest focus on the lack of benefits and withholding of payroll taxes --, Aymes concluded that the programmer was an independent contractor and the program was not a work for hire. Id. at 864.
In the present case, the evidence indicates that Graham, contrary to his assertions, had little control over or supervision of James. As is noted supra, he had done little more than show James the Anderson version of NIGHT.EXE and explain what he sought from James, enough so that James would meet his needs, but nothing more. The later idea of creating the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE was James's after he gained a fuller appreciation of what Graham sought. While James did some programming work at Graham's residence, most was done at his own   home or while he was driving a taxi and, quite possibly, prior to creating the James- QuickBASIC version. Further, it is clear that Graham is not a computer programmer; at the preliminary injunction hearing he was unable to explain even what the acronym "DOS" signified -- viz., Disk Operating System. He thus would have been unable to interject himself into the details of James's work or to exercise any meaningful control over such. While he also states that Ralph Markwardt, at his direction, had supervised and instructed James in the development of the James-C version, it is clear that Markwardt lacked the qualifications in programming to have been a supervisor in any meaningful sense. There is thus no credibility to Graham's assertion that he had controlled the manner and the means of creating the James-C version or of the subsequent support work James conducted thereanent. It would appear that even CCNV had exerted more control over Reid -- see supra and 490 U.S. at 733- 735, 752 -- than had Graham over James. This factor weighs in favor of a finding that James was not Graham's employee.
With regard to the right to assign other projects, it is clear that Graham did not possess   such right. The agreement which led to the James-QuickBASIC version of NIGHT.EXE was a discrete transaction -- a CD-ROM disk drive in exchange for the program. James proposed the idea of the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE to Graham; Graham did not assign such project to James. It was another and entirely discrete project initiated by James and accepted by Graham. Although Graham argues that the subsequent payments (Pltf's Exh 12) to James represented his monthly salary and evidence an employee-employer relationship, both contentions are rejected. The taped telephone conversation (Pltf's Exh 16) wherein, inter alia, James offered to do some additional work for Graham, further indicates that the parties had proceeded on a project-by-project basis with James's role being that of an independent party simply performing successively contracted tasks for Graham, often at his own behest and unlike the relevant facts of Aymes. Such weighs in favor of a finding that James was not Graham's employee.
It is clear that James possessed a modicum of skill as a self-taught computer programmer and that of such skill Graham had little to none. This Court concludes, however, that the level of programming   skill necessary to perform the work requested hardly seems as elevated as that at issue in Aymes. Nonetheless, it was not something that Graham himself could accomplish; he needed and sought a programmer therefor and was referred to James. This factor weighs in favor of a finding that James was not Graham's employee but is given less weight because of the program's simplicity.
Also noted is the fact that, although such circumstance was accorded little weight in Aymes, Graham was not in the business of writing software; his was the business of publishing and selling CD-ROMs (see, e.g., Pltf's Exh 5 (copyright screen: "NIGHTOWLS Communications & CDROM Publisher"). He successively hired several programmers to perform such genetic tasks, all of whom appear to have been free-lance, independent contractors, and not employees. Like James, each appears to have been hired by Graham on a per-project basis and for a relatively short period of time. James's work for Graham extended only from March through September 1991. There was no set schedule of hours or days during which James was required to work for Graham. There appears not to have been any deadlines set for the completion   of the James-C version or defined phases thereof. Finally, that James might have used certain pieces of Graham's hardware or software to complete his program, as Graham posits, is of little or no relevance. The fact that James did not hire any assistants is of no relevance.
The linchpin herein, as it was in Aymes, was Graham's failure to provide employee benefits or withhold payroll taxes from the five payments made to James. Graham attempts to distinguish Aymes by noting that the retailer therein was a multi-store retailer with many employees, while Graham did not have any regular employees and was less equipped to handle payroll deductions when he became involved with James. He also posits that such could not be effected because James had refused to provide his Social Security number to Graham, although Graham's accountant had nonetheless begun the process by which withholding could be effected. The evidentiary record is devoid, however, of testimony of Graham's accountant or any documentary evidence of an initiation of such process. Hence and in light of Graham's lack of credibility, his position is unsupported and rejected. In any event, Graham testified that such process   had not begun until September (II:1752/9 to II:1754/3) and that he hadn't expected to have it "up and running" until October 15th. He failed to withhold payroll taxes or to provide employee benefits. There are no other indicia of an employer-employee relationship. Additionally, four of the five checks paid to James and comprising Pltf's Exh 12 are dated in September -- after James had delivered the James-C version of the program to Graham in July 1991. Such indicate installment payments under the agreement, rather than "monthly" paychecks. Of final note is Graham's own testimony:

"Q Now, when exactly did Mr. James become your employee? A Full time employee, I'd say September 1st. Q Well, when did he become your employee in any sense? A Well, he worked for us in April. Q Do you know what an independent contractor is? A I do. Q Was he an independent contractor in April, or was he an employee? A I'd say independent. THE COURT: Independent? THE WITNESS: Independent. BY MR. OSTROWSKI: Q And when did he become your employee then? A September." II:1737/18 to II:1738/6.

Because this Court concludes that James was an independent contractor and not an employee of   Graham, it further concludes that the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE is not a work for hire and that the copyright vests in James, not in Graham.
It must now be determined which, if any, of Graham's later CD-ROM releases incorporated programs that were copies of the James-C program.  To establish copying, a party must show either (1) direct evidence of copying or (2) that the other party had access to the copyrighted work and that the other party's work is substantially similar to the work. Computer Associates, 982 F.2d at 701. This Court has found that Pltf's Exh 19 is a copy of Deft's Exh 2 and that such was copied at Graham's direction. Graham's own's testimony was that Pltf's Exh 19 was James's code with minor alterations effected by Martin. Further, a simple visual comparison of the three exhibits shows that Pltf's Exh 19 is very nearly identical to the others. By merely picking out the spelling errors in the documents, a novice would reach the same conclusion. Thus, even if this direct evidence did not support a finding of literal copying, it would nonetheless also point this Court to finding a substantial similarity among Deft's Exhs 1 and 2 and Pltf's Exh 19. Coupled with   the undisputed fact that Graham had access to James's code -- specifically Deft's Exh 2 --, both before and after the termination of their business relationship, the evidence noted leads this Court to infer copying.
With regard to the source code of the NIGHT.EXE versions used in NOPV-7, NOPV-8 and NOPV-9 (Pltf's Exhs 20 & 21), James states that, because he has shown that Graham had access to his source code, "the Court should impose a heavy burden on Graham to show he made no use of the program for the NOPV series" -- Defendant's Proposed Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, at 12 -- and that he has failed to carry that burden. Such is incorrect. If James is to prevail on his infringement claim with regard to these later versions of NIGHT.EXE, the burden falls on him to prove the substantial similarity of such versions to Deft's Exhs 1 and 2. See Computer Associates, 982 F.2d at 701, 714 (although defendant had access to program, plaintiff still required to prove substantial similarity); Durham Industries, Inc. v. Tomy Corp., 630 F.2d at 911 ( in order to prove infringement, a plaintiff must show valid copyright and copying; the latter may be shown by proof of access and   substantial similarity). James has presented no credible evidence that the computer programs represented by the source codes in Pltf's Exhs 20 or 21 are substantially similar to those represented in Deft's Exhs 1 and 2. Due to an earlier protective order imposed by this Court, James was denied access to the source codes contained in Pltf's Exhs 20 and 21. Thus, he was unable to offer his own comparison of such to the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE contained in Deft's Exh 1 and 2. He also failed to call his other expert. Instead, he gave only a partial demonstration of the asserted similarities of one non-literal element -- viz., the computer-user interface of the program. This Court finds such unconvincing on the issue of substantial similarity. This failure of proof prevents this Court from even conducting an analysis in line with Computer Associates, supra, as it apparently prevented James from doing in his Proposed Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law. This Court also rejects James's contention that Graham's experts testified that either Pltf's Exh 20 or 21 was substantially similar to Deft's Exh 1 and 2. They testified to the contrary. Further, a comparison of the source   code contained in Pltf's Exh 20 or 21 with Deft's Exh 1 and 2 is not helpful to James's case. This Court considers itself qualified to find only that the patent substantial similarity of the code that was apparent in Pltf's Exh 19 and Deft's Exh 1 and 2 is absent here.
In anticipation of such a conclusion, James seeks to reopen the evidentiary record so that he might present expert testimony of the substantial similarity of NOPV-7's, NOPV-8's and NOPV-9's file retrieval system to the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE. This Court will decline to do so. Firstly, it is noted that it is unclear under what rule of procedure James is making such motion, possibly somewhere between or under FRCvP 52(b) and 59(a)(2), although neither rule is exactly applicable. See 6A J. MOORE, MOORE'S FEDERAL PRACTICE, at 59.04[13] (1996). To the extent that it might be   said that a party may reopen under the instant circumstances, the decision to allow such is committed to the sound discretion of this Court. See Zenith Radio Corp. v. Hazeltine Research, Inc., 401 U.S. 321, 331-332, 28 L. Ed. 2d 77, 91 S. Ct. 795, reh'g denied, 401 U.S. 1015, 28 L. Ed. 2d 552, 91 S. Ct. 1247 (1971); Air Et Chaleur, S.A. v. Janeway, 757 F.2d 489, 495 (2d Cir. 1985). While the authority for such a motion is scant, John v. Sotheby's, Inc., 858 F. Supp. 1283, 1288 (S.D.N.Y. 1994), aff'd without op., 52 F.3d 312 (2d Cir. 1995), is instructive in noting that a Court may consider whether the moving party's failure to submit evidence was the result of that party's lack of diligence, the extent to which reopening the record might unduly or unfairly prejudice the non-movant and the interests of justice. Therein, the burden was placed on the movant to demonstrate the above. This Court will do the same.
James asserts that he did not present expert evidence in support of his position because he could not afford the requisite witness or witnesses. He states that, if he prevails on the other of his claims, he will thereafter have the wherewithal to   retain and pay an expert or experts. Such rationale, even if sincere, is rejected. As the record makes clear, James did avail himself of the services of at least one expert who, for whatever reason, did not testify. Although it facially appears that little unfairness would be worked upon Graham, who initiated this lawsuit and still enjoys the protection of this Court's preliminary injunction, the lack of any probative evidence that the program represented by Pltf's Exh 20 or 21 is substantially similar to the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE leads this Court to conclude that a reopening might not be unfairly and unduly prejudicial to Graham, but would be an improvident use of this Court's time and other resources. Further and while the interests of justice would clearly favor James if this inquiry were focused on Pltf's Exh 19 and the claims of infringement thereanent, such interests do not so favor him with respect to Pltf's Exh 20 or 21. This Court has given the parties ample opportunity to present their respective cases, in hindsight well beyond what might reasonably have been called for in light of the primitive nature of the programs in question. Further, James presented himself as   an expert and left this Court unconvinced. Based on the above, this Court considers that James would be unable -- and should be barred from trying -- to present the evidence he seeks to secure and submit. He has had his bite at the apple and has failed to carry his burden with regard to Pltf's Exh 20 or 21 and his claims of resultant or demonstrated infringement.
Implicit in and throughout the above analysis is this Court's conclusion that Graham's claims of infringement are meritless and warrant no further discussion.
Under the Act and for Graham's infringing activity, James is entitled   to recover

 "the actual damages suffered by him *** as a result of the infringement, and any profits of the infringer that are attributable to the infringement and are not taken into account in computing the actual damages. In establishing the infringer's profits, the copyright owner is required to present proof only of the infringer's gross revenue, and the infringer is required to prove his or her deductible expenses and the elements of profit attributable to factors other than the copyrighted work." 17 U.S.C. § 504(b). James's actual damages for infringement mirror his contract damages as concluded above, with one exception: Graham's failure to credit him with authorship of the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE.
James seeks actual damages for this failure to credit. Such an award is permissible and appropriate in this instance. 3 NIMMER ON COPYRIGHT, supra, at § 14.02[B] & fn.50 (1996). This damage amount is placed at $ 25,000 and goes uncontested. Such will be granted.
With respect to Graham's profits, James seeks $ 90,000, based essentially and simply on Graham's assertions during the Preliminary Injunction hearing that the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE was   worth $ 60,000 to $ 120,000. Such an award is permitted under the Act to prevent an infringing party from unfairly benefitting from a wrongful act. NIMMER, supra, at § 14.03. Further and as is also apposite to the present case, an award of only actual damages can provide little incentive to protect one's copyright. Profits may not, however, be speculative or remote and must be attributable to the infringement. Graham has the burden of proving deductible expenses and that all or part of his profits was attributable to something other than his unauthorized use of the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE. 17 U.S.C. § 504(b); NIMMER, supra, at § 14.03[A], [B] & [C].
In line with section 504(b) of the Act, this Court has been able to approximate Graham's gross revenue and the number of disks sold for the relevant time period. Graham estimates that his manufacturing and premanufacturing costs came to about $ 5.70 per disk. The figures on which he base such calculation appear to be inflated (e.g., fees paid to programmers to review the files to be included on the various releases) and, in light of Graham's overall lack of credibility, such figure will be reduced to four dollars   per disk.  Multiplying the total number of relevant disks sold (12,866) by $ 4, this Court finds that Graham has proven deductible expenses of $ 51,464. Because there undoubtably was an element "of profit attributable to factors other than the copyrighted work" (17 U.S.C. § 504(b)) -- e.g., that Graham probably would have sustained a modicum of profit even if he had continued to market the James-QuickBASIC version --, such figure will be rounded up to $ 55,000. Thus, this Court concludes that Graham's gross profits amount to $ 112,258.74 for the relevant period. Because such figure would have been reduced by royalty payments made to James and such are already taken into account in this Court's calculations of actual damages, James's entitlement to Graham's gross profits will be reduced by $ 17,716 to $ 94,542.74.
James has also shown the need for a permanent injunction against future infringing activity on the part of Graham. 17 U.S.C. 502. To the extent that Graham might deem it unnecessary in light of what he asserts to be superior   and later-released programs, the injunction will also be harmless. Such will be granted.
Accordingly, it is hereby FOUND, CONCLUDED and ORDERED that the defendant's motions to amend his Answer and Counterclaim is granted as noted above, that the defendant's motion to reopen for the further submission of evidence is denied, that the Preliminary Injunction is dissolved, that the Complaint is dismissed in its entirety, that the Third and Fourth and Fifth Counterclaims are dismissed, that the plaintiff and his corporation and their respective officers, partners, agents, servants, employees and all other persons in concert or participation with them are enjoined from producing, selling, marketing or otherwise using or distributing any file retrieval program that is substantially similar to the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE, from producing, selling, marketing or otherwise using or distributing any CD-ROM -- particularly, PDSI-004-1, PDSI-004-1 (recut), PSDI-004-2, PDSI-005, PDSI-006, PDSI- 006-1 and NOPV-6 -- containing such program and from otherwise infringing the defendant's copyright to such program, that all copies of programs substantially similar to the James-C version of NIGHT.EXE   in any form (particularly those CD-ROMs listed above) in the possession of plaintiff Graham, plaintiff Night Owl's Publisher, Inc. or either's officers, partners, agents, servants, employees and all other persons in concert or participation with either of them shall be immediately impounded, that the defendant is entitled to an award of $ 137,258.74 and attorney's fees to be determined by this Court at a later date and shall file and serve proper substantiation of same forthwith  and that the defendant shall be awarded his costs and disbursements in this action upon submission of proof of such to the Clerk of this Court.

WOOD, D.J.

This action arises out of defendants' March 1995 release and sale of an album entitled Soca Party 3 (the "Album") that included a song entitled "On the Road" (the "Song") written by Austin Lyons ("Lyons"). Plaintiff, Ice Music Limited ("Ice Music") is a music publishing company incorporated in Antigua. Defendant Michael Schuler ("Schuler") is the managing director of defendant Coral Recording Services Ltd. ("Coral Studios"), which is incorporated in Trinidad. Schuler and Coral Studios   manufactured and distributed the Album, which includes a recording of the Song performed by Ronnie McIntosh ("McIntosh") with a band known as Massive Chandelier.

Ice Music contends that it owns the exclusive copyright to the Song and that defendants' allegedly unauthorized use of the Song on the Album infringed that copyright. Defendants contend in response that their use of the Song did not constitute copyright infringement because they duly licensed the Song from Lyons.

For the reasons set forth below, I find that defendants are liable for copyright infringement.
2. The Publishing Agreement Between Ice Music and Lyons

On July 1, 1992, Ice Music and Lyons signed a publishing agreement (the "Publishing Agreement") in which Lyons assigned to Ice Music all copyrights for all musical works composed by him prior to March 31, 1993 "or during the continuance of any recording or license agreement between [Ice Music] and [Lyons] (. . .) pursuant to which Ice Music Ltd is entitled to release [Lyons's] sound recordings."  See Publishing Agreement Schedule B. At trial, Ice Music attempted to demonstrate that the Publishing Agreement had been extended and was still in effect when Lyons wrote the Song in late 1994 and/or early 1995.
The Publishing Agreement provided for a three-year extension of the agreement pursuant to certain conditions precedent:

[Lyons] hereby grant[s] to [Ice Music] an option to extend the Term of this Agreement for a period of three years commencing upon April 1st 1993, (the "Option Period"). [Ice Music] will exercise it's [sic] option (if at all) by notice in writing to [Lyons] to be given at any time prior to March 31st 1993. If during the Term [Lyons] receive[s] a bona fide written offer from a third party offering to publish musical works to be written by [Lyons] during the Option Period [Lyons] will deliver a copy of such offer to [Ice Music] and [Ice Music] will only be entitled to exercise it's [sic] option hereunder if [Ice Music] matches the royalty and advance provisions of the third party offer. In the event there is no third party offer then [Ice Music] will pay [Lyons] an advance of $ 5,000 (five thousand U.S. Dollars) within seven days of the commencement of the Option Period. Publishing Agreement Schedule B.
Thus, the Publishing Agreement provided two possible methods by which it could be extended. Pursuant to the first method   ("Method One"), Ice Music could exercise its option to extend the contract by fulfilling two conditions precedent: (1) giving Lyons notice prior to March 31, 1993 and (2) matching any other offer received by Lyons or, in the event that Lyons receives no other offers, paying Lyons an advance of $ 5000 within seven days of April 1, 1993. See Publishing Agreement Schedule B. Pursuant to the second method ("Method Two"), the Publishing Agreement was automatically extended "during the continuance of any recording or license agreement between [Ice Music] and [Lyons] (. . .) pursuant to which Ice Music Ltd is entitled to release [Lyons's] sound recordings." See Publishing Agreement Schedule B.
a. Extension of the Publishing Agreement Pursuant to Method One

At trial, Ice Music attempted to introduce into evidence a document dated December 11, 1992 that appeared to be a letter (the "Dolan Letter") authored by Michael A.P. Dolan, Ice Music's company director, to establish that the first condition precedent to Ice Music exercising its option to extend the Publishing Agreement -- notice in writing to Lyons -- had been satisfied. The Dolan Letter was addressed to Lyons in care   of Denzil Patterson ("Patterson") and purported to give notice that Ice Music was exercising its option to extend the term of the Publishing Agreement. However, I sustained defendants' objection to the admission of this letter. Tr. at 30. Dolan was not called as a witness. Lyons testified that he "could have seen" the Dolan Letter, but had no specific memory of it. Tr. 128-29. Patterson testified that he did not receive the Dolan Letter and that the address on the letter was incorrect. Tr. 58, 52. Without the admission of the Dolan Letter, Ice Music was unable to establish that first condition precedent to extending the Publishing Agreement -- notice in writing to Lyons of Ice Music's exercise of the option -- had been satisfied. 

In addition, Ice Music was unable to elicit testimony from any witness with personal knowledge, and offered no evidence, that the remaining condition precedent to Ice Music's exercise of its option -- payment of $ 5000 to Lyons within seven days of April 1, 1993 -- had been satisfied.
b. Extension of the Publishing Agreement Pursuant to Method Two

Ice Music also attempted to introduce into evidence a document dated December 1992 entitled "Exclusive  Artist Recording Agreement" (the "Recording Agreement"), in order to demonstrate that the Publishing Agreement had been extended pursuant to Method Two and thus was in effect when Lyons wrote the Song.

i. The Admissibility of the Recording Agreement

Ice Music never formally moved to have the Recording Agreement received as evidence. However, defendants' only objection to the admission of the Recording Agreement was unfair surprise. Ice Music produced the Recording Agreement only during the course of the trial, not during discovery or in the joint pretrial order, although defendants had requested all contracts and agreements between Ice Music and Lyons during discovery.

 Unfair surprise is not a sufficient reason for excluding otherwise relevant evidence, because any prejudice resulting from unfair surprise can almost always be counteracted by a continuance. Fed. R. Evid. 403 advisory committee's note (noting that surprise was intentionally excluded from Rule 403's list of factors in decision whether to exclude relevant evidence because "the granting of a continuance is a more appropriate remedy than exclusion of the evidence" in the face of claims of unfair surprise).

Defendants   did not request any additional time to prepare a response to Ice Music's introduction of the Recording Agreement, although I offered such time.    Thus, unfair surprise does not lead me to reject the Recording Agreement. However, the facsimile copy of the Recording Agreement that Ice Music attempted to introduce must be shown to fit into an exception to the "best evidence" rule. See Fed. R. Evid. 1002. It does so: The  facsimile copy is a duplicate that "is admissible to the same extent as an original unless (1) a genuine question is raised as to the authenticity of the original or (2) in the circumstances it would be unfair to admit the duplicate in lieu of the original." Fed. R. Evid. 1003. Here, defendants raised no question as to the authenticity of the original Recording Agreement. Moreover, given that two of the three people who signed the Recording Agreement  -- Lyons, the recording artist, and Patterson, a witness -- testified that the Recording Agreement was authentic, see Tr. 98-99, 129-30, there is no reason to doubt its authenticity. Thus, I now admit the Recording Agreement into evidence.
ii. Duration of the Recording Agreement

Article 2.1 of the Recording Agreement defines the Recording Agreement's duration:

The Term of this agreement will commence upon the full execution of this Agreement and shall continue for one Contract Period. The Company shall have and the Artist hereby grants to the Company the option in the first Contract Period and each successive Contract Period up to and including the fourth to extend the Term subject to the Company's full and proper performance of its obligations hereunder by one further separate and successive Contract Period so that the Term may extend for a total of five Contract Periods.    Each of the options shall be exercisable by notice in writing to the Artist before the end of the then current Contract Period of the Agreement. The Artist agrees that if the Artist has not received any such notice from the Company by the date upon which the then current Contract Period would otherwise   expire such Contract period shall automatically be extended until the Artist shall so advise the Company in writing and the Company shall have seven (7) days from receipt of that notice in which to exercise its option. In the event of the Company exercising the relevant option following receipt of the notice aforesaid the Term hereof shall be deemed to have continued up to the date of such exercise by the Company. Recording Agreement art. 2.1. Thus, the Recording Agreement, which was originally signed in December of 1992, was extendable for a total of as many as five Contract Periods. A "Contract Period" is defined as:


whichever shall be the longer of a period of twelve months or a period of six (6) months from the fulfillment of the recording commitment in such Contract Period PROVIDED THAT no Contract Period shall exceed two years. Recording Agreement art. 1.3.

Because a Contract Period can be twelve months long, and the Term of the Recording Agreement is automatically extended for up to a total of five Contract Periods if no action is taken by either Ice Music or Lyons, the Recording Agreement could still have been in effect at the time of the actions challenged,    and indeed could remain in effect until December 1997. Moreover, no evidence was presented at trial to demonstrate that either Ice Music or Lyons took any action that would have resulted in the termination of the Recording Agreement. Indeed, Lyons testified that he is an Ice Music recording artist and has been one for the last few years. Tr. 126-27.
B. Defendants' Attempts to Establish that They Obtained a Non-Exclusive License With Respect to the Song

Lyons began to write the Song sometime in December 1994, and it was recorded at Coral Studios in early January 1995. At around the time the Song was written and recorded, Noel Monsegue ("Monsegue"), representing Sorrel Records  and Coral Studios, made a number of payments to Lyons in exchange for Lyons' writing and producing the Song

When these payments were made no written record was made to memorialize the transactions. However, in July 1995, after this action was filed, Patterson signed a receipt (the "Receipt") indicating that on December 15, 1994, he received 800 Trinidad and Tobago Dollars from Monsegue as the initial payment in exchange for Lyons writing the Song for Sorrel Records and Coral Studios. The Receipt memorializing this alleged payment, which is dated December   15, 1994 but was not actually executed until July 1995, states:

Received from Noel Monsegue the sum of eight hundred T&T Dollars as deposit payment towards song composition by Austin Lyons "Superblue" for Ronnie McIntosh. It is signed "Denzil Patterson." Patterson testified that he signed the Receipt in Canada.

Patterson testified that he served as Lyons's manager from sometime in 1986 to sometime in 1995. Tr. 41. He testified that his duties included "taking [Lyons] to shows, collecting money, booking [Lyons]    on shows, whatnot." Tr. 42. Patterson also testified that in December 1994 he received money from Monsegue on behalf of Lyons for the composition of the Song. Tr. 43-44. Lyons testified that Patterson was his "road manager," acted as his promoter and producer at times, and performed certain management    functions, including collecting money, but that his actual manager was Patricia Joseph. Tr. 109-10, 118. Lyons also testified that he, Lyons, received the payments from Monsegue directly for the composition of the Song around the time the Song was written and produced. Tr. 119-20.


Lyons and Patterson contradict each other's testimony as to (1) whether Monsegue paid the money to Patterson or directly to Lyons and (2) whether at least a portion of the money was paid on December 15, 1994, or whether the first payment was made sometime in January 1995 during the course of the performance and recording of the Song. Although Lyons's testimony was often unclear and difficult to follow, based on Lyons's demeanor and the specificity of his testimony with respect to how Monsegue made payments to him during the course of the recording of the Song, I find him more credible than Patterson with respect   to these questions.
II. Analysis

A. Liability

 A prima facie case of copyright infringement consists of proof that the plaintiff owns a valid copyright and the defendant has engaged in unauthorized copying. Novelty Textile Mills, Inc. v. Joan Fabrics Corp., 558 F.2d 1090, 1092 (2d Cir. 1977).

 In any judicial proceedings the certificate of a [copyright] registration made before or within five years after first publication of the work shall constitute prima facie evidence of the validity of the copyright and of the facts stated in the certificate.

17 U.S.C. § 410(c). By submitting its Certificate, Ice Music has produced prima facie evidence that it owns a valid copyright. It is undisputed that Ice Music did not authorize defendants to record the Song. Thus, Ice Music has established a prima facie case of copyright infringement.

Defendants argue, however, that their publication of the Song did not constitute copyright infringement because, they allege, they own a non-exclusive license from Lyons to publish the Song that prevails over Ice Music's copyright.  When a defendant in a copyright action seeks to justify copying by establishing that it was  granted authority to copy by a third party, the defendant bears that burden of establishing that such other person was entitled to grant the authority. See, e.g., Von Tilzer v. Jerry Vogel Music Co., 53 F. Supp. 191, 195 (S.D.N.Y. 1943), aff'd sub nomine, Gumm v. Jerry Vogel Music Co., 158 F.2d 516 (2d Cir. 1946); see also 3 Melville B. Nimmer & David Nimmer, Nimmer on Copyright § 12.11[D] (1996).

Specifically, defendants argue that Lyons granted them a non-exclusive license that, pursuant to 17 U.S.C. § 205(e), prevails over the transfer of copyright ownership from Lyons to Ice Music. Section 205(e) states that:

 [a] nonexclusive license, whether recorded or not, prevails over a conflicting transfer of copyright ownership if the license is evidenced by a written instrument signed by the owner of the rights licensed or such owner's duly authorized agent, and if --

(1) the license was taken before execution of the transfer; or (2) the license was taken in good faith before recordation of the transfer and without notice of it.

Defendants contend that the Receipt is the written instrument evidencing the grant of the license; that Lyons  was at the relevant time "the owner of the rights licensed"; and that Patterson signed the Receipt as Lyons's duly authorized agent.  Ice Music contends that the December 15, 1994 exchange of money between Patterson and Monsegue that the Receipt purports to memorialize never took place, that even if the exchange    had taken place the Receipt did not satisfy the written instrument requirement of § 205(e) because (1) it was neither timely nor sufficient, (2) Lyons was not "the owner of the rights licensed" at the time Patterson allegedly received money from Monsegue, and (3) Patterson was not Lyons's duly authorized agent (a) when he allegedly received the money in December 1994 and (b) when he signed the Receipt in July 1995.


  I find Patterson's testimony with respect to the existence of this alleged December 15, 1994 payment unbelievable, and thus necessarily find that the Receipt is not evidence of any such payment. I thus hold that the Receipt does not satisfy the requirement of a written instrument evidencing the assignment of a non-exclusive license pursuant to § 205(e). Having found that the December 15, 1994 did not occur, I need not address the other issues raised by Ice Music.

Thus, for the reasons set forth above, I hold (1) that the defendants's unauthorized use of the Song constituted infringement on Ice Music's copyright and (2) that defendants have not established that Lyons assigned them a non-exclusive license with respect to the Song that prevails over Lyons's transfer of his copyright in the Song to Ice Music pursuant to 17 U.S.C. § 205(e).
B. Damages

Ice Music requests that I find that defendants were unjustly enriched by their copyright infringement in the amount of at least $ 7,950.00.  If a copyright owner who prevails in a statutory infringement action does not choose statutory damages, he is entitled to recover "any profits of the infringer that are attributable to the  infringement and are not taken into account in computing the actual damages." 17 U.S.C. § 504(b). Ice Music has not submitted any evidence of actual damages. Thus, Ice Music can recover only that portion of defendants' profits from the sale of the Album that is attributable to the infringement.

Ice Music has submitted three invoices recording transactions between Coral Studios and three different record dealers, in amounts totaling $ 7,950.00. Subtracting the price of an unrelated record included on those invoices, the invoices reflect $ 6550.00 in gross revenue attributable to the Album at issue here.

 Copyright law puts the burden on the infringer "to prove his or her deductible expenses" that may then be deducted from gross revenue to result in the ultimate damage award. 17 U.S.C. § 504; see Abeshouse v. Ultragraphics, 754 F.2d 467, 470 (2d Cir. 1985). Defendants have submitted no evidence of deductible expenses. Because defendants have defaulted on this element, I have the discretion to deduct no expenses from the gross revenue, considering the entire amount as profit. However, because Ice Music has previously submitted an affidavit to this court -- in conjunction with its   request that the preliminary injunction bond that Ice Music was required to post be lowered -- stating that defendants' total cost to produce each unit of the Album sold would be approximately $ 6.59, August 25, 1995 Dolan Aff. P 7, I will subtract that amount of cost per unit from the amount of gross revenue established by Ice Music. Thus, the total amount of profit on the Album that Ice Music has established is $ 1607.50.

The Song is only one among many songs on the Album.  Copyright law puts the burden on defendants to prove "the elements of profit attributable to factors other than the copyrighted work." 17 U.S.C. § 504; see Lottie Joplin Thomas Trust v. Crown Publishers, Inc., 592 F.2d 651, 657 (2d Cir. 1978). Defendants have also submitted no evidence relevant to establishing which portion of the profits results from the non-infringing recordings that were included on the Album with the infringed compositions. Because defendants have defaulted on this element and there is no evidence before the court that could form the basis for a reasoned apportionment of the profits to infringing and non-infringing portions of the Album, I will treat the entire amount of profit as resulting   from the infringing Song. Thus, I award Ice Music $ 1607.50 in damages.

Ice Music also requests that I award it attorney fees. I find that an award of attorney fees is not appropriate in this case. Due to Ice Music's failure to produce the Recording Agreement until the trial of this action had already begun, it was not clear that Ice Music actually had a contract granting it rights to the Song that was in effect before the alleged non-exclusive license was granted until Ice Music belatedly produced the Recording Agreement. Thus, defendants cannot wholly be faulted for proceeding to trial in this action, as it appeared prior to trial that they might possess a meritorious defense. See Roy Export Co. Establishment v. Columbia Broadcasting Sys. Inc., 503 F. Supp. 1137, 1155 (S.D.N.Y. 1980), aff'd, 672 F.2d 1095 (2d Cir. 1982) (propriety of attorney fee award turns on substantiality of defense offered).
III. Conclusion

For the reasons stated above, I find that defendants are liable for copyright infringement. Thus, I grant Ice Music's request for a permanent injunction. Defendant Coral Sound and defendant Michael Schuler in his capacity as managing director of Coral Sound,    and their agents, affiliates, licensees, and distributors, are hereby enjoined from:

1) manufacturing, distributing, advertising, importing, selling or shipping any copy of, or derivative work containing, the musical composition "On the Road," including but not limited to the "Soca Party 3" album (in all recorded formats); and

2) using any material copied from and substantially similar to the musical composition "On the Road" in any of defendants' audio and/or audio-visual products.

The clerk is directed to release the bond posted by Ice Music in the amount of $ 2,000.00. I award Ice Music damages in the amount of $ 1607.50. The clerk of court is directed to close this case.

SO ORDERED.

August 19, 1996

Kimba M. Wood

United States District Judge

It is not necessary that an individual perform the songs in order to be held liable for copyright infringement. Finally, Khalifa argues that the district court abused its discretion in awarding statutory damages of $ 5000 for the five instances of copyright infringement. This contention is meritless.  The statute allows an award of up to $ 20,000 per violation. § 504(c). Within the parameters set by § 504(c), the awarding of statutory damages is solely within the discretion of the court. See Oboler, 714 F.2d at 213. The record supports the court's finding that the infringement was willful and, further, the award is well within the statutorily permissible range.
