BOYCE F. MARTIN, JR., Chief Judge, dissenting. This case presents for me one of the more obvious examples of how laudable societal objectives, recognized by both the Constitution and statute, have been thwarted by a decided lack of judicial prudence. Copyright protection as embodied in the Copyright Act of 1976 is intended as a public service to both the creator and the consumer of published works. Although the Act grants to individuals limited control over their original works, it was drafted to stimulate the production of those original works for the benefit of the whole nation. The fair use doctrine, which requires unlimited public access to published works in educational settings, is one of the essential checks on the otherwise exclusive property rights given to copyright holders under the Copyright Act. [****1651]
Ironically, the majority's rigid statutory construction   of the Copyright Act grants publishers the kind of power that Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution is designed to guard against. The Copyright Clause grants Congress the power to create copyright interests that are limited in scope. Consequently, the Copyright Act adopted the fair use doctrine to protect society's vested interest in the sharing of ideas and information against pursuits of illegitimate or excessive private proprietary claims. While it may seem unjust that publishers must share, in certain situations, their work-product with others, free of charge, that is not some "unforeseen byproduct of a statutory scheme;" rather, it is the "essence of copyright" and a "constitutional requirement." Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Tel. Serv. Co., 499 U.S. 340, 349, 113 L. Ed. 2d 358, 111 S. Ct. 1282 (1991).
Michigan Document Services provided a service to the University of Michigan that promoted scholarship and higher education. Michigan Document Services was paid for its services; however, that fact does not obviate a fair use claim under these facts. Requiring Michigan Document Services to pay permission fees in this instance is inconsistent with the primary mission of the Copyright Act. The individual   rights granted by the Act are subservient to  [***24]  the Act's primary objective, which is the promotion of creativity generally. We must therefore consider the fair use provision of Section 107 of the Act in light of the sum total of public benefits intended by copyright law. In this instance, there is no adverse economic impact on Princeton University Press that can outweigh the benefits provided by Michigan Document Services. Indeed, to presume adverse economic impact, as has the majority, is to presume that the $ 50,000 in fees currently earned by plaintiff is mandated by the Act in every instance -- something I hesitate to presume.
That the majority lends significance to the identity of the person operating the photocopier is a profound indication that its approach is misguided. Given the focus of the Copyright Act, the only practical difference between this case and that of a student making his or her own copies is that commercial photocopying is faster and more cost- effective. Censuring incidental private sector profit reflects little of the essence of copyright law. Would the majority require permission fees of the Professor's teaching assistant who at times must copy,    at the Professor's behest, copyrighted materials for dissemination to a class, merely because such assistant is paid an hourly wage by the Professor for this work?
The majority's strict reading of the fair use doctrine promises to hinder scholastic progress nationwide. By charging permission fees on this kind of job, publishers will pass on expenses to colleges and universities that will, of course, pass such fees on to    students. Students may also be harmed if added expenses and delays cause professors to opt against creating such specialized anthologies for their courses. Even if professors attempt to reproduce the benefits of such a customized education, the added textbook cost to students is likely to be prohibitive.
The Copyright Act does not suggest such a result. Rather, the fair use doctrine contemplates the creation and free flow of information; the unhindered flow of such  [***25]  information through, among other things, education in turn spawns the creation and free flow of new information.
In limiting the right to copy published works in the Copyright Act, Congress created an exception for cases like the one before us. When I was in school, you bought your books and   you went to the library for supplemental information. To record this supplemental information, in order to learn and benefit from it, you wrote it out long-hand or typed out what you needed --not easy, but effective. Today, with the help of free enterprise and technology, this fundamental means of obtaining information for study has been made easier. Students may now routinely acquire inexpensive copies of the information they need without all of the hassle. The trend of an instructor giving information to a copying service to make a single set of copies for each student for a small fee is just a modern approach to the classic process of education. To otherwise enforce this statute is nonsensical. I therefore dissent.
[***26]  MERRITT, Circuit Judge, dissenting. The copying done in this case is permissible under the plain language of the copyright statute that allows "multiple copies for classroom use:" "The fair use of a copyrighted work . . . for purposes such as . . . teaching (including multiple copies for classroom use), . . . is not an infringement of copyright." 17 U.S.C. § 107 (emphasis added). Also, the injunction the Court has upheld exceeds the protections provided   by the Copyright Act of 1976 regardless of whether the use was a fair use and is so grossly overbroad that it violates the First Amendment.
I.

This is a case of first impression with  [****1652]  broad consequences. Neither the Supreme Court nor any other court of appeals has interpreted the exception allowing "multiple copies for classroom use" found in § 107 of the copyright statute. There is no legal precedent and no legal history that supports our Court's reading of this phrase in a way that outlaws the widespread practice of copying for classroom use by teachers and students.
For academic institutions, the practical consequences of the Court's decision in this case are highly unsatisfactory, to say the least. Anyone who makes multiple copies for classroom use for a fee is guilty of copyright infringement unless the portion copied is just a few paragraphs long. Chapters from a book or articles from a journal are verboten. No longer may Kinko's and other corner    copyshops, or school bookstores, libraries and student- run booths and kiosks copy anything for a fee except a small passage. I do not see why we should so construe plain statutory language that on its face permits "multiple copies for classroom use." The custom of making copies for classroom use for a fee began during my college and law school days forty years ago and is now well- established. I see no justification for overturning this long-established practice.
[***27]  I disagree with the Court's method of analyzing and explaining the statutory language of § 107 providing a fair use exception.  Except for "teaching," the statute is cast in    general, abstract language that allows fair use for "criticism," "comment," "news reporting" and "research." The scope or extent of copying allowed for these uses is left undefined. Not so for "teaching." This purpose, and this purpose alone, is immediately followed by a definition. The definition allows "multiple copies for classroom use" of copyrighted material. The four factors to be considered, e.g., market effect and the portion of the work used, are of limited assistance when the teaching use at issue fits squarely within the specific language of the statute, i.e., "multiple copies for classroom use." In the present case that is all we have -- "multiple copies for classroom use."
There is nothing in the statute that distinguishes between copies made for students by a third person who charges a fee for their labor and copies made by students themselves who pay a fee only for use of the copy machine. Our political economy generally encourages the division and specialization of labor. There is no reason
why in this instance the law should discourage high schools, colleges, students and professors from hiring the labor of others to make their copies any more than there is a reason to discourage lawyers from hiring paralegals to make copies for clients and courts. The Court's distinction in this case  [***28]  based on the division of labor -- who does the copying -is short sighted and unsound economically.
Our Court cites no authority for the proposition that the intervention of the copyshop changes the outcome of the case. The Court errs by focusing on the "use" of the materials made by the copyshop in making the copies rather than upon the real user of the materials -- the students. Neither the District Court nor our Court provides a rationale as to why the copyshops cannot "stand in the shoes" of their customers in making copies for noncommercial, educational   purposes where the copying would be fair use if undertaken by the professor or the student personally.
Rights of copyright owners are tempered by the rights of the public. The copyright owner has never been accorded complete control over all possible uses of a work. Generally, "the monopoly privileges [of copyright] that Congress may authorize are neither unlimited nor primarily designed to provide a special private benefit," Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, Inc., 464 U.S. 417, 429, 78 L. Ed. 2d 574, 104 S. Ct. 774 (1984), a statement the Court more fully explained as follows:
The limited scope of the copyright holder's statutory monopoly, like the limited copyright duration required by the Constitution, reflects a balance of competing claims upon the public interest: Creative work is to be encouraged and rewarded, but private motivation must ultimately serve the cause of promoting broad public availability of literature, music, and the other arts . . . . When technological change has rendered its literal terms ambiguous, the Copyright Act must be construed in light of its basic purpose. [****1653]

Twentieth Century Music Corp. v. Aiken, 422 U.S. 151, 156, 45 L. Ed. 2d 84, 95 S. Ct. 2040 (1975) (footnotes omitted).    The public has the right to make fair use of a copyrighted work and to exercise that right without requesting permission from, or paying any fee  [***29]  to, the copyright holder. The copyshop makes its money based on the number of pages copied, not the content of those pages. The Copyright Act both establishes a general grant of monopoly powers to holders of copyrights and codifies the "fair use" doctrine as an exception to that broad grant. Section 106 of the Copyright Act confers exclusive rights upon individual creators to distribute and produce their original copyrighted work and "derivative works based upon the copyrighted work." 17 U.S.C. § 106. However, section 107 carves out an  [****1656]  exception to the exclusive rights conferred in section 106, permitting members of the public to use copyrighted works for "fair" purposes.  17 U.S.C. § 107. Whether a challenged use qualifies as a "fair use" is to be determined by considering section 107's four fair use factors, which are set forth in the majority opinion, as well as any other relevant considerations. The four fair use factors, and any other relevant factors, must be applied and weighed together "in light of the purposes of copyright" protection.  Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569, 114 S. Ct. 1164, 1171, 127 L. Ed. 2d 500  [***37]  (1994) (citing Pierre N. Leval, Toward a Fair Use Standard, 103 HARV. L. REV. 1104, 1110-11 (1990)).
"The primary objective   of copyright is not to reward the labor of authors, but 'to promote the Progress of Science and useful Arts.'" Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Tel. Serv. Co., 499 U.S. 340, 349, 113 L. Ed. 2d 358, 111 S. Ct. 1282 (1991) (quoting U.S. CONST. art. I, § 8, cl. 8). This court has explained:

The question that must ultimately be answered is whether that which is a fair use for a student--copying--is not a fair use if done for the student by another, and for a profit.
Plainly, the Copyright Act explicitly anticipates that use of a work by "reproduction in copies . . . for purposes such as . . . teaching (including multiple copies for classroom use)," will sometimes be a fair use even though teaching is commonly conducted for profit.  17 U.S.C. § 107.
Thus, MDS's copying of materials, which indisputably are for "teaching (including multiple copies for classroom use)," must be tested for fair use under the four "factors to be considered" in section 107. Id.
The first factor that courts must evaluate in a fair use determination is "the purpose and character of the use, including whether such use is of a commercial   nature or is for nonprofit educational purposes." 17 U.S.C. § 107(1).
[***39]  There are two parts to section 107's first factor: (1) the degree to which the challenged use has transformed the original, and (2) the profit or nonprofit character of the use. Both a non-transformative use determination and a "commercial" use determination weigh against a finding of fair use, though by no means conclusively.

Ordinarily, analysis of transformative character under the first prong of the first factor centers on "whether the new work merely 'supersedes the objects' of the original creation . . . or instead adds something new, with a further purpose or different character, altering the first with new expression, meaning, or message; it asks, in other words, whether and to what extent the new work is 'transformative.'" Ct. at 1170; Harper & Row, 471 U.S. at 549-53, does not diminish in any measure the rule that legislative history is not a proper source of authority for this court when the language of the statute is not analogous. The majority substitutes language contained only in pre-enactment political maneuvering of Congress for our obligation to rely, as we are required to do, on the rich body of case law that properly guides our application of the statutory factors to the specific facts of a case. In Campbell, 114 S. Ct. at 1170, the Court noted that "the task is not to be simplified with bright-line rules, for the statute, like the doctrine it recognizes, calls for case-by-case analysis." The case for copyright infringement is very weak indeed if the court must rely on the unenacted theater of Committee Reports to find infringement. In sum, even if the four statutory factors of section 107 are not "models of clarity" and their application to the facts of this case is "troublesome"--a challenge of the kind federal appellate judges are paid to face every day--the four factors are not ambiguous. Therefore, we may not properly resort to legislative history. I am satisfied to rely exclusively upon the evidence and lack of evidence on the record before us and the plain language of the Copyright Act and its construction in the case law; and they lead me to conclude that MDS's compilation into coursepacks of excerpts selected by professors is a "fair use" of the copyrighted materials.

For all the foregoing reasons, I conclude that MDS did not infringe upon the copyrights of the publishers.

Bolton incurred and paid the following business and personal management fees in connection with his infringing profits: $ 2,389,872 with respect to the album; $ 8,210 with respect to the single; and $ 115,913 with respect to publishing. (Id. at 6-7). Bolton paid income taxes of $ 2,803,909 on his combined profits.
Bolton is entitled to deduct the income tax payments and the business management and personal  management fees. (Id. at 6-7, 9 (COL 4, 7)). After permissible deductions, appropriate allocation of the income taxes, and the jury's apportionment, Plaintiff is entitled to recover from Bolton $ 716,601 from the album profits, (id.), and $ 216,323 from the single and publishing profits, (id. at 8.).
3. Goldmark

Goldmark realized profits from the song only, in the amount of $ 570,000, exclusive of income taxes and business management fees. Goldmark paid income taxes with respect to his infringing profits of $ 206,954. Goldmark incurred and paid business management fees in connection with that income of $ 28,523. (Id. at 5.) The income tax payments and management fees are allowable deductions. (Id. at 5, 9 (COL 4, 8).) After the deductions and based on the jury's apportionment, Plaintiff is entitled to recover from Goldmark $ 220,785 in profits from the song. (Id. at 5-6.)
C. The Parties' Objections

The parties, in their respective filings, object to various legal conclusions and related facts contained in the Report and the Amended Report. Taken together, the objections and responses address two major issues. The first is whether Bolton, Goldmark, and Sony are entitled to deduct, from   the profits on which the award to Plaintiff is to be based, income tax expenses or liabilities incurred in connection with profits from their infringing activities. The second is whether Bolton and Goldmark are entitled to deduct certain business and personal management fees.
1. Deductibility of Bolton's and Goldmark's Income Tax Payments and Sony's Income Tax Liability

This series of objections and responses raises two questions. The first is whether, as a general matter, a copyright infringer is entitled to deduct, from the profits on which an award to the copyright owner is based, income tax expenses incurred in connection with profits from infringing activities. The second is whether a reduction in an NOL in connection with tax liability for profits from infringing activities is an income tax expense, and therefore deductible.
Defendants contend that the profits upon which a copyright owner's award is based should be after-tax profits. Defendants thus approve of the Special Master's Conclusion that Bolton and Goldmark are entitled to deduct income tax payments they made. Defendants object, however, to the Special Master's conclusion that Sony is not entitled to deduct from its profits the amount of income tax it would have paid on its infringing   profits but for the NOL. Defendants contend that the reduction in the NOL is a deductible income tax expense.
Plaintiff, on the other hand, argues that the copyright owner's award should come from pre-tax profits. Plaintiff thus objects to the Special Master's conclusion that Bolton and Goldmark are entitled to deduct from their profits income tax payments made in connection with profits from their infringing activities. Plaintiff agrees, however, with the Special Master's conclusion that Sony is not entitled to deduct the reduction in the NOL. Plaintiff and the Special Master assert that the NOL reduction is not a deductible income tax expense.
a. Legal Standards

i. Statute

 A copyright owner bringing an infringement action can seek both actual damages suffered as a result of the infringement and any profits of the infringer attributable to the infringement that are not taken into account in computing actual damages. 17 U.S.C. § 504(b). The plaintiff bears the burden of proving the gross revenues received by the defendant, while the defendant has the burden of proving its "deductible expenses" and the portion, if any, of profits attributable to sources other than the copyrighted work. Id.   The Copyright Act does not define the term "profit." It also does not specify which expenses will be regarded as deductible costs; that task has fallen to the courts. See 3 Melvin B. Nimmer & David Nimmer, Nimmer on Copyright § 14.03[B] (1996).

 "Any doubt as to the computation of costs or profits is to be resolved in favor of the plaintiff. If the infringing defendant does not meet its burden of proving costs, the gross figure stands as the defendant' profits." Frank Music Corp. v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Inc., 772 F.2d 505, 514 (9th Cir. 1985).
ii. Case Law: Circuit Split

In the case at bar, Plaintiff elected to seek profits rather than actual damages. (Amended Report at 12.) In addition, the jury, in Phase I, concluded that Defendants had not willfully infringed. This case thus raises the question of whether a non-willful copyright infringer, in calculating the amount of profits from which a copyright owner's award is to be determined, is entitled to deduct income tax payments made in connection with profits made from infringing activity.
The Special Master noted   that the law is clear that when infringers have acted in a willful, conscious, and deliberate manner, they are not entitled to deduct income tax expense in determining profits from their infringement. (Amended Report at 10 (citing Larson Co. v. Wrigley Co., 277 U.S. 97, 48 S. Ct. 449, 72 L. Ed. 800, 1928 Dec. Comm'r Pat. 273 (1928) and Alfred Bell & Co. v. Catalda Fine Arts, Inc., 191 F.2d 99, 106 (2d Cir. 1951).) In Larson, the Supreme Court held that:

It would be unjust to charge an infringer with the gross amount of his sales without allowing him for the materials and labor that were necessary to produce the things sold, but it does not follow that he should be allowed what he paid for the chance to do what he knew that he had no right to do. . . . Even if the only relief that the [infringer] can get is a deduction from gross income when the amount of its liability is finally determined the [victim] will have to pay a tax on the . . . profits when it receives them, and in a case of what has been found to have been one of conscious and deliberate wrongdoing, we think it just that the further deduction should not be allowed.

Larson, 277 U.S. at 100.
There is a split of authority, however, on whether an infringer who was not found to have acted   willfully is entitled to deduct income taxes. (See Pl.'s Objections at 5 & n.2) Neither the Special Master nor any of the parties points to a Ninth Circuit case addressing this issue.  (See Pl.'s Objections at 5; Amended Report at 10-11 (discussing relevant case law).) Courts in the Second and Sixth Circuits have reached different conclusions when faced with the issue.
(a) Schnadig

In Schnadig v. Corp. Gaines Mfg. Co., 620 F.2d 1166, 1169-71 (6th Cir. 1980), a patent infringement case, the Sixth Circuit held that an infringing defendant, whether or not willful, is required to pay pre-tax profits to the plaintiff. The court noted that the case was one of first impression in the Sixth Circuit, and that, at the time, no other court had squarely   addressed the issue in a published opinion. Id. at 1168.
The Schnadig court relied in part on the statutory provision governing awards of profits in patent infringement cases then in place. Under that provision, the infringer of a design patent "'shall be liable to the owner to the extent of his total profit.'" Id. at 1169 (quoting 35 U.S.C. § 289). Observing that section 289 did not distinguish between willful and negligent infringers, the court read Larson broadly to bar deduction by both types of infringers. Schnadig, 620 F.2d at 1171.
The Schnadig court stated that although an award of pre-tax profits appears to require that an infringer pay more in damages than he was able to gain from the infringement, id. at 1169, "disallowing consideration of the immediate tax consequences to the infringer does not penalize; it merely assures that the profit to the wrongdoer is fully extracted," id. at 1171. This is in part because payments of damages for patent infringement   are deductible from the income of the infringer, id. at 1169 (citing I.R.C. § 162), and includible in the gross income of the patentee, Schnadig, 620 F.2d at 1169 (citing I.R.C. § 61). It was also in part because, under net operating loss carry-back and carry-forward rules, a taxpayer can generally utilize a loss to the taxpayer's advantage. Schnadig, 620 F.2d at 1170. If an infringer is permitted to deduct income tax payments from the profit on which the victim's award is based, "the infringer [might be able to] net[] as much as his victim, and perhaps even more if the dynamics of the money market are considered." Id. at 1169.
The court acknowledged that "the actual dollar impact of a damage award on the taxes of either party will naturally depend upon the party's overall tax situation. Tax rates will vary, and offsetting losses could conceivably bar use of the deduction or negate any tax effect of the award." Id. at 1169-70. Nevertheless, the court concluded, because of the time periods within which taxpayers can use losses, "the vast majority of infringers should be able to utilize the deductions." Id. at 1170. "By recovering an infringer's pre-tax profits, the patentee will in fact   be treated as though he had gained the profits from the exploitation of his patent. We find this to be the result intended by the statute . . . ." Id. at 1171.
(b) In Design

In Design v. K-Mart Apparel Corp., 13 F.3d 559 (2d Cir. 1994). There, the court read Larson more narrowly, concluding that the Larson Court "carefully limited the breadth of its holding recognizing that there could be cases where the circumstances of the. infringer's conduct dictated that such a tax deduction would be proper." Id. at 566. Rejecting the reasoning in Schnadig, the In Design court held that  a non-willful infringer may deduct income tax payments. The court concluded that "when a claim is made for infringing profits, '[t]his means profits actually made. A book profit of a dollar is not a profit actually made when from the dollar the government takes twenty cents as the price for the right to make any profit at all.' Hypothetical discussions of possible indirect tax ramifications do not change that basic fact."  Id. at 567 (quoting Macbeth-Evans Glass Co. v. L.E. Smith Glass Co., 23 F.2d 459, 463 (3d Cir. 1927)).
b. Discussion

In the case at bar, the Special Master concluded that Plaintiff did not seek actual damages, and presented no evidence with respect to actual damages. (Amended Report at 12.) Plaintiff seeks only Defendants' profits.
i. Deductibility of Income Tax Payments

(a) Defendants' Position

As might be expected, Defendants do not object to the Special Master's general conclusion of law that income taxes are deductible expenses, or to his conclusion that Bolton and Goldmark are entitled to deduct their income tax payments. Defendants, showing their support for the In Design rule, argue that income tax payments generally should be deductible from profits. Defendants' expert  testified that income   taxes are deductible under generally accepted accounting principles in arriving at profits. (Amended Rep. at 12-13.) Defendants would place profits from which copyright infringement awards are made within the scope of those principles.
Defendants also argue that the denial of a deduction gives a windfall to Plaintiff. (Def.s' Mot. at 8.) They base this argument on three grounds. First, Defendants invested time, effort, and resources in producing the album and song profits, while Plaintiff did not. (Id. at 8-9.) Second, Plaintiff produced no evidence that it derived any publishing or performance income from the song. (Id. at 8.) Third, because of the standard indemnification provisions included in his agreements with Sony, Bolton will bear the ultimate liability for Sony's losses. (Id. at 9-10.)
(b) Plaintiff's Position

Plaintiff, by contrast, would follow Schnadig.   Plaintiff argues that, as a general matter, no deductions should be allowed for income taxes in the calculation of profits in copyright infringement actions. Plaintiff would apply that principle to Sony, as the Special Master did, and to Bolton and Goldmark, which the Special Master declined to do.
Specifically, Plaintiff claims that the Special Master failed to recognize that a copyright infringer who pays an award to a copyright holder can be reimbursed for all taxes they have paid on their infringing profits, a factor on which the Schnadig court relied. (Pl.'s Objections at 3.) The Special Master concluded that any such reimbursement for Bolton and Goldmark, in the form of a future tax savings, was too speculative to support denying those defendants a. deduction for income tax payments they have made. (Amended Report at 13-14.) Plaintiff challenges that conclusion, arguing that the ability to deduct payments of damages pursuant to court awards gives infringers the potential to earn a profit despite paying the award. (Id. at 7-8.) Disallowing the deduction, in Plaintiff's view, will both provide the copyright owner with the appropriate award and still permit complete reimbursement   for the infringer. (Id. at 8-9.) Finally, Plaintiff maintains that permitting the deduction of income tax payments results in the shifting of a potential tax liability created by infringing activities from the infringer to the innocent copyright owner. (Id. at 11.)
With regard to the question of a windfall, Plaintiff argues that the points Defendants make are irrelevant to the issue of calculating the award to which an innocent copyright holder is entitled. According to Plaintiff, Defendants' investment in the production of the album and song profits has no bearing on the determination of damages in this action.
Plaintiff also contends that the extent to which it generated revenues from its original work is immaterial. "Nowhere in the vast body of Copyright law is there articulated a principle that a copyright holder must receive a lower damage award than the jury verdict where the copyright holder shows little or no revenue from its original work." (Pl.'s "Reply" at 10.) To adopt such a principle would be to treat the infringement of works that produced little income for their copyright owners as something less than complete infringement. (Id.) Plaintiff notes that it will have to pay tax on the profit award it ultimately receives from Defendants. (Pl.'s Objections at 9.)
Finally, Plaintiff argues that the nature of the contractual arrangement between Bolton and Sony is irrelevant: "It is not for Plaintiff, as the innocent copyright holder, to bear the risk of loss sustained by the Defendant infringers  as a result of their infringement or the consequences of their personal financial contracts and agreements among themselves." (Pl.'s "Reply" at 9.)
(c) Conclusion

The Court must determine whether, as a general matter, profits in non-willful copyright infringement cases are to be calculated pre-tax or after-tax; that is, the Court must choose between the Schnadig rule (pre-tax) and the In Design rule (after-tax).
On balance, the In Design approach advocated by Defendants better reflects  the usual meaning of the term "profit" as the amount that is left over after all expenses are deducted.  It also provides a more convincing reading of Larson, which emphasizes willfulness as a part of its holding. The Schnadig court's interpretation of Larson's discussion of willfulness as merely descriptive does not accurately reflect the language and tone of that discussion.
Accordingly, the Court herein follows the In Design rule of after-tax profits. The Court thus adopts the Special Master's conclusions regarding Bolton and Goldmark: they are entitled to deduct income tax payments they have made. The Court reaches the question of whether Sony's reduction of its NOL, in connection with the realization of profits from infringing activity, amounts to a deductible income tax expense.
ii. Reduction of NOL as an Income Tax Expense

(a) Defendants' Position

Defendants object to the Special Master's Conclusion of Law number 5:

Having failed to establish that it paid income taxes with respect to revenues it received from its infringing activities, Sony is not entitled to a deduction for income taxes in the computation of its profits from infringement.

(Id. at 9.) Defendants argue that Sony did "pay" income tax, by reducing the NOL by the amount of its infringing profits. (Def.s' Mot. at 5.)
Defendants challenge the Special Master's   conclusion that the projection of a future tax expense for Sony resulting from the diminution of its NOL is too speculative to demonstrate a deductible income tax expense related to its income from infringement. (Amended Report at 15.) The Special Master stated:

Just as it would be speculative to consider the possible tax savings to Bolton and Goldmark from the payment of a pre-tax award, it would be unduly speculative to project a future tax expense for Sony Music resulting from the diminution of its net operating loss carry-forward. It may be that Sony Music will never incur a federal income tax liability. In any event, Sony Music has not met its burden of proving that it suffered a deductible income tax expense related to its income from infringement.

(Id.)
Defendants contend that, under generally accepted accounting principles, taxes become a cost when the liability to pay them is incurred.  (Def.s' Mot. at 5.) They further argue that an NOL is a salable asset. (Id. at 7.) See Chugach Alaska Corp. v. United States, 34 F.3d 1462, 1468 (9th Cir. 1994) (recognizing that NOLs can be sold to profitable corporations). As such, any reduction in it has "an immediate and concrete impact   on the company's financial condition." (Def.s' Mot. at 7-8.) See In re Standard Brands Paint Co., 154 B.R. 563, 565 (Bankr. C.D. Cal. 1993) (stating, with regard to parent company and four wholly owned subsidiaries, that "[t]he debtors would suffer negative tax consequences if the debts between/among the debtors were permanently cancelled [because] [c]ancellation of debt would affect debtors' state net operating loss carryovers and their adjusted basis in property"); In re Beery, 116 B.R. 808, 810 (D. Kan. 1990) (holding that bankruptcy court properly allowed trustee to use loss carry-forwards on estate return and stating that "[t]he debtor's estate did generate considerable income, and the loss carryforwards were a valuable asset of the estate").
"[The album and song] profits generated a tax expense -- a cost in   the years received, regardless of when taxes are paid, and reduced the amount of the NOL, an asset of the company, thereby hastening the day on which Sony Music will pay taxes." (Def.s' Mot. at 6.) Defendants draw an analogy with the situation in which an infringing company has a tax credit which it reduces rather than make a cash payment to the taxing authorities. (Def.s' Reply at 3.)
Following the accounting principles, Defendants maintain that the profits Sony earned on the album and the single reduced its NOL in the year the income was received, regardless of when the income tax is ultimately paid. (Def.s' Mot. at 4-5.) Thus, Defendants conclude, tax liabilities generated by income from the album and the single "immediately diminished an asset of the company by the amount of the tax expense associated with that income." (Def.s' Mot. at 5.)
Defendants also argue that the Special Master erred in drawing a parallel between the reduction of Sony's NOL and the ability of Bolton and Goldmark, as individuals, potentially to claim tax deductions in the future for the amounts they may pay to Plaintiff. The Special Master treated both situations as involving equally speculative future events.
With   regard to Bolton and Goldmark, the Special Master concluded that "[t]o deny an infringer a deduction for income taxes in computing profits on the ground that an infringer might realize tax savings at a future time would be engaging in unwarranted speculation." (Amended Report at 13.) In reaching that determination, the Special Master referred to the following unpredictable variables:

(1) the availability of income against which a payment can be deducted; (2) time constraints on the filing of an amended return; (3) the ability to take advantage of net operating loss rules, which ability itself depends on such variables as carry-back and carry-forward time limitations and, for an individual taxpayer, the character of the deduction as a business or non-business deduction or non-business capital loss;  and (4) the possibility that the infringer's applicable tax rate in the year in which the infringer pays the profit award might differ from the applicable rate in the year in which the infringer received the profits.

(Id., at 13-14.) He stated that "it can be argued that an infringer who realizes a tax savings by deducting from unrelated income the amount of the profit payment made to the copyright   owner is simply realizing additional profit on the unrelated activity, rather than a greater profit on the infringing activity." (Id. at 14.) Following that reasoning, the Special Master concluded that Bolton and Goldmark are entitled to deduct income taxes that they had actually paid on income they received from infringing activities. (Id. at 12-13.)
According to Defendants, however, there was no evidence at the hearing that those factors apply to Sony. (Def.s' Reply at 2.) As an example, Defendants note that Sony's parent company would never have any "non-business" income or deductions, nor would it be required to file an amended return once its NOL is utilized. (Id. at 2-3.) In addition, Defendants argue, there was evidence that companies like Sony's parent manage their NOLs to ensure that they are used. (Id. at 3.)
Defendants contend that the prospect of Sony paying income tax, in some form, on profits from infringing activities is far less speculative than the prospect of Bolton and Goldmark receiving a future tax benefit from any payments they make to Plaintiff. (Def.s' Mot. at 7.) It was thus inconsistent, Defendants assert, for the Special Master to permit   Bolton and Goldmark to deduct but not Sony--Defendants argue that all three are entitled to the deduction.
(b) Plaintiff's Position

Plaintiff argues that even if the Court concludes that income tax deductions should be permitted in general, Sony is not entitled to such a deduction. Plaintiff asserts that the reason the Special Master found Sony not to be entitled to a deduction is that Sony did not pay any income tax on profits it made from infringing activities. In Plaintiff's view, a reduction in an NOL is not equivalent to an income tax payment. Plaintiff argues that, even if, as Defendants maintain, an NOL is a corporate asset, "[t]he calculation of profits in the instant matter is not concerned with the diminution in the value of corporate assets, but with out-of-pocket expenses actually paid by the infringer." (Pl.'s "Reply" at 6.)
In addition, Plaintiff agrees with the Special Master's conclusion that Sony's reduction of the NOL in accordance with its infringing profits is at least as speculative as Bolton's and Goldmark's future realization of a tax deduction for an award payment made to Plaintiff: "[A]ttributing a present value does not make Sony's potential realization of its  carry-over tax burden any more concrete or less speculative." (Id. at 6.) "Defendants cannot with any certainty say that the day will ever arrive when the taxes on this infringing work will be paid by Sony, and Defendants certainly cannot define the amorphous term 'hastening.'" (Id. at 7.) Plaintiff argues that the same criteria that the Special Master applied to the Bolton and Goldmark future potential tax deductions should be applied to the Sony NOL reduction, with the same result: no deduction. (Id.)
(c) Conclusion

On balance, Plaintiff and the Special Master make the better argument. Although the reduction in the NOL may be immediate, it cannot be known when, if ever, that reduction will have a concrete financial impact on Sony. The In Design court concluded that  "when a claim is made for infringing profits, '[t]his means profits actually made.'" In Design, 13 F.3d at 567 (quoting Macbeth-Evans Glass, 23 F.2d at 463). Similarly, when an argument is made for a deduction from the infringing profits, the expense to be deducted must be one that was actually incurred.
Defendants have the burden of proving their deductible expenses, 17 U.S.C. § 504(b), and "[a]ny doubt as to the computation   of costs or profits is to be resolved in favor of the plaintiff," Frank Music, 772 F.2d at 514. The Special Master correctly concluded that Defendants did not carry their burden of showing the deductibility from their infringing profits of the NOL reduction.
2. Deductibility of Bolton's and Goldmark's Business and Personal Management Fees

It appears that the source of the parties differences with regard to this issue is a marked difference in interpretation of what the Special Master actually   found and concluded. He may have determined that all of the fees paid to Bolton's and Goldmark's managers for all of the managers' work are deductible, on the ground that the entirety of a manager's work is related to the success of any individual project.  That would be clearly erroneous. In the alternative, he may have meant only that all of the commissions the managers received from sales of the infringing works are deductible.  That conclusion would agree with governing authority. A careful reading of the Amended Report reveals that the Special Master followed the latter, correct approach.
a. Legal Standards

 In determining the impact of overhead expenses on an award of a non-willful infringer's profits to the copyright owner, "[t]he real question . . . is whether any of the overhead expenses were caused by the production or sale of the infringing goods, not the proportionate amount of sales of the goods in relation to total sales." Kamar Int'l, Inc. v. Russ Berrie & Co., Inc., 752 F.2d 1326, 1332 (9th Cir. 1984).   A non-willful infringer may deduct overhead "only when the infringer can demonstrate it was of actual assistance in the production, distribution or sale of the infringing product." Id.; see also Nimmer & Nimmer, supra, § 14.03, at 14-38 ("In general, it may be said that only those expenses that are proven with some specificity to relate to the infringing work may be deducted in determining the profits attributable to such work."). To be entitled to deduct overhead from the profit award, the infringer must show that the overhead costs "actually contributed to sales of the infringing work." Frank Music, 772 F.2d at 516. "This is a factual determination to be made by the district court . . . ." Kamar, 752 F.2d at 1332.
Deductions have been allowed for management fees that took the form of commissions based on a percentage of the gross income earned by the artist/infringer. See Abkco Music, Inc. v. Harrisongs Music, Ltd., 508 F. Supp. 798, 801 (S.D.N.Y. 1981), affirmed with modification, 722 F.2d 988 (2d Cir. 1983). In Abkco Music, the Court simply applied the percentage the managers received in commission generally to the infringing profits, and reduced those profits accordingly.
b. The   Amended Report

The Special Master found that Bolton and Goldmark paid personal and business management commissions with respect to their income from infringement. In so finding, the Special Master appears to have followed the testimony of Defendants' expert that, under generally accepted accounting principles, commissions paid to personal or business managers are appropriately allocable to revenues in arriving at profits. (Amended Report at 17.) The expert also testified that, in his opinion, the commission rates paid by Bolton and Goldmark were reasonable under industry standards. (Id.)
With regard to Bolton, the Special Master found that Contemporary Communications Corporation ("Contemporary") and Louis Levin ("Levin"), then a Contemporary employee, began managing Bolton in 1980, after Bolton had made four unsuccessful albums and when his recording career was in disarray. (Id. at 18.) Contemporary and Levin obtained a five-album record contract for Bolton, the contract that produced the profits to Bolton from the album and the song at issue in this case. (Id.) In 1988, Bolton left Contemporary and Levin began managing Bolton, as Bolton's personal manager, through Louis Levin Management.   (Id.) Levin continued to develop and guide Bolton's career, and had significant involvement with the development, promotion, and sale of the album and the single. (Id. at 18-19.) "During the time Levin and Contemporary rendered their respective management services, their management efforts contributed to the enhanced stature of Bolton as a recording artist. Undoubtedly, Bolton's artistic statute played a part in the commercial success of the album." (Id.) Similarly, the Special Master found that David Feinstein, to whom Bolton paid business management fees, managed Bolton's financial affairs, was intimately involved with the negotiation and renegotiation of Bolton's contract with Sony, and analyzed all of Bolton's royalty statements relating to the album and the song. (Id. at 19.)
With regard to Goldmark, the Special Master found that Padell-Nadell managed all of Goldmark's business affairs to enable Goldmark to concentrate on creative musical work. (Id. at 19-20.) Padell-Nadell was also involved in Goldmark's contract negotiations with Warner-Chappell and made sure that Goldmark received all income due to him from the song. (Id. at 20.)
In sum, the Special Master found that "Bolton   paid personal and business management commissions with respect to the income he received from infringement, and Goldmark paid business management commissions with respect to Goldmark's infringement income." (Id. at 16.) The Special Master concluded that: "Bolton and Goldmark have demonstrated that the subject management expenses are sufficiently related to the exploitation of the infringing work to be deductible in the computation of profits. The management commissions are directly related to infringement income."  (Id.) In his conclusions of law, he stated that:

7. The allocable personal management and business management expenses paid by Bolton are deductible in computing Bolton's profits from infringement. 8. The allocable business management expenses paid by Goldmark are deductible in computing Goldmark's profits from infringement.

(Id. at 9.)
c. Discussion

Plaintiff appears to argue that commissions based on sales are never "attributable directly" to those sales: "All of the commissions at issue are   not 'variable costs, attributable directly to sales of the infringing item,' but rather, are contingent fees that are related to sales of the infringing work." (Pl.'s Objections at 13 (quoting Def.s' Brief to Special Master at 5).) That argument not only runs against the plain meaning of the phrase "attributable directly to", but also, as the discussion of the case law above suggests, is contrary to relevant law.
Plaintiff also asserts that it was "erroneous and unfair" for the Special Master to conclude that all of the fees directly attributable to the infringing work are deductible. (Pl.'s Objections at 14.) It is Plaintiff's arguments, however, that are erroneous.
Plaintiff's line of reasoning is somewhat obscure at times. Nevertheless, Plaintiff seems to assert that the Special Master concluded that Bolton and Goldmark are entitled to deduct fees paid to their managers for work done by the managers on projects or tasks unrelated to the album and the song. (Id. at 14-16.) As the passages from the Amended Report quoted above indicate, however, the Special Master recommended the deduction only of those fees that he found were related to the album and the song.
Plaintiff's real challenge   may be to the Special Master's factual findings that the management fees at issue were related to the generation of the infringement profits. As the Special Master's lengthy description of the managers' involvement in the generation of the infringing profits reveals, those factual findings are not clearly erroneous. (Amended Report at 17-20.) Given the managers' extensive involvement, fees in the form of commissions based on those profits are clearly costs that "actually contributed to sales of the infringing work." Frank Music, 772 F.2d at 516.
Plaintiff also assumes that the Special Master made the factual finding that the total compensation Bolton's and Goldmark's managers received from Bolton and Goldmark, for all of the managers' work, was a commission based on revenues from "Love is a Wonderful Thing" and Time, Love and Tenderness. (Pl.'s Objections at 14.) Based on that contention, Plaintiff argues that only a portion of even the fees that are directly attributable to the infringing work should be deductible. (Id. at 15-16.) The Special Master, however, found that Bolton and Goldmark paid their managers for the work the managers did in relation to the album and the song through commissions   based on income generated by the album and the song. (Amended Report at 16.) That finding is not clearly erroneous.
Where, as here, an artist's manager is paid by commissions tied to sales of the artist's works, that arrangement provides a convenient way to measure the portion of overall management fees attributable to the manager's efforts on any particular work, including an infringing work. Accordingly, because the law permits the infringer to deduct management fees attributable to the infringing work, and commissions on sales are a permissible way to structure those fees, the Special Master correctly calculated the management fee deductions to which Bolton and Goldmark are entitled.
LOURDES G. BAIRD

Finally, defendant Gemmy moves to dismiss claim five, copyright infringement, for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Gemmy claims that plaintiff has alleged only acts of infringement which took place outside the United States, that extraterritorial acts do not violate the Copyright Act, and that therefore, this court lacks jurisdiction over this claim. Plaintiff counters that it has alleged that Gemmy authorized the Chinese factory's activities from within the United States and that this authorization is sufficient to bestow jurisdiction on this court over the extraterritorial   acts of infringement.
Federal courts have original jurisdiction over any civil action arising under federal copyright law. 28 U.S.C. § 1338(a) (1994). "It is well established that copyright laws generally do not have extraterritorial application." Update Art, Inc. v. Modiin Publ'g, Ltd., 843 F.2d 67, 73 (2d Cir. 1988); see Capitol Records, Inc. v. Mercury Records Corp., 221 F.2d 657, 662 (2d Cir. 1955). However, the Second Circuit has recognized a narrow exception to this rule:  Where an individual commits an act of infringement in the United States that permits further reproduction outside the United States -- such as when an individual makes unauthorized copies of copyrighted material and then sends them out of the country -- a court may assert jurisdiction over those foreign acts and a plaintiff may recover damages for the infringing acts that took place extraterritorially.  Update Art, Inc., 843 F.2d at 73.
For this exception to apply, a plaintiff must first demonstrate that the domestic predicate act was itself an act of infringement in violation of the copyright laws. See id. In Update Art, for example, an owner of the rights to artwork sued an Israeli   corporation and its American subsidiary for copyright infringement. The artwork had appeared in both the American and Israeli editions of the weekend magazine section of the newspaper owned by the defendants. Id. at 68-69. The defendants argued that the Court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over the portion of the controversy involving the Israeli edition of the newspaper, and that, as   a result, damages could not be assessed for this extraterritorial infringement.
The Second Circuit found that the key issue was where the initial reproduction of the artwork took place. If it took place in the United States, the Court had jurisdiction to award damages for the Israeli newspaper's infringement; if it took place in Israel, the Court lacked jurisdiction to award such damages. Id. at 73. The Court reasoned that the initial reproduction of the artwork in the United States established the Court's jurisdiction over the extraterritorial infringing acts because such reproduction was an independent copyright violation that contributed to the extraterritorial infringement. Because the defendants did not demonstrate that the illegal reproduction had occurred in Israel rather than in the   United States, the Court found that it had jurisdiction. Id.
Thus,  in order to establish jurisdiction over extraterritorial acts, the act taking place in the United States at the very least must itself violate the Copyright Act. See Update Arts, 843 F.2d at 73; Robert Stigwood Group Ltd. v. O'Reilly, 530 F.2d 1096, 1101 (2d Cir. 1976) (holding that the preparations within the United States for performances in Canada were insufficient to confer jurisdiction over the extraterritorial violations because these preparations were not themselves violations of the Copyright Act), cert. denied, 429 U.S. 848, 50 L. Ed. 2d 121, 97 S. Ct. 135 (1976); see also Allarcom Pay Television, Ltd. v. General Instrument Corp., 69 F.3d 381, 387 (9th Cir. 1995); Subafilms, Ltd. v. MGM-Pathe Communications Co., 24 F.3d 1088, 1094 (9th Cir.) (en banc) ("In these cases, liability is not based on contributory infringement, but on the theory that the infringing use would have been actionable even if the subsequent foreign distribution that stemmed from that use never took place."), cert. denied, 115 S. Ct. 512 (1994); De Bardossy v. Puski, 763 F. Supp. 1239, 1243   (S.D.N.Y. 1991); 3 Nimmer on Copyright, § 17.02, at 17-20  ("If, and to the extent, a part of an "act" of infringement occurs within the United States, then, although such act is completed in a foreign jurisdiction, those parties who contributed to the act within the United States may be rendered liable under American copyright law.").
Here, plaintiff's allegations, construed liberally, present two domestic acts: 1) transport of a sample of the Bank from the United States to the Chinese factory; and 2) authorization and approval of the Chinese factory's activities from within the United States. Neither, however, constitutes copyright infringement.
Gemmy's transport of the sample Bank to the Chinese factory did not violate the copyright laws.  "Anyone who violates any of the exclusive rights of the copyright owner as provided in Sections 106 through 118 . . . is an infringer of the copyright . . . ." 17 U.S.C. § 501(a) (1994). Section 106 gives the copyright owner exclusive rights to, inter alia, reproduce, prepare derivative works of, or distribute copies of copyrighted work to the public. 17 U.S.C. § 106 (1994). Transporting the Bank from the United States to China was   not a copyright violation. It did not involve the illegal reproduction of the copyrighted work, preparation of derivative works, or distribution of copies of the copyrighted work to the public. See 17 U.S.C. § 106 (1994).
Further,  mere authorization and approval of copyright infringements taking place outside the United States is not a copyright violation and does not create jurisdiction over those extraterritorial acts. Plaintiff relies on Peter Starr Prod. Co. v. Twin Continental Films, Inc., 783 F.2d 1440, 1443 (9th Cir. 1986), which held that the authorization of extraterritorial acts from within the United States was sufficient to create jurisdiction over the foreign acts.

However, plaintiff's reliance is misplaced because Peter Starr was overruled by Subafilms, which held that  allegations that defendant authorized within the United States infringing conduct that occurred entirely abroad was insufficient to create subject matter jurisdiction over the foreign acts. 24 F.3d at 1094-95. The Subafilms Court stated that "the addition of the words 'to authorize' in the Copyright Act was not meant to create a new form of liability for 'authorization' that was   divorced completely from the legal consequences of authorized conduct, but was intended to invoke the preexisting doctrine of contributory infringement." Id. at 1092.  Under the doctrine of contributory infringement, a person cannot be held liable "unless the authorized or otherwise encouraged activity itself could amount to infringement." Id. Because extraterritorial infringements are not violations of the Copyright Act, authorization of such acts is not a copyright violation in and of itself and cannot confer jurisdiction on federal courts.  Id. at 1093-94; see also Nimmer on Copyright, § 12.04[A][3][b], at 12-88-12-94. Although the Second Circuit has never adopted this rule, the persuasiveness of the Ninth Circuit's reasoning and the Second Circuit's traditionally narrow view of liability for   extraterritorial infringement recommends acceptance of Subafilms's holding. See Update Art, 843 F.2d at 73; Robert Stigwood Group, 530 F.2d at 1101. Because plaintiff has failed to allege an infringement within the United States that led to extraterritorial infringement, the general rule that extraterritorial infringements are not violations of the Copyright   Act applies, and the extraterritorial acts of infringement are not within this court's jurisdiction. Plaintiff has therefore failed to allege sufficient jurisdictional facts and claim five must be dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
Here, sanctions under Rule 11 are not warranted. Plaintiff should have indicated that Peter Starr had been overruled, and its failure to do so is, to say the least, disturbing. However, the Second Circuit has never directly addressed the legal issue raised by plaintiff's claim: whether authorization from within the United States of infringement outside the United States is sufficient to create subject matter jurisdiction over extraterritorial copyright violations. Although I have   declined to exercise jurisdiction in such a situation, and although Peter Starr is no longer good law in the Ninth Circuit, a panel of the Ninth Circuit did adopt such a rule, and thus reasonable minds might find such domestic authorization sufficient to grant a court jurisdiction over the extraterritorial acts of infringement. See Curb v. MCA Records, Inc., 898 F. Supp. 586, 595 (M.D. Tenn. 1995) ("A better view . . . would be to hold that domestic violation of the authorization right is an infringement . . . whenever the authorizee has committed an act that would violate the copyright owner's § 106 rights.").
As to the factual contentions, plaintiff's assertion that Gemmy possessed some authority over the actions of the Chinese factory did not lack evidentiary support. The ongoing relationship between the factory and Gemmy, the specific arrangement with regard to the manufacture of the Can, and the fact that Gemmy supplied the factory with the Bank sample which was used to produce the counterfeit Bank justifies an allegation that Gemmy knew of, supervised or asserted some control over the factory's activities. Gemmy argues that plaintiff's allegations lacked good faith   because I denied plaintiff's contempt motion based on defendant's alleged violation of the preliminary injunction. Although I rejected defendant's contempt motion in part because defendant failed to demonstrate with convincing clarity that Gemmy was responsible for the factory's sale of counterfeit Banks, that determination was not dispositive on the issue of defendant's authorization or control of the Chinese factory's actions. First, in denying plaintiff's contempt motion, I merely found that plaintiff had not demonstrated ownership or control by clear and convincing evidence, a standard above the preponderance of the evidence standard that governs this action. Second, the contempt hearing took place before the parties completed discovery, which might have revealed additional information to support plaintiff's allegations. Thus, although I have dismissed plaintiff's copyright claim, I find that sanctions are not justified under Rule 11 or 28 U.S.C. § 1927.

A. Unclean Hands
Sherman complains that Yang gained access to MAPHIA under a pseudonym, and argues that such access amounts to unclean hands which should prevent summary judgment. The Court disagrees.
Yang's access to MAPHIA under the informant's pseudonym was consistent with all users' anonymous access. Thus, no misrepresentation occurred. Even characterized as misrepresentation, however, such actions do not provide a defense to copyright or trademark infringement. See, e.g., Reebok Int'l Ltd. v. Jemmett, 1988 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 16504, 6 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1715, 1717 (S.D. Cal. 1988) (no unclean hands where Reebok employee falsely represented name and occupation to get evidence of infringement).
I. Copyright Infringement
Sega contends that Sherman is liable for copyright infringement under direct, contributory, and vicarious liability theories. Sherman admits that users of the MAPHIA BBS were allowed to upload and download Sega games with the authorized password, but maintains that this copying fits under the fair use defense because it was nothing more that the use of the games at people's homes, and that any copyright violation was de minimis.
A. Direct Infringement
To establish a prima facie case of direct copyright infringement, Sega must prove (1) ownership of a valid copyright in the infringed work, and (2) "copying" by the defendant. See Sid & Marty Krofft Television Productions, Inc. v. McDonald's Corp., 562 F.2d 1157, 1162 (9th Cir. 1977); Religious Technology Center v. Netcom On-line Communication Services, Inc., 907 F. Supp. 1361, 1366-67 (N.D. Cal. 1995).
A certificate of copyright registration establishes a presumption that the copyright is valid. 17   U.S.C. § 410(c). Sega has submitted several certificates of copyright registration for its video games, including certificates for Jurassic Park and Sonic Spinball. These certificates establish a presumption that Sega owns a valid copyright in those video game programs. Apple Computer, Inc. v. Formula Int'l Inc., 725 F.2d 521, 523 (9th Cir. 1984).
The Ninth Circuit has held that  "copying," for the purposes of copyright law, occurs when a computer program is transferred from a permanent storage device to a computer's random access memory. Mai Systems Corp. v. Peak Computer, Inc., 991 F.2d 511, 518 (9th Cir. 1993), cert. dismissed, 510 U.S. 1033 [***1712]    (1994). In this case, copies were made when the Sega game files were uploaded to or downloaded from Sherman's BBS. Thus, copying by someone is established.
This does not end the inquiry, however, because it does not establish whether Sherman, as the BBS operator, is directly liable for the copying. In Netcom, the court found that the Internet provider was not directly liable for copyright infringement of a copyrighted work posted and distributed through its system. Netcom, 907 F. Supp. at 1368-70. The Netcom court held   that "although copyright is a strict liability statute, there should be some element of volition or causation which is lacking where a defendant's system is merely used to create a copy by a third party." Id. at 1370. "Where the infringing subscriber is clearly directly liable for the same act, it does not make sense to adopt a rule that could lead to the liability of countless parties whose role in the infringement is nothing more that setting up and operating a system that is necessary for functioning of the Internet," even where the Internet provider has knowledge of potential copyright infringement by its subscribers. Id. at 1372-73.
While Sherman's actions in this case are more participatory than those of the defendants in Netcom, the Court finds Netcom persuasive. Sega has not shown that Sherman himself uploaded or downloaded the files, or directly caused such uploading or downloading to occur. The most Sega has shown is that Sherman operated his BBS, that he knew infringing activity was occurring, and that he solicited others to upload games. However, whether Sherman knew his BBS users were infringing on Sega's copyright, or encouraged them to do so, has no   bearing on whether Sherman directly caused the copying to occur. Id. at 1372. Furthermore, Sherman's actions as a BBS operator and copier seller are more appropriately analyzed under contributory or vicarious liability theories. Therefore, because Sega has not shown that Sherman directly caused the copying, Sherman cannot be liable for direct infringement.
948 F. Supp. 923, *931; 1996 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 20385, **19; 41 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1705, ***1711
B. Contributory Infringement
Just because Sherman is not liable for direct infringement, however, does not mean that he is free from liability.  Although the Copyright Act does not expressly impose liability on anyone other than direct infringers, courts have long recognized that in certain circumstances, liability for contributory infringement will be imposed. Fonovisa, Inc. v. Cherry Auction, Inc., 76 F.3d 259, 261 (9th Cir. 1996) (citing Sony v. Universal City, 464 U.S. 417, 435, 78 L. Ed. 2d 574, 104 S. Ct. 774 (1984). Contributory copyright infringement stems from the notion that one who directly contributes to another's infringement should be held liable. 76 F.3d at 264. Such liability is established where the defendant, "with knowledge of the infringing activity, induces, causes or materially contributes to the infringing conduct of another." Id. (quoting Gershwin Publishing Corp. v. Columbia Artists Management, Inc., 443 F.2d 1159, 1162 (2nd Cir. 1971)); see also Religious Technology Ctr. v. Netcom On-Line Communication Serv., Inc., 907 F. Supp. 1361, 1372 (N.D. Cal. 1995) (quoting Gershwin, 443 F.2d at 1162).
To impose liability on Sherman for   contributory infringement, Sega must first establish that the users of Sherman's MAPHIA BBS directly infringed Sega's copyright. Second, Sega must establish that (i) with knowledge of the users' infringing activity, (ii) Sherman induced, caused, or materially contributed to their infringing activity.
1. Direct infringement by MAPHIA BBS users
As discussed above, Sega has established that copies were made when unauthorized    copies of Sega game files were downloaded from, or uploaded to, Sherman's BBS by Sherman's BBS users. Therefore, Sega has established direct copyright infringement by Sherman's BBS users.
2. Sherman's knowledge of his users' activities
The standard for the knowledge requirement is objective, and is satisfied where the defendant knows or has reason to know of the infringing activity. Casella v. Morris, [***1713]  820 F.2d 362, 365 (11th Cir. 1987) (quoting Gershwin, 443 F.2d at 1162.) Here, it is undisputed that Sherman had knowledge that his users were copying the games. Sherman admits that users were allowed to upload and download Sega games from his MAPHIA BBS. Moreover, evidence of a screen printout of user uploading and downloading statistics from the   MAPHIA BBS shows that Sherman tracked, or at least had the ability to track, user uploads and downloads. Thus, Sega has established that Sherman knew of the infringing conduct by MAPHIA BBS users.

Fonovisa, 76 F.3d at 264. In this case, Sherman provided the BBS as a central depository site for the unauthorized copies of games, and allowed subsequent distribution of the games by user downloads. He provided the facilities for copying the games by providing, monitoring, and operating the BBS software, hardware, and phone lines necessary for the users to upload and download games.
However, even under an alternative and higher standard of "substantial participation," Sherman is liable. Under this standard, Sherman is only liable if he knew of the users' infringing actions, and yet substantially participated by inducing, causing or materially contributing to the users' infringing conduct. Netcom, 907 F. Supp. at 1382. In this case,    Sherman did more than provide the site and facilities for the known infringing conduct. He actively solicited users to upload unauthorized games, and provided a road map on his BBS for easy identification of Sega games available for downloading. Additionally, through the same MAPHIA BBS medium, he offered copiers for sale to facilitate playing the downloaded games Another court has found that the sale of such copying devices

constitutes contributory infringement. Nintendo of America, Inc. v. Computer and Entertainment, Inc., 1996 WL 511619, *4 (W.D. Wash. 1996). Moreover, Sherman's business, Parsec Trading, had a policy of providing limited free downloading of games and thereafter selling downloading privileges to customers who had purchased copiers. Thus, Sherman's role in the copying, including providing facilities, direction, knowledge, encouragement, and seeking profit, amounts to a prima facie case of contributory copyright infringement.
Because the Court finds that Sega has established a prima facie case of contributory copyright infringement liability, it need not address whether Sherman is also liable under the theory of vicarious liability.
C. Fair Use Defense
Sherman argues that the copying done by the MAPHIA BBS users was fair because there is no evidence that the users went beyond simply playing the games in their own homes, nor any evidence that the users further distributed the games.
Under the fair use defense, there is no infringement, even where a person violates one of the copyright holder's exclusive rights, if that person's use is a fair one. 17 U.S.C. § 107.  In determining whether a use is fair, the following four, non-exclusive factors are considered: the purpose and character of the use; the nature of the copyrighted work; the amount and substantiality of the copyrighted work used; and the effect of the use upon the potential market for the copyrighted work. Title 17 U.S.C. § 107; Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569, 114 S. Ct. 1164, 1170-71, 127 L. Ed. 2d 500 (1994).  Because fair use is an affirmative defense, Sherman carries the burden of demonstrating it. Acuff-Rose, 114 S. Ct. at 1177.
In considering this defense, the Court will consider whether Sherman has shown that either his actions or the users' actions constitute fair use. If the users' actions constitute fair use, they will not be considered  direct infringers. Then, Sherman cannot be contributorily liable because contributory infringement requires direct infringement by someone. Fonovisa, 76 F.3d at 264. If the users' actions do not constitute fair use, Sherman may still avoid liability if his contributing actions qualify as fair use. Netcom, 907 F. Supp. at 1378.
1. Purpose and character of use
With respect to Sherman's activities, the evidence shows that Sherman encouraged uploading and downloading of Sega's games in order to induce sales of copiers. Such a use is clearly commercial. Sherman intended to profit directly from the content of the information made available on his BBS because his copier customers could use the game files to play the games rather than purchase Sega game cartridges. This distinguishes Sherman from the Internet provider in Netcom who did not gain anything from the content of the information available to subscribers. Id. at 1379 (fact  that the Internet provider did not directly gain anything from the content of the information available to its subscribers on the Internet helps weigh [***1714]  this factor in its favor despite commercial character of Internet provider's use). This factor   weighs against a finding of fair use with respect to Sherman's activities.
The BBS users were encouraged to download games from the BBS in order to avoid having to buy video game cartridges from Sega. Such a purpose weighs against the fair use defense. See American Geophysical Union v. Texaco, Inc., 802 F. Supp. 1, 14-16 (S.D.N.Y. 1992), aff'd 60 F.3d 913 (2nd Cir. 1994), cert. dismissed 116 S. Ct. 592 (1995) (no fair use where scientists photocopied publication to avoid cost of purchasing additional copies from publisher). Because the BBS users were able to avoid purchasing the Sega cartridges, their copying is distinguished from that in Lewis Galoob, where the users did have to purchase an authorized game cartridge. See Lewis Galoob Toys, Inc. v. Nintendo of America, Inc., 964 F.2d 965, 970 (9th Cir. 1992), cert. denied, 507 U.S. 985, 123 L. Ed. 2d 149, 113 S. Ct. 1582 (1993) (fair use found where users necessarily had to purchase Nintendo's game cartridges in order to use a device called the "Game Genie," which altered features of Nintendo's copyrighted games during home play.)
Furthermore, this case is distinguishable from Sega Enter., Ltd. v. Accolade,     Inc., 977 F.2d 1510 (9th Cir. 1992), where the court found reverse engineering to be a fair use, in part because the reverse engineering

promoted a growth in creative expression. Id. at 1523. In contrast, in this case, there is no evidence of any actual reverse engineering or any intent on the part of the users to do so. Southeastern Express Co., 64 F.3d 1330, 1336 (9th Cir. 1995), cert. denied 134 L. Ed. 2d 96, 116 S. Ct. 1015 (1996).
2. Nature of the copyrighted work
This factor provides that the closer the copyrighted work is to the core of intended copyright protection, the more difficult it is to establish the fair use defense.  Acuff-Rose, 114 S. Ct. at 1175. In assessing this factor, one consideration is whether the copyrighted work is informational or creative.  Netcom, 907 F. Supp. at 1379. Because the Sega video games are for entertainment uses and involve fiction and fantasy, which are more creative than informational, consideration of the nature of the copyrighted work weighs against a finding of fair use. See Harper & Row     Publishers, Inc. v. Nation Enterprises, 471 U.S. 539, 563, 85 L. Ed. 2d 588, 105 S. Ct. 2218 (1985); Stewart v. Abend, 495 U.S. 207, 237-38, 109 L. Ed. 2d 184, 110 S. Ct. 1750 (1990); Playboy Enter. Inc. v. Frena, 839 F. Supp. 1552, 1558 (M.D.Fla. 1993).
3. Extent of the work copied
The third factor concerns both  the percentage of the original work that was copied, and whether what was copied constitutes the "heart" of the copyrighted work. Netcom, 907 F. Supp. at 1379 (citing Harper    & Row, 471 U.S. at 564-65). Although not a per se rule, the copying of an entire work will ordinarily militate against a finding of fair use. Id. (citing Sony, 464 U.S. at 449-450).
Here, Sega has shown that the BBS users copied virtually entire copyrighted works by way of their uploads and downloads of Sega games, and that Sherman made these games available through his BBS. While this does not per se preclude a finding of fair use, Sherman has not shown any public benefit nor explanation for the complete copying. Cf. Sega Enter., Ltd. v. Accolade, Inc., 977 F.2d 1510, 1526-27 (9th Cir. 1992) (fair use found despite total copying where total copying was necessary to   carry out the defendants' beneficial purpose of reverse engineering software to get at the ideas found in the source code). Therefore, this factor weighs against a finding of fair use.
4. Effect of the use upon the market
The fourth and final statutory factor concerns  whether unrestricted and widespread conduct of the sort engaged in by the defendant would result in a substantially adverse impact on the potential market for the copyrighted work. Campbell, 114 S. Ct. at 1177. While all factors must be weighed together, id. at 1171, the fourth factor is the most important consideration. Los Angeles News Service v. Tullo, 973 F.2d 791, 798 (9th Cir. 1992) (citing Harper & Row, 471 U.S. at 566).
By utilizing the MAPHIA BBS, users are able to download and distribute one or more copies of Sega video game programs from a single copy of a Sega video game program on the MAPHIA BBS, and thereby obtain unauthorized copies of Sega's copyrighted video game programs.
This unauthorized copying of Sega video game programs works to decrease Sega's sales of video game cartridges. The Super Magic Drives could be used for copying Sega's video game programs onto disks. Sherman admits   users were allowed to upload and download Sega games through the MAPHIA BBS onto magnetic media like floppy disks, and that users who had Sega [***1715]  games on disks could play them directly using the copiers. The copiers sold and advertised by Sherman through his business Parsec Trading came with downloading privileges to the purchaser, giving the purchaser the ability to copy Sega copyrighted video game programs from the MAPHIA BBS. Copier purchasers were thus able to duplicate and play the games without purchase of Sega game cartridges. The copiers in conjunction with the MAPHIA BBS supplanted the need to purchase the genuine Sega video games.
While Sherman contends that the copiers have other non-infringing uses, the Court is unpersuaded by this argument. It is unlikely that customers would pay $ 350 to back up the Sega game cartridges, which are not
948 F. Supp. 923, *934; 1996 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 20385, **30; 41 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1705, ***1714
susceptible to breakdown and which sell for between $ 30 and $ 70. The Court finds that the only substantial use of the copiers is to avoid having to buy video game cartridges from Sega by copying the video game program and playing such unauthorized, copied games. See Nintendo, 1996 WL 511619 at *4 (finding that there were no substantial   non- infringing uses for a game-copying device such as the Super UFO, which copies Nintendo games from cartridges to disk).
Sherman also argues that, because there are only a limited number of BBS users that have copiers, and these users would likely play the games only in their own homes, their use should be considered de minimis. He contends that because there is no evidence that these users are further distributing the games, these users' actions cannot be considered to have a tendency to dilute Sega's sales.
The Court finds this argument unpersuasive. Even if the users are only playing the games in their own homes and even if there are currently only a limited number of users that have copiers, unrestricted and widespread conduct of this sort would result in a substantial adverse impact on the market for the Sega games. See Playboy, 839 F. Supp. at 1558-59 (finding that providing a BBS from which users could and did download Playboy copyrighted pictures would adversely affect the market if the conduct became    widespread.) By downloading the games from the BBS, users avoid paying for the games. Sherman's conduct in providing the BBS for uploading and downloading games,    and offering for sale the copiers on which to play these unauthorized games, facilitated the users' conduct. This conduct, if widespread, would adversely impact the market for Sega games.
5. Analysis
All of the factors discussed above weigh against the application of the fair use defense. Because the fair use defense does not apply, and Sega has met its burden to show contributory copyright infringement by Sherman, the Court GRANTS Sega's motion with respect to its copyright claim.
D. Willfulness
Sega contends that Sherman's actions show that he willfully infringed upon their copyrights, which would entitle it to greater damages under 17 U.S.C. § 504(c)(2).
Infringement is willful if the responsible party acts with knowledge that he or she is infringing a copyright. Peer Intl. Corp. v. Pausa Records, Inc., 909 F.2d 1332, 1335 (9th Cir. 1990), cert. denied 498 U.S. 1109, 112 L. Ed. 2d 1100, 111 S. Ct. 1019 (1991); Twin Peaks Productions, Inc. v.
