Plaintiffs request and suggest that a judgment in the amount of $ 1,000 per infringement would, under the circumstances, be just and reasonable in the instant case. In addition, plaintiffs maintain that defendants are not entitled to rely on the "innocent infringer" defense because "each and every infringing videocassette seized from defendants contained a notice of copyright." Further, in their reply brief in support of their motion for summary judgment, plaintiffs represent that "for purposes of this motion only, plaintiffs hereby abandon their claim of willful infringement."
In response, defendants do not dispute plaintiffs' entitlement to statutory damages under the Copyright Act. However, defendants do contest the applicability of § 504(c)(1). Defendants argue that § 504(c)(2) is appropriate in the instant case and request a hearing on this matter. In particular, defendants maintain that they did not "willfully infringe" plaintiffs' respective copyrights.    In their answer to plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment, defendants "maintain that their actions were not willful and that they did not recklessly disregard the plaintiffs' copyright[s]." Defendants rely on an "innocent infringement" defense in mitigation of statutory damages. Defendants "suggest to the court that a full hearing [should] be held on the issue of 'willfulness' in order to determine whether or not Section 504(c)(2) should be applied in determining statutory damages." Defendants posit that if such a hearing is held, "evidence will show that these defendants were not willful in their infringement of the plaintiffs' motion pictures." In so doing, defendants direct this court's attention to this court's decision in Zakarian, 1991 WL 93889, at *5, wherein the court denied a plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on the issue of statutory damages in connection with a copyright infringement claim for the illegal distribution of unauthorized duplicates of videocassettes containing copyrighted motion pictures. Defendants posit that, as in Zakarian, this court should set the matter for a hearing.
This court grants plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment on the   issue of statutory damages in connection with plaintiffs' copyright infringement action. This court recognizes  § 504(c) of the Copyright Act allows a copyright holder to elect statutory damages in lieu of actual damages. See 17 U.S.C. § 504(c)(1); see also Video Views, Inc. v. Studio 21, Ltd., 925 F.2d 1010, 1013 (7th Cir. 1991); Landa, 974 F. Supp. at 14; Zakarian, 1991 WL 93889, at *4. If a defendant is found to have infringed and statutory damages have been elected, § 504(c)(1) states that a plaintiff is entitled to:

an award of statutory damages for all infringements involved in the action, with respect to any one work, for which any one infringer is liable individually, or for which any two or more infringers are liable jointly and severally, in a sum of not less than $ 500 or more than $ 20,000 as the court considers just.

17 U.S.C. § 504(c)(1); see also Video Views, Inc., 925 F.2d at 1013; Landa, 974 F. Supp. at 14; Zakarian, 1991 WL 93889, at *4. At the same time, however,  § 504(c)(2) empowers a district court with the discretion, in certain circumstances, to grant an enhanced award of up to $ 100,000 per infringement or to make   a reduced award as low as $ 200 per infringement. In particular, § 504(c)(2) provides as follows:

In a case where the copyright owner sustains the burden of proving, and the court finds, that infringement was committed willfully, the court in its discretion may increase the award of statutory damages to a sum of not more than $ 100,000. In a case where the infringer sustains the burden of proving, and the court finds, that such infringer was not aware and had no reason to believe that his or her acts constituted an infringement of a copyright, the court [in] its discretion may reduce the award of statutory damages to a sum of not less than $ 200.  The court shall remit statutory damages in any case where an infringer believed and had reasonable grounds for believing that his or her use of the copyrighted work was a fair use under section 107, if the infringer was: (i) an employee or agent of a nonprofit educational institution, library, or archives acting within the scope of his or her employment who, or such institution, library, or archives itself, which infringed by reproducing the work in copies or phone cords; or (ii) a public broadcasting entity which or a person who, as   a regular part of the nonprofit activities of a public broadcasting entity (as defined in subsection (g) of section 118) infringed by performing a published nondramatic literary work or by reproducing a transmission program embodying a performance of such a work.

17 U.S.C. § 504(c)(2).
This court initially notes that the first sentence of § 504(c)(2) is inapplicable in the instant case and, as such, this court does not consider whether to exercise its discretion to award plaintiffs an enhanced amount of statutory damages based on a finding of willfulness. As stated, § 504(c)(2) states that in instances where a copyright infringement plaintiff sustains its burden of proving, and the court finds, "that infringement was committed willfully, the court in its discretion may increase the award of statutory damages to a sum of not more than $ 100,000." Id. In this case, plaintiffs, in their reply brief in support of their motion for summary judgment, represent that for purposes of the instant motion for summary judgment "plaintiffs hereby abandon their claim of willful infringement." As a result, consideration as to whether to award plaintiffs an enhanced amount up to $ 100,000   for each of defendants' infringement under § 504(c)(2) is improper in the instant case because plaintiffs do not claim that defendants' infringement was willful. See Landa, 974 F. Supp. at 15 (district court did not consider whether to award plaintiffs an enhanced amount under § 504(c)(2) where the plaintiffs did not seek a finding that the infringing acts were willful) compare Zakarian, 1991 WL 93889, at *5 (considering a claim by plaintiffs that defendants' infringement was willful in connection with motion for summary judgment on the issue of statutory damages).
Defendants, however, claim that the amount of statutory damages provided for in § 504(c)(1), i.e., between $ 500 and $ 20,000, is inappropriate in the instant case and seek a reduced sanction for each infringement under § 504(c)(2). In this regard, defendants claim that their infringement was not willful and that they "never knowingly possessed any illegal videocassette tapes, but rather were in possession of said videocassette tapes, having purchased said videocassette tapes from various sources, including, vendors, flea market sales, private owners and other video rental stores." In so doing, defendants   request a hearing and rely  on the second sentence in § 504(c)(2) which, as previously referenced, allows a court to exercise its discretion to reduce the award of statutory damages below the $ 500 minimum amount provided for in § 504(c)(1) to a sum of not less than $ 200 in instances where "the infringer sustains the burden of proving, and the court finds, that such infringer was not aware and had no reason to believe that his or her acts constituted an infringement of a copyright." 17 U.S.C. § 504(c)(2).
Despite defendants' reliance on the second sentence in § 504(c)(2) in an attempt to reduce the amount of statutory damages, this court finds that, given the record in the instant case, § 401 of the Copyright Act renders the second sentence of § 504(c)(2) inapplicable in the instant case.  § 401(d) of the Copyright Act provides that:

If a notice of copyright in the form and position specified by this section appears on the published copy or copies to which a defendant in a copyright infringement suit had access, then no weight shall be given to such a defendant's interposition of a defense based on innocent infringement in mitigation of actual or statutory damages, except as provided in the last sentence of section 504(c)(2).


17 U.S.C. § 401(d).  With respect to the "form of notice" referenced in § 401(d), § 401(b) provides as follows:

(b) Form of Notice. -- If a notice appears on the copies, it shall consist of the following three elements: (1) the symbol Copr. (the letter C in a circle), or the word "Copyright," or the abbreviation "Copr."; and

(2) the year of first publication of the work; in the case of compilations or derivative works incorporating  previously published material, the year date of first publication of the compilation or derivative work is sufficient. The year date may be omitted where a pictorial, graphic, or structural work, with accompanying text matter, if any, is reproduced in or on greeting cards, postcards, stationary, jewelry, dolls, toys, or any useful articles; and (3) the name of the owner of copyright in the work, or an abbreviation by which the name can be recognized, or a generally known alternative designation of the owner.

17 U.S.C. 401(b).  Relative to the "position of notice" referenced by § 401(d), § 401(c) states the following:

(c) Position of Notice. -- The notice shall be affixed to the copies in such a manner and location as to give reasonable notice to the claim of copyright. The Register of Copyrights shall prescribe by regulation, as examples, specific methods of affixation and positions of the notice on various types of works that will satisfy this requirement, but these specifications shall not be considered exhaustive.

17 U.S.C. § 401(c).
In this case, plaintiffs have submitted the affidavit of Douglas S. Buck, one of plaintiffs' attorneys, which supports plaintiffs' position that the infringing videocassettes seized from defendant Tucker's Video Connection contained a notice of copyright published in conformity with § 401. Defendants have not provided any evidence to the contrary. As stated, with respect to the "form of notice" requirement, § 401(b) provides that the following appear on the copies: (i) the symbol Copr. (the letter C in a circle), the word "copyright," or the abbreviation "Copr.;" (ii) the year of the first publication of the work; and (iii) the name of the work's copyright owner, an abbreviation by which the name can be recognized, or a generally known alternative designation of the owner. See 17 U.S.C. § 401(b). In Buck's affidavit, Buck testified that on August 14, 1995, he personally reviewed every videocassette seized from Tucker's Video Connection. Buck stated that upon his review of the seized videocassettes, he observed that, except for six of the videocassettes seized, the outside label of every videocassette "bares a notice of the copyright" and that "these notices consist of the letter   C in a circle, or the word 'Copyright,' the year of first publication of the work and the name of the copyright owner." Buck stated that while notice of this information is illegible on the outside cassette label of the other six videocassettes, such notice "is displayed during the credits of the movie itself." Moreover, according to Buck's affidavit, all six of these videocassettes "bare an FBI warning on the outside of the cassette which reads in part, 'all … rights reserved …. Federal law provides severe civil and criminal penalties for the unauthorized reproduction, distribution or exhibition of copyrighted motion pictures, video tapes or laser discs." As such, this court finds that plaintiffs have established the "form of notice" requirement of § 401(b) because Buck's uncontroverted affidavit reflects that notice of plaintiffs' copyright appears on each of the seized videocassettes, along with the year of first publication of the work and the name of the copyright owner.
This court also finds that Buck's uncontroverted affidavit establishes that the "position of notice" requirement of § 401 has been satisfied in the instant case. Relative to this requirement,  § 401(c)    states that "the notice shall be affixed to the copies in such a manner and location as to give reasonable notice of the claim of copyright" and that "the Register of Copyrights shall prescribe by regulation, as examples, specific methods of affixation and positions of the notice on various types of works that will satisfy this requirement, but these specifications shall not be considered exhaustive." 17 U.S.C. § 401(c).  Examples of methods of affixation and positions of the copyright notice on various types of works that will satisfy the notice requirement of § 401(c) is found in 37 C.F.R. § 201.20. Subdivision (h) of that regulation governs positions of copyright notice for "motion pictures and other audiovisual works." 37 C.F.R. § 201.20(h). In particular, this subdivision provides, in pertinent part, as follows:

(1) The following constitute examples of acceptable methods of affixation and positions of the copyright notice on motion pictures and other audiovisual works: A notice that is embodied in the copies by a photomechanical or electric process, in such a position that it ordinarily would appear whenever the work is performed in its entirety, and that is located: (i)    With or near the title; (ii) with the cast, credits, and similar information; (iii) at or immediately following the beginning of the work; or (iv) at or immediately preceding the end of the work. …. (3) In the case of a motion picture or other audiovisual work that is distributed to the public for private use, the notice may be affixed, in addition to the locations specified in paragraph (h)(1) of this section, on the housing or container, if it is a permanent receptacle for the work.

37 C.F.R. § 201.20(h).
In the instant case, Buck's affidavit establishes that notice of copyright for all of the seized videocassettes is positioned in accordance with subsection (h) of 37 C.F.R. § 201.20, and therefore in conformity with the requirements of § 401(c). With respect to the six videocassettes which, as Buck's affidavit states, contains copyright notice during the credits of each movie, the notice of copyright in these videocassettes, as described in Buck's uncontroverted affidavit, is in accordance with paragraph (h)(1). That paragraph indicates that an acceptable method of affixation and position of copyright notice on motion pictures and other audiovisual works is a notice   of copyright appearing "with the cast, credits, and similar information." 37 C.F.R. § 201.20(h)(1). Buck's affidavit states that these six videocassettes have notice of copyright "displayed during the credits of the movie itself" and therefore in conformity with paragraph (h)(1) of § 201.20. As for the other videocassettes seized at Tucker's Video Connection, Buck's affidavit represents that these copies contain a notice of copyright positioned in accordance with paragraph (h)(3) which states that notice may be affixed "on the housing or container, if it is a permanent receptacle for the work." 37 C.F.R. § 201.20(h)(3). According to Buck's affidavit, with the exception of the aforementioned six videocassettes, the other videocassettes contain a notice of copyright "printed on a label located out of the videocassette itself." As a result, these videocassettes contain a notice of copyright positioned in accordance with paragraph (h)(3) of § 201.20.
This court therefore finds that, given Buck's uncontroverted affidavit, § 401 of the Copyright Act renders the second sentence of § 504(c)(2), i.e., defendants' "innocent infringement" defense to statutory damages, inapplicable  to the instant case. Buck's affidavit establishes that the seized videocassettes complied with both the "form of notice" and the "position of notice" requirements of § 401 and, as such, § 401(d) requires that "no weight … be given to [defendants'] interposition of a defense based on innocent infringement in mitigation of actual or statutory damages…." 17 U.S.C. § 401(d). As a result, this court finds that a reduced damages award pursuant to § 504(c)(2) based on "innocent infringement" is inappropriate in the instant case. See also Columbia Pictures Industries, Inc. v. Richardson, 95-C-0868-C, at pp. 8-9 (W.D. Wis. 1996). Therefore, this court predicates plaintiffs' statutory damages award on § 504(c)(1).
This court denies defendants' request for a hearing on the issue of statutory damages in the instant case. As stated, defendants, in requesting a hearing on the issue of statutory damages, relies on this court's decision in Zakarian. In their "memorandum in opposition of plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment," defendants assert that in Zakarian this court "denied an award of statutory damages and set the matter for hearing on the issue of whether 17 U.S.C.   Section 504(c)(2) should be applied to determine a lesser sanction for innocent infringement." Defendants posit that they "seek the same relief."
This court finds no merit to defendants' reliance on Zakarian in support of their request for a hearing on the issue of whether a lesser sanction is warranted for "innocent infringement." In Zakarian, this court granted plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment on the issue of copyright infringement, but denied plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment on the issue of statutory damages and set the matter for a hearing. See Zakarian, 1991 WL 93889, at *4-5. On the issue of copyright infringement, this court found defendant, an owner of a video rental store, liable for violating plaintiffs' exclusive right to reproduce and to distribute copies of the subject motion pictures, i.e., copyright infringement. See Zakarian, 1991 WL 93889, at *4. On the issue of statutory damages, plaintiffs argued that defendants' infringements were committed "willfully and with knowledge of the illegality of said actions" and sought an enhanced award of statutory damages "of not less than $ 500 nor more than $ 100,000 for each infringement."   See id. at *5. As such, the plaintiffs sought an enhanced amount of statutory damages pursuant to § 504(c)(2) based on a finding of willfulness. See id. This court, however, determined that, based on the evidence of willful infringement in the record which was largely circumstantial, it could not determine "whether Zakarian knew that she was infringing plaintiffs' copyrights or whether she was acting in reckless disregard of those copyrights." Id. This court therefore found that "Zakarian's intent and her state of mind, both crucial to the willfulness determination, are issues of fact to which Zakarian has presented a genuine issue." Id.
Zakarian is distinguishable from the instant case for two significant reasons. First, defendants in the instant case apparently misconstrue this court's decision in Zakarian as concluding that the defendant in that case was entitled to a hearing on the issue of "innocent infringement." Zakarian, however, did not conclude that there was a genuine issue of material fact on the issue of whether defendants are entitled to pay a lesser sanction based on a finding of "innocent infringement." See id. Rather, the court in Zakarian   found that there was a genuine issue of material fact on the issue of whether plaintiffs were entitled to an enhanced award of statutory damages pursuant to § 504(c)(2), i.e., an award between $ 500 and $ 100,000 per infringement, based on a finding of "willful infringement." See id. Therefore, this court denies defendants' request for a hearing on the issue of innocent infringement because § 401 renders that issue inapplicable. Even assuming arguendo that § 401 of the Copyright Act did not render the "innocent infringement" defense in mitigation of statutory damages inapplicable, this court finds that an award of statutory damages pursuant to § 501(c)(1) is appropriate in the instant   case. See Landa, 974 F. Supp. at 14. what is just in   the particular case, considering the nature of the copyright, the circumstances of the infringement and the like, … but with the express qualification that in every case the assessment must be within the prescribed [maximum or minimum].

Peer International Corporation v. Pausa Records, Inc., 909 F.2d 1332, 1336 (9th Cir. 1990) (quoting F.W. Woolworth Co. v. Contemporary Arts, Inc., 344 U.S. 228, 232, 73 S. Ct. 222, 225, 97 L. See id.; Haines and Company, Inc., 905 F.2d at 1089.
Given the pervasive nature of defendants' illegal activity, i.e., 115 infringements and 261 illegal videotapes available to the public for rental, this court finds that an award of $ 1,000 per infringement is just and proper. Cf.  Landa, 974 F. Supp. at 15-16. Since defendants collectively infringed upon 115 individual movie titles, this court will award plaintiffs a total award of $ 115,000. See id. (citing to Hodge E. Mason and Hodge Mason Maps, Inc. v. Montgomery Data, Inc., et al, 967 F.2d 135, 144 n.11 (5th Cir. 1992)   (noting that the text and legislative history of section 504(c)(1) make clear that statutory damages are to be calculated according to the number of works infringed)). In support of this motion, plaintiffs contend that "due to the magnitude of defendants' infringement and the ease with which such infringement is perpetuated, the threat of defendants' continuing   infringement is substantial." Any court having jurisdiction of a civil action arising under this title may, subject to the provisions of section 1498 of title 28, grant temporary and final injunctions on such terms as it may deem reasonable to prevent or restrain infringement of a copyright.

17 U.S.C. § 502(a). A permanent   injunction is appropriate under § 502 of the Copyright Act when liability has been established and there still exists the threat of continuing or ongoing infringements of plaintiff's rights. See Landa, 974 F. Supp. at 16; Columbia Pictures Industries, Inc. v. Babella, 1996 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 7990, 1996 WL 328015, at *4; Columbia Pictures Industries, Inc. v. Zuniga, 1995 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 15824, 1995 WL 632249, at *5 (N.D. Ill. 1995); Zakarian, 1991 WL 93889, at *6; Broadcast Music, Inc. v. Niro's Palace, Inc., 619 F. Supp. 958, 963 (N.D. Ill. 1985). In assessing whether a permanent injunction is appropriate, a large number of infringements is a factor which courts consider. See Landa, 974 F. Supp. at 16; Zuniga, 1995 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 15824, 1995 WL 632249, at *5; Zakarian, 93889, at *6.

As stated, plaintiffs have established 115 infringements of their copyrights, and 261 illegally duplicated video cassettes were seized from defendants' store on September 15, 1994. See Zuniga,   1995 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 15824, 1995 WL 632249, at *5. Defendants have put forth no reason why an injunction should not issue in these circumstances.  Accordingly, plaintiffs' motion for a permanent injunction pursuant to § 502 of the Copyright Act is granted and this court will enter an order enjoining defendants from further infringement of the copyrights owned by plaintiffs. See Landa, 974 F. Supp. at 16; Zuniga, 1995 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 15824, 1995 WL 632249, at *5-6. In that connection, plaintiffs are directed to file with the court proposed language for the permanent injunction within fourteen days of the entry of this memorandum and order. See Landa, 974 F. Supp. at 17.
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, this court:    grants plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment on their copyright infringement claim; grants plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment on the issue of statutory damages in connection with plaintiffs' claim for copyright infringement; grants plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment on plaintiff's claim for a permanent injunction; grants plaintiffs' motion for costs; and denies plaintiffs' motion for attorney's fees. It is further ordered that plaintiffs file with the court proposed language for the permanent injunction, as well as a bill of costs, within twenty-eight days of the date of the entry of this memorandum and order and defendants are granted twenty-eight days following receipt of the bill of costs to file any objections as to the reasonableness of the costs submitted.

Defendants Ives and Ellis also testified, however, that the infringements were innocent. They maintained that identification and elimination of all PEI images was impossible and therefore that no infringement might be termed "willful."
The Court disagrees. Elimination by manual monitoring would have been difficult and expensive, but not impossible, particularly for images as obviously infringing as the ones at issue here. The evidence shows that Webbworld implemented substantial effort to combat the infringement. Notwithstanding its "compliance program," Webbworld chose to continue to copy from a newsgroup that essentially advertised by its "centerfolds" name that it carried PEI images. After it was on notice of infringement, Webbworld chose to stay in business without implementing a system that would   reliably delete even such obvious transgressions. Such an action constitutes willful infringement. See Broadcast Music, Inc., 855 F.2d at 236 (holding that a music vendor's choice to stay in business and thereby to continue to infringe copyrighted music was patently willful). For the five copyright registrations infringed by the many images Webbworld copied from the "centerfolds" newsgroup after the TRO was entered in this case, the Court makes a finding of willfulness.

PEI claims that each of the individual Defendants should be held vicariously liable for Webbworld's infringement.  Participants in copyright infringement are jointly and severally liable as tortfeasors.  Swallow Turn v. Wilson, 831 F. Supp. 575, 579 (E.D. Tex. 1993).  To show vicarious liability, a plaintiff must prove that a defendant (1) has a direct financial interest in the infringing activity, and (2) has the right and ability to supervise the activity which causes the infringement. Id. As with direct copyright infringement, intent or knowledge of the infringement is not an element of a claim for    vicarious liability.  Peer Int'l Corp. v. Luna Records, Inc., 887   F. Supp. 560, 565 (S.D.N.Y. 1995). "Innocence," therefore, is no defense.  Swallow Turn Music, 831 F. Supp. at 578-79.
991 F. Supp. 543, *553; 1997 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 21264, **18; 45 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1641, ***1647

On summary judgment in this case, Judge Saffels held Defendants Ellis and Ives vicariously liable for the sixty-two direct infringements decided at that time. See Webbworld, 968 F. Supp. at 1177. Nothing in the evidence adduced at trial argues against holding these two similarly liable for the remaining infringements. Ellis testified that he had full control of the day-to-operations of the Netpics site throughout the relevant time period. Furthermore, he created and controlled operation of the ScanNews software that was the heart of the Webbworld enterprise, and he chose which newsgroups would serve as sources of material. In return, Ellis collected 50% of Webbworld's net profits. Ellis is vicariously liable for the infringements in this case.
Defendant Ives, until late January 1997, owned 100% of the outstanding Webbworld shares of stock and was Webbworld's president and director. He handled most of the legal and financial aspects of the business. Ives testified at trial that he had no involvement in the day-to-day operations of the business. He kept his   full-time position with the United States Postal Service and devoted only about 20 hours per week to Webbworld. He viewed the Netpics site only a "couple of times" per week, typically when a change was made or a question raised. His testimony, corroborated by Defendant Gurkin, was that operational decisions were made only by consensus and that Ives did not -- and did not believe he had the authority to -- give orders to Ellis regarding operation of the business. Ives testified that he could "make suggestions" but could not control Ellis.

Supp. at 578-79 (defining liability as the "right and ability" to exercise   control) (and cases cited therein). In this case, Ives's ownership of 100% of the business and his position, therefore, as Ellis's employer, invested him with supervisory authority over all Webbworld operations, including the infringing activities. Even though he declined to exercise such authority, his right and ability to exercise it is sufficient for vicarious liability to attach.
It is undisputed that Ives received a significant and direct financial reward of 25% of Webbworld net profits for his efforts. Accordingly, Ives, along with Ellis, is vicariously liable for each of the remaining infringements at issue in this case.
The analysis with regard to Defendant Gurkin reaches a different result. Gurkin, who formerly worked for the United States Postal service and owned a security agency, contributed start-up capital to Webbworld. He derived significant financial benefit from the business in the form of 25% of the net income. With regard to establishing the requisite supervisory authority over the infringing activity, however, PEI has not met its burden as to Gurkin.
Gurkin worked as Webbworld's customer service representative, spending approximately 3-5 hours per day fielding   and responding to subscribers' e-mail. Although the parties have stipulated that Gurkin, along with Ellis and Ives, "had the right, authority and ability to control the operations of the Netpics website," the Court finds that Gurkin did not have authority or supervision over the actual infringing activities. Moreover, PEI did not connect him to any decision-making ability regarding which newsgroups the site used as sources of material. Accordingly, the Court finds that Gurkin should not be held vicariously liable for any of the infringements.

PEI has elected to pursue statutory damages for its established claim of copyright infringement.  A copyright owner whose copyright has been infringed may, at any time before judgment, elect to recover either actual damages or statutory damages.  17 U.S.C. § 504; see Central Point Software, 903 F. Supp. at 1060-61. Supp. at 1061. For the violations the Court has found to be willful, the maximum statutory award is raised to $ 100,000 per infringement. See id.
Within the range defined by the statutory maximum and minimum, the court   has virtually unfettered discretion in setting the damage award.  F.W. Woolworth Co. v. Contemporary Arts, 344 U.S. 228, 231, 97 L. Ed. 276, 73 S. Ct. 222 (1952); see Broadcast Music, Inc. v. Star Amusements, Inc., 44 F.3d 485, 487-89 (7th Cir. 1995) (holding that the standard of review for an award of statutory damages is even more deferential than an abuse of discretion standard) (citing Douglas v. Cunningham, 294 U.S. 207, 210, 79 L. Ed. 862, 55 S. Ct. 365 (1935)). HN20[

Co., 807 F.2d 1110, 1117 (2nd Cir. 1986).
In this case, the evidence shows that in its 9-month existence, Webbworld generated approximately $ 670,000 after some but not all expenses, and before taxes. According to further testimony   from Defendant Ives, Webbworld's net income was between $ 400,000 and $ 450,000 for the relevant period. The testimony is not clear to what extent, if at all, appropriating PEI images rather than generating original images served to decrease Webbworld's operating expenses.
The weight of the evidence establishes that even after becoming aware of obvious infringements, Webbworld continued to operate overall at approximately the same pace, and with an increasing clientele, while declining to develop software or an effective manual monitoring plan to eliminate copying of PEI images. A simple reduction in the number of newsgroups covered would have facilitated lawful operation. Under those circumstances, continuing to operate virtually unrestrained showed, at best, reckless disregard of PEI's legal rights.

As a somewhat mitigating factor, the Court finds that Webbworld and its principals attempted to put a "compliance plan" in place after entry of the TRO to reduce the risk of infringement. Specifically, the images do not appear for the most part in proximity to a title, phrase or emblem connecting them to PEI. PEI appears to find great negative significance in that Defendants made a relatively large amount of money for a relatively small investment of capital and time. On the contrary, the Court finds no reason to deter [***1655] capitalism in the technological or any other arena.
Copyright infringement, however, must not be allowed to serve as the cornerstone of a profitable business. Under all of the circumstances of this case, the Court awards to PEI $ 1,000 for each of the 29 copyrights at issue at trial. B. Permanent Injunction

In addition to damages, PEI asks the Court to enter a permanent injunction.  Under the Copyright Act, a court may "grant   temporary and final injunctions on such terms as it may deem reasonable to prevent or restrain infringement of a copyright.  17 U.S.C. § 502(a). Permanent injunctive relief is "never lightly given." Posada v. Lamb County, Tex., 716 F.2d 1066, 1070 (5th Cir. 1983). To establish entitlement to permanent injunctive relief, a party must demonstrate the following: (1) actual success on the merits; (2) no adequate remedy at law; (3) that the threatened injury outweighs any damage to the defendant; and (4) that the injunction will not disserve the public interest.  Caroline T. v. Hudson School Dist., 915 F.2d 752, 755 (1st Cir. 1990); Picker Int'l v. Blanton, 756 F. Supp. 971, 978 (N.D. Tex. 1990); see also DSC Comms. Corp. v. DGI Tech., Inc., 81 F.3d 597, 600 (5th Cir. 1996) (applying the traditional factors to a preliminary injunction application for copyright infringement).
In this case, PEI has prevailed in its case for copyright infringement. The burden that would be imposed on Defendants -- merely to refrain from further infringement -- is light in comparison to the threatened injury to PEI should such infringement occur. Furthermore, the Court finds that the public   interest, to the extent it is involved at all in this private business matter, is affirmatively served by requiring continuing, strict adherence to intellectual property law in the relatively uncharted arena of Internet commerce.
It remains to be decided only whether PEI has an adequate remedy at law in this case. To prevail on this issue, PEI must show a significant threat of cognizable injury and that money damages would not fully repair the threatened harm.  Humana, inc. v. Avram A. Jacobson, M.D., P.A., 804 F.2d 1390, 1394 (5th Cir. 1986); see Danden Petroleum, Inc. v. Northern Natural Gas Co., 615 F. Supp. 1093, 1099 (N.D. Tex. 1985)  ("Injuries which can be compensated by money damages at a later time are not irreparable and do not warrant the extraordinary remedy of an injunction.").
In analyzing the evidence in this case, the Court revisits Robert Perkins's testimony    that PEI's reputation would be damaged by continued display of PEI images in close conjunction with "hard-core pornography." Although the Court did not find the past harm to have risen to the level of tarnishment required for dilution of trademark under all the circumstances, the evidence is at least probative   on the issue of potential harm for which legal remedy is inadequate. See Valley v. Rapides Parish Sch. Bd., 118 F.3d 1047, 1053-56 (5th Cir. 1997) (holding potential damage to reputation to constitute irreparable harm). Additionally, the Court finds a strong suggestion that Defendants Webbworld, Ives, and Ellis may not be in a position to provide future monetary relief if required. The assets of Webbworld, its computers and files, have been seized; and the ScanNews software, the heart of Webbworld's business, has been sold to the Yehudi company in California. Of course, these facts may argue equally that no serious danger of recurrent violation exists. See United States v. W.T. Grant Co., 345 U.S. 629, 633,
991 F. Supp. 543, *561; 1997 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 21264, **47; 45 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1641, ***1654

97 L. Ed. 1303, 73 S. Ct. 894 (1953) (requiring for permanent injunction that there be "something more than the mere possibility which serves to keep the case alive").
On the other hand, a finding of willful infringement has been made in this case. Defendants have not shrunk from continuing their activities even when put on notice of infringement. See Dream Dealers Music v. Parker, 924 F. Supp. 1146, 1152 (S.D. Ala. 1996) (awarding a permanent injunction against the   owner of a broadcast station who "willfully and flagrantly" persisted in infringing conduct). Moreover, Defendant Ellis, who wrote the ScanNews software, is capable of and amenable to re-creating it for the same purpose. See Ives Depo. (noting that Ellis continued to look for a way to profit from the ScanNews software before the sale to Yehudi); Ellis Depo II, at 41 (indicating that as of August 11, 1997, Ellis continues to write Internet-related software).
Under all of these circumstances, PEI has made a sufficient showing of the potential for irreparable harm and the substantial likelihood of further infringement. See Marvin Music Co. v. BHC Ltd Partnership, 830 F. Supp. 651, 655 (D. Mass. 1993) (noting that once liability for [***1656]  copyright infringement has been established, courts generally grant a permanent injunction if there is a substantial likelihood of continuing infringement). By separate order, Defendants Webbworld, Ellis and Ives will be permanently enjoined from infringing PEI's copyrighted images.

YOUNG, D.J.

December 31, 1997

The Plaintiff, Claire Murray ("Murray"), brought suit against the Defendant, Shaw Industries, Inc., ("Shaw"), alleging copyright infringement and violation of the Lanham Act, 15 U.S.C. §§ 1125(a)(1)(A) and 1125(a)(1)(B). After a jury trial, the jury found liability on both theories and awarded Murray compensatory damages of $ 386,875    for the infringement of four separate copyrights. Thereafter, the Court awarded statutory damages of $ 100,000 for each copyright infringed. Pursuant to 17 U.S.C. § 504, Murray elected   to receive statutory damages for each of three copyrights infringed, and for the infringement of the fourth copyright, the "Noah's Ark" design, she elected the jury's award in the amount of $ 235,585.75. In addition, the jury awarded compensatory damages under the Lanham Act in the amount of $ 58,000. Murray now moves for the entry of judgment in the case awarding her both her elected copyright damages of $ 535,585.75 and her Lanham Act damages of $ 58,000, along with attorney's fees and costs, plus interest from the commencement of suit.
DISCUSSION

The question before the Court is whether Murray is entitled to all of the relief that she seeks, or merely a part of that relief.
1. Damages

Murray asserts, correctly, that  courts in some instances may award damages for both copyright infringement and violation of the Lanham Act in the same action. See Nintendo of America, Inc. v. Dragon Pacific Int'l, 40 F.3d 1007, 1010-11 (9th Cir. 1994) (upon which Murray relies), cert. denied sub nom.  Sheng v. Nintendo of America, Inc., 515 U.S. 1107, 132 L. Ed. 2d 263, 115 S. Ct. 2256 (1995). An award under the Lanham Act, however, is expressly made "subject to the principles of equity,"    15 U.S.C. § 1117(a); see Johnson v. Jones, 921 F. Supp. 1573, 1587 (E.D. Mich. 1996). The plaintiff ought not obtain a double recovery where her injuries stemming from the infringement of her copyright and the violation of her rights under the Lanham Act are coextensive. Cf.  Computer Assocs. Int'l, Inc. v. Altai, Inc., 982 F.2d 693, 720 (2d Cir. 1992) (so noting in the context of copyright infringement and trade secret appropriation).
The issues of copyright infringement and violation of the Lanham Act were both submitted to the jury, and the jury found liability under both theories. At no point during the proceedings, however, did Murray offer any proof of direct economic damages, such as lost profits or diminution in the value of her intellectual property flowing from either the infringement or the Lanham Act violation. As a result, both of the verdicts were based entirely on the profits Shaw earned selling Murray's designs. Likewise, the Court's award of statutory damages, although crafted in part to punish and deter the defendant, was necessarily premised on the disgorgement [***1155]  of Shaw's profits, in view of the absence of proof of other damages.
Because the only available   theory of damages in this case was based on the surrender of Shaw's profits attributable to the sale of Murray's designs, the measure of damages for the violation of the Lanham Act is coextensive with the measure of damages for copyright infringement. This is not a case, like Nintendo, in which the statutory damages for copyright infringement represent different theories of harm or punishment from the Lanham Act damages. Rather, copyright infringement and violation of the Lanham Act served as alternate legal bases for imposing liability and obtaining the recovery of what was essentially the same measure of damages. This Court concludes that it would be inequitable to allow Murray to recover under the Lanham Act in addition to her copyright damages. Although Shaw's actions may have constituted "two wrongs" under the separate statutory schemes governing copyright and trademark, Nintendo, 40 F.3d at 1010, those wrongs produced a single harm. Murray is adequately compensated, and Shaw is adequately punished and deterred, by the combination of statutory and actual copyright damages that Murray has elected. This court therefore limits Murray's award to damages for the infringement   of her copyrights in the amount of $ 535,585.75.

At the conclusion of this non-jury trial the Court found that the defendants wilfully infringed plaintiff's copyright. Since there were questions concerning the legal standards to be applied in determining damages, the Court requested additional briefs on those issues.
Under the Copyright Act, a copyright owner is entitled to recover from an infringer "the actual damages suffered by him or her as a result of the infringement, and any profits of the infringer that are attributable to the infringement and are not taken into account in computing actual damages . . . ."   17 U.S.C. § 504(b). The specific questions presented here are whether the defendant is entitled to a deduction for overhead in computing the amount of profit it realized on the infringing sales and whether the plaintiff must deduct overhead in computing the damages it suffered as the result of   lost sales.
While the plaintiff in a copyright action is entitled to recover the "profits" of the defendant, the plaintiff does not have to prove the actual amount of the profit. It is only required to prove the gross income that the defendant derived from sales on the infringing goods. 17 U.S.C. § 504(b); In Design v. K-Mart Apparel Corp., 13 F.3d 559, 563 (2d Cir. 1994). The burden then shifts to the defendant to prove that it had costs associated with the production of the goods that should be deducted in determining the profit it realized on the sales of those goods. 17 U.S.C. § 504(b); In Design, 13 F.3d at 563.
In cases such as this, where the the defendant's infringment is found to be wilful the courts are divided on the question of the defendant's right to deduct "overhead" expense in calculating the profit that the plaintiff is entitled to recover.

Some courts have adopted the "full absorption" approach, which permits the defendant to deduct all overhead expenses in the same percentage as the sales of the infringing goods bears to its total sales. See, e.g., Warner Bros., Inc. v. Gay Toys, Inc., 598 F. Supp. 424, 428-29 (S.D.N.Y. 1984); Stevens Linen Associates,     Inc. v. Mastercraft Corp., 1980 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 15653, 79 Civ. 2016 (CBM), 1980 WL 1174 (S.D.N.Y. Dec. 17, 1980), modified on other grounds, 656 F.2d 11 (2d Cir. 1981). Other courts allow the defendant to deduct only "incremental" overhead costs, that is, those costs which can be shown to be directly related to the production of the infringing goods.  Levin Bros. v. Davis Mfg. Co., 72 F.2d 163 (8th Cir. 1934); With Love Designs, Inc. v. Dressy Tessy, Inc., 1992 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 15629, 91 Civ. 4717 (RPP), 1992 WL 309578 (S.D.N.Y. Oct. 9, 1992); Jarvis v. A & M Records, 827 F. Supp. 282 (D.N.J. 1993).
The law in this Circuit finds its genesis in the statement of Judge Learned Hand in Sheldon v. Metro-Goldwyn Pictures Corp., 106 F.2d 45, 54 (2d Cir. 1939):

The correct rule upon this point is stated in Levin Bros. v. Davis Mfg. Co., 72 F.2d 163, 8 Cir., and in substance it is this.  'Overhead' which does not assist in the production of the infringement should not be credited to the infringer; that which does, should be; it is a question of fact in all cases. In the case at bar the infringing picture was one of over forty made by the defendants, using the same supervising staff and organization, which had to be maintained   if the business was to go on at all. Without them no picture could have been produced; they were as much a condition upon the production of the infringing picture as the scenery, or the plaintiffs' play itself. Levin Bros. v. Davis Mfg. Co., supra, did not hold otherwise; nor did Haiss Mfg. Co. v. Link- Belt Co., 63 F.2d 479, 3 Cir.
While this passage has been cited by some courts as supporting the full absorption approach, see, e.g., Warner Bros., Inc. v. Gay Toys, Inc., supra; Softel, Inc. v. Dragon Medical and Scientific Communications, Ltd, 891 F. Supp. 935 (S.D.N.Y. 1995), a close analysis of that opinion suggests that a deduction for overhead should be the exception rather than the rule.
It is important to note that Judge Hand begins his analysis of the issue by stating "The correct rule upon this point is stated in Levin Bros. v. Davis Mfg. Co., 72 F.2d 163, 8 Cir." As the following passage from that opinion demonstrates, the Eighth Circuit in Levin Bros. clearly adopted an "incremental" approach:

It is quite obvious that an inclusion, in all cases, of all overhead would be very unfair to the patentee. The profit on the patented articles is the difference   between the cost of producing them and the price received for them. To put into this cost an overhead expense, in nowise caused thereby, would be an improper inclusion. It often happens that overhead expenses are applicable to and should be spread over the entire business but where a business is established and in operation and another line is taken on without increase of overhead expenses it is just to the patentee that the actual situation be applied and none of such overhead be charged as an expense of the added line except as it participated in manufacture or sale of the infringing article.
Part of the difficulty is determining whether "overhead" should be deducted   arises from the fact that the term "overhead" embraces a variety of expenses, only some of which the infringer should   be allowed to deduct. The term overhead is defined in Webster's, Third New International Dictionary as "those general charges or expenses in a business which cannot be charged up as belonging exclusively to any particular part of the work or product (as rent, taxes, insurance, lighting, heating, accounting and other office expenses, and depreciation)." Thus, the term overhead embraces some expense which may be essential to the production of the infringing item and some that would be incurred even if no infringing items were produced. Logic suggests that it is only the former that the infringer should be allowed to deduct and this appears consistent with Judge Hand's statement in Sheldon that "'Overhead' which does not assist in the production of the infringement should not be credited to the infringer; that which does, should be . . . ." As Judge Hand noted, "it is a question of fact in all cases. Sheldon, 106 F.2d at 54; Wilkie v. Santly Bros., Inc., 139 F.2d 264 (2d Cir. 1943).
If the infringer were allowed to deduct expenses that would have been incurred even if the infringing goods were not produced, it would, in effect, be profiting from the infringement because it   would be passing part of its fixed cost on to the copyright holder. For example, assume that an infringer owns a store for which it pays $ 1,000 per month in rent and that it sells $ 100 in legitimate merchandise and $ 900 in infringing merchandise per month. If it did not sell the infringing merchandise it would lose $ 900 per month. By allowing the infringer to deduct a proportionate amount of its rent in computing the damages to be paid as a result of its infringing activity, the Court would thus allow the infringer to turn a $ 900 loss into a break even operation. In that instance the infringer should not be permitted to deduct the rent expense in calculating its profit from the infringement.
The issue is complicated by the fact that, depending on the circumstances, the same category of expense may be deductible in one case and not in another. For example, using the above hypothetical, if the infringer had to rent additional space to display the infringing works that rent would be deductible.
Thus,  in any particular case the Court must examine the facts to determine those incremental cost of the infringer that were increased as a direct result of the production and sale of the   infringing goods and are, therefore, deductible and to separate them from those fixed costs that would have been incurred in any event. The infringer "must carry the burben of demonstrating a sufficient nexus between each expense claimed and the sales of the unlawful goods." Manhattan Indus. v. Sweater Bee by Banff, Ltd., 885 F.2d 1 (2d Cir. 1989); In Design, 13 F.3d at 563.
The above analysis also compels the conclusion that  the copyright holder should not be required to deduct overhead costs in calculating the damage it suffered as the result of sales lost to the infringers product. Once a copyright holder has sufficient sales so that its income is sufficient to cover all of its costs, including overhead, additional sales will increase its profits to the extent that the sales proceeds exceed the costs of goods sold and any other incremental expenses. Thus the damage done to a copyright holder when it loses sales to an infringer should be determined by the gross amount of the lost sales less such incremental costs as the copyright holder would have had to incur to produce and sell those additional units.
Plaintiff seeks damages of $ 240,782 from defendant GFI of which $ 149.823 represents its calculation of its gross profits on the sale it claims it could have made to those of its customers who purchased infringing goods from GFI. GFI argues that plaintiff would not have made these sales because its goods were priced above what the market was willing to pay. There appears to be some merit to this argument. Moreover, as plaintiff concedes it may not recover its profit on these alleged sale and defendant' profit on the sale to these companies. In these

circumstances, it appears more accurate to measure plaintiff's lost profit on these sales by looking to the incremental profit that defendant actually realized on its sales to these accounts. Therefore, plaintiff will be fully compensated on its claims against GFI by an award of $ 201,049 which is the full profit realized by GFI on all infringing sales using an incremental approach to the calculation of its profit.
Plaintiff has also submitted evidence establishing that it is entitled to recover damages in the amount of $ 28,836 from SGS and $ 67,106 from J.C. Penney.
