THE COURT: Plaintiff Nihon Keizai Shimbun, who I will refer to as "Nihon," seeks permanently to enjoin defendant Comline Business Data, Inc., who I will refer to as "Comline," along with three of its principals and/or directors, individual defendants Yoshinobu Okuma, Hiroyuki Takagi, and Haruhisa Morimoto from marketing and disseminating news articles that have be extracted in whole or in part from articles previously contained in certain business and financial publications produced by the Nihon, and from using Nihon's trademarks in connection with those abstract articles. The Amended Complaint asserts claims for copyright infringement under the Copyright Act of 1976, 17 U.S.C. Section 101 et seq., trademark infringement under the Lanham Act, 15 U.S.C. Section 1114, and a declaration that the defendants' activities constitute a violation   of the Copyright Act. In addition to a permanent injunction and declaration, Nihon also seeks other forms of equitable relief, including the recall or destruction of all infringing materials and an accounting and payment over for all gains from infringing acts, as well as statutory damages. The precise issue here is whether creating a translation in English of a Japanese article that is protected under United States copyright law infringes the copyright of the original work when that translation is not literal, but instead seeks to convey the meaning of the translated work as effectively as possible in the English language.
By way of an Order dated March 5, 1998, the Court granted final judgment to Nihon against Terry Silveria, who had been named in the original complaint as a fourth individual defendant, but with whom Nihon subsequently reached an agreement permanently enjoining him from engaging in the infringing conduct asserted in the complaint. In the course of discovery, Nihon also waived any claim for actual damages on its copyright cause of action, leaving as its only damages claim a request for statutory damages under 17 U.S.C. Section 504 (c).
On March 20, 1998, Nihon moved pursuant   to Rule 15 (a) to amend its complaint to add a count for declaratory relief. This proposed third count sought a declaration that the defendants' "near-verbatim" copying of 28 articles set forth in the original complaint, as well "as any additional exhibits introduced at trial evidencing Comline's copying," constituted a violation of the Nihon's rights under the Copyright Act. At a final pretrial conference on April 7, 1998, the Court granted in part the motion to amend, ruling that Nihon could add a declaratory judgment claim as to the 28 articles referenced in, and appended to, the original complaint, but that it could not add such a claim as to the 50 or so articles offered in Nihon's pretrial exhibits as additional examples of Comline's infringement. The Court withheld judgment, however, as to whether those additional articles would be considered for purposes of damages, were they to be admitted into evidence at trial.
Nihon strives to ensure the quality of its news reporting, and to preserve its reputation and good will in its name and products, through several measures, including issuing guidelines to its reporters concerning proper journalistic practices; providing its employees with a copyright handbook describing policies on the use of sources and materials; requiring applicants for reporter   positions to pass a rigorous test; and hiring as reporters only those who have acquired, in almost all cases, at least one college degree. Nihon asserts that it is the practice of its reporters, when writing a story, to verify facts independently, to use multiple sources, and to study the general background of the industries upon which they write. The preparation and expertise of Nihon's reporters fundamentally affects, and determines, the content and style of the finished articles. Nihon presently has approximately 1400 employees engaged in the news gathering and editing activities; the articles produced by these individuals constitute works for hire.
In August 1997, Nihon began filing periodic applications with the United States Copyright Office for registration of articles issues in Nihon Keizai Shimbun, Nikkei Kinyu Shimbun, Nikkei Sangyo Shimbun, and the Nikkei Weekly. Some certificates of copyright registration have been issued, and others are pending. Nihon has also federally registered the following trademarks in connection with its news publications: "Nikkei" and "Nikkei Weekly," as well as the Japanese characters representing the names "Nihon Keizai Shimbun," "Nikkei Sangyo   Shimbun," and "Nikkei Ryutsu Shimbun."
Defendant Comline was founded in 1992, and has conducted its operations in New York City since December 1, 1993. According to the defendants, Comline's business involves "abstraction of factual news from various news services, including published newspapers and commercial databases, for inclusion in abstracts written, translated and edited by Comline BD. The abstracts are supplied by Comline BD to its customers, including business and individual subscribers, as well as commercial data base suppliers in the United States, Japan and Europe, who include Comline BD's product for the information products they in turn provide to their customers."
One of Comline's services provides English translations for Nikkei Telecom articles in such a way that the translations appear in Japan literally at the same time that the Nihon Japanese newspapers arrive on a businessperson's desk. Comline takes the original stories (in Japanese) off the Nikkei Telecom news service the night before the paper versions come out, which is the previous morning in the U.S., translates them overnight in the U.S. or wherever its translators live, and sends   out the translations on its Tokyo Financial Wire by approximately 8 a.m. Tokyo time.
The crux of this dispute concerns the manner and form in which Comline prepares and disseminates its articles, and the degree to which it relies upon, or copies, Nihon's publications and materials in doing so. Generally speaking, Comline's articles are one paragraph long, contain at the top a signature line and stating COMLINE, with the relevant date, followed by a more specific headline, and the then the text of the article. At the end of, and below, the text follows a reference line that lists the publications or sources from which the article was derived. The reference line may include several references, although all of those in this litigation, obviously, include at least one reference to a Nihon publication. The reference line might read, for example: "Ref: Nikkei Sangyo Shimbun, 8/21/97."
The content, style, and organization of Comline's articles, and whether or not those elements in combination constitute an infringement of Nihon's copyrights and/or trademarks, will be addressed the Discussion section below. The purpose here is to set forth the manner in which Comline has created those articles   during the period at issue in this litigation. Comline editors scan the Nikkei Telecom and selects stories of interest to Comline's customers. The editor also reviews materials culled by staff in Japan and sent to her daily. In the next step, the editor shortens the articles to near the pre-set length desired by Comline, a suggested length of approximately 110 words, and then sends batches of these shortened articles to translators "around the world." The translators, who are native English speakers, are instructed to read the piece sent to them until they understand it and then to translate it into English so that the meaning is well conveyed in English. The translators are to avoid a literal translation of the article if that would result in a an article that would be appear awkwardly phrased to a native English speaker. The written instructions that translators receive include the following:
"When you are ready to translate: Please spend five to ten minutes reading each of the Japanese-language articles that were sent to you, and highlight key points as you go along. When you translate the materials, you should organize your thoughts beforehand and write them down (anywhere between   90 to 110 words). Do not try to translate the Japanese-language article verbatim as this will cause more trouble in your translation work. Each translation may take ten to 15 minutes."
After creating the articles in English, translators send them to "rewriters" who edit them into a consistent Comline style. The rewriters may also call the companies which are the subjects of the articles to check on the spellings of names. An editor edits 50 to 70 articles a day; a translator, who is paid between six to seven dollars per article, translates 25 to 35 articles per day; an editor spends on average six minutes per article; a translator spends approximately 15 minutes per article; and a rewriter spends another 15 minutes per article. All together then, it takes approximately 36 minutes to transform a Nikkei Telecom article into a Comline article.
Comline states that it published over 17,000 total articles, based on all sources, in 1997. Approximately 30 percent of these articles cite as at least one of the references in the "ref" line a Nihon publication. That is, conservatively, over 5,000 Comline pieces in that year relied on Nihon as a source. According to Morimoto, Comline's practice   of printing a reference to the article's original sources is "similar to a byline," and is done so as to enable Comline's customers "to obtain and review the original source when they require further information."
Once the articles are created, they are distributed either electronically or via fax or mail to Comline's customers, namely, 16 commercial database vendors. These vendors, in turn, distribute Comline's articles to business and individual subscribers of their own. Comline is compensated for providing its articles by "typically entering into subscription and/or licensing agreements with each of its customers," i.e., the database vendors. Under Comline's own subscription agreements, the very practices that it engages in by storing and transmitting Nihon's articles are forbidden. Morimoto asserts that Comline "was willing to accept a license" from Nihon, "for a nominal amount," in order to continue using Nihon's articles for its own articles. Nihon currently licenses one Comline customer called Thomson to copy its articles "for about $ 40 per story. " Expecting that Nihon would refuse it access, Comline has obtained access to Nikkei Telecom through sharing that service with   the company, Ulmer Brothers, from which it sublets office space, Comline has seen the company's subscription agreement with Nihon and is aware that its use of the articles that it retrieves off the Nikkei Telecom service violates several provisions of the Nihon subscription agreement.
Finally, Morimoto sets forth the allegations underlying Comline's counterclaims against Nihon. Almost immediately after the commencement of this action, counsel for Nihon sent letters to at least three of Comline's customers advising them that Nihon had filed suit against Comline on January 29, 1998, for copyright and trademark infringement; expressing Nihon's belief that the allegations of copying in the Complaint, a copy of which was attached, were well founded; asserting the legal proposition that subsequent publishers of infringing material may be liable for infringement; and stating Nihon's "intention to fully enforce its rights in all its products." According to Morimoto, Nihon's letters were "extremely detrimental" to Comline's reputation and business to the extent that the letters caused Comline's customers, who depend on "uninterrupted service" of accurate news articles, to believe that its   service would be interrupted or delayed. Indeed, Morimoto states that, after receiving Nihon's letter, two of Comline's customers, Dialine MRI Information Network, Inc. and Chemical Abstracts Service, served notice that they would terminate their contracts with Comline, and that a third entity, an Internet search company, dropped all references to Comline after being contacted by Nihon.
Let me now review the prior litigation that has been the subject of certain testimony in this case.
In 1992, Nihon brought suit in Japan against an entity known as Comline International Corp., or "Comline IC," for infringement of Nihon's copyrights in various articles appearing in its publications. According to Morimoto's affidavit in this case, Comline IC was in the business of preparing news abstracts similar to that of Comline, the defendant here. At some point in 1992, after the commencement of Nihon's Japanese infringement action, Comline IC dissolved. The defendant Comline was established approximately one month thereafter, and, as noted above, has been operating at least in New York City since December 1, 1993. During the pendency of Nihon's Japanese action, Comline IC move to have Comline   added as a party, but subsequent withdrew that motion.
The decision of the Japanese court, issued on February 18, 1994, essentially found that Comline IC had infringed Nihon's copyrights in 11 articles that were the subject of that suit. The basic allegations of the case were identical to those here. The court rejected Comline IC's argument that its abstracts provided only raw facts extracted from various information sources to which no copyright applied, or that, due to the technical nature of the subjects reported, there were only few, in any, different means available for expressing the same facts. In addition, the court found insufficient evidence that Comline IC had relied on information sources other than Nihon's articles, or that Comline IC had independently verified the information it had reported. By way of relief, the court granted Nihon an amount equivalent to the minimum fee that it received (from its licenses) for its articles approximately one hundred dollars in U.S. currency. Based upon this Court's reading of the Japanese decision, there is no ground for finding, as Comline initially asserted in this litigation, that the Japanese court denied a request by Nihon for   an injunction. Indeed, Comline's principal witness conceded at trial that he understood Nihon to have withdrawn that request.
The court that ruled on the suit against Comline IC was one of only two courts in Japan with special jurisdiction in their respective locales over intellectual property cases, thus imbuing the court's decisions with great weight in Japan among practitioners in the field. Comline, however, disputes the relevance to this case of the prior litigation, in part based upon the contention that Comline IC was "not Comline BD's predecessor." Indeed, notwithstanding the close similarity in essential purpose, functioning, and methodology of these two entities, Comline asserts that it "did not acquire the business of Comline IC," and that it is instead "a separate corporation with different owners and officers which acquired some assets of Comline IC after Comline IC was dissolved." Nevertheless, there is exists a substantial overlap, at the least, between Comline IC and the defendant Comline. For instance, when Comline was created, all of its employees including its General Manager Morimoto came from Comline IC. Comline essentially took one half of the Comline IC work   force. In addition, Comline used the Comline IC logo for several years. Moreover, Comline represents that its services have been offered, not since the date of its own founding, but instead since 1986, the date Comline IC began to provide such services. Pointing to additional facts that show the similarity and the overlap and the continuity between the organizations, Comline's publications have the same names as those published by Comline IC, and, of course, its product is the same sort of product that had been offered by Comline IC.
As indicated above, Nihon's Amended Complaint, which I will refer hereafter as the "Complaint," asserts essentially two causes of action: Copyright infringement and trademark infringement. Nihon's third claim is really only an additional claim for relief, a declaration that the specific articles referenced in the Complaint constitute infringements of Nihon's copyrights. Comline opposes Nihon's action on numerous grounds, including, one, that news abstracts cannot constitute copyright infringement, two, that in any event Comline's abstracts do not constitute infringements   because they fall within the "fair use" doctrine, three, that Comline's use of Nihon's trademarks as source references either does not constitute trademark use or constitutes fair use; and, four, that Nihon's claims are barred under principals of laches and acquiescence. Comline also contends that Nihon is entitled to only nominal statutory damages for infringement, and that Nihon may not, consistent with the Constitution, secure an injunction restraining Comline's future publication of news abstracts. Finally, Nihon opposes Comline's counterclaims on the ground that the letters sent to Comline's customers were wholly truthful.
Tuning first to the governing legal standards for copyright infringement.
Section 106 of the Copyright Act grants owners of valid copyrights, as is Nihon here, at least with respect to 22 articles referenced in its Complaint, the "exclusive rights" to reproduce the copyrighted work or to prepare "derivative works" thereof.  17 U.S.C. Section 106. Derivative works are defined by the Act to include "translation[s], … abridgement[s], condensation[s], or any other form in which a work may be recast, transformed, or adapted." 17 U.S.C. Section 101.
As defense   counsel concedes, the copyright laws protect translations from one language to another, of original written work and abridgements of original works. In order to prove infringement of these "exclusive rights" under Section 501 of the Act, a plaintiff with a valid copyright must demonstrate, "one, that the defendant has actually copied the plaintiff's work and, two, that the copying is illegal because a substantial similarity exists between the defendant's work and the protectible elements of plaintiff's." Knitwaves, Inc. v. Lollytogs, Ltd. 71 F.3d 996 at 1002. See generally 1 Nimmer on Copyright, Section 3.06.
As to the first element, actual copying may be established either by direct evidence of copying or by indirect evidence, such as "access to the copyrighted work, similarities that are probative of copying between the works, and expert testimony." Laureyssens v. Idea Group, 964 F.2d 131 at 140. See also Fisher-Price v. Well Made Toy Manufacturing, 25 F.3d 119 at 123. In the second step, assuming that copying has been shown, the plaintiff "must also show illegality … (which) requires a sharper focus: The court must find a substantial similarity between the   protectible elements of the two works." Id. at 123. The test most often used to determine "substantial similarity" is so-called "ordinary observer test," which asks "whether an average lay observer would recognize the alleged copy as having been appropriated from the copyrighted work." Warner Brothers v. ABC, 654 F.2d 204 at 208. Ultimately, the court must determine under this test whether "the ordinary observer, unless he set out to detect the disparities, would be disposed to overlook them…." Peter Pan Fabrics v. Martin Weiner, 274 F.2d 487 at 489.
Where copyrighted work, however, contains both protectible and unprotectible elements, as is alleged here, courts in this Circuit apply what has been described as "a more discerning" version of the "ordinary observer" test, Harbor Software v. Applied Systems, 936 F. Supp. 167 at 170. This test requires the Court to "exclude comparison of the unprotectible elements from (its) application of the ordinary observer test," Fisher-Price, 25 F.3d at 123, and ask "whether the protectible elements, standing alone, are substantially similar," Knitwaves 71 F.3d at 1002.
Nevertheless, under either analysis the Court   must bear in mind the axiom that "copyright protection does not extend to ideas; it protects only the means of expression employed by the author." CCC Information Servs., Inc v. Maclean Hunter Market Reports, Inc, 44 F.3d 61 at 68. Thus,  in examining two works for substantial similarity, the "focus must be, on the similarity of the expression of an idea or fact, not on the similarity of the facts, ideas or concepts themselves." Rogers v. Koons, 960 F.2d 301 at 308. This distinction is more easily stated than applied, see, for example, Walker v. Time Life Films, Inc., 784 F.2d 44 at 48. And courts confronting the issue often invoke the language of Judge Learned Hand, sometimes referred to as his "abstractions test":
"Upon any work … a great number of patterns of increasing generality will fit equally well, as more and more of the incident is left out. The last may perhaps be no more than the most general statement of what the play is about, and at times consist only of its title; but there is a point in this series of abstractions where they are no longer protected, since otherwise the playwright could prevent the use of his 'ideas', to which, apart from their   expression, his property is never extended." Nichols v. Universal Pictures Corp., 45 F.2d 119 at 121. While the legal question focuses on the existence of similarities between the works, the Second Circuit has observed that "'numerous differences tend to undercut substantial similarity.'" Warner Bros., Inc. v. ABC, 720 F.2d 231 at 241.
Finally,  although the governing test requires exclusion of unprotectible ideas, the Court must examine the "total concept and feel" of the executed works.  Knitwaves, Inc, 71 F.3d at 1062 to 1063. The more discerning ordinary observer test therefore is not an invitation to dissect a work into its constituent elements or features; rather, the works as a whole must be compared to each other, inasmuch as "a work may be copyrightable even though it is entirely a combination of unprotectible elements. What is protectible then is 'the author's original contributions' -- the original way in which the author has 'selected, coordinated, and arranged' the element of his or her own work." Id. at 1003-04. And in evaluating the "total concept and feel" of two works for infringement purposes, courts customarily resolve the question of substantial   similarity "primarily through detailed viewing or reading of the works themselves," Walker v. Time Life, 784 F.2d 44 at 52; that is, without examining lists of similarities, Id., or relying on expert testimony. See Computer Associates Int'l. Inc. v. Altai, Inc., 982 F.2d 693 at 713.
I conclude that Nihon has carried its burden under the foregoing standards of proving copyright and trademark infringement; and that none of the defendants'    arguments, including their claims under the "fair use" doctrine, alter this result; and that the defendants' counterclaims are without merit. I will address each of these issues in turn.
At the outset it is important of course to resolve which of the Nihon's works are protected by valid, extant copyrights. In its Complaint, Nihon identified 27, well, really, 28 articles, but 27 of them were offered in evidence at trial, only 22 of which are covered by a U.S. copyright registration.  An action for infringement cannot be asserted unless a certificate of registration has been issued Fonar Corp. v. Domenick, 105 F.3d 99 at 103, and Whimsicality, Inc. v. Rubie's Costume, 891 F.2d 452 at 455. The following analysis of infringement, therefore, will discuss the 22 protected articles, that is Plaintiff's Exhibits 1 to 5, 7 to 9, 12 to 15, 17 to 19, and 21 to 27. Nihon contends that a registration is unnecessary where it has applied for copyright protection, but where registration has not yet issued. Nihon relies on two District Court cases, both of which in turn rely on a Fifth Circuit decision in Apple Barrel Products, Inc. v. Beard, 730 F.2d 384 at 386 to 387.
The Fifth Circuit   opinion appears to offer minimal precedential value, especially today. As Judge Kaplan of this Court has pointed out, the statement in Apple Barrel regarding the necessity of actual registration was based solely on "the then-current edition of Nimmer[,] … yet that authoritative text now quite clearly indicates that registration is a precondition to the commencement of an infringement action except in limited circumstances that do not pertain to this case." Robinson v. Princeton Review, 1996 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 16932, 41 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1008, at 1015. In short, Nihon has offered no persuasive authority to sustain its claim that it can rely simply on the application for a copyright.
Turning then to the substance of the copyright infringement claim.
It is undisputed that Nihon has valid, extant copyrights in 22 articles referenced in the Complaint. In addition, there is no real issue as to whether Nihon has demonstrated actual copying of its articles, as Comline has admitted its access to, and use of, Nihon's articles in preparing its articles. Thus the sole question for purposes of establishing copyright infringement is whether Comline has copied Nihon's articles "illegally" within the meaning of the Copyright Act, that is, whether a "substantial similarity" exists between Comline's own articles and the protectible elements of Nihon's articles. Because Comline argues that those articles contained many unprotectible elements, namely, the facts and ideas comprising the news being reported therein, the Court conducts this analysis pursuant to the standards of the "more discerning" "ordinary observer."
Without recounting on the record a line-by-line comparison works at issue, it is sufficient for present purposes to state that the Court reviewed in detail   the 22 sets of articles that were appended to the Complaint, and in addition examined the other sets offered by Nihon as trial exhibits. Furthermore, for purposes of this evaluation the Court studied both parties' translations of the original 22 Nihon articles, so as to alleviate Comline's concerns regarding Nihon's use of false or misleadingly similar translations in the original complaint and Order to Show Cause. Indeed, for purposes of this analysis, I have relied primarily on the translations of the Nihon articles proffered by the defendants. Based on this comparative analysis, the Court finds it abundantly clear in 20 of the 22 articles that, under any translation, substantial similarity exists between Nihon's articles and Comline's articles, even with respect to their "protectible elements, standing alone." Nihon therefore has shown that Comline "appropriated [Nihon's] particular means of expressing an idea, not merely that [Comline] expressed the same idea." While the Comline articles are usually shorter than the Nihon articles and thus frequently omit certain facts and information, what information the Comline articles do provide almost invariably is presented with the   same structure and organization, follows the same chronological and substantive grouping of facts, and results in the same conclusions or resolutions, and in addition often employs identical phraseology and word choice, as in the original Nihon articles. In short, the Court has little hesitation in finding that Comline's articles unlawfully infringe Nihon's exclusive rights under Section 106 (2) of the Copyright Act, to prepare derivative works based on its copyrighted articles.
The Court finds this conclusion to be supported in particular by the Second Circuit's decision in the highly analogous case of Wainwright Securities, Inc. v. Wall Street Transcript Corp. 558 F.2d 91. The plaintiff in Wainwright produced for its subscribing clients in-depth analytical reports providing market evaluations and predictions regarding numerous industrial and financial corporations; it brought an action for copyright infringement against the publisher of a weekly financial newspaper that ran a "Wall Street Roundup" column based on abstracts of institutional research reports, including those of the plaintiff. One of the defendant's arguments in opposing entry of a preliminary injunction was   virtually identical to Comline's principal claim here, namely, that publication of the abstracts was "simply financial news coverage entitled to the protection of the first amendment," especially since the reports themselves have been reported as news event in other publications. The Wainwright court acknowledged the well-settled rule that "'news event' may not be copyrighted," but stated that, " in considering the copyright protections due a report of news events or factual developments, it is important to differentiate between the substance of the information contained in the report, i.e., the event itself, and 'the particular form or collocation of words in which the writer has communicated it.'… What is protected is the manner of expression, the author's analysis or interpretation of events, the way he structures his material and marshals facts, his choice of words, and the emphasis he gives to particular developments. Thus, the essence of the infringement lies not in taking a general theme or in coverage of the reports as events, but in appropriating the "particular expression through similarities of treatment, details, scenes, events and characterization." (emphasis   added)
This discourse, which is entirely consistent with the standards noted above for applying the more discerning ordinary observer test, demonstrates precisely what is impermissible about Comline's activities here. Indeed the Second Circuit's conclusions as to the basis of the defendants liability in Wainwright are every bit as applicable in this case, and could just as easily serve as the holding here:
"The [defendants] did not bother to distinguish between the events contained in the reports and the manner of expression…. Moreover, [Comline's articles] did not provide independent analysis or research; [they] did not solicit comments on the same topics from other financial analysts; and [they] did not include any criticism, praise, or other reactions by industry officials or investors. Rather, [Comline's articles] appropriated almost verbatim the most creative and original aspects of the reports, the financial analyses and predictions, which represented a substantial investment of time, money and labor."
As in Wainwright, the defendants here appropriated protectible elements of Nihon's articles, their means of expression, structuring, and marshaling of facts;    and even if Comline's abstracts condensed the articles and altered some of the words, the "total concept and feel" of those abstracts nonetheless manifest substantial similarity to the original Nihon articles, and thus constitute impermissible infringements.
In light of these findings, Comline's initial argument, that "news abstracts based on news items extracted from news sources are not copyright infringements," has little merit, to the extent that it is not simply irrelevant. Once again, it is "axiomatic that 'news events' may not be copyrighted," Wainwright, 558 F.2d at 95, and Nihon has never claimed that Comline's extraction of "news items" from its publications constitutes an infringement. What is at issue here is Comline's appropriation of the protectible elements of Nihon's articles, which are separate from, and do not include, the facts or ideas comprising the bare items of "news." In other words, Comline's argument that it has not copied "'constituent elements of [Nihon's] work that are original,' for the simple reason that news is not original," is misplaced; Nihon's action is based not on Comline's copying of "the news," but its copying of the means of expression,    organizational structuring, and marshaling of facts that make up Nihon's reporting of the news.
For similar reasons, the defendants are also incorrect in their claim that the CCC Information case is inapplicable because "Comline has abstracted pre-existing facts merely reported by [Nihon]. There is no editorial creativity or other original creation." To the contrary, Comline has fallen far short of showing that Nihon based its articles solely, wholly, or to any significant degree upon pre-existing company press releases. But even if that were the case, and even if those press releases set forth factual information about the companies or industries at issue and Nihon "merely reported" those facts, Nihon's  articles would still be entitled to copyright protection, as Comline concedes, if the "selection and arrangement of data in [those articles] displayed amply sufficient originality." CCC Information, 44 F.3d at 67. Having reviewed the relevant 11 articles for which there were press releases, the Court concludes that, in any event, Nihon's particular use of the releases shows "amply sufficient originality" to merit protection of its articles.
Let me address briefly defendants'    argument that a translation of a Japanese article is harder to protect than a translation of a Romance language article since it is more difficult to translate Japanese in a verbatim translation that. makes its meaning comprehensible. I reject such an argument.  The copyright statute's protection for derivative works reaches just as broadly to works whose origin is in Japanese as other languages with which we may be more familiar or which may seem more accessible. At root, the defendants ordered their translators to do very little more than translate. They were ordered to translate the Japanese text in a way that rendered their meaning intelligible and were told it would take on average 15 minutes to do so. The resulting product was, not surprisingly, substantially similar to the text from which it was produced and is therefore protected.
Let me now turn to Comline's argument, that its copying of Nihon's articles "constitutes permissible fair use under the Copyright law."  The fair use doctrine "permits other people to use copyrighted material without the owner's consent in a reasonable manner for certain purposes." Leibovitz v. Paramount Pictures Corp., 137 F.3d 109, 1998 WL 73116, Second   Circuit, 1998. See also Twin Peaks Prods., Inc. v. Publications Int'l, Ltd., 996 F.2d 1366 at 1373. The doctrine of fair use is codified at Section 107 of the Copyright Act, which sets forth "an illustrative list of the purposes for which the doctrine may be invoked" -- such as criticism, comment, news reporting and research -- and in addition lists the factors that courts are to consider in determining whether a use is 'fair.'" The four "fair use" factors are:
"(1) the purpose and character of the use, including whether such use is of a commercial nature or is for nonprofit educational purposes;
"(2) the nature of the copyrighted work; "(3) the amount and substantiality of the portion used in relation to the copyrighted work as a whole; and
"(4) the effect of the use upon the potential market for or the value of the copyrighted work."
The Second Circuit recently emphasized that, under the Supreme Court's clarification of the doctrine in Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569, 127 L. Ed. 2d 500, 114 S. Ct. 1164 (1994), "fair use determination 'calls for case-by-case analysis,'" employing "an aggregate weighing of all four fair use factors."    Leibovitz, 1998 WL 73116 at *3-4. Pursuant to this standard this Court will address each factor in turn, with the "'results weighed together.'"
The issue under the "purpose" analysis "is not simply whether a challenged work serves one of the non- exclusive purposes identified in Section 107,… but whether it does so to an insignificant or substantial extent." Twin Peaks at 1374. The focus of the inquiry, in other words,
"should be on whether the copying work "merely 'supersede[s] the objects' of the original …, or instead adds something new, with a further purpose or different character, altering the first with knew expression, meaning, or message." Leibovitz, 137 F.3d 109, 1998 WL 73116, at *3.
Thus the standard is whether the copying use is "transformative." Id. Finally, while Campbell has made clear that commercial uses of copyrighted material are no longer considered to be presumptively unfair, commercial use nevertheless remains "a separate factor that tends to weigh against a finding of fair use." Leibovitz, 137 F.3d 109, 1998 WL 73116, at *3.
In this case, it is manifest that the purpose of Comline's copying is commercial. Its entire business, apparently, involves   the sale and distribution to other database vendors of news articles, many of which are based on Nihon's original articles. But more important than the fact that Comline makes a great deal of money by piggy- backing onto Nihon's labor is that Comline's use is not in the least "transformative." That is, in merely taking excerpts from Nihon's articles and rendering the most effective translation of those excerpts, or rearranging the order of the very same words and phrases, Comline in no way "adds something new, with a further purpose or different character, altering the first with new expression, meaning, or message." Leibovitz, 137 F.3d 109, 1998 WL 73116, at *3. To the contrary, Comline reports the very same news as does Nihon, in highly similar terms, and with almost exactly the same expression and structure Once again, copyright owners possess the exclusive right to prepare "derivative works" of their copyrighted works, such as the Comline articles at issue here. It is for this reason that  an "abridgement of a copyrighted work is … likely to be found to be prima facie infringing," especially where, as here, "the abridgement serves no transformative function and elaborates in detail   far beyond that which is required to serve any legitimate purpose" of comment or criticism. Twin Peaks at 1376. In such cases, "the first factor cannot be weighted in favor of the fair use defense." Id.
Although the claim is not fleshed out, Comline appears to argue that Nihon's use is not original because it merely copies facts or news from company or industry press releases. As noted above, this contention is groundless. A comparison of the press releases that were provided for the Nihon articles reveals that the articles do not simply copy the press releases; that they do indeed add information ostensibly from other sources; that they alter the structure and tone of the often self-laudatory releases; and that they are themselves therefore "transformative." Moreover, with the exception of one exhibit, and that is exhibit 19, each of the articles that Comline produced quoted material that was added by Nihon to its stories that did not appear in the original press releases. In short, I find that Nihon's articles are creative and original works.
Turning to the third factor,  that factor requires an examination of the "quantity and value of the material used in relation to the   [copyrighted] work as a whole." Sandoval v. New Line Cinema Corp., 973 F. Supp. 409 at 413. The relevant issue concerns "the amount and substantiality of the copyrighted expression that has been used, not the factual content of the material in the copyrighted works." Rogers, 960 F.2d at 311. In other words, "more critical than the quantity is the qualitative degree of the copying: What degree of the essence of the original is copied in relation to its whole." Id. The Court concludes that this factor also weighs against a finding of fair use. Although, as noted, Comline's articles often omit material appearing in the, original Nihon articles, and thus are shorter, the more important point is that the information that is copied invariably includes the crucial facts and ideas -- again, structured and expressed in a manner substantially similar to the original -- that pertain to the very reason for writing the article in the first place. Thus the "degree of the essence" of Nihon's original articles that is copied, i.e., the amount and substantiality of the articles' protectible expression that reappears in Comline's articles, is extremely high "in relation to   the copyrighted work as a whole." For essentially the same reason that the "total concept and feel" of Comline's articles shows substantial similarity to Nihon's articles, this factor favors a finding of infringement.
The final fair use factor requires an examination of the effect that the infringing work will have on the market for the original work, taking into consideration "not only the extent of market harm caused by the specific use in question, but the effect that would occur if that type of use became widespread," Sandoval 973 F. Supp. at 414, and in addition, "not only the primary market for the copyrighted work but the current and potential market for derivative works," Twin Peaks, 996 F.2d at 1377. This factor is no longer deemed "the single most important element of fair use," but instead varies with the amount of harm and "relative strength of the showing on the other factors," Leibovitz, 137 F.3d 109, 1998 WL 73116, at *4.
The "effect of use" factor favors Nihon perhaps most clearly of all. The parties' products are highly similar substantively, have similar and overlapping means of distribution, and serve a similar consumer market for timely and concise business,    financial, and industry news specifically relating to Japanese firms and markets. Moreover, Comline's production of articles based on Nihon's articles, which summarize, condense, and/or copy portions of those articles, almost by definition damages Nihon's potential market for derivative works. In these circumstances, where the parties are essentially market competitors in the same products "or at least derivations thereof), the harmful effect upon the, copyright owner's potential markets is virtually beyond dispute. The fact that Nihon currently publishes its articles in English on a weekly, instead of a daily basis, does not alter my analysis of this factor.
Based on foregoing analysis, the aggregate assessment of fair use factors presents little difficulty in this case. Inasmuch as every factor favors Nihon to a significant extent, the Court concludes that Comline's production of abstracts or articles from Nihon's articles is not a fair use under the Copyright Law.
Laches   is an appropriate defense in the context of an application for injunctive relief in an intellectual property case. But, as in the case of a claim for monetary damages, the existence and operation of a laches defense in a case involving a request for injunctive relief under a federal statute is in part dependent on whether the action was instituted within the relevant statute of limitations.  Conopco, Inc. v. Campbell Soup Co., 95 F.3d 187 at 191. If the applicable statute of limitations has elapsed, then there is a presumption of laches. If the applicable limitations period has not elapsed, then defendant bears the burden of proving this affirmative defense.
The Court concludes that Comline has failed to carry its burden of showing that laches should bar Nihon's claim for an injunction where, as here, Nihon has filed its action well within the period of limitations, and Comline, as explained elsewhere in this opinion, is held to have the knowledge of Nihon's prior victory in a copyright infringement action for precisely the conduct at issue here. Comline places great emphasis on the fact that Nihon scrutinized its activities in the period 1993-94 and decided that at that time Comline   could not successfully be charged with copyright infringement. The Court does not have evidence of the articles published by Nihon and Comline in that period to assess whether Nihon's view was well-founded or misguided. Far from indicating that Nihon just sat on its rights, however, this scrutiny can just as easily be evidence of Nihon's vigilance and yet caution about proceeding with litigation unless confident that Comline's practices did violate the law. Even if Nihon's excuse for delay is weak, or non-existent, Comline has failed to show any prejudice from that delay. The evidence shows that Comline was formed very shortly after the dissolution of Comline IC in 1992, and based largely on the remnants of that former entity. For at least a full year during the pendency of the Japanese action, Comline conducted its operations in New York for the very purpose of avoiding the weight of enforcement of Japanese copyright laws. Even after the Japanese Court reached a decision in February 1994, finding Comline IC's conduct to be infringing, Comline continued what were essentially the identical infringing practices.
Thus Comline cannot demonstrate  prejudice under the prevailing Second Circuit   standard, which requires a showing that "the defendant has changed his position in a way that would not have occurred if the plaintiff had not delayed." Conopco, 95 F.3d at 192. Although Comline claims that it "set up shop in the United States and grew a viable business" while Nihon delayed, in reality, Comline's persistence in continuing to create infringing articles during and after the Japanese litigation strongly indicates that its "change [in] position," if any, had nothing to do with Nihon's delay, but was based entirely on Comline's knowing and intentional flaunting of the copyright laws. In other words, based upon Comline's past conduct in the face of an adjudication that practices identical to its own were unlawful, Comline would likely have continued its "viable business" of creating infringing abstracts whether or not Nihon had delayed. Because Comline cannot show prejudice in these circumstances, its laches defense fails.
In any event, under traditional equitable principles, Comline, as a "non-innocent" or "deliberate" infringer cannot claim the benefit of a laches defense. "Deliberate" in these circumstances means "something greater than simply not unintentional   copying, connoting perhaps piratical construct." 3 Nimmer on Copyright, Section 12:06. For reasons explained more fully elsewhere, Comline's infringement satisfies these standards.
In reference to this issue of law, I rely also on Harlequin Enterprises v. Gulf & Western, 644 F.2d 946 at 950, a Second Circuit 1981 case, that declined to apply a laches defense in a trademark action where the infringer was non-innocent or deliberate.
The copyright misuse argument is equally unavailing. Such a  defense "prevents a copyright owner from recovering from infringement where he has impermissibly extended the copyright monopoly in a manner that constitutes an unreasonable restraint of trade." Coleman v. ESPN, Inc., 764 F. Supp. 290 at 295. In other words, the argument might prevail where a copyright infringement defendant could prove that the copyright owner "used its legal monopoly to assert economic control over uncopyrighted products." Broadcast Music, Inc. v. Hearst/ABC
Viacom Entertainment Servs., 746 F. Supp. 320 at 328, a case that notes that its research revealed no case where misuse of copyright prevented recovery on an infringement claim. Simply put, the defendants   have failed to adduce anywhere near the quantity or quality of evidence necessary to show the type of unreasonable restraint of trade that is required for a misuse defense. In particular, the defendants have failed to allege the sort of illegal "tying" arrangement that is the hallmark of the patent misuse defense, which is the basis for the copyright misuse doctrine -- if indeed the doctrine has any viability at all. Comline's complaint that Nihon readily licenses others to use its articles is altogether insufficient as a defense to a new infringement action absent evidence that Nihon has gained such market dominance over its copyrighted articles that it has the ability to, and does, assert economic control over uncopyrighted articles. It would surely be extraordinary to claim that Nihon has such power in the market as to control the reporting of the news, an extraordinarily competitive market. In sum, Comline is liable for copyright infringement with respect to the articles of Nihon that are at issue in this case, and Comline has no defense to that liability.
Let me turn to the relief sought.
Nihon's principal claim for relief seeks a permanent injunction prohibiting the defendants from marketing, disseminating, publishing, et cetera, the articles it currently creates from Nihon's articles, bearing Nihon's marks.  A plaintiff is entitled to such permanent injunctive relief under Section 502 (a) of the Copyright Act, where he   establishes both liability and the threat of continuing violation. Nihon has amply satisfied both of these criteria, and therefore is entitled to the injunction it seeks, in light of the evidence adduced at trial of Comline's established method of producing its abstracts. Indeed, to avoid repeating the infringing activity, Comline would have to change radically its organizational structure and practices so that it either became more of a traditional news or research agency, or agreed to translate solely, and condense articles solely, from sources that had granted it licenses.
The defendants' chief argument against entry of such a "broad injunction" is that "prohibiting any use of [Comline's] news stories in the future … is impermissible as a prior restraint on the publication of news." The court in Wainwright, however, upheld a preliminary injunction against a similar argument that "publication of the abstracts … is simply financial news coverage entitled to the protection of the first amendment." 558 F.2d at 95. The Second Circuit concluded that, under either a fair use analysis or "a free speech theory," the defendants "failed to demonstrate that their use of the [plaintiff's]    reports either was reasonable or pursuant to legitimate news reporting that implicates first amendment interests." Id. at 97. The same analysis holds true here; Comline's unlawful copying of Nihon's articles does not constitute genuine news reporting deserving of full First Amendment protection. Stenograph filed its initial complaint on January 20, 1995, in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, and its First Amended Complaint on May 22, 1995, against, as pertinent to this appeal, Bossard Associates and Dennis K. Bossard (collectively "defendants"). See Ex. 1. Bossard Associates is a court reporting and litigation support service located in Washington, D.C. Before his death in August 1997, Mr. Bossard owned all of the stock of Bossard Associates and served as the company's president and treasurer. Stenograph sought compensatory and punitive damages and an injunction for copyright infringement and state law claims of trade secret misappropriation and conversion. These claims arose from allegations that, from April 1992 through November 1994, Mr. Bossard illicitly purchased Stenograph's Premier Power software and eleven keys from one of Stenograph's sales representatives, John Baker, with checks made payable to Baker personally, at a substantial discount from Stenograph's normal retail price.
A jury trial commenced on November   20, 1996. Stenograph presented evidence that Mr. Bossard obtained the keys and software from Baker during the alleged time periods.  See Trial Tr. (11/21/96) at Appendix ("App.") 164-66, 200; id. (11/22/96) at App. 228-36. Stenograph also presented evidence that defendants used the software and one or more of the keys obtained from Baker, gave four keys to independent contractors for them to use (at least partly for Bossard related jobs), and resold two other keys, all notwithstanding Mr. Bossard's knowledge that Stenograph required users of its software to enter into licensing agreements. See id. (11/22/96) at App. 222-26; id. (11/25/96) at App. 440-46. Baker testified that Stenograph fired him on November 4, 1994, after he admitted that he sold Premier Power software and keys to Mr. Bossard for his own personal benefit. See id. (11/21/96) at App. 164- 66; Ex. 6, at 1. Stenograph did not seek damages for any time after 1995, because in 1996 Christopher Bossard, the son of Mr. Bossard, obtained a Premier Power key from another court reporter and paid Stenograph for a license transfer. See id. (11/22/96) at 22728; Br. of Appellee at 16.
At trial, Mr. Bossard   defended largely on the theory that he did not know either that the products obtained from Baker belonged to Stenograph, or that Baker lacked authority to make the sales in question. Baker had had a fifteen year sales relationship with defendants, during which time Baker legitimately sold other Stenograph goods to Bossard Associates. See Trial Tr. (11/21/96) at App. 163, 173-74; Br. of Appellee at 11. With respect to the eleven keys, Mr. Bossard testified that Baker told him that Baker was merely serving as a "broker" for third parties who wished to get rid of the products. See Trial Tr. (11/21/96) at App. 212. It is undisputed, however, that after Baker was fired in November 1994, Stenograph asked defendants to either pay for or return the Premier Power keys,
The District Court denied Bossard's motion for judgment as a matter of law made at the conclusion of Stenograph's case and renewed at the end of trial. See id. (11/22/96) at App. 282; id. (11/26/96) at App. 539-40. On December 12, 1996, the   jury returned a verdict for Stenograph on all counts. The jury awarded damages in the amount of $ 1,500,000 for copyright infringement; compensatory damages of $ 710,000 and punitive damages of $ 750,000 for trade secret misappropriation; and compensatory damages of $ 44,000 and punitive damages of $ 178,000 for conversion. See Stenograph Corp. v. Bossard Assocs., Civ. No. 95-0141(NHJ) (D.D.C. filed Feb. 12, 1997) ("Order"), reprinted at Ex. 3. The District Court subsequently denied defendants' motion for a new trial or, alternatively, to amend the judgment and to stay the enforcement of the judgment. See id. The Court also entered a separate judgment    as a matter of law in favor of Stenograph on other claims alleged in the lawsuit. See id. The District Court then entered a judgment on the jury verdict and awarded Stenograph monetary relief in the total amount of $ 3,198,016.17 against Mr. Bossard and Bossard Associates. See Ex. 4.
A. Copyright Infringement
Most of Bossard's numerous challenges   to the District Court's judgment are plainly meritless and thus do not warrant treatment in this opinion. We do, however, address appellants' contention that the District Court erred in presenting Stenograph's copyright infringement claim to the jury, on the ground that Stenograph failed to present sufficient evidence of impermissible "copying" of Premier Power software by Bossard.  In reviewing the denial of a judgment as a matter of law, "the standard we apply is the same as that applied by a district court considering the motion in the first instance. Viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving party, we must ask ourselves whether any reasonable jury could find in its favor." Harbor Ins. Co. v. Schnabel Foundation Co., 292 U.S. App. D.C. 56, 946 F.2d 930, 935 (D.C. Cir. 1991);  see also Smith v. Washington Sheraton Corp., 328 U.S. App. D.C. 367, 135 F.3d 779, 782 (D.C. Cir. 1998); Scott v. District of Columbia, 322 U.S. App. D.C. 75, 101 F.3d 748, 752 (D.C. Cir. 1996). This entails an examination of "all uncontradicted evidence offered by the moving party, as well as all evidence introduced by the non-moving party." Harbor Ins., 946 F.2d at 935.
A plaintiff seeking   to establish copyright infringement must prove "(1) ownership of a valid copyright, and (2) copying of constituent elements of the work that are original." Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Tel. Serv. Co., 499 U.S. 340, 361, 113 L. Ed. 2d 358, 111 S. Ct. 1282 (1991); Fonar Corp. v. Domenick, 105 F.3d 99, 104 (2d Cir.), cert. denied, 139 L. Ed. 2d 191, 118 S. Ct. 265 (1997). The copying must be beyond the scope of a license possessed by the defendant.  See MAI Systems Corp. v. Peak Computer, Inc., 991 F.2d 511, 517 (9th Cir. 1993). In the instant case, the first element is not in dispute, because Stenograph's certificates of registration for Premier Power, see Ex. 5, at 9-12, constitute  prima facie evidence of the validity of the copyright of the software, and Bossard makes no argument that such certificates were improvidently issued. See 17 U.S.C. § 410(c); Fonar, 105 F.3d at 104 ("possession of a registration certificate creates a rebuttable presumption that the work in question is copyrightable" (internal quotation omitted)). As to the second element, appellants argue that Stenograph never demonstrated that Bossard copied the protected elements   of Premier Power--i.e., the original parts of the software for which Stenograph validly held copyright protection.
Case law supports the general proposition that  unoriginal portions of a software program can be copied without resulting in copyright infringement. See Lotus Develop. Corp. v. Borland Int'l, 49 F.3d 807, 815 (1st Cir. 1995) (holding copying of uncopyrightable subject matter of software not copyright infringement), aff'd by an equally divided court, 516 U.S. 233, 116 S. Ct. 804, 133 L. Ed. 2d 610 (1996); Gates Rubber Co. v. Bando Chemical Indus., Ltd., 9 F.3d 823, 832 (10th Cir. 1993) (copyright plaintiff had to show that "those elements of the program that have been copied are protected expression and of such importance to the copied work that the appropriation is
144 F.3d 96, *98; 1998 U.S. App. LEXIS 11483, **5; 46 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1936, ***1937
actionable"); see generally Rogers v. Koons, 960 F.2d 301, 307 (2d Cir. 1992) ("That a whole work is copyrighted does not mean that every element of it is copyrighted; copyright protection extends only to those components of the work that are original to the creator."). Drawing on these principles, appellants posit that Stenograph failed to meet its evidentiary burden on the copying issue, because Stenograph did not show that   use of Premier Power in tandem with the keys resulted in [***1939]  the copying of the protected elements of the software to a Bossard computer's random access memory ("RAM"). In support of this    point, appellants contend that Stenograph did not present an expert witness who could testify competently on the manner in which Premier Power software worked inside Bossard's computers.
Appellants' argument on copying--particularly their attention to the issue of whether protected elements of Premier Power were copied to random access memory--is a nonstarter. Appellants conceded at oral argument, and this court agrees, that  if someone loads validly copyrighted software onto his or her own computer without the owner's permission, and then uses the software for the principal purposes for which it was designed, there can be no real doubt that the protected elements of the software have been copied and the copyright infringed. In other words, the only real question in this case is whether the jury had sufficient evidence to find that Bossard installed and used Stenograph's software for its principal purposes.
As an analytical matter, there are two different ways to describe the impermissible "copying"    that occurred in this case. First, it can be concluded, quite simply, that copying occurred when appellants installed and used the software for the principal purposes for which it was intended. Alternatively, following a line of analysis adopted by a number of courts, it can be concluded that appellants copied the software when it was booted up for use for its principal purposes, and thereby loaded into RAM. These two theories may be two ways of saying the same thing; but in either of them, the jury's verdict against appellants was fully justified.
1. Installation
The language of the Copyright Act, case law, and common sense support the proposition that the installation of software onto a computer results in "copying" within the meaning of the Copyright Act. See 17 U.S.C. § 101 (defining "copies" as "material objects … in which a work is fixed by any method now known or later developed, and from which the work can be perceived, reproduced, or otherwise communicated, either directly or with the aid of a machine or device"); 2 MELVILLE B. NIMMER & DAVID NIMMER, NIMMER ON COPYRIGHT § 8.08[A][1], at 8-113 (1997) ("NIMMER") (the Act's language "makes clear that the input   of a work into a computer results in the making of a copy"); cf.  Vault Corp. v. Quaid Software Ltd., 847 F.2d 255, 260 (5th Cir. 1988) ("the act of loading a program from a medium of storage into a computer's memory creates a copy of the program"). Appellant does not argue that the installation of software onto a single computer workstation differs from the installation of software onto an office network, for purposes of infringement analysis. Moreover,  if an entire program is thus copied, certainly the "protectible elements" of the program are also copied. See Fonar, 105 F.3d at 106 (summary judgment for defendants inappropriate assuming they made "complete copies" of plaintiff's software); Triad Systems Corp. v. Southeastern Express Co., 64 F.3d 1330, 1335 (9th Cir. 1995) (where defendant's conduct "involved copying entire programs, there is no doubt that protected elements of the software were copied").
The question in the instant case, then, is how installation could be proven. Here, Mr. Bossard admitted outright at trial that Premier Power was installed on his company's computer network. See Trial Tr. (11/22/96) at App. 232-33. During Mr. Bossard's testimony,    after a series of exchanges between Stenograph's counsel and Mr. Bossard on the issue of how Bossard originally obtained the software and keys, Stenograph's counsel elicited the following testimony:

Q You have your Premier Power software installed on the network. Correct? A I'll agree to that, okay?

Id. According to appellants, Mr. Bossard's statement only established that Premier Power was installed on the company's network as of the time of trial--i.e., November 1996. Thus, they argue, Mr. Bossard's statement does not constitute persuasive evidence of infringement, because earlier in 1996 Christopher Bossard had obtained a license for the software. See Reply Br. at 7-8.
Appellants' self-serving reading of the record is not enough to overcome the jury verdict    in this case. First, Mr. Bossard never claimed that his company's installation of Premier Power occurred only after a license for its use had been obtained. Second, and more important, Mr. Bossard essentially conceded all of the points in issue when he testified that Bossard had possessed and used Premier Power software since 1993.
Bossard does not dispute that a court reporter who seeks   to use the software first must insert a disk containing stenographic notes "into a computer on which the Premier Power  resides." Br. of Appellee at 7 (emphasis added); also see Trial Tr. (11/22/96) at App. 322. This is hardly surprising, because it is consistent with the way in which software [***1940]  is typically used. See 2 NIMMER, § 8.08[B][1], at 8-118 ("Installing programs from floppy disks onto the hard drive (instead of booting them from the floppy drive every time they are desired) has become almost universal…."). Indeed, even if it were possible to use Premier Power without prior installation onto a computer, Bossard makes absolutely no suggestion that it did so in this case. Furthermore, Bossard makes no claim that it used only computers located in other offices, on which Premier Power already was installed pursuant to a license from Stenograph. In these circumstances, where installation of the software is a prerequisite to its use, Stenograph could show that Bossard installed and therefore copied the software by demonstrating that Bossard used the software and keys for their principal purposes during the relevant time periods.
There is substantial evidence   in the record showing that Bossard used Premier Power for the principal purposes for which it was designed--i.e., to convert stenographic notes into English text and produce transcripts for sale. First, Mr. Bossard testified that his company initially obtained Premier Power in 1993, when Bossard also obtained its first software protect key from Baker. See Trial Tr. (11/22/96) at App. 23435. In addition, Stenograph elicited testimony from Mr. Bossard that numbered keys were kept in Bossard's offices.  See id. at 229. On those occasions when Bossard would purchase a key from Baker, the key would "ultimately go to [Bossard's] computer room" if Baker did not first take it there himself. Id. (11/25/96) at 381-82. At one point in his testimony Mr. Bossard admitted that software had been used from "whenever [the company] got the first Premier Power key from John Baker." Id. (11/22/96) at 234.  Mr. Bossard separately admitted that a Bossard Associate employee used the software and a key in the company's computer room to process files and cause transcripts to be printed for sale to customers. See id. (11/25/96) at 445-46. From these statements, the jury easily   could conclude that Bossard--through both its regular employees and independent contractors-used the software in tandem with the keys prior to 1996.
In sum, the evidence supports the finding that Bossard impermissibly copied Premier Power by installing and using the software for its principal purposes during the time in question.
2. Loading Into RAM
It is also evident that copying of Premier Power occurred through the loading   of the software into the random access memories of Bossard's computers while the software was in use. Courts that have addressed the issue agree that  the loading of software from some permanent storage medium, such as a floppy disk or a computer's hard drive, to the computer's random access memory ("RAM") when the software is "booted up" causes a copy to be made. See MAI Systems Corp. v. Peak Computer, Inc., 991 F.2d 511, 518 (9th Cir. 1993) (defendant's "loading of copyrighted software into RAM creates a 'copy' of that software in violation    of the Copyright Act"); Triad Systems Corp. v. Southeastern Express Co., 64 F.3d 1330, 1335 (9th Cir. 1995); Advanced Computer Servs. v. MAI Systems Corp., 845 F. Supp. 356, 363 (E.D. Va. 1994); 2 NIMMER § 8.08[A][1], at 8-113 to 8-114 (describing trend recognizing that reproduction of program in RAM constitutes "copy"); see generally, Jane C. Ginsburg,  Putting Cars on the "Information Superhighway": Authors, Exploiters, and Copyright in Cyberspace, 95 COLUM. L. REV. 1466, 1476 (1995) ("Copies of a work are made … when a temporary copy is received into the
144 F.3d 96, *100; 1998 U.S. App. LEXIS 11483, **13; 46 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1936, ***1939
memory of [a] computer."). Appellants erroneously argue in   their brief that the holding in MAI Systems has no bearing on the instant case because it only addressed the issue of whether a computer program in RAM is "fixed" under the Act, independent of the issue of whether the RAM reproduction constitutes a "copy."  See Br. of Appellant at 9. On the contrary, MAI Systems held that  a RAM reproduction was a copy precisely because it was fixed under the Act. See 17 U.S.C. § 101 (defining the terms "copies" and "fixed"); MAI Systems, 991 F.2d at 518; Advanced Computer, 845 F. Supp. at 362-64 (rejecting contention that program in RAM was not "fixed").
We do not read appellants' arguments to seriously challenge the holding in MAI Systems [***1941]  and other cases that a RAM reproduction constitutes a copy, although this holding has drawn some criticism. See, e.g., Jessica Litman, The Exclusive Right to Read, 13 CARDOZO ARTS & ENT. L.J. 29, 40 (1994) (protesting result in which all acts of reading or viewing a digitalized work with the use of computer involves "actionable reproduction"); see generally, Ginsburg, 95 COLUM. L. REV. at 1476 n.39 (citing critics). Rather, appellants complain that Stenograph failed   to prove that the protected elements of Premier Power were reproduced into RAM in the first instance. But this argument is specious, because, at oral argument, appellants conceded that the protected elements of Premier Power were copied if in fact the software was used for the principal purposes for which it was designed. As described above, there was ample evidence from which the jury could conclude that Bossard used Premier Power to convert stenographic notes into English text and produce transcripts for sale, without a license from Stenograph. Equally important, appellants do not argue that they had any reason to use Premier Power other than for the software's principal purposes. Thus, evidence of Bossard's use of Premier Power served as sufficient evidence that protected elements were copied, insofar these elements were reproduced into RAM. On the current record, it is simply irrelevant that Stenograph never presented an expert witness who could testify that specific parts of Premier Power were reproduced into RAM when the software was used by Bossard.
Contrary to appellants' contentions, this conclusion is not in tension with Fonar Corp. v. Domenick, 105 F.3d 99 (2d Cir.1997),   cert. denied, 139 L. Ed. 2d 191, 118 S. Ct. 265 (1997). In Fonar, the plaintiff sued for copyright infringement on the theory that the defendant copied plaintiff's software when the defendant booted up the software for use. Although the district court granted summary judgment to the defendant primarily on the ground that plaintiff failed to establish a valid copyright, the court of appeals reversed and stated, in pertinent part, "at trial Fonar will undoubtedly have to break down its software into its constituent parts in order to allow the examination of these parts" for protected elements.  105 F.3d at 104.  That a copyright plaintiff should have to demonstrate a software's protected elements for purposes of establishing a valid copyright does not lend support to Bossard's contention that the same plaintiff must specifically show reproduction of these elements into RAM during defendant's unauthorized use of the software, for purposes of showing "copying." Indeed, the  Fonar court assumed, in reversing the district court, that loading a program into RAM resulted in "wholesale copying," id. at 103, and that therefore whatever protected elements that were contained in   the software were copied during the software's use. See id. at 106. Thus, Fonar supports, rather than undermines, our position that impermissible copying occurs when a validly copyrighted program is used for its principal purposes.
Our holding in this case does not address a situation in which it might be claimed that no    copying occurred through prior installation. See, e.g., Fonar, 105 F.3d at 101-02 (infringement action brought against company that uses programs residing on third parties' computer systems); MAI Systems, 991 F.2d at 517 (same). Nor does this case involve a claim that defendant used only the unoriginal--or unprotected--portions of a program. In other words, a defendant might claim that he or she used only those elements of a software program that are common to other programs and, therefore, by themselves, not copyrightable. In such a case, it might be argued that such limited use of the software by the defendant does not support an action for infringement, because the limited use did not cause any of the software's protected elements to be reproduced into RAM. We leave these questions for another day. B. Damages
The total damages awarded by the   District Court to Stenograph reflected, in part, the jury's awards of $ 1,500,000 for copyright infringement and "$ 710,000 for actual losses and unjust enrichment" on the claim of trade secret misappropriation. Order, at 1. Appellants' arguments attacking these and other aspects of the total damages award are without merit.
The amount of $ 1,500,000 presumably represents Bossard Associates' total revenues ($ 1,700,000) for the time period under dispute (December 1994 through December 1995), minus an estimation of expenses related to the use of Premier Power software (approximately $ 200,000). Bossard's challenge to the $ 1,500,000 figure is meritless because,  after Stenograph introduced the statement containing Bossard Associates' gross revenues for the relevant time period, see Ex. 5, at 25-27; Trial Tr. (11/22/96) at App. 236-37, the burden shifted to Bossard under 17 U.S.C. § 504(b) to "prove his or her deductible expenses and the elements of profit attributable to factors other than the copyrighted work." Id. Because appellants [***1942]  clearly failed to carry their burden under § 504(b), we have no reason to disturb the copyright infringement award of $ 1,500,000. See   § 504(b), Notes of the Committee on the Judiciary on Actual Damages and Profits; cf.  Blackman v. Hustler Magazine, Inc., 255 U.S. App. D.C. 135, 800 F.2d 1160, 1163 (D.C. Cir. 1986) (holding, where defendants failed to meet burden under 1909 Copyright Act, that "the gross figure is left to stand as the profit factor" (internal quotation omitted)).
