Based on the evidence in the pleadings and in the supplemental declaration, the Court finds that personal jurisdiction is proper as to Defendant Major League, but not as to Defendant Evans. The Court therefore recommends that the Motion be DENIED as to Defendant Evans. Because the Court finds   that the balance of the factors enumerated by the Ninth Circuit weigh in favor of entering default judgment against Defendant Major League, the Court recommends that the Motion be GRANTED as to Major League.
II. BACKGROUND

Plaintiff is a jazz saxophonist who resides in California. First Amended Complaint ("FAC") ¶ 4. He is the sole composer and owner of the copyright in the composition "Free Soul." Id. A copyright to "Free Soul" was issued to Heavy Music, Inc., by the Register of Copyrights on April 29, 1969. FAC ¶ 10; see also Ex. A. Plaintiff recorded the song on his 1969 LP entitled Blowing Gold. FAC ¶ 13. In 1978, Heavy Music assigned the rights to the composition "Free Soul" to Remohj Music, the music publishing business Plaintiff operates as a sole proprietorship. FAC ¶ 11; see also Ex. B.
Plaintiff brought suit in the instant matter under the Copyright Act of 1976, 17 U.S.C. §§ 101 et seq., ("the Copyright Act") for Defendants' allegedly infringing use of "Free Soul." FAC ¶ 1. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that Defendants copied "qualitatively and quantitatively substantial excerpts" from "Free Soul" in the song: "Clothes, Hoes N Liquer" [sic]. That composition allegedly "digitally samples and 'loops'"   substantial passages from Plaintiff's 1969 recording of "Free Soul." FAC ¶ 16.
"Free Soul" is one of Plaintiff's "signature songs." FAC ¶ 14. In the past, Plaintiff has licensed the use of digital samples of "Free Soul" to various hip hop recording artists under a standard licensing agreement. FAC ¶ 14; Declaration of John Klemmer filed in support of Plaintiff's Motion for Default Judgment ("Klemmer Decl.") ¶¶ 5, 6. In this case, no Defendant asked Plaintiff's permission to sample "Free Soul." FAC ¶ 17. In any event, Plaintiff declares that he would not have licensed "Free Soul" for use in the composition "Clothes, Hoes N Liquer," because he found the lyrics to that composition objectionable. Klemmer Decl. ¶ 7.
Defendant Jabari Evans is the composer of the musical composition and performer of the sound recording of the allegedly infringing derivative work, "Clothes, Hoes N Liquer." FAC ¶6. Evans created the composition in or around 2006. FAC ¶ 16. Using the pseudonym "Naledge," Evans performs as one half of the duo "Kidz in the Hall." FAC ¶ 2; Declaration of Alan Korn in Support of Plaintiff's Motion for Default Judgment ("Korn Decl.") ¶ 16. In about 2006 or 2007, Evans entered "a recording   and/or distribution deal" with Defendant Major League Entertainment N.Y.C., Inc., ("Major League") regarding the composition, "Clothes, Hoes N Liquer." FAC ¶ 19.
Major League is a record company that authorized the reproduction and distribution of "Clothes, Hoes N Liquer." FAC ¶¶ 7, 9. Plaintiff voluntarily dismissed his claims against a second record company, Rawkus Records, LLC, that apparently also distributed copies of "Clothes, Hoes N Liquer," pursuant to full performance of settlement conditions. See Docket #34.
On April 29, 2008, prior to filing the Complaint in the instant matter, Plaintiff's attorney sent a letter to Defendants informing them of the unauthorized use of "Free Soul" and attempting to resolve the dispute informally. Korn Decl. ¶ 12, Ex. 1. Approximately six weeks later, on May 27, 2008, Plaintiff's attorney re-sent the letter, and advised Defendants that Plaintiff was prepared to initiate a lawsuit if they failed to respond. Id. Plaintiff's attorney also spoke with Evans's manager, Matthew Marcus of Major League,   on at least two separate occasions. Korn Decl. ¶ 13.
Plaintiff filed a Complaint on August 5, 2008. On September 10, 2008, Plaintiff filed the First Amended Complaint. The First Amended Complaint sought the following relief: (1) a permanent injunction barring Defendants or their agents from future infringing use of "Free Soul"; (2) mandamus directing Defendants to file with the Court a "report setting forth the manner and form in which" they would comply with the injunction; (3) damages of either (a) actual damages sustained by Plaintiff, together with any of Defendants' profits that are attributable to the infringement, or (b) statutory damages of no less than $30,000 and as much as $150,000 for each willful infringement; (4) an order directing Defendants to provide an accounting of gross receipts based on sales of the infringing works; (5) equitable relief including the imposition of a constructive trust on profits that result in Defendants' unjust enrichment; and (6) reasonable attorney's fees and costs.
A Summons and a copy of the First   Amended Complaint were served on Major League's designated agent for service in New York on September 18, 2008. Defendant Evans was personally served with a Summons and the First Amended Complaint in Missoula, Montana, on October 12, 2008.
Neither of the Defendants answered or filed another response to the First Amended Complaint with the Court. Accordingly, Plaintiff moved for entry of default. The Clerk of the Court entered a default against Major League on October 16, 2008. On November 5, 2008, the Clerk of the Court entered default as to Evans.
Plaintiff filed this Motion on November 24, 2008, seeking entry of default judgment and the relief prayed for in the First Amended Complaint. Plaintiff has elected to receive statutory damages under the Copyright Act in lieu of actual damages, and seeks damages of no less than $30,000 and up to $150,000 for willful infringement. Plaintiff also seeks an order requiring the destruction of all infringing goods; this relief was not specifically requested in the First Amended Complaint. See Memorandum of Points and Authorities in support of Plaintiff's Motion for Default Judgment ("MPA") at 4; FAC at 9-10. Plaintiff served Defendants with the Motion for Default   Judgment by mail on November 24, 2008.
III. ANALYSIS
A. Personal Jurisdiction

Plaintiff is a resident of California. FAC ¶ 4. Plaintiff alleges that Major League is a New York corporation. FAC ¶ 7. The record contains no evidence of where Defendant Evans is domiciled. Evans was served with process in Missoula, MT. Docket #20. Plaintiff alleges that this Court has jurisdiction over Defendants based on their contacts with the State of California and with this judicial district. Because a court has a duty to inquire as to the existence of its own jurisdiction, the Court, as an initial matter, considers the evidence supporting the exercise of personal jurisdiction over Defendants. After examining the evidence in the record, including the supplemental declaration filed on February 11, 2009, the Court concludes that it has personal jurisdiction over Major League based on its contacts with the forum, but that the record does not contain sufficient evidence of minimum contacts to support this Court's exercise of jurisdiction over Defendant Evans.
A federal court may exercise personal jurisdiction in the manner provided by the state law of the state in which it sits. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(k)(1). Under California's long-arm   statute, Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 410.10, federal courts located in California my exercise jurisdiction to the extent permitted by the Due Process Clause of the Constitution. Core-Vent Corp. v. Nobel Indus. AB, 11 F.3d 1482 (9th Cir. 1993). The Due Process Clause, in turn, allows federal courts to exercise jurisdiction where either: 1) the defendant has continuous and systematic contacts with the forum state sufficient to subject him or her to the general jurisdiction of the court; or 2) the defendant has sufficient minimum contacts to subject him or her to the specific jurisdiction of the court. Id.
1. Major League

The Court finds that Major League has sufficient minimum contacts with the forum to support specific jurisdiction.
Courts apply a three-part test to determine whether specific jurisdiction exists:

(1) The non-resident defendant must purposefully direct his activities or consummate some transaction with the forum or resident thereof; or perform some act by which he purposefully avails himself of the privileges of conducting activities in the forum, thereby invoking the benefits and protections of its laws; (2) the claim must be one which arises out of or relates to the defendant's forum-related activities; and

(3) the exercise of jurisdiction must comport with fair play and substantial justice, i.e., it must be reasonable.

Schwarzenegger v. Fred Martin Motor Co., 374 F.3d 797, 802 (9th Cir. 2004).   In the context of tort claims, the Supreme Court has held that the purposeful direction requirement is met where the defendants intended to and did indeed cause injury within the forum state, even though the actions that gave rise to the effects took place outside the forum. Calder v. Jones, 465 U.S. 783 (1984). In the copyright infringement context, courts have applied the purposeful direction test expansively. See 3 M. B. Nimmer & D. Nimmer, Nimmer on Copyright § 12.01(c) (citing Editorial Musical Latino Americana, S.A. v. Mar Int'l Records, Inc., 829 F. Supp. 62, 64 (S.D.N.Y. 1993) ("Offering one copy of an infringing work for sale in New York, even if there is no actual sale, constitutes commission of a tortious act within the state sufficient to imbue this Court with personal jurisdiction over the infringers."). Personal jurisdiction may flow from a single contact with the forum state if the claim "arise[s] out of that particular purposeful contact of the defendant with the forum state." Lake v. Lake, 817 F2d 1416, 1421 (9th Cir. 1987).
Plaintiff alleges that jurisdiction is proper based on Defendants' contacts with the forum state and the judicial district in which the Court sits. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges that Major League has "conducted substantial business in California and in the Bay Area, including licensing deals with iTunes, IODA, Emusic and other Bay Area Companies involved in   the digital distribution of recordings, including Clothes, Hoes N Liquer." MPA at 4; see FAC, ¶ 7, Exh. D-3, D-4, E-1. Plaintiff alleges that Defendant Major League has sold copies of the infringing works within this district and that copies may be downloaded from third party providers, such as iTunes, within the district. MPA at 4; Korn Decl. ¶¶ 15, 17.
a. Purposeful Direction

Under the first prong of the specific jurisdiction test, Plaintiff must establish that defendants either purposefully availed themselves of the privilege of conducting activities in California, or purposefully directed their activities toward California. See Schwarzenegger, 374 F.3d at 803. Purposeful availment and purposeful direction are distinct concepts. Courts typically apply purposeful availment analysis to contract claims, and analyze tort claims under a purposeful direction inquiry. Id. at 802. Because Plaintiff has alleged the intentional infringement of his copyright, a tort, the Court applies a purposeful direction inquiry. See, e.g., IO Group, Inc., v. Pivotal, Inc., No. C 03-5286 MHP, 2004 WL 838164, at * 5 (N.D. Cal. April 19, 2004).
Purposeful direction is itself demonstrated according to a three-part "effects" test, which "requires that the defendant   allegedly have (1) committed an intentional act, (2) expressly aimed at the forum state, (3) causing harm that the defendant knows is likely to be suffered in the forum state." Schwarzenegger, 347 F.3d at 803. "In Columbia Pictures, the Ninth Circuit essentially deemed the effects/purposeful direction test satisfied when the defendant is being sued for copyright infringement, the plaintiff brings suit in the forum where the plaintiff resides, and the defendant knows that the plaintiff resides there." Brayton Purcell, LLP v. Recordon & Recordon, No. C-04- 4995 EMC (N.D. Cal. Mar. 18, 2005) (citing Columbia Pictures Television v. Krypton Broadcasting of Birmingham, Inc., 106 F.3d 284 (9th Cir. 1997) overruled on other grounds by Feltner v. Columbia Pictures Television, 523 U.S. 340 (1998)). With regard to Major League, all three parts of the purposeful direction test have been met in the instant case. First, Plaintiff must allege an intentional act. Plaintiff has alleged that Major League copied and distributed "Clothes, Hoes N Liquer" knowing that the work was covered by copyright. MPA at 7. This allegation is sufficient to establish in intentional act under the first part of the test. See Brackett v. Hilton Hotels Corp., 88 U.S.P.Q.2d 1012, 1016 (N.D. Cal. 2008) (finding that hotel chain's act of copying artist's limited edition prints constituted intentional act).
Second, Plaintiff must show that Major League's intentional acts were expressly aimed at the   forum. Plaintiff has provided evidence that Major League purposefully directed its activities towards the Northern District by entering distribution agreements with Bay Area music retailers and selling sound recordings and digital music files to California residents in the Bay Area. MPA at 4. A number of courts in this district have found that the sale of infringing goods within the forum satisfies the requirement that the acts be aimed at the forum. See, e.g., IO Group, 2004 WL 838164, at * 6 (alleged infringer's act of posting material on its website and "attempting to profit from sales to California residents" sufficed); Expert Pages v. Buckalew, No. C-97-2109 VRW, 1997 WL 488011, at * 3 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 6, 1997) (holding that defendant directed his activities at the plaintiff in the forum state even though defendant "did not enter [the forum state] or conduct business with [plaintiff]" when defendant copied material from plaintiff's website); Walker v. University Books, Inc., 382 F. Supp. 126, 129 (N.D. Cal. 1974) (plaintiff's allegations that defendant marketed and sold allegedly infringing book in California was sufficient to confer personal jurisdiction over foreign defendant).
Third, Major League's acts must have caused harm that they knew would likely be suffered in the forum. This is because the   "goal of the effects test is to establish jurisdiction where the effects of a defendant's contacts are felt . . . ." Brackett, 88 U.S.P.Q.2d at 1017 (citing Calder, 456 U.S. 783). Here, there is no evidence in the record that Defendants knew that Plaintiff resided in the forum until they received the cease and desist letter in the spring of 2008. However, this does not bar a finding that they purposely directed their activities at the forum. Following receipt of the cease and desist letter, Plaintiff alleges that Major League continued "to engage in the unauthorized reproduction, distribution and exploitation of Klemmer's copyrighted song "Free Soul" in the derivative recordings of Clothes, Hoes N Liquer." Korn Decl. ¶ 20. As a result, Major League knew that the brunt of the harm resulting from its conduct would likely be felt in California. See IO Group, 2004 WL 838164, at * 6 (plaintiff adequately demonstrated that defendants knew that harm would be felt in the state where defendants continued to display copyrighted images on their website after receipt of a cease and desist letter). Therefore, the Court finds that the record contains sufficient evidence that Major League purposefully directed its activities towards California.
b. "Arising out of" Defendant's Forum   Activities

The second prong of the test for specific jurisdiction requires that the claim be one that arises out of or relates to the defendant's activities in the forum. This requires a showing of "but for" causation. Panavision Int'l v. Toeppen, 141 F.3d 1316, 1322 (9th Cir. 1998). Here, there is sufficient evidence that Plaintiff would not have been injured "but for" Major League's conduct directed toward him in the forum. See Brayton Purcell, 361 F. Supp.2d at 1143 (noting factor was "easily met" where defendant's copyright infringement "reached into this District" and "affected [the plaintiff] in this District"); IO Group, 2004 WL 838164, at * 4 (sales to California residents concluded via website that displayed infringing images sufficient to establish that claim was related to defendant's activities within the forum).
c. Fair Play and Substantial Justice

Last, the third prong of the test for specific jurisdiction provides that the exercise of jurisdiction must comport with fair play and substantial justice. To determine whether the exercise of jurisdiction over a non-resident defendant comports with fair play and substantial justice, a court must consider seven factors:

(1) the extent of the defendants' purposeful interjection into the forum state's affairs; (2) the burden on the defendant of defending in the forum;   (3) the extent of conflict with the sovereignty of the defendants' state; (4) the forum state's interest in adjudicating the dispute; (5) the most efficient judicial resolution of the controversy; (6) the importance of the forum to the plaintiff's interest in convenient and effective relief; and (7) the existence of an alternative forum.

Core-Vent Corp. v. Nobel Indus., 11 F.3d 1482, 1487-88 (9th Cir. 1993). There is a presumption that the exercise of jurisdiction is reasonable when the first two prongs of the specific jurisdiction test have been met. See Schwarzenegger, 374 F.3d at 802 (stating that after the plaintiff meets his burden to satisfy the first two prongs, the burden then shifts to the defendant to present a "compelling case" that jurisdiction is unreasonable); Haisten v. Grass Valley Medical Reimbursement, 784 F.2d 1392, 1397 (9th Cir. 1986) ("[T]here is a presumption of reasonableness upon a showing that the defendant purposefully directed his activities at forum residents . . . .").
Here, Major League has made no appearance and therefore has not offered any argument to overcome the presumption of reasonableness. Additionally, the reasonableness factors enumerated in Core-Vent weigh in favor of finding that the exercise of jurisdiction comports with fair play and substantial justice. First, Plaintiff is a California resident; accordingly, the forum   state has a strong interest in adjudicating the dispute. See Microsoft Corp. v. Very Competitive Computer Prods. Corp., 671 F. Supp. 1250, 1256 (N.D. Cal. 1987) (finding that state had strong interest in resolving dispute over Taiwanese defendants where California plaintiff alleged copyright infringement). Second, the "burden to the defendant" factor carries less weight when the defendant has "direct and ongoing business activities" within the forum. Id. Major League has transacted substantial business within the forum, and has entered into contracts with forum businesses relating to the sale of the allegedly infringing work. FAC ¶ 7. Therefore, the Court concludes that the exercise of specific jurisdiction over Defendant Major League is reasonable.
Additionally, as to Major League, specific jurisdiction would be proper under a theory of purposeful availment. "A commercial actor need not physically enter the forum state to purposefully avail himself of the privilege of conducting business there." Very Competitive Computer Prods., 671 F. Supp at 1254. "[It is an inescapable fact of modern commercial life that a substantial amount of business is transacted solely by mail and wire communication across state lines, thus obviating the need for physical presence . . . ." Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz, 471 U.S. 462, 476 (1985).
Major league entered contracts with businesses within the district   to promote and sell copies of the infringing work. FAC ¶¶ 3, 7; MPA at 4. Plaintiff has alleged that Major League has collected revenue from sales of Clothes, Hoes N Liquer to California customers through these arrangements. FAC ¶ 7. Accordingly, having availed itself of the benefits and protections of California's laws in order to conduct business within the state, Major League could reasonably anticipate being haled into court within the state. See Very Competitive Computer Prods., 671 F. Supp. at 1255 (finding personal availment where Taiwanese company directed its product into California); IO Group, 2004 WL 838164, at * 4 (commission-based contracts with five California corporations and sales in the amount of $754.42 to California residents supported finding of purposeful availment). If Major League had breached its obligations to one of the Bay Area distributors of its products, including products containing copies of "Clothes, Hoes N Liquer," Major League would be subject to suit in California. Similarly, Major League could also foresee the likelihood of being haled into court for copyright infringement based on sales of the infringing product within the state. Very Competitive Computer Prods., 671 F. Supp. at 1255-56.
2. Evans

In contrast, the record does not provide enough evidence of sufficient contacts to support this Court's  exercise of personal jurisdiction over Defendant Evans. First, there is insufficient evidence of continuous and systematic contacts that would support the exercise of general jurisdiction over Evans. General jurisdiction exists when the defendants contacts are so extensive he or she would be subject to suit even where the cause of action was unrelated to the contacts with the forum. Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia, S.A. v. Hall, 466 U.S. 408, 414 n. 9 (1984). Here, Plaintiff has alleged that Evans has "performed numerous times in the Bay Area . . . ." MPA at 4; Korn Decl. ¶ 16, Exh. 3. Plaintiff also alleges that Evans has made other "substantial business transactions" in the forum. Korn Supp. Decl. ¶¶ 11-14. Plaintiff does not allege that these transactions relate to the conduct that gives rise to this action. These allegations of sporadic contacts are insufficient to confer general jurisdiction. See Schwarzenegger, 374 F.3d at 801 (stating that a defendant must engage in continuous and systematic contacts that "approximate physical presence" in order for a court to exercise general jurisdiction over the defendant).
Second, there is insufficient evidence to support a finding of specific jurisdiction. Unlike Major League, who entered contracts with California companies for the purpose of distributing   the infringing composition, there is no evidence in the record indicating that Evans had a contractual relationship regarding the sale and distribution of "Clothes, Hoes N Liquer" with anyone other than Major League. See FAC ¶ 19. There is no evidence that Evans directed the distribution and sale of the infringing goods in California. Rather, the record suggests that Evans authorized Major League to market and distribute his composition. See FAC ¶ 19. Without evidence that Evans specifically directed the sale of infringing goods towards California, the fact that the goods ended up being sold in the state is insufficient to demonstrate purposeful availment. See Asahi Metal Indus. Co. Ltd v. Superior Ct., 480 U.S. 102, 112 (1987) ("The placement of a product into the stream of commerce, without more, is not an act of the defendant purposefully directed toward the forum State."); Neogen Corp. v. Neo Gen Screening, Inc., 282 F.3d 883, 891 (6th Cir. 2002) (stating that "passive availment" of a state's opportunities was not "purposeful availment"); Bridgeport Music, Inc. V. Still N the Water Publ'g, 327 F.3d 472, 480-81 (6th Cir. 2003) (declining to find purposeful availment where music publishing company knew that its products were marketed nationwide but did not specifically direct the marketing to the forum state).
Plaintiff has provided evidence that Evans has performed several times in California, including   "well-promoted appearances at Shoreline Amphitheater in Mountain View, California on August 18, 2008" in order to promote his recordings, including albums containing the infringing work at issue. Korn Supp. Decl. ¶ 6. Korn Supp. Decl. However, this performance took place after the Complaint was filed on August 5, 2008. The Ninth Circuit has held that when considering contacts with a foreign state for purposes of establishing personal jurisdiction over a non- resident defendant, only contacts occurring prior to the event causing the litigation may be considered. Overton v. Vanzant, No. CV 01-624, 2001 WL 1911359, at * 3 (D. Or. December 13, 2001) (citing Steel v. United States, 813 F.2d 1545, 1549 (9th Cir. 1987) ("[T]he fair warning that due process requires arises not at the time of the suit, but when the events that gave rise to the suit occurred.")). Thus the Court determines that Plaintiff has failed to provide sufficient evidence of Evans's contacts with the forum state. See Steel, 813 F.2d at 1549.
C. Eitel Factors Plaintiff has alleged that Major   League, a limited liability company, is not a minor, incompetent person, or in military service. Korn Decl. ¶¶ 5, 6. After examining the Eitel Factors, the Court finds that they weigh in favor of entering default judgment against Major League.
1. Prejudice to Plaintiff

With regard to the first factor, the Court concludes that the Plaintiff will be prejudiced if default judgment is not entered against Major League. Without entry of default judgment, Plaintiff would be denied the right to judicial resolution of his claims and would likely be without other recourse for recovery. See Phillip Morris, USA, Inc. v. Castworld Prods., Inc., 219 F.R.D. 494, 499 (C.D. Cal. 2003). Furthermore, Plaintiff has alleged that Major League continues to infringe upon Plaintiff's copyright in "Free Soul" despite Plaintiff's cease and desist letters and this action for infringement. MPA at 7, 8-9; Korn Decl. ¶ 20, Exh. 7. Thus, without entry of default judgment, Plaintiff could not be granted injunctive relief and Defendant's infringement could continue. See Capitol Records v. Barrera, 2007 WL 1113949, at *2 (N.D. Cal. April 13, 2007). Accordingly, the Court finds that Plaintiff would suffer prejudice if default judgment were not entered.
2. Sufficiency of the Complaint and the Merits of Plaintiff's Claims

Plaintiff has adequately stated and supported his claim for copyright infringement.   To establish copyright infringement, a plaintiff must prove two elements: (1) ownership of a valid copyright; and (2) that the alleged infringer has violated at least one exclusive right granted to the copyright holder by the Copyright Act. Mardar v. Lopez, 450 F.3d 445, 454 (9th Cir. 2006) (citing A & M Records, Inc. V. Napster, Inc., 239 F.3d 1004, 1013 (9th Cir. 2001)). Section 106 of the Copyright Act grants a copyright owner "the exclusive rights to do or authorize any of the following: (1) to reproduce the copyrighted work in copies or phonorecords; (2) to prepare derivative works based upon the copyrighted work; (3) to distribute copies or phonorecords of the copyrighted work to the public . . . ." 17 U.S.C. § 106. In addition, section 501 of the Copyright Act provides that "anyone who violates any of the exclusive rights of the copyright owner as provided by [section] 106 . . . is an infringer of the copyright" and that the copyright owner is entitled "to institute an action for any infringement . . . ." 17 U.S.C. § 501(b).
Here, Plaintiff has made sufficient factual allegations, taken as true on Defendants' default, to establish both elements of a copyright infringement claim. First, Plaintiff owns the copyright to the musical composition at issue, described in Exhibits A and B filed with the First Amended Complaint. Second, Plaintiff has alleged, and has presented   evidence to support his allegations, that Defendant Evans copied original elements of "Free Soul" in creating the derivative composition, "Clothes, Hoes N Liquer." See 17 U.S.C. § 106(2); Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Tel. Serv. Co., Inc., 499 U.S. 340, 361 (1991). Plaintiff has also alleged that Major League authorized the reproduction and distribution of the copyrighted work. See 17 U.S.C. § 106(1), (2).
The Court also considers the likelihood that Defendant could raise a meritorious defense. See Rashidi v. Albright, 818 F. Supp. 1354, 1356 (D. Nev. 1993) (in evaluating motion for default judgment, considering whether the court would later be obliged to set aside judgment). Here the Court evaluates the potential defense of fair use under section 107 of the Copyright Act and concludes that such a defense would be unlikely to succeed based on the record before the Court.

See 17 U.S.C. § 106 (granting copyright owner exclusive rights to, among other things, make reproductions of the work).

The grant of a license may be    implied by "objective conduct that would permit a reasonable person to conclude that an agreement [to use copyrighted work] had been reached." SHL Imaging, Inc. v. Artisan House, Inc., 117 F. Supp. 2d. 301, 317 (S.D.N.Y. 2000) (internal quotations omitted). The particular circumstances of how and when ISPI contends that a license was implied are vague, but there appear to be essentially four arguments. None of them is meritorious.
20. First, ISPI argues that it was granted a license prior to the Bankruptcy Stipulation, when ISPI was a distributor for SimplexGrinnell and   when ISPI was provided with programming software without any limitation or restriction. (Ex. D P 5.) This rejection clearly terminates any licenses granted prior to the Bankruptcy Stipulation.

Second, ISPI argues that it was granted an implied license after the Bankruptcy Stipulation, by virtue of the fact that SimplexGrinnell did not demand the return of the physical disks containing the programming software. But,  physical possession of a copyrighted work does not by itself entitle one to use that work however one wishes. See 17 U.S.C. § 202 ("[O]wnership of any material object   . . . does not of itself convey any rights in the copyrighted work embodied in the object.")  Under certain circumstances, giving over a software disk might imply a general license to use such software, but not in the circumstances of this case. ISPI, after all, did have and continues to have a right to use programming software with respect to customers on the ISPI Customer List, so SimplexGrinnell would not have been within its rights to demand the physical return of the disks containing that software. 22. Third, ISPI argues that it was granted an implied license because ISPI continued to have access to the Programmers through the SimplexGrinnell website. (D. Mem. 21.) For the same reasons that the failure   to request a return of the disks do not imply a license, neither does the failure to promptly deactivate ISPI's password. Again, the fact that ISPI had physical access to the Programmers does not by itself imply an unrestricted license to use it. There is no credible evidence that SimplexGrinnell even knew that ISPI continued to have such access. In light of the explicit rejection of all prior agreements in the Stipulation, the mere failure to turn off access does not permit a reasonable inference of an ongoing license    to use the Programmers for new customers.
23. Fourth, ISPI argues that a license is implied by the fact that SimplexGrinnell knew about and acquiesced in its use of the Programmers.  A non-exclusive copyright license may be implied from "a lack of objection" where the copyright owner knows about the use of the work. Keane Dealer Services Inc. v. Hartz, 968 F. Supp. 944, 947 (S.D.N.Y. 1997), quoting I.A.E., Inc. v. Shaver, 74 F.3d 768, 775 (7th Cir. 1996). ISPI   points to two letters sent by SimplexGrinnell in the summer of 2006 to two of ISPI's new customers as evidence of SimplexGrinnell's knowledge of ISPI's use of programming software. The letters refer generally to "nonqualified technicians chang[ing], alter[ing], modify[ing], or adjust[ing]" the customer's system, and one letter refers specifically
D. SimplexGrinnell is Not Estopped From Asserting Its Copyright Claims
26. Finally, ISPI argues that even if it does not have a license to use the    programming software, SimplexGrinnell should be estopped from asserting its copyright claim because of its prior conduct.  A copyright holder may be estopped from asserting a copyright claim where:
(1) plaintiff had knowledge of the defendant's [infringing] conduct; (2) plaintiff either (a) intended that defendant rely on plaintiff's acts or omissions [suggesting authorization], or (b) acted or failed to act in such a manner that defendant had a right to believe it was intended to rely on plaintiff's   conduct; (3) defendant was ignorant of the true facts; and (4) defendant relied on plaintiff's conduct to its detriment.
27. ISPI has not shown that SimplexGrinnell intended for ISPI to continue to use the Programmers for new customers; indeed, the letters to ISPI's customers warning them not to use ISPI to service their systems are inconsistent with such a conclusion. Nor has SimplexGrinnell acted in a way that would reasonably cause ISPI to believe that it was authorized to use the programming software. As noted above,  physical possession of a copyrighted work does not result in a grant of any of the rights protected by copyright law. See 17 U.S.C. § 202. Moreover, SimplexGrinnell's failure to demand the return of the disks containing the Programmers is entirely consistent with the fact that ISPI has the right to use such software for existing customers but not for new customers.  The same is true with respect to its failure to turn off website access. The letters SimplexGrinnell sent
to ISPI customers do seem to suggest that SimplexGrinnell was at least   aware of ISPI's unauthorized use of the Programmers as of the summer of 2006. Again, however, a nine month period between the time of such awareness and the initiation of this lawsuit is insufficient to establish that ISPI reasonably believed SimplexGrinnell intended it to continue its unauthorized usage. Indeed, Guarino did not even testify that he believed that SimplexGrinnell intended to provide ISPI an unrestricted license to use the 4100U Programmer beyond the ISPI Customer List.
28. Moreover, even if there were reasonable reliance, ISPI has not shown such reliance to be detrimental. ISPI has derived significant revenue over the last four years from its unauthorized use of the Programmers for new customers. To be sure, prohibiting ISPI from continuing to use the software   for new customers will harm ISPI. But there is no evidence that such prohibition would put ISPI in a worse place than if ISPI had never used the Programmers in this manner in the first place. Warner Bros. Entm't, 575 F. Supp. 2d at 553.  Fourth and finally, there is no public harm in preventing ISPI from using SimplexGrinnell's copyrighted

Dream Games of Arizona ("Dream Games") prevailed in its lawsuit against PC Onsite for copyright infringement of "Fast Action Bingo," an electronic video bingo game, and was awarded statutory damages. We must decide whether (1) the district court properly allowed the jury to see unprotectable elements of the game without identifying the protectable elements; (2) the jury should have been allowed to hear evidence that Fast Action Bingo was operated illegally in two states; (3) statutory damages were available to Dream Games despite the illegal operation; and (4) the district court erred in dismissing claims against PC Onsite's majority owner for lack of evidence of direct infringement. We have jurisdiction, 28 U.S.C. § 1291, and we affirm the district court's rulings. [***1195]
Dream Games and American Software Development Company, a licensor of Fast Action Bingo, filed a complaint in the United States District Court for the District of Arizona, alleging copyright infringement under 17 U.S.C. § 501, common law breach of contract, and unjust enrichment, and seeking injunctive relief and damages. Specifically, Dream Games alleged that PC Onsite, Casey Hagon, and Garland Piece (collectively, "PC Onsite"), "having full knowledge of the copyright rights of Dream Games, have infringed Dream Games' copyrights by manufacturing, displaying, distributing, . . . selling, [and] licensing . . . an electronic video bingo game known as 'Quick Play Bingo.'" Dream Games obtained a preliminary injunction against PC Onsite, enjoining it from infringing Dream Games's copyright.
A six day jury trial began on November 7, 2006. During trial, PC Onsite moved for Judgment as a Matter of Law ("JMOL"), arguing that Garland Pierce was not liable for copyright infringement because he did not directly distribute Quick Play Bingo to the public or participate in its development, and that Dream Games was not entitled to damages because Fast Action Bingo was operated illegally. During oral argument on the motion, Dream Games argued for the first time that Garland Pierce was secondarily liable for infringement. The district court granted judgment as a matter of law in favor of Pierce and dismissed him from the case. The court further ruled that Dream Games could not recover actual damages for Fast Action Bingo's lost profits because the game was offered illegally in Utah and Wyoming, but that Dream Games was entitled to recover statutory damages to be determined by the jury.
The jury found PC Onsite and Hagon liable for willful copyright infringement. It awarded $ 25,000 to Dream Games in statutory damages. Final judgment was entered on March 30, 2007, in favor of Dream Games. Dream Games subsequently moved to amend the judgment for an error correction and to enter a permanent injunction. It also filed a motion for a new trial on Pierce's liability for inducement. On May 2, 2007, the district court amended its judgment to correct the clerical error and to order a permanent injunction, and denied Dream Games's motion for a partial new trial. [***1196]
PC Onsite timely appeals. Dream Games and Affordable Video Systems cross-appeal the district court's denial of Dream Games's motion for a partial new trial on Pierce's liability.
A. Evidence of Unprotectable Elements Before the Jury

Because "copyright protects only an author's expression of an idea," Data E. USA, Inc. v. Epyx, Inc., 862 F.2d 204, 207 (9th Cir. 1988), "elements of expression that necessarily follow from an idea, or . . . expressions that are as a practical matter, indispensable or at least standard in the treatment of a given idea" are not protected, id. at 208 (alteration and internal quotation marks omitted). We have held, however, that a claim of copyright infringement can be based on infringement of a combination of unprotected elements. See Apple Computer, Inc. v. Microsoft Corp., 35 F.3d 1435, 1446 (9th Cir. 1994). "It is well settled that a jury may find a combination of unprotect[a]ble elements to be protect[a]ble . . . because 'the over-all impact and effect indicate substantial appropriation.'" Three Boys Music Corp. v. Bolton, 212 F.3d 477, 485 (9th Cir. 2000) (quoting Sid & Marty Krofft Television Prods., Inc. v. McDonald's Corp., 562 F.2d 1157, 1169 (9th Cir. 1977), superseded on other grounds by 17 U.S.C. § 504(b)). To allow the possibility of such a finding, the jury must be allowed to see the complete work. Apple Computer and its progeny do, however, require that the unprotected elements be identified to the jury. See, e.g., Apple Computer, 35 F.3d at 1446 ("[T]he unprotectable elements have to be identified, or filtered, before the works can be considered as a whole.").
1. District Court's Refusal to Limit Evidence To Protectable Elements

PC Onsite argues that the district court abused its discretion in allowing the jury to see the unprotectable elements of Fast Action Bingo. Unprotectable elements such as Bingo [***1197] cards and game function buttons, i.e., "Log Out," were introduced into evidence as part of the complete printouts of Fast Action Bingo screen displays. Because it is appropriate for the jury to see unprotected elements of a copyrighted work so that it may assess whether the combination of such elements warrants protection, the district court did not abuse its discretion in allowing into evidence complete Fast Action Bingo screen displays that include unprotectable elements.
2. Identification of Protectable Elements in Jury Instructions

PC Onsite argues that the district court erred by failing to identify in the jury instructions the specific elements of FasHN9[ ] t Action Bingo that are protected by copyright. "[P]rejudicial error results when, looking to the instructions as a whole, the substance of the applicable law was not fairly and correctly covered." Gambini v. Total Renal Care, Inc., 486 F.3d 1087, 1092 (9th Cir. 2007) (internal quotation marks omitted).
PC Onsite relies primarily on Harper House, Inc. v. Thomas Nelson, Inc., 889 F.2d 197 (9th Cir. 1989), to support its argument that the jury instructions did not fairly and correctly cover the applicable law. In Harper House, the district court "refused to give defendants' proposed jury instructions that portions of the organizers were not

561 F.3d 983, *988; 2009 U.S. App. LEXIS 8274, **7; 90 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1193, ***1196

protected by copyright." Id. at 200. We held that because organizers were "copyrightable as compilations" that consisted "mainly or entirely of uncopyrightable elements," id. at 204, it was error for "the jury instructions . . . [to fail to] adequately distinguish between protectable and unprotectable material," id. at 207-08. However, as PC Onsite concedes, Harper House did not address whether merely instructing a jury as to the protectable elements is sufficient without also identifying those elements.
Consideration of the whole work is proper under Apple Computer as long as "the unprotectable elements [are] identified." Apple Computer, 35 F.3d at 1446 (emphasis added). No case law or legal theory requires that "protectable" elements be identified as well. Here, the jury instructions properly identified the "unprotectable" elements of Fast Action Bingo. The district court instructed the jury that "to establish that PC Onsite is liable for infringement, Dream Games must show that the accused screen displays are virtually identical to protected elements of corresponding screen displays of the Fast Action Bingo game." It further instructed that "even a combination of unprotectable elements may be entitled to some copyright protection if the works are virtually identical." Finally, the district court identified in detail those elements of the copyrighted work that are not protected: "Functions such as 'Add user,' 'Games Menu' and 'Done' are not copyrightable . . .," "Bingo cards, called numbers (often printed on balls), a key describing winning patterns and corresponding prizes, and the player's balance and winnings, are all elements of a video bingo game that are not protected by copyright." The district court correctly rejected PC Onsite's proposed instructions that listed four specific protected elements of Fast Action Bingo because they would have improperly limited the jury's consideration to four aspects of Fast Action Bingo, as opposed to the whole work.
Because the district court specifically identified the unprotected elements, the jury instructions fairly and sufficiently explained the theory of the case and did not misstate the law. Neither party argues that the district court abused its discretion in formulating the exact wording of the instructions, and the text of the instructions supports this conclusion. Therefore, the district court did not abuse its discretion in giving the jury instructions.
B. Impact of Illegal Operation on Award of Damages

During the relevant time period, Dream Games operated Fast Action Bingo in two states, Wyoming and Utah. While Dream Games's lawsuit was pending, the Wyoming Supreme Court ruled that Fast Action Bingo was illegal in that state. See Fraternal Order of Eagles Sheridan Aerie No. 186, Inc. v. State ex rel. Forwood, 2006 WY 4, 126 P.3d 847 (Wyo. 2006). The State of Utah also prohibits gambling, and has seized several Fast Action Bingo machines operated in one particular bingo hall, but has not declared the game illegal without regard to operation. Before trial, the district court concluded that because Fast Action [***1198] Bingo is definitely illegal in Wyoming, "there is no potential recovery" in that state, but whether there is recovery in Utah "really depends upon the facts." Ruling on PC Onsite's subsequent JMOL motion, the district court first noted that it "resolved that Fast Action Bingo is illegal" in Utah. It nevertheless held that because "the illegality I have found is not, per se, so it only pertains to the actual damages for violation of a copyright," Dream Games "may recover statutory damages."
1. Availability of Actual or Statutory Damages

Although we have not previously addressed whether illegal use or operation of a work by the copyright owner precludes the award of actual or statutory damages for copyright infringement, analogous case law persuades us that it does not.
Previously, we have held thatHN11[ ] fraudulent content is not a basis for denying copyright protection to a work, and is not a defense to infringement. See Belcher v. Tarbox, 486 F.2d 1087, 1088 (9th Cir. 1973) (refusing to deny copyright protection to fraudulent advertising). "[T]he currently prevailing view" is that "no works are excluded from copyright by reason of their content." 1 Melville B. Nimmer & David Nimmer, Nimmer on Copyright § 2.17 (2008)

561 F.3d 983, *989; 2009 U.S. App. LEXIS 8274, **11; 90 U.S.P.Q.2D (BNA) 1193, ***1197

(citing Mitchell Bros. Film Group v. Cinema Adult Theater, 604 F.2d 852, 863 (5th Cir. 1979)); see also Belcher, 486 F.2d at 1088 (explicitly disagreeing with a Fifth Circuit case later overruled by Mitchell). Dismissing the defense of obscenity to a claim of copyright infringement, the Fifth Circuit concluded in Mitchell that "[t]he maxim of unclean hands is not applied where plaintiff's misconduct is not directly related to the merits of the controversy between the parties, but only where the wrongful acts 'in some measure affect the equitable relations between the parties in respect of something brought before the court for adjudication.'" 604 F.2d at 863 (quoting Keystone Driller Co. v. Gen. Excavator Co., 290 U.S. 240, 245, 54 S. Ct. 146, 78 L. Ed. 293, 1934 Dec. Comm'r Pat. 639 (1933)). It held that "[t]he alleged wrongdoing of the plaintiff does not bar relief unless the defendant can show that he has personally been injured by the plaintiff's conduct." Id.; see also Fuller v. Berger, 120 F. 274, 278 (7th Cir. 1903) ("[I]f the defendant can do no more than show that the complainant has committed some legal or moral offense, which affects the defendant only as it does the public at large, the court must grant the equitable remedy and leave the punishment of the offender to other forums."); Jartech, Inc. v. Clancy, 666 F.2d 403, 406 (9th Cir. 1982) (recognizing that obscenity is not a defense to copyrightability).
As Professor Nimmer has written, the defense of illegality or unclean hands is "recognized only rarely, when the plaintiff's transgression is of serious proportions and relates directly to the subject matter of the infringement action. For instance, the defense has been recognized when plaintiff misused the process of the courts by falsifying a court order or evidence, or by misrepresenting the scope of his copyright to the court and opposing party." 4 Nimmer on Copyright § 13.09[B] (citing L.A. News Serv. v. Tullo, 973 F.2d 791, 799 (9th Cir. 1992)) (internal footnotes omitted).
Sound policy reasons support the "Congressional intent to avoid content restrictions on copyrightability." 1 id. § 2.17. In Belcher, we explained that "[t]here is nothing in the Copyright Act to suggest that the courts are to pass upon the truth or falsity, the soundness or unsoundness, of the views embodied in a copyrighted work." 486 F.2d at 1088. We noted that "[t]he gravity and immensity of the problems, theological, philosophical, economic and scientific, that would confront a court if this view were adopted are staggering to contemplate." Id. Similarly, the Mitchell court was concerned that the broad use of the illegality defense would swallow the entire right to copyright protection. See Mitchell, 604 F.2d at 864 ("[L]imiting copyright protection on a broad public injury rationale would lead to absurd and unacceptable results. . . . Arguably an infringer could defend on the ground that the work had been transported into the state in the copyright owner's truck that does not meet federal safety and pollution requirements . . . . The possibilities are well nigh limitless.").

The theory of secondary liability is distinct from the theory of direct infringement. While direct infringement requires proof of unlawful copying, contributory infringement requires proof that a defendant "(1) has knowledge of a third party's infringing activity, and (2) induces, causes, or materially contributes to the infringing conduct." Perfect 10, Inc. v. Visa Int'l Serv. Ass'n, 494 F.3d 788, 795 (9th Cir. 2007) (internal quotation marks omitted). Implied consent is also ruled out because the evidence introduced at trial, to the extent it was relevant to secondary liability, was also relevant to direct liability for infringement. See id. ("[W]hen the evidence that is claimed to show that an issue was tried by consent is relevant to an issue already in the case, . . . and there was no indication at trial that the party who introduced the evidence was seeking to raise a new issue, the pleadings will not be deemed amended under . . . P. 16(e) (2006) ("This order shall control the subsequent course of action unless modified . . . to prevent manifest injustice."). IV. CONCLUSION

The district court properly admitted evidence of unprotectable elements and did not err in failing to more specifically identify the protectable elements to the jury. The district court did not err in excluding evidence of illegal operation of the copyrighted work from the jury's consideration. Nor did the district court err in dismissing Garland Pierce on a motion for judgment as a matter of law.

III. DISCUSSION
Plaintiffs' motion for final default judgment seeks relief based on three provisions of the Copyright Act. Specifically, Plaintiffs seek statutory damages under 17 U.S.C. § 504, an injunction pursuant to 17 U.S.C. § 502 and costs under 17 U.S.C. § 505. The undersigned will address each in turn.
Section 504 imposes liability against an infringer of copyright for either actual or statutory damages. 17 U.S.C. § 504(a). The statute permits recovery of not less than $750 or more than $30,000 per work infringed. Id. § 504(c). Plaintiffs must satisfy two requirements to present a prima facie case of direct infringement: (1) they must show ownership of the allegedly infringed material; and (2) they must demonstrate the alleged infringers violate at least one exclusive right granted to copyright holders under 17 U.S.C. § 106. See id. § 501(a) (infringement occurs when alleged infringer engages in activity listed in section 106). Activities listed in section 106 include reproduction of copyrighted work   in copies, as well as distribution of copies of the copyrighted work to the public by sale or other transfer of ownership, or by rental, lease, or lending. Id. § 106(1) & (3).
Plaintiffs allege Defendant Wolf has, without permission, used an online media distribution system to download music recordings in which they own a copyright, distribute them to the public, and/or make them available for distribution to others. (Plf. ¶ 14). By virtue of her default, Defendant Wolf has admitted to the truth of this allegation. Therefore, the Court finds Plaintiffs have established a cause of action under § 504(a). See In re Aimster Copyright Litig., 334 F.3d 643, 645 (7th Cir. 2003) (swapping of computer files containing copyrighted music, which involves making and transmitting a digital copy of the music, infringes copyright, with swappers being the direct infringers); A&M Records, Inc. v. Napster, Inc., 239 F.3d 1004, 1014 (9th Cir. 2001) (users of online file sharing system who upload file names to the search index for others to copy violate copyright holders' distribution rights, users who download files containing copyrighted music violate copyright holders' reproduction rights).
Having concluded Plaintiffs are entitled to default judgment on their § 504(a) claim, the Court turns to the question of relief. As a general rule, courts may enter a default   judgment awarding damages without a hearing only if the amount of damages is a liquidated sum, an amount capable of mathematical calculation, or an amount demonstrated by detailed affidavits. James v. Frame, 6 F.3d 307, 310 (5th Cir. 1993); United Artists Corp. v. Freeman, 605 F.2d 854, 857 (5th Cir. 1979). It is a matter within the court's discretion whether to hold a hearing before awarding damages in a default judgment. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 55(b)(2) (in determining amount of damages entered in default, court may conduct such hearings or order such references to determine amount of damages "as it deems necessary and proper"); James, 6 F.3d at 310 (district court has wide latitude in deciding whether to require evidentiary hearing before entering default judgment). Here, Plaintiffs have not requested a hearing and have moved only for statutory, and not actual, damages. Accordingly, the Court finds a hearing is not necessary to calculate damages.
Section 504(c) states, in pertinent part:
the copyright owner may elect, at any time before final judgment is rendered, to recover, instead of actual damages and profits, an award of statutory damages for all infringements involved in the action, with respect to any one work, for which any one infringer is liable individually, or for which any two or more infringers are liable jointly and severally, in a sum of   not less than $750 or more than $30,000 as the court considers just.
17 U.S.C. § 504(c)(1). Plaintiffs allege Defendant downloaded six separate Copyrighted Recordings. (Plf. Compl. ¶ 14 & Ex. A). They seek only the minimum damages authorized by statute for each infringement. Accordingly, Plaintiffs are entitled to $4,500 in statutory damages. See Broadcast Music, Inc. v. Xanthas, Inc., 855 F.2d 233, 237 (5th Cir. 1988) (under § 504(c) trial court must award damages according to number of separate works infringed).
Plaintiffs further seek entry of a permanent injunction prohibiting Defendant from any further infringing activities concerning the Copyrighted Recordings. Plaintiffs maintain Defendant's conduct is causing and, unless enjoined, will continue to cause, Plaintiffs great and irreparable injury such that monetary damages will be inadequate. As such, pursuant to 17 U.S.C. §§ 502 and 503, Plaintiffs seek injunctive relief prohibiting Defendant from further infringing Plaintiffs' copyrights, including any obtained on works later created, and ordering Defendant to destroy all copies of sound recordings made in violation of Plaintiffs' exclusive rights. (Plf. Compl. ¶¶ 15 & 19). The Copyright Act permits a court to "grant temporary and final injunctions on such terms as it may deem reasonable to prevent   or restrain infringement of a copyright." 17 U.S.C. § 502(a). A grant of injunctive relief requires the requesting party to establish: (1) a substantial likelihood of success on the merits; (2) a substantial threat that failure to grant the injunction will result in irreparable injury; (3) the threatened injury outweighs the threatened harm the injunction may cause the opposing party; and (4) the injunction will not disserve the public interest. Enrique Bernat F., S.A. v. Guadalajara, Inc., 210 F.3d 439, 442 (5th Cir. 2000). In copyright cases, irreparable harm is presumed on a showing of reasonable likelihood of success on the merits. Lexmark Int'l, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 387 F.3d 522, 532-33 (6th Cir. 2004); MyWebGrocer, LLC v. Hometown Info, Inc., 375 F.3d 190, 193 (2nd Cir. 2004); Elvis Presley Enters., Inc. v. Passport Video, 349 F.3d 622, 627 (9th Cir. 2003). Because the default against Defendant satisfies the element of success on the merits, Plaintiffs need not make any additional showing of irreparable harm. See NXIVM Corp. v. Ross Inst., 364 F.3d 471, 476 (2nd Cir. 2004) (to demonstrate likelihood of success on merits of copyright claim, plaintiff must establish ownership of valid copyright and unauthorized copying by defendant).
As to the third factor, Plaintiffs allege damages will not adequately compensate them for the harm caused. The Court agrees. Defendant's use of an online media distribution system with millions of potential users has made Plaintiffs' sound recordings vulnerable to further acts of infringement by countless others who can readily  download and distribute the Copyrighted Recordings at issue. Further, there is no evidence Defendant has stopped infringing Plaintiffs' recordings, nor any evidence Defendant will stop, absent an injunction. Moreover, Defendant's failure to respond to Plaintiffs' complaint suggests Defendant does not take seriously the illegality of the infringing activity. Thus, without an injunction, Plaintiffs' copyrighted recordings would remain vulnerable to continued, repeated infringement by Defendant. See Fermata Int'l Melodies, Inc. v. Champions Golf Club Inc., 712 F. Supp. 1257, 1262 (S.D. Tex. 1989), aff'd, 915 F.2d 1567 (5th Cir. 1990) (in short, injunction appropriate if liability established and there is substantial likelihood of further infringement of plaintiffs' copyrights).
Finally, injunctions are regularly issued pursuant to the mandate of section 502 because the "public interest is the interest in upholding copyright protections." Autoskill, Inc. v. Nat'l Educ. Support Sys., Inc., 994 F.2d 1476, 1499 (10th Cir. 1993). See Apple Computer, Inc. v. Franklin Computer Corp., 714 F.2d 1240, 1255 (3d Cir. 1983) (public interest can only be served by upholding copyright protections, thus preventing misappropriation of skills, creative energies, and resources invested in protected work). An injunction is necessary to preserve the integrity of the copyright laws which seek to encourage individual efforts and creativity by granting valuable enforceable rights. Atari Inc. v. Am. Philips Consumer Elec. Corp., 672 F.2d 607, 620 (7th Cir. 1982). An injunction will not harm the   public interest, but rather, serve it.
Thus, all four factors necessary for the grant of injunctive relief are satisfied in this action. Because Defendant has knowingly infringed and shared Plaintiffs' copyrighted works, and no evidence has been presented showing Defendant has ceased the unauthorized activities, the injunction is proper in order to prevent further downloading and distribution of the copyrighted material.
Plaintiffs additionally argue, because they continually create new copyrighted works similarly vulnerable to infringement, an injunction limited to existing works would require repetitive litigation to redress future infringements. They, therefore, request the injunction be addressed both to existing and future works. This Court agrees with Plaintiffs, and finds such an injunction is warranted. See, e.g., Princeton Univ. Press v. Michigan Document Servs., 99 F.3d 1381, 1392-93 (6th Cir. 1996) (weight of authority supports extension of injunctive relief to future works); Olan Mills, Inc. v. Linn Photo Co., 23 F.3d 1345, 1349 (9th Cir. 1994) (permanent injunction includes works created in the future). Accordingly, Plaintiffs' request for present and future injunctive relief should be granted in the language in their motion for default judgment.
IV. RECOMMENDATION
The undersigned RECOMMENDS that the District Court GRANT Plaintiff's Application for Entry of Default Judgment by the Court (Clerk's Dkt. #10) against Defendant Denise Wolf on their claim under 17 U.S.C. § 504, and award statutory damages in the amount of $4,500 and costs in the amount of $480.00. The undersigned FURTHER RECOMMENDS the District Court permanently enjoin Defendant from future violations of the Copyrighted Recordings pursuant to 17 U.S.C. §§ 502 & 503.
